### [1] [STATERA: Hidden Mass Estimation via Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Kinematics using Frozen Temporal Tubelets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00003)
*Animesh Varma*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: STATERA is a method for localizing center-of-mass (CoM) of opaque, asymmetric rigid bodies from short monocular videos, where surface cues and point tracking fail due to self-occlusion. It adapts a pretrained video backbone (V-JEPA) with a lightweight temporal tubelet mixer. The HiddenMass Benchmark (50K simulation + 63 real-world sequences) supports this task. Results show significant improvement in CoM localization (25.2% vs 41.7% error) and physics capture (41.0% vs 2.6%), though with a trade-off between phase-aware and phase-agnostic supervision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision models pretrained for frame-level appearance struggle to infer hidden physical properties (like center-of-mass) from motion when self-occlusion occurs, making surface cues and point tracking unreliable.

Method: STATERA adapts a pretrained video backbone (V-JEPA) with mostly frozen weights and adds a lightweight temporal tubelet mixer to predict per-frame CoM heatmaps and trajectories. The HiddenMass Benchmark provides 50K MuJoCo trajectories and 63 real-world sequences with physically calibrated CoM ground truth.

Result: In simulation, STATERA-50K-Sigma reduces normalized CoM error from 41.7% (DINOv2) to 25.2%. In zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, phase-aware targets (STATERA-50K-Crescent) show consistent movement toward true hidden offset, improving physics capture from 2.6% to 41.0%, though with slight absolute error increase due to overshoot artifact.

Conclusion: Frozen temporal representations can better separate inertial dynamics from visual geometry for hidden-parameter estimation. There's a fundamental trade-off in supervision: phase-aware targets can cause bimodal predictions but capture physics better, while phase-agnostic targets may collapse toward safe centroids.

Abstract: Vision models pretrained for frame-level appearance often struggle to infer hidden physical properties from motion. We study center-of-mass (CoM) localization for opaque, asymmetric rigid bodies from short monocular videos, where surface cues and point tracking are unreliable under self-occlusion. We propose STATERA, which adapts a pretrained video backbone (V-JEPA) with mostly frozen weights and a lightweight temporal tubelet mixer to predict per-frame CoM heatmaps and trajectories. To support this task, we introduce the HiddenMass Benchmark, comprising 50K MuJoCo trajectories and a 63-sequence real-world test set with physically calibrated CoM ground truth. In simulation, STATERA-50K-Sigma improves normalized CoM error from 41.7% (DINOv2) to 25.2%. In zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, we observe a fundamental trade-off in supervision: phase-aware targets can induce bimodal predictions, while phase-agnostic targets can collapse toward statistically safe centroids. Nevertheless, our phase-aware STATERA-50K-Crescent is the only evaluated method that demonstrates consistent movement toward the true hidden offset. While this leads to a monocular vector overshoot artifact that marginally increases absolute Euclidean error compared to a static geometric centroid, it improves physics capture from 2.6% to 41.0%. These results suggest that frozen temporal representations can better separate inertial dynamics from visual geometry for hidden-parameter estimation.

</details>


### [2] [Emergent Object Binding Has a Finite Spatial Horizon](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00006)
*Mayank Singal*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Self-supervised Vision Transformers learn to bind image patches belonging to the same object, but this binding is spatially local with a finite range described by exponential decay. This local binding property explains several behaviors that aggregate accuracy metrics obscure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper investigates whether pretrained Vision Transformers encode object-level information (whether two patches belong to the same object) and why a single accuracy number fails to capture the true structure of this "IsSameObject" signal in frozen patch embeddings.

Method: The authors probe frozen patch embeddings from DINO and CLIP backbones using three probe families on ADE20K and COCO datasets. They control for confounders and map various behaviors including object size effects, class separation, part-whole grouping, and occlusion handling.

Result: Binding is spatially local: the probability that two patches of the same object are decoded as bound decays exponentially with distance, reaching a nonzero floor. This local spatial coherence explains why binding weakens on large objects, separates same-class objects less reliably than different-class objects, and groups parts with wholes. Occlusion has no effect once object size is controlled.

Conclusion: Object binding emerges from self-supervised pretraining alone. The local spatial coherence with finite range is a fundamental property of the representation, not the decoder. Additional observations about depth organization in DINOv2 vs DINOv3 are reported as preliminary.

Abstract: Pretrained Vision Transformers encode whether two image patches belong to the same object. This IsSameObject signal is decodable from frozen patch embeddings at high accuracy, which suggests that object binding emerges from self-supervised pretraining alone. We show that this single accuracy number hides the structure of the signal. Binding is local: the probability that two patches of the same object are decoded as bound falls off monotonically with the distance between them and levels off at a nonzero floor, a falloff well described by an exponential with a finite length scale. This decay holds across object sizes, across three families of probe, on both ADE20K and COCO, and across DINO and CLIP backbones, which indicates that it is a property of the representation rather than of the decoder. Reading binding as local spatial coherence with a finite range accounts for a set of behaviors that the aggregate score leaves unexplained: binding weakens on large objects, separates distinct objects of the same class less reliably than objects of different classes, and groups object parts with their wholes. It is, by contrast, unaffected by occlusion once object size is controlled. We map each behavior with confounds controlled. As a preliminary observation, the horizon and its floor are organized at different depths in DINOv2 and DINOv3, which we report as suggestive given the small number of layers probed and the confound between the two models.

</details>


### [3] [Spatial Lifting for Dense Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00017)
*Mingzhi Xu,Tao Zhou,Yong Li,Yizhe Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Spatial Lifting (SL) is a novel methodology that lifts standard inputs (e.g., 2D images) into higher-dimensional space and processes them using networks designed for that dimension (e.g., 3D U-Net), achieving better performance with fewer parameters and lower inference costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dense prediction tasks in vision typically use 2D networks. The authors propose that lifting inputs to higher dimensions (e.g., 2D → 3D) can paradoxically improve performance while reducing computational costs and model parameters.

Method: The method involves: (1) Lifting standard inputs into a higher-dimensional space; (2) Processing with networks designed for that dimension (e.g., 3D U-Net); (3) Leveraging intrinsically structured outputs along the lifted dimension for dense supervision during training; (4) Using single-forward-pass self-consistency for quality and uncertainty estimation at test time.

Result: SL achieves good performance on benchmark tasks compared to conventional approaches, while reducing inference costs and drastically lowering the number of model parameters. The framework enables dense supervision and self-consistency-based quality/uncertainty estimation.

Conclusion: Spatial Lifting offers a simple and general modeling strategy that provides a promising path toward more efficient, accurate, and reliable deep networks for dense prediction tasks in vision.

Abstract: We present Spatial Lifting (SL), a novel methodology for dense prediction tasks. SL operates by lifting standard inputs, such as 2D images, into a higher-dimensional space and subsequently processing them using networks designed for that higher dimension, such as a 3D U-Net. Counterintuitively, this dimensionality lifting allows us to achieve good performance on benchmark tasks compared to conventional approaches, while reducing inference costs and \textbf{drastically lowering the number of model parameters}. The SL framework produces intrinsically structured outputs along the lifted dimension. This emergent structure facilitates dense supervision during training and enables single-forward-pass self-consistency-based quality and uncertainty estimation at test time. Spatial Lifting introduces a simple and general modeling strategy that offers a promising path toward more efficient, accurate, and reliable deep networks for dense prediction tasks in vision.

</details>


### [4] [Encoded but Disconnected: Decomposing Vision-Language Model Failures under a Patching Null](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00024)
*Genpei Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents a negative result study testing whether mid-layer representations in vision-language models are causally relevant to final predictions. Across three VLM architectures, while ground-truth answers are encoded in mid layers (68-91% of errors), causal interventions (residual-stream patching) yield zero meaningful effects, suggesting these representations are not actively used for predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors investigate a fundamental question in mechanistic interpretability: whether intermediate layer representations that encode task-relevant information are actually used (causally active) for model predictions. This addresses the distinction between "encoding" (information present in representations) versus "causal relevance" (information actually used for outputs).

Method: The study uses residual-stream patching across three VLM architectures (LLaVA-1.5-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3-8B) on the POPE benchmark. They test both layer-level and per-head-level interventions, and categorize errors into three operationally defined failure modes using oracle labels.

Result: Key findings: (1) Mid layers encode ground-truth answers in 68-91% of errors but patching yields 0% non-trivial flips at layer level for all architectures; (2) Per-head patching shows 0/12,600 flips for Qwen; (3) One exception: InternVL3 layer-20 head-2 (self-attending, localized, p < 1e-4); (4) Three failure modes (Perception Failure, Encoded-but-Disconnected, Prior-Override) are learnable above 60% on all architectures; (5) Architecture prior direction predicts intervention response.

Conclusion: The study provides evidence that encoding in mid-layers does not imply causal relevance for predictions. The three identified failure modes appear mechanistically real (not statistical artifacts), as shown by category-specific responses to interventions under oracle labels. This challenges assumptions in interpretability research that encoded information is necessarily used by the model.

Abstract: Across three vision-language model architectures (LLaVA-1.5-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3-8B), we report a universal negative finding for mid-layer interpretability. On POPE -- the benchmark common to all three -- the mid layers encode the ground-truth answer in 68-91% of errors, yet this signal is not causally active for the final prediction: residual-stream patching yields 0% non-trivial flip at the layer level on all three architectures, and on two of three at the per-head level (Qwen: 0/12,600 patched forwards). The lone exception, InternVL3 layer-20 head-2, is a non-vocab, self-attending head whose effect is localized to that specific head (p < 1e-4). Despite the null, the errors separate operationally into three failure modes -- Perception Failure, Encoded-but-Disconnected, Prior-Override -- learnable above 60% on all three architectures, and the architecture's prior direction predicts which of two interventions elicits a category-specific response. We report these mitigation effects under oracle labels as evidence the categories are mechanistically real, not as a deployable method.

</details>


### [5] [Domain generalization and synthetic data in object detection: the enabler, the probe, and the gap](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00030)
*Elfi I. S. Hofmeijer,Ella P. Fokkinga,Friso G. Heslinga,Klamer Schutte,Jörgen M. Karlholm*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents an object detection-centric review of Domain Generalization (DG), examining the role of synthetic data from three perspectives: as an enabler through diversification/alignment strategies, as a probe for identifying failure modes, and addressing the synthetic-to-real gap. It argues for representation-aware methods that address both localization and classification under domain shift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Object detection models suffer performance degradation under distribution shifts (weather, environment, object appearance changes), yet DG research focused specifically on object detection is scarce. Existing DG approaches fail to address the unique challenges of localization and multi-scale representations in detection tasks.

Method: Review-based analysis examining synthetic data's role in DG for object detection from three complementary perspectives: (1) diversification and alignment strategies for robustness, (2) controlled experimentation to identify failure modes, and (3) addressing the synthetic-to-real domain shift.

Result: Identified limitations of current DG approaches for object detection, highlighting that future research requires representation-aware methods that explicitly handle both localization and classification under domain shift conditions.

Conclusion: Future DG research for object detection must develop representation-aware methods that explicitly address the dual challenges of localization and classification under distribution shifts, moving beyond classification-focused approaches.

Abstract: Object detection models often experience performance degradation when deployed under distribution shifts, caused by for example changes in weather type, operational environment, or object appearance. Domain Generalization (DG) aims to develop models that remain robust under such shifts and generalize well to unseen domains. DG research specifically focused on object detection models is scarce, although these models face additional challenges around localization and multi-scale representations. Synthetic data is a promising tool to support in DG, by enabling large-scale generation of diverse new samples. In this paper, we present an object detection-centric review of DG and examine the role of synthetic data from three complementary perspectives. First, synthetic data acts as an enabler of DG through diversification and alignment strategies that aim to improve robustness to distribution shifts. Second, it serves as a probe that enables controlled experimentation to identify and understand failure modes. Third, we discuss the synthetic-to-real gap, a particularly challenging form of domain shift that arises when models trained on synthetic imagery are deployed on real-world data. Through reviewing these perspectives, we identify limitations of current DG approaches for object detection and argue that future research requires representation-aware methods that explicitly address both localization and classification under domain shift.

</details>


### [6] [Seeing the City or Recognizing the Place? What Street-View Imagery Adds Beyond Existing Urban Data in VLM Urban Sensing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00031)
*Kaizhen Tan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper compares street-view image-based predictions with existing urban data sources across seven attributes (road damage, curb ramps, house price, population, building type, building function, and low-rise floor count) using five public data resources and three vision-language models (VLMs). The study evaluates whether images add predictive value beyond already-available data for the same locations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors address a critical gap in urban sensing research: while street-view imagery is widely used to predict urban attributes, it remains unclear whether images actually contribute new information beyond existing data sources (task context, nearby observations, public records). The motivation is to determine when and why image-based predictions are valuable versus redundant.

Method: The study compares image-based predictions with existing urban data across seven attributes using:
1. Five public data resources and three VLMs
2. Evaluations on the same urban units using four approaches: images alone, task context, nearby observations, and public records
3. Two experimental tests: image replacements (removing images to test reliance) and conflicting records (testing model behavior when data sources disagree)
4. OpenFACADES floor annotations generated with OpenStreetMap floor values for validation

Result: Key findings:
- Existing urban data matched or exceeded image-only models for: road damage, curb ramps, and house price
- Neighbouring official statistics nearly matched the best image result for population
- Images were more informative for: building type, building function, and low-rise floor count
- For floor count, image advantage increased by 5.7 percentage points per doubling of distance to the nearest labeled building
- Image advantage declined for tall buildings whose rooflines often fell outside the frame
- Models frequently followed conflicting records
- OpenFACADES showed opposite height-dependent error pattern from image-only results

Conclusion: Street-view image value depends on two key factors: (1) visual legibility of the target attribute (images help for building characteristics but not for already-documented attributes like road damage), and (2) local data coverage (images provide advantage when existing data is sparse). The study concludes that comparing images with existing urban data should guide image collection priorities and clarify the provenance of derived urban maps. The method of comparing images against existing data sources should become standard practice in urban sensing research.

Abstract: Street-view imagery is increasingly used to infer urban attributes, but predictive accuracy alone does not reveal how much a photograph contributes beyond data already available for the same place. We compare image-based predictions with existing urban data across seven attributes from five public resources and three VLMs. The same urban units are evaluated using images, task context, nearby observations, and public records, while image replacements and conflicting records test source reliance. Existing urban data matched or exceeded image-only models for road damage, curb ramps, and house price, while neighbouring official statistics nearly matched the best image result for population. Images were more informative for building type, building function, and low-rise floor count. For floor count, image advantage increased by 5.7 percentage points per doubling of distance to the nearest labelled building and declined for tall buildings whose rooflines often fell outside the frame. Models frequently followed conflicting records. OpenFACADES floor annotations were generated with OpenStreetMap floor values and showed the opposite height-dependent error pattern from image-only reruns. Street-view image value therefore depends on visual legibility and local data coverage. Comparing images with existing urban data can guide image collection and clarify the provenance of derived urban maps.

</details>


### [7] [Soundwich: Video Generation with Layered and Controllable Audio](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00691)
*Zhuo Ning,AmirHossein Naghi Razlighi,Sagi Polaczek,Daniel Cohen-Or,Ali Mahdavi-Amiri*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Soundwich is a training-free framework that transforms joint audio-video generative models into generators of multiple synchronized, independently editable audio stems (speech, music, sound effects, ambient sounds) coupled to a shared video, enabling source-level editing while maintaining audiovisual coherence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current joint audio-video models generate audio as a single mixed track, limiting source-level control. This differs from practical workflows where different audio elements (speech, music, SFX, ambient) are represented as separate editable tracks.

Method: 1) Transform a frozen joint audio-video flow-matching model into a multi-stem generator. 2) Introduce a shared scene representation to communicate global audiovisual context across stems while preserving source-level separation. 3) Route cross-modal interactions between each audio stem and its corresponding visual source to improve audiovisual consistency.

Result: Experiments and human evaluations show improved temporal control, source separation, and naturalness, while enabling flexible source-level editing (retiming, muting, replacing, remixing) within coherent audiovisual generation.

Conclusion: Soundwich successfully enables independent control over multiple audio stems while maintaining synchronization with video, bridging the gap between generative audiovisual models and practical editing workflows.

Abstract: Recent joint audio-video generative models can synthesize realistic videos with synchronized sound, but typically generate audio as a single mixed track. This limits source-level control and differs from practical audiovisual workflows, where speech, music, sound effects, and ambient sounds are represented as separate editable tracks. We introduce Soundwich, a training-free framework that transforms a frozen joint audio-video flow-matching model into a generator of multiple synchronized, independently editable audio stems coupled to a shared video. Soundwich generates separate audio stems with explicit control over their temporal activity. To keep separately generated sounds coherent, we introduce a shared scene representation that communicates global audiovisual context across stems while preserving their source-level separation. We further route cross-modal interactions between each audio stem and its corresponding visual source, improving audiovisual consistency. The resulting stems remain synchronized with the video and can be independently retimed, muted, replaced, or remixed. Experiments and human evaluations show improved temporal control, source separation, and naturalness, while enabling flexible source-level editing within coherent audiovisual generation. Code is available at https://github.com/CodyNing/Soundwich.

</details>


### [8] [DSSR-3D: Decoupled Reasoning for View-Dependent Referring in 3D Gaussians](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00040)
*Thanh-Khoi Nguyen,Thien-Phuc Tran,Minh-Triet Tran*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DSSR-3D is an inference-time framework for view-dependent referring segmentation on 3D Gaussian fields. It addresses the limitation that existing methods embed language features in a view-invariant space, making them unable to resolve observer-centric spatial relations (e.g., "to the left of"). The framework uses two interfaces - pose-invariant semantic localization and pose-conditioned spatial reasoning - instantiated via temperature-sharpened softmax localization and projection-based directional scoring, fused without training. It also introduces ViewRef-GS benchmark for evaluating view-dependent segmentation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing 3D Gaussian Splatting methods for open-vocabulary and referring segmentation embed language features in a globally view-invariant space, which fundamentally cannot resolve observer-centric spatial relations (e.g., "to the left of", "in front of") that depend on camera pose. This limits their ability to handle viewpoint-dependent spatial grounding tasks.

Method: DSSR-3D formalizes view-dependent referring segmentation as two interfaces: (1) pose-invariant semantic localization - to identify semantic content in the scene, and (2) pose-conditioned spatial reasoning - to resolve spatial relations based on camera pose. The method instantiates these with: (a) a temperature-sharpened softmax localization mechanism for semantic localization, and (b) a projection-based directional scoring function for spatial reasoning. These are fused via a lightweight, training-free step. The framework requires no retraining of the underlying semantic field and no discrete geometric proxies like bounding boxes.

Result: Experiments show consistent gains over existing 3DGS-based referring methods, with no additional training beyond the base semantic field. The method can transfer zero-shot to structurally distinct semantic fields without adaptation. The work also introduces ViewRef-GS benchmark (augmented with Ref-LERF) as a comprehensive testbed for viewpoint-dependent spatial grounding.

Conclusion: DSSR-3D successfully enables view-dependent referring segmentation on continuous 3D Gaussian fields through a principled two-interface framework. The training-free approach achieves superior performance over existing methods while generalizing zero-shot to different semantic fields. The proposed benchmarks (ViewRef-GS and augmented Ref-LERF) provide standardized evaluation for this task.

Abstract: Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting have enabled open-vocabulary and referring segmentation by distilling semantic knowledge from 2D foundation models into 3D representations. However, existing referring fields embed language features in a globally view-invariant space, making them fundamentally unable to resolve observer-centric spatial relations (e.g., "to the left of") that depend on camera pose. We propose DSSR-3D, an inference-time framework for view-dependent referring segmentation on continuous 3D Gaussian fields, formalized as two interfaces - pose-invariant semantic localization and pose-conditioned spatial reasoning - such that any pair of functions satisfying these constraints yields a valid instantiation, requiring no retraining of the underlying semantic field and no reliance on discrete geometric proxies such as bounding boxes. We instantiate the two interfaces with a temperature-sharpened softmax localization mechanism and a projection-based directional scoring function, fused via a lightweight, training-free step, and show they transfer zero-shot to structurally distinct semantic fields without adaptation. We further propose ViewRef-GS, a benchmark isolating view-dependent segmentation on 3D Gaussian fields, evaluated jointly with an augmented Ref-LERF to provide a comprehensive testbed for viewpoint-dependent spatial grounding. Experiments show consistent gains over existing 3DGS-based referring methods, with no additional training beyond the base semantic field

</details>


### [9] [Supervising Sound Localization by In-the-wild Egomotion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01388)
*Anna Min,Ziyang Chen,Hang Zhao,Andrew Owens*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A method for learning binaural sound localization using egomotion as supervisory signal, where camera motion across video frames provides supervision for training an audio model to predict sound directions, combined with traditional binaural cues, validated on a new real-world dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sound localization is important for robotics and AR/VR applications, but traditional methods rely on explicit supervision or limited binaural cues. The authors propose using egomotion (camera movement) as a weak but plentiful form of supervision, since the camera's direction to a sound source changes as the camera moves.

Method: 1) Use traditional multi-view geometry methods to estimate camera motion (egomotion) from video
2) Train an audio model to predict sound directions that are consistent with these visual motion estimates
3) Combine this supervision with traditional binaural cues
4) Evaluate on a new dataset of real-world audio-visual videos with egomotion

Result: The model can successfully learn from real-world data and performs well on sound localization tasks.

Conclusion: Egomotion can serve as an effective supervisory signal for learning binaural sound localization, providing a weak but plentiful form of supervision that works with real-world data.

Abstract: We present a method for learning binaural sound localization using egomotion as a supervisory signal. Over the course of a video, the cameras direction to a sound source will change as the camera moves. We train an audio model to predict sound directions that are consistent with visual estimates of camera motion, which we obtain using traditional methods from multi-view geometry. This provides a weak but plentiful form of supervision that we combine with traditional binaural cues. To evaluate this method, we propose a dataset of real-world audio-visual videos with egomotion. We show that our model can successfully learn from real-world data and that it performs well on sound localization tasks

</details>


### [10] [Reachability Is Not Generalization: Understanding Verb--Noun Decomposition in Assembly Action Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00064)
*Changyi Li,Yu Xiao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates why verb-noun decomposition only partially generalizes to unseen action combinations in assembly tasks. Through systematic analysis across three datasets (MECCANO, HAViD, IMPACT), the authors find that decomposition's gains come mainly from interpolating within densely supported regions of the compositional space, not true recombination. Failures stem from three connected factors: primitive support (co-occurrence patterns), vocabulary asymmetry (bottleneck on larger component), and component entanglement in shared encoders.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assembly actions combine manipulations with parts/tools, but atomic classifiers assign zero probability to novel combinations. While verb-noun decomposition is widely adopted, its generalization under compositional shift remains poorly understood. The authors aimed to systematically analyze why decomposition achieves only partial compositional generalization in practice.

Method: The authors conducted a systematic analysis of verb-noun decomposition across three assembly datasets (MECCANO, HAViD, IMPACT). They evaluated performance on unseen compositions, analyzed the relationship between performance and training data co-occurrence structure, compared independent vs. shared-encoder training, and examined how vocabulary asymmetry affects generalization.

Result: Decomposition escapes the atomic ceiling but generalization extends only partially beyond it. Unseen-composition performance remains strongly tied to training data co-occurrence patterns, indicating gains arise from interpolation within densely supported regions rather than unconstrained recombination. Failures concentrate on the larger-vocabulary component (e.g., IMPACT's verb-heavy vocabulary reverses the bottleneck from nouns to verbs). Shared-encoder training introduces component entanglement, encouraging reliance on co-occurrence patterns that transfer poorly to unseen compositions, trailing independent recombination by up to 6.0× in harmonic mean.

Conclusion: Verb-noun decomposition achieves only partial compositional generalization in practice due to three connected sources of error: (1) primitive support - performance tied to co-occurrence structure; (2) vocabulary asymmetry - failures concentrate on larger-vocabulary component; (3) component entanglement - shared encoders create dependencies that transfer poorly. The authors provide a portable diagnostic framework for studying compositional recognition beyond aggregate accuracy.

Abstract: Assembly actions are compositional: they combine a manipulation with a part or tool. In deployment, systems routinely encounter novel combinations of familiar components, yet an atomic action classifier assigns every unseen combination exactly zero probability by construction. The prevailing solution is verb--noun decomposition, which predicts components separately and recombines them to reach unseen actions. While widely adopted, how decomposition generalizes under compositional shift remains poorly understood. We present a systematic analysis of verb--noun decomposition across three assembly datasets (MECCANO, HAViD, and IMPACT). Although decomposition escapes the atomic ceiling, its generalization extends only partially beyond it. Unseen-composition performance remains strongly tied to the co-occurrence structure of the training data, indicating that much of the observed gain arises from interpolation within densely supported regions of the compositional space rather than from unconstrained recombination. Across datasets, failures consistently concentrate on the larger-vocabulary component, and IMPACT's verb-heavy vocabulary reverses the bottleneck from nouns to verbs. We further show that shared-encoder training introduces component entanglement, encouraging reliance on co-occurrence patterns that transfer poorly to unseen compositions and trailing independent recombination by up to $6.0\times$ in harmonic mean. Taken together, these findings explain why decomposition achieves only partial compositional generalization in practice. By identifying primitive support, vocabulary asymmetry, and component entanglement as connected sources of error, we provide a portable diagnostic framework for studying compositional recognition beyond aggregate accuracy. Code: https://github.com/hisalaheiyo/assembly.

</details>


### [11] [Exploring Weaknesses of Generative Image Watermarks against Latent Frequency Masking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02010)
*Kirill Aistov,Khaled Abud,Irina Serzhenko,Egor Kovalev,Aleksey Yakushev,Aleksandr Akimenkov,Dmitry Obydenkov,Yury Markin,Sergey Lavrushkin,Dmitriy Vatolin,Anastasia Antsiferova*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A new attack called Latent Frequency Masking removes AI image watermarks by manipulating Fourier coefficients in latent representations, defeating six watermarking methods while maintaining image quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Invisible watermarking is used for tracing AI-generated images, but its robustness against adaptive removal attacks is uncertain. Need to identify vulnerabilities in current watermarking methods.

Method: Latent Frequency Masking attack - replaces selected Fourier coefficients in latent representation of watermarked images. Two sampling methods: Gaussian noise (efficient) or diffusion regeneration (better image preservation). Includes theoretical distortion bound analysis.

Result: Attack removes or substantially weakens watermarks from six diffusion watermarking methods while preserving perceptual quality and achieving favorable runtime compared to existing attacks.

Conclusion: Latent frequency manipulation represents a practical attack surface for AI-generated image watermarks, requiring inclusion in robustness evaluations. The attack successfully removes/weakens multiple watermarks while preserving perceptual quality.

Abstract: Invisible watermarking has become a central tool for tracing AI-generated images, but its robustness against adaptive removal attacks remains an open security question. We introduce Latent Frequency Masking, an attack that erases watermark evidence by replacing selected Fourier coefficients in the latent representation of a watermarked image. The replacement can be sampled from Gaussian noise for efficiency or derived from diffusion regeneration for improved image preservation. We provide a theoretical distortion bound relating the change between the reconstructed adversarial image and the masked latent-frequency perturbation. We evaluate the proposed attack against six diffusion watermarking methods on images generated from DiffusionDB and MS-COCO prompts. Latent Frequency Masking removes or substantially weakens several watermarks while preserving perceptual quality and achieving favorable runtime compared with existing attacks. These results identify latent-frequency manipulation as a practical attack surface and highlight the need to include such attacks in robustness evaluations of generative image watermarking.

</details>


### [12] [Robust Online Aero-Engine Blade Defect Detection via Dual-Alignment Test-Time Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00067)
*Zhaoyang Wang,Haiyong Chen,Dongying Li,Yining Wang,Huapeng Wu,Xinwei Lv,Atik Shahariar*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Aero-engine Blade Defect Detector (ABDD) is an online adaptive detection framework that addresses domain shift problems in visual inspection for aero-engine blade manufacturing. It uses test-time adaptation to handle variations in production lines, imaging conditions, blade poses, and surface backgrounds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to solve the domain shift problem in aero-engine blade defect detection, where deep defect detectors degrade in reliability during online inspection due to mismatches between training and deployment data. The challenge is amplified by sparse defects in blade images, making pseudo-label-based adaptation vulnerable to noise.

Method: The proposed method ABDD incorporates three key components: 1) Dual-Alignment Strategy combining feature-statistics alignment with pseudo-box alignment to adapt global visual style and local defect morphology; 2) Uncertainty-aware Box Filtering mechanism evaluating pseudo boxes using classification confidence, classification entropy, and localization entropy; 3) Lightweight Sparse Dilated Mona module for parameter-efficient delta tuning while limiting source-domain forgetting. Evaluation is performed on CD-AeBD and HD-AeBD datasets under multiple domain-shift scenarios using RT-DETR + Swin-T architecture.

Result: ABDD consistently improves detection robustness under domain shifts. The method's practicality is further validated on an industrial inspection platform.

Conclusion: The proposed ABDD framework effectively addresses domain shift challenges in aero-engine blade visual inspection through test-time adaptation, demonstrating consistent robustness improvements across various domain-shift scenarios and practical applicability in industrial settings.

Abstract: Reliable visual inspection is essential for quality assurance in aero-engine blade manufacturing, where defect appearance may vary across production lines, imaging conditions, blade poses, and surface backgrounds. Such domain shifts cause a mismatch between training and deployment data and degrade the reliability of deep defect detectors in online inspection. This problem is particularly challenging because aero-engine blade images usually contain sparse defects, making pseudolabel-based adaptation vulnerable to noisy or missing predictions. To address this issue, we propose Aero-engine Blade Defect Detector (ABDD), an online adaptive detection framework based on test-time adaptation. ABDD introduces a Dual-Alignment Strategy to jointly adapt global visual style and local defect morphology by combining feature-statistics alignment with pseudo-box alignment. To reduce error accumulation from unreliable pseudo labels, an Uncertainty-aware Box Filtering mechanism evaluates pseudo boxes using classification confidence, classification entropy, and localization entropy. In addition, a lightweight Sparse Dilated Mona module enables parameter-efficient delta tuning while limiting source-domain forgetting. ABDD is evaluated on CD-AeBD and HD-AeBD under multiple domain-shift scenarios, with TTA strategies compared under a unified RT-DETR + Swin-T architecture. Experiments show that ABDD consistently improves detection robustness under domain shifts, and its practicality is further validated on an industrial inspection platform.

</details>


### [13] [What Builds the Scene? Luminance Dominates Geometry Formation in 3D Gaussian Splatting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00749)
*Rezvan Joshaghani,Steven Cutchin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates how luminance and chrominance contribute to 3D Gaussian Splatting geometry learning. The authors find that geometry formation is strongly luminance-dominated but not luminance-exclusive, with luminance-only supervision producing geometry only 0.085 dB below RGB-trained models, while chroma-only supervision yields geometry 3.9-5.5 dB worse. Chromatic appearance can largely be recovered after spatial support forms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting learns geometry and appearance jointly from RGB supervision, making it difficult to isolate how luminance and chroma contribute to the learned representation. This study aims to understand the relative importance of luminance versus chrominance in geometry formation and appearance fitting.

Method: The authors trained 3DGS models under different channel supervision regimes (luminance-only, chroma-only, RGB), froze non-appearance parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity), and re-estimated appearance with the same solver before comparing held-out reconstruction quality across eleven benchmark scenes with four independent runs each.

Result: Geometry learned from luminance alone supports held-out reconstruction 0.085 dB below RGB-trained geometry on average. Higher-order spherical harmonics improve PSNR by 1.44 dB for luminance versus only 0.19 dB for chroma. Chroma-only supervision produces geometry 3.9-5.5 dB worse than luminance-only supervision. Deleting chroma from a trained model and re-fitting it on frozen geometry can recover original quality or slightly better. Densification partially explains the gap between chroma-only and luminance-only supervision.

Conclusion: Geometry formation in standard 3DGS is strongly luminance-dominated but not luminance-exclusive. Luminance plays a dominant role in spatial support formation, while chromatic appearance can be largely recovered after geometry has been established. This findings have implications for understanding neural rendering representations and potential applications in efficient geometry learning.

Abstract: Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) learns geometry and appearance jointly from RGB supervision, making it difficult to isolate how luminance and chroma contribute to the learned representation. We study this by training models under different channel supervision, freezing their non-appearance parameters (position, scale, rotation, and opacity), and re-estimating appearance with the same solver before comparing held-out reconstruction. Across eleven benchmark scenes with four independent runs each, geometry learned from luminance alone supports held-out reconstruction 0.085 dB below RGB-trained geometry on average. If chroma is deleted from a trained model, a sufficiently expressive solver can re-fit it on the frozen geometry to the original quality or slightly better. Higher-order spherical harmonics contribute much more reconstruction quality to luminance than to chroma, improving PSNR by 1.44 dB versus 0.19 dB on average, although on mirror-like surfaces hue does still change with viewpoint. The luminance advantage is even larger when geometry is being formed. Chroma-only supervision produces geometry 3.9-5.5 dB worse than luminance-only supervision after the same appearance solve; densification explains part of this gap. Overall, geometry formation in standard 3DGS is strongly luminance-dominated but not luminance-exclusive, and much of the chromatic appearance can be recovered after spatial support has formed.

</details>


### [14] [A Framework for Egocentric and Exocentric Procedural Understanding via Temporal Segmentation and Semantic Abstraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00069)
*Vivek Chavan,Jörg Krüger*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A compact framework that converts continuous multimodal workplace video into a structured Procedural State Memory (Work Environment Model) by detecting event boundaries using multimodal cues and representing segments as evidence-linked event cards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon ego/exo workplace video data is rich in procedural evidence but suffers from redundancy, noise, and high processing/retainment costs, necessitating a compact representation approach.

Method: The framework detects event boundaries using changes in visual context, location, motion, narration, gaze/object interaction, and optional exocentric workspace evidence (inspired by event segmentation theory). Each segment is abstracted into an evidence-linked event card containing actor, interval, location, action, objects/tools, pre/post state, confidence, and provenance. Implementation uses frozen DINOv2 and VJEPA-2 encoders with a local language model.

Result: The framework enables compact, auditable documentation and retrieval under on-premise privacy constraints, with the WEM incrementally updated through event cards.

Conclusion: The design provides a scalable solution for procedural memory representation from multimodal workplace video, with evaluation criteria outlined for segmentation quality, memory compression, retrieval fidelity, and long-horizon QA.

Abstract: Long-horizon ego/exo data contains rich procedural evidence, but are redundant, noisy, and costly to process or retain. We propose a compact framework that converts continuous multimodal workplace video into a structured Procedural State Memory, implemented as a Work Environment Model (WEM). Inspired by event segmentation theory, we detect boundaries using changes in visual context, location, motion, narration, gaze/object interaction, and optional exocentric workspace evidence, rather than fixed windows or visual novelty alone. Each segment is abstracted into an evidence-linked event card containing actor, interval, location, action, objects/tools, pre/post state, confidence, and provenance. These event cards incrementally update the WEM, enabling compact, auditable documentation and retrieval under on-premise privacy constraints. We instantiate the design with frozen DINOv2 and VJEPA-2 encoders and a local language model, and outline evaluation criteria for segmentation quality, memory compression, retrieval fidelity, and long-horizon QA.

</details>


### [15] [DramaAgent: Agentic Storytelling Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00097)
*Ting Huang,Biao Wu,Ronghao Chen,Zeyu Zhang,Tengfei Cheng,Qizhen Lan,Huacan Wang,Hao Tang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DramaAgent is a hierarchical agentic framework that improves long-form text-to-video-and-audio generation by adding an upper-level control layer on top of existing video generation backbones. It decomposes the generation process into story planning, persistent character conditioning, scene-wise synthesis, and reflection-guided targeted repair to address narrative drift, character identity instability, weak cross-scene continuity, and audio-visual mismatch.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current text-to-video models struggle with coherent long-form story videos with consistent characters and aligned audio. Existing methods suffer from narrative drift, unstable character identity, weak cross-scene continuity, and audio-visual mismatch over extended sequences.

Method: DramaAgent introduces a hierarchical, agentic, and model-agnostic framework that acts as an upper-level control layer. It decomposes generation into: (1) story planning, (2) persistent character conditioning, (3) scene-wise synthesis, and (4) reflection-guided targeted repair. The framework maintains reusable story and character states across scenes, diagnoses failures (identity drift, missing semantics, temporal discontinuity, cross-modal mismatch), and repairs problematic clips in a stage-specific manner.

Result: Experiments across multiple video generation backbones show that DramaAgent improves long-horizon coherence, character consistency, narrative fidelity, and scene-level audio-visual consistency over direct generation and strong baselines.

Conclusion: Hierarchical agentic control is a practical direction for controllable long-form audiovisual generation. DramaAgent provides a model-agnostic approach that can work with various video generation backbones while maintaining coherence and consistency across extended video sequences.

Abstract: Recent diffusion and autoregressive models have substantially improved text-to-video generation, yet producing coherent long-form story videos with consistent characters and aligned audio remains challenging. Existing methods often suffer from narrative drift, unstable character identity, weak cross-scene continuity, and audio-visual mismatch over extended sequences. We propose DramaAgent, a hierarchical, agentic, and model-agnostic framework for long-form text-to-video-and-audio generation. Rather than improving the underlying video backbone itself, DramaAgent introduces an upper-level control layer that decomposes generation into story planning, persistent character conditioning, scene-wise synthesis, and reflection-guided targeted repair. The framework maintains reusable story and character states across scenes, diagnoses failures such as identity drift, missing scene semantics, temporal discontinuity, and cross-modal mismatch, and repairs problematic clips in a stage-specific manner. Experiments across multiple video generation backbones show that DramaAgent improves long-horizon coherence, character consistency, narrative fidelity, and scene-level audio-visual consistency over direct generation and strong baselines. These results suggest that hierarchical agentic control is a practical direction for controllable long-form audiovisual generation. Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/DramaAgent. Website: https://aigeeksgroup.github.io/DramaAgent.

</details>


### [16] [LiteReality-Agent: An Agentic System for Interactable 3D Indoor Scene Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01863)
*Zhening Huang,Yueyan Li,Johnathan Chiu,Xiaoyang Lyu,Matt Zhou,Yuxin Yao,Joan Lasenby,Shangzhe Wu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LiteReality-Agent is an agentic system that reconstructs real indoor environments into realistic, articulated, and simulation-ready 3D scenes from RGB-D scans by formulating reconstruction as a coding problem where a coding agent iteratively edits a Python script (Room.py) using specialized tools within an observe-edit-verify framework.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for high-quality, simulation-ready 3D digital twins of real indoor environments for embodied AI tasks and real-to-sim applications. Current frontier models (Astra, Fable) lack sufficient geometric accuracy, visual realism, and simulation compatibility.

Method: Formulates 3D reconstruction as a coding problem using a coding agent that gathers evidence through specialized tools and iteratively edits a Python script (Room.py) that generates the 3D scene. Implements a robust observe-edit-verify harness supporting evidence gathering, measurement, verification, layout optimization, simulation readiness, and quality control throughout the reconstruction process.

Result: LiteReality-Agent produces reconstructions that are more geometrically accurate, visually realistic, and simulation-compatible than recent frontier models (Astra and Fable). The system provides a strong orchestration framework with specialized tools, structured workflows, and verification mechanisms for future agents.

Conclusion: LiteReality-Agent represents a practical and important building block for robust real-to-sim systems, providing an extensible framework that improves reconstruction quality and reliability as agent capabilities continue to advance. Source code and data-capture application are publicly available.

Abstract: We present LiteReality-Agent, an agentic system for reconstructing real indoor environments as realistic, articulated, and simulation-ready 3D scenes from RGB-D scans. At its core, LiteReality-Agent formulates 3D reconstruction as a coding problem, in which a coding agent gathers evidence using specialised tools and iteratively edits a Python script, Room.py, which can be executed to produce a 3D digital twin of the room. With this formulation, we develop a robust observe-edit-verify harness that supports evidence gathering, measurement, verification, layout optimisation, simulation readiness, and quality control throughout the reconstruction process. LiteReality-Agent produces high-quality reconstructions suitable for simulation and downstream embodied AI tasks. Furthermore, as agent capabilities continue to improve rapidly, the system introduced by LiteReality-Agent remains a strong orchestration framework for future agents: it equips them with specialised tools, structured workflows, and robust verification mechanisms that substantially improve reconstruction quality and reliability. We demonstrate that LiteReality-Agent produces reconstructions that are more geometrically accurate, visually realistic, and simulation-compatible than those generated by recent frontier models, such as Astra and Fable. We therefore view LiteReality-Agent as a practical and important building block for robust real-to-sim systems. Both the source code and the data-capture application are publicly available. Code:https://github.com/LiteReality/LiteReality-Agent/

</details>


### [17] [A Low Grounding Score Is Not an Ungrounded Judge: Identifying the Perceptibility Confound in Multimodal Oversight](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00111)
*Rasul Khanbayov,Hasan Kurban*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper identifies a fundamental flaw in counterfactual probes used to measure visual grounding in multimodal model judges. The probe edits images to flip ground truth while holding reasoning fixed, then checks if the verdict follows. However, the authors show this score is systematically biased downward - it can only make judges appear less grounded than they actually are, creating false alarms where auditors reject usable judges. They propose using a detection probe on unedited images as a complementary upper bound that can identify and certify false alarms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors aim to address a critical issue in evaluating multimodal reasoning models: whether the "model judges" that supervise these systems actually use visual evidence. Current counterfactual probes of visual grounding claim to measure this, but the authors suspected the measurement itself was flawed.

Method: The authors formalize the counterfactual probe as the "Verdict Grounding Score" and prove theoretically that it has a one-sided error property - it can only underestimate grounding. They show the missing quantity (true grounding) can be identified from three quantities already collected in standard audits. They validate this by auditing nine judges and comparing detection rates on edited vs. unedited images.

Result: The predicted ordering holds strictly across all nine judges audited. The typical judge acts on only about half of the edits whose attribute it can otherwise resolve. Using a conservative rejection threshold, several cells are certified as false alarms outright - the clearest being a judge that detects injected errors almost every time while still scoring as if it had not used the image at all.

Conclusion: The key conclusion is that image-side counterfactual scores should never be reported alone. A detection probe on the unedited image should always be included as an upper bound to certify false alarms. This costs nothing extra to run and prevents discarding usable overseers based on flawed measurements.

Abstract: Model judges now supervise multimodal systems at scale, filtering training data, selecting outputs, and supplying the reward that shapes multimodal reasoning models. Trusting one means first checking that it uses its evidence, and that check is itself worth scrutinizing, so we ask whether a counterfactual probe of visual grounding measures what it claims to. The probe edits the image so the ground truth flips, holds the reasoning trace fixed, and asks whether the verdict follows. We formalize it as the Verdict Grounding Score and show it cannot be read the way such scores are read. A verdict responds only to an edit that reaches the judge's decision-relevant reading, so the score is capped by how perceptible the edit is, and unless editing makes the attribute easier to read, the error is one-sided: the score can only make a judge look less grounded than it is. The practical failure is therefore a false alarm, an auditor discarding a usable overseer. Under assumptions we state, we show this missing quantity is not merely bounded but identified from three quantities the same audit protocol already collects, which makes the false-alarm rate directly measurable rather than merely a concern. Auditing nine judges, we find the predicted ordering holds strictly across our entire primary pool, and the typical judge there acts on only about half of the edits whose attribute it can otherwise resolve. Applying a conservative rejection threshold certifies several cells as false alarms outright, the clearest being a judge that detects the injected error essentially every time while still scoring as if it had not used the image at all. The rule that follows is that an image-side counterfactual score should never be reported alone: a detection probe on the unedited image upper-bounds it, certifies its false alarms, and costs nothing extra to run.

</details>


### [18] [MosaiChunk: Compositing Spatio-Temporal Memory for Autoregressive Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02153)
*Yiwen Zhang,Haocheng Xi,Michael Tian-Yue Liu,Alexei A. Efros,Hadar Averbuch-Elor,Qianqian Wang,Haiwen Feng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MosaiChunk introduces a spatio-temporal memory mechanism that composes a mosaic of historical key-value entries to handle long-horizon video generation where objects/scenes reappear after falling out of context. It uses a lightweight router to select historical sections under a fixed memory budget, keeping the video generator frozen.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon autoregressive video generation is limited by finite context windows. When objects or scenes fall out of context, their fine-grained visual details are lost and difficult to recover upon reappearance. Existing methods like sliding-window inference or whole-chunk retrieval have limitations in maintaining visual consistency for long-horizon videos.

Method: 1) Spatio-temporal memory mechanism composing a mosaic of selected historical KV entries across space and time. 2) Leverages the observation that a frozen video generator can directly consume non-contiguous historical KV and recover visual content. 3) Keeps the generator fixed and learns only a lightweight router to determine which historical sections to include in the mosaic under a fixed active-memory budget. 4) Introduces RememBench benchmark with T2V (text-to-video) and I2V (image-to-video) splits for long-horizon revisits.

Result: MosaiChunk consistently improves revisit consistency over both sliding-window inference and whole-chunk retrieval under matched memory budgets, across both T2V and I2V settings.

Conclusion: The proposed MosaiChunk approach effectively addresses the context window limitation in long-horizon video generation by selectively retaining and reusing historical visual information through a learned router, achieving improved consistency when objects/scenes reappear after being out of context.

Abstract: Long-horizon autoregressive video generation is limited by a finite context window. When an object or scene falls out of context, its fine-grained visual details may be lost and difficult to recover upon reappearance. To retain access to such visual details, we introduce MosaiChunk, a spatio-temporal memory mechanism that composes a mosaic of selected historical key-value (KV) entries across space and time. Our approach is motivated by the observation that a frozen video generator can directly consume such non-contiguous historical KV and recover the corresponding visual content. We therefore keep the generator fixed and learn only a lightweight router that determines which historical sections to include in the mosaic under a fixed active-memory budget. We further introduce RememBench, a benchmark of long-horizon revisits with prompt-driven text-to-video (T2V) and camera-driven image-to-video (I2V) splits. Our experiments show that MosaiChunk consistently improves revisit consistency over both sliding-window inference and whole-chunk retrieval under matched memory budgets, across both T2V and I2V settings.

</details>


### [19] [Evaluating the Robustness of Anti-UAV Detection under Controlled Fog Degradation: Fog-Aware Training and Clear-Sky Tradeoff](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00141)
*Gur Levy Birkental,Seyed Sahand Mohammadi Ziabari,Ali Mohammed Mansoor Alsahag*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents the first severity-controlled fog benchmark for vision-based anti-UAV detection, applying 10 levels of synthetic fog to the Anti-UAV300 dataset. The study reveals that detection performance degrades sharply and non-linearly with fog severity, with a 96% reduction in mAP@0.5:0.95 from clear to thickest fog. Fog-aware training improves performance across all severities but cannot prevent collapse under extreme fog conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current anti-UAV benchmarks use only clear-sky footage, and prior robustness studies treat adverse weather as a simple present/absent condition. This leaves a critical gap in understanding how fog severity specifically impacts ground-to-air UAV detection, which is essential for real-world deployment reliability.

Method: Synthetic fog at ten severity levels was applied to the RGB modality of the Anti-UAV300 dataset. A clear-trained YOLOv5m baseline was compared to a fog-aware model trained on both clear and foggy images. Performance was evaluated using mAP@0.5:0.95 and mAP@0.5 metrics.

Result: Detection performance degrades sharply and non-linearly. Degradation is front-loaded across light-to-moderate fog (beta ≈ 0.05-0.10), with a 96% reduction in mAP@0.5:0.95 from clear to thickest fog, primarily due to lost recall and confidence. On mAP@0.5, this collapse exceeds the most extreme rain degradation reported in prior benchmarks. Fog-aware training boosts detection across all severities (up to +0.320 mAP@0.5:0.95) with only a 9.1% drop in clear-sky accuracy, but cannot prevent collapse under extreme fog.

Conclusion: Reliability is lost within a narrow visibility range, and simple clear vs adverse tests underestimate operational risk. The study highlights the need for severity-controlled benchmarks to properly assess anti-UAV system robustness in real-world fog conditions.

Abstract: Vision-based anti-UAV systems must function in poor visibility, yet most benchmarks use only clear-sky footage, and previous robustness studies treat adverse weather as a simple present/absent condition. As a result, the impact of fog severity on ground-to-air UAV detection remains poorly understood. This work presents the first severity-controlled fog benchmark for this task: synthetic fog at ten severity levels is applied to the RGB modality of the Anti-UAV300 dataset, comparing a clear-trained YOLOv5m baseline to a fog-aware model trained on both clear and foggy images. Detection performance drops sharply and non-linearly: degradation is front-loaded across light-to-moderate fog (beta approximately 0.05-0.10), with a 96% reduction in mAP@0.5:0.95 from clear to thickest fog, mainly due to lost recall and confidence. On the comparable metric (mAP@0.5), this collapse exceeds the most extreme rain degradation reported in the closest prior benchmark. Fog-aware training boosts detection across all severities (up to +0.320 mAP@0.5:0.95) with only a 9.1% drop in clear-sky accuracy, raising the threshold for reliable detection while not preventing collapse under extreme fog. Since reliability is lost within a narrow visibility range, simple clear vs adverse tests underestimate operational risk.

</details>


### [20] [GPEC: Efficient Pre-LLM Gaussian Process Embedding Correction for Cardiac Video Caption Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00196)
*Arefeh Rezaei*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: GPEC is a pre-LLM error-correction method that improves cardiac ultrasound caption generation by VideoChat2. It learns a residual correction using sparse variational Gaussian Process to move visual representations toward annotation-guided targets, without requiring end-to-end fine-tuning. The method adds minimal inference overhead (<0.05s) while improving caption similarity and content alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) show performance decline in specialized medical imaging domains like echocardiography. There's a need for a computationally efficient method to improve visual representations for medical video captioning without requiring end-to-end fine-tuning of the pretrained backbone.

Method: GPEC is inserted between the visual projection layer and the language model. It learns a residual correction using sparse variational Gaussian Process with inducing points, natural-parameter variational updates, and a block-wise linear kernel. The target is constructed by converting structured video annotations into qualitative attributes, generating fixed-format reference captions, and mapping them into the language-model embedding space. Original VideoChat2 components remain frozen.

Result: GPEC improves caption similarity and content alignment compared to original VideoChat2, while adding less than 0.05s inference-time overhead per video. The method was evaluated using representation-level, caption-level, content-oriented, and execution-time metrics.

Conclusion: GPEC can improve caption generation in specialized medical video domains with minimal computational cost, without requiring end-to-end fine-tuning of the pretrained multimodal backbone. This demonstrates the potential of modular, computationally efficient correction methods for adapting MLLMs to specialized medical domains.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown strong potential for video understanding and caption generation, but their performance may decline in specialized medical imaging domains such as echocardiography. This work introduces Gaussian Process Embedding Correction (GPEC), a modular and computationally efficient pre-LLM error-correction method that improves the visual representations used by VideoChat2 for cardiac ultrasound caption generation. GPEC is inserted between the visual projection layer and the language model and learns a residual correction that moves the projected visual representation toward an annotation-guided target. The target is constructed by converting structured video annotations into qualitative attributes, generating a fixed-format reference caption, and mapping it into the language-model embedding space. The correction is modeled using a sparse variational Gaussian Process with inducing points, natural-parameter variational updates, and a block-wise linear kernel, while the original VideoChat2 components remain frozen.The method is evaluated using representation-level, caption-level, content-oriented, and execution-time metrics by comparing the original VideoChat2 with VideoChat2 + GPEC under identical input and reference conditions. Results show improved caption similarity and content alignment after applying the proposed correction. Furthermore, GPEC adds less than 0.05 s of inference-time overhead per video in the evaluated setting. These findings indicate that GPEC can improve caption generation in specialized medical video domains with minimal computational cost, without requiring end-to-end fine-tuning of the pretrained multimodal backbone.

</details>


### [21] [Query Independent Variable Rate Visual Token Coding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00204)
*Hongbo Zhang,Zihao Yang,Liuyang Song,Daqian Yang,Haoyang Yao,Yan Wen,Zhengtao Yao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a new approach to visual-token compression for vision-language models that uses transform coding (varying compression rate per token) instead of token selection/pruning. The method creates a single compressed representation that works for any query, solving the problem where attention-based pruning only works for the specific question it was optimized for.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current visual-token compression methods treat the problem as token selection (keep vs discard), using attention scores from the language model as ranking criteria. This approach has a critical flaw: the ranking depends on the specific question being asked. While this is invisible in single-turn benchmarks, it becomes decisive when a compressed representation is reused across multiple queries (e.g., cached conversation turns or transmitted between devices). The authors sought a method that creates a single, query-agnostic compressed representation.

Method: The authors propose a transform coding approach that keeps every token but varies its compression rate. They measure each token's distortion-rate curve and distribute a fixed bit budget across tokens using exact integer rate-distortion optimization. This approach requires no text/prompt information in the compression pipeline, enabling one compressed representation to serve any query.

Result: At equal bit budgets, on two datasets and two capacities, the method preserves the model's output distribution and answers better than: (1) uniform-rate coding, (2) closed-form water-fill, and (3) distortion-ranked pruning. It matches attention-ranked pruning on the specific question that pruning was tuned for, and significantly outperforms it when the compressed image must answer a different question about the same image.

Conclusion: Transform coding with per-token rate allocation outperforms selection-based pruning methods for multi-query scenarios. Since no text enters the compression pipeline, one compressed representation can serve any downstream query, making it practical for caching and transmission applications. The key insight is that the "other half of the classical transform-coding toolkit" (rate allocation) provides complementary benefits to token selection.

Abstract: Visual-token compression for vision--language models is posed almost entirely as a selection problem: decide which tokens to keep and discard the rest. The criteria that work best rank tokens by the attention the language model pays them, which makes the ranking a function of the question being asked. That is invisible in a single-turn benchmark and decisive whenever a compressed representation is written once and read many times, as when it is cached across the turns of a conversation or transmitted between a device and a server. We take the other half of the classical transform-coding toolkit instead: keep every token and vary its rate. A transform code exposes each token's measured distortion--rate curve, and a fixed bit budget is distributed across tokens by exact integer rate--distortion optimisation on those curves. No text enters the pipeline, so one compressed representation serves any query. At equal bit budgets, on two datasets and two capacities, it preserves the model's output distribution and its answers better than uniform-rate coding, the closed-form water-fill and distortion-ranked pruning. It matches attention-ranked pruning on the question pruning was tuned for, and overtakes it once the compressed image must answer a different question about the same image.

</details>


### [22] [Multi-Resolution Feature Fusion U-Net for Magnetic Resonance Imaging Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00279)
*Eirini Cholopoulou,Dimitrios E. Diamantis,Dimitris K. Iakovidis*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A novel deep learning architecture MRFFU-Net with Multi-Resolution Feature Fusion (MRFF) module is proposed for MRI segmentation. The MRFF module can be integrated into any U-Net-like architecture to capture both fine-grained details and global contextual information at multiple resolutions, outperforming state-of-the-art models on CSF spinal MR and left atrium cardiac segmentation datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing U-Net and its extensions struggle with preserving fine-grained details and global contextual information in MRI segmentation. This is particularly challenging for MRI data where anatomical structures have irregular boundaries and variations in shape, contrast, and scale.

Method: The proposed MRFFU-Net architecture integrates a novel Multi-Resolution Feature Fusion (MRFF) module into all levels of an encoder-decoder structure, combined with attention mechanisms and skip connections. This enables multi-resolution feature extraction to capture both fine details and global context.

Result: Experimental results on two benchmark MRI datasets (CSF spinal MR segmentation and left atrium cardiac segmentation from MSD challenge) show that MRFFU-Net outperforms state-of-the-art models across multiple evaluation metrics.

Conclusion: The MRFFU-Net architecture effectively addresses the challenge of preserving fine-grained details and global contextual information in MRI segmentation, demonstrating its effectiveness across different anatomical structures.

Abstract: The segmentation of anatomical structures in medical images and particularly in MRI scans, is essential for clinical diagnosis and monitoring disease progression. While Deep Learning (DL) architectures, such as U-Net and its extensions are very effective in medical image segmentation tasks, they often struggle with preserving fine-grained details and global contextual information. This is especially challenging for MRI data segmentation, where anatomical structures are characterized by irregular boundaries and variations in shape, contrast, and scale. To address this challenge, we propose a novel DL architecture for MRI segmentation across different anatomical structures. Specifically, the architecture introduces a module, named Multi-Resolution Feature Fusion (MRFF), that can be easily integrated into any U-Net-like architecture. The MRFF is integrated in all levels of an encode-decoder structure, along with attention mechanisms and skip connections to extract features at multiple resolutions, enabling the model to capture both fine-grained details and global contextual information. We evaluate the MRFFU-Net on two publicly available benchmark MRI datasets of different anatomical targets; one for Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) segmentation in spinal MR scans, and one for left atrium cardiac segmentation, from the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) challenge. Experimental results indicate that MRFFU-Net outperforms state-of-the-art models across multiple evaluation metrics, demonstrating its effectiveness in MRI segmentation.

</details>


### [23] [LENS-GRF: Permutation-Invariant Lesion Evidence Network with Gated Residual Fusion for Acne Severity Grading and Multi-Rater Clinical Oracle Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00294)
*Muhammad Muhtasim Shahriar,M. F. Mridha*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LENS-GRF is an interpretable multi-stage framework for 4-class acne severity grading that combines global Vision Transformer with permutation-invariant Lesion Set Transformer and Gated Residual Fusion. Achieves 95.89% accuracy with ground-truth annotations on ACNE04 but only 35% in zero-shot cross-dataset evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Acne severity grading requires both whole-face context and fine-grained lesion evidence. Existing methods lack interpretability and struggle with cross-domain generalization.

Method: LENS-GRF integrates Adaptive Facial Skin Segmentation, global Vision Transformer prior, Lesion Set Transformer for localized lesion patches with spatial geometry, and Gated Residual Fusion for adaptive local-global combination. Uses YOLOv11s for lesion detection.

Result: On ACNE04: 80.82% accuracy (automated), 95.89% ± 0.59% accuracy with QWK 0.9753 (ground-truth annotations). On PLSBRACNE01 zero-shot: 35.00% vs 42.50% baseline. Oracle analysis showed 47.97% accuracy max with 0.5799 QWK. Data audit found 15 duplicate pairs including 5 with conflicting labels.

Conclusion: High performance on ACNE04 degrades significantly in cross-dataset zero-shot evaluation (35% vs 42.50% baseline), revealing detector domain shift and annotation variability issues. Oracle agreement (49.32-66.22%) highlights cross-criterion mismatch between dermatologists. Ground-truth lesion inputs substantially improve oracle accuracy.

Abstract: Automated acne severity grading requires both whole-face context and fine-grained lesion evidence. We propose LENS-GRF (Lesion Evidence Network with Set-Transformer and Gated Residual Fusion), an interpretable multi-stage framework for four-class acne severity grading. The method combines Adaptive Facial Skin Segmentation and a global Vision Transformer prior with a permutation-invariant Lesion Set Transformer that encodes localized lesion patches and spatial geometry. Gated Residual Fusion adaptively controls the local residual contribution and reduces to the global prediction when the gate is zero. On ACNE04, fully automated LENS-GRF with YOLOv11s achieved 80.82% accuracy; with ground-truth lesion annotations, it achieved 95.89% +/- 0.59% accuracy and a Quadratic Weighted Kappa of 0.9753. A data-integrity audit identified 15 cross-split duplicate image pairs, including five with conflicting severity labels. In locked zero-shot evaluation on the full PLSBRACNE01 cohort (200 subjects, 600 views), automated LENS-GRF achieved 35.00% accuracy versus 42.50% for the global baseline. On the 148-subject common cohort used for three-dermatologist oracle analysis, ground-truth lesion inputs increased the best oracle accuracy to 47.97%, while the highest oracle QWK was 0.5799. Pairwise oracle agreement ranged from 49.32% to 66.22%, highlighting detector domain shift, annotation variability, and cross-criterion mismatch.

</details>


### [24] [Decoding the Disaster: Multi-Task Geospatial Reasoning with Vision-Language Models and Crowdsourced Imagery for Disaster Mapping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00302)
*Wenping Yin,Fabian Desuer,Ziqi Liu,Naixia Mou,Weijia Li,Pedram Ghamisi,Xiao Xiang Zhu,Hao Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes GRDisaster, a multi-task Geospatial Reasoning Disaster mapping framework that leverages vision-language models (VLMs) to understand, geolocalize, and reason over crowdsourced disaster imagery. The framework uses a new benchmark dataset of 26,340 images (PhotoMappers-derived) organized as VGI-SVI-RS) cross-view triplets, combining deterministic and probabilistic cross-view geolocalization with multi-view fusion.
