Method: The proposed VEI method works as an inference pipeline with three components: (1) Video Preview (dense low-resolution frames for global coverage), (2) Video Evidence Indexing (a policy that jointly performs evidence localization and budget planning to select high-resolution frames), and (3) Answer Generation (combines preview and evidence set for VQA). The method uses privileged self-distillation where an answer-aware teacher guides the test-time policy on student-generated indexing traces. A single policy is trained to support previews at 1, 6, 12, and 24 visual tokens per frame.

Result: Video Evidence Indexing improves accuracy under limited visual budgets, and self-distillation further improves both QA accuracy and temporal evidence localization.

Conclusion: The proposed VEI approach effectively addresses the token budget constraint in long-video QA by intelligently selecting relevant moments using low-resolution previews, and the self-distillation mechanism enhances both answer accuracy and evidence localization without requiring frame-level supervision.

Abstract: Long-video question answering is limited by the high cost of visual tokens and by the fixed context width of current VLMs. A long-video question may require broad temporal coverage, but the answer is often supported by only a compact set of moments. To locate these moments efficiently, we propose token-budgeted Video Evidence Indexing (VEI): given a dense low-resolution Video Preview, the model constructs a compact high-resolution Evidence Set for final reasoning. We treat VEI as a policy that must jointly solve \textit{evidence localization}, which finds question-relevant moments, and \textit{budget planning}, which decides where to spend the limited high-resolution frame budget. We implement this idea with an inference pipeline: the Video Preview provides cheap global coverage, Video Evidence Indexing constructs the Evidence Set, and Answer Generation combines both inputs for final VQA. To address missing frame-level supervision, we adopt privileged self-distillation, where an answer-aware teacher guides the normal test-time policy on student-generated indexing traces. We explore previews at 1, 6, 12, and 24 visual tokens per frame, training a single policy that supports all four resolutions. Experiments show that Video Evidence Indexing improves accuracy under limited visual budgets, and self-distillation further improves both QA accuracy and temporal evidence localization.

</details>


### [47] [VTV-FM: Flow Matching through Variational Terminal-Velocity Closure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00785)
*Haoyang Jiang,Yuheng Li,Di Yang,Yanhai Xiong,Haipeng Chen,Yi He*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Flow matching (FM) learns generative transport by fitting continuous-time motion from a simple source distribution to the data distribution. Most existing methods use first-order bridges: once a source and a target sample are paired, the path is a straight motion with constant velocity. FM with optimal transport (OT) improves the pairing, but the bridge itself remains linear, limiting its ability to model curved motion, acceleration, and changing directions. A natural remedy is to use second-order phase-space dynamics; however, learning the bridge requires target-side terminal-velocity information that static datasets do not provide. We propose Variational Terminal-Velocity Flow Matching (VTV-FM), a second-order FM framework that derives the missing velocity by minimizing acceleration energy, yielding a closed-form closure for static data. The same minimum-acceleration variational construction also defines the OT pairing cost and the acceleration targets used for training. Experiments on low-dimensional datasets, PDE-governed physical fields, and CIFAR-10 show that VTV-FM improves transport geometry and generation quality over first-order and high-order FM baselines.

</details>


### [48] [Paying for Too Many Tokens? Valid and Cost-Efficient Multimodal LLM Annotation with Simple Heuristics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00809)
*Zhixi Zhu,Kristina Gligoric*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper systematically evaluates cost-saving heuristics for Vision-Language Model (VLM) video annotation in computational social science tasks. The authors test various frame sampling, video compression, and modality strategies on sentiment and topic classification tasks, assessing accuracy, inference validity, and token costs. They find that accuracy and validity can diverge, text-only models may suffice, and a single 2×8 image grid can achieve near full-video performance at ~15% cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-Language Models enable video annotation at scale but incur high token costs when processing short-form videos (e.g., 60-second videos at 1 fps = millions of tokens). Researchers rely on heuristics (frame sampling, image grids, single modality) to reduce costs, but it's unclear which methods save costs while preserving downstream conclusions. The authors address this gap by systematically evaluating these heuristics.

Method: The authors conducted a systematic evaluation of various cost-saving heuristics using short-form videos on two CSS tasks: sentiment and topic classification. They evaluated each configuration along three axes: (1) classification accuracy, (2) validity of downstream inference, and (3) per-video token cost. They tested different approaches including frame sampling, video compression into image grids, and single vs. multi-modality configurations.

Result: Three key findings: (1) Accuracy and validity diverge—the highest-accuracy configuration can produce wrong conclusions; (2) Modality value is not guaranteed—text alone can yield strong performance, meaning adding modalities can add cost without adding signal; (3) Cost can be decoupled from video length—a single 2×8 image grid using simple shot-transition detection achieves full-video understanding (κ within ~0.05) at ~15% of the token cost.

Conclusion: The authors derive guidelines for cost-aware VLM annotation in CSS. The key insight is that practitioners can significantly reduce token costs (by ~85%) while maintaining inference validity by using simple shot-transition detection to create a 2×8 image grid. The paper emphasizes that accuracy alone is insufficient—downstream inference validity must also be considered when selecting annotation strategies.

Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable video annotation at scale, but costs accumulate quickly: processing a typical 60-second short-form video at one frame per second requires millions of tokens. To reduce costs, researchers rely on heuristics such as sampling a subset of frames, compressing videos into image grids, or using only a single modality. However, it remains unclear which heuristics save cost, and whether they preserve the downstream conclusions these annotations enable. To address this gap, we conduct a systematic evaluation of these heuristics using short-form videos, on two computational social science (CSS) tasks: sentiment and topic classification. We evaluate each configuration along three axes the literature typically treats separately: classification accuracy, validity of downstream inference, and per-video token cost. First, we find that accuracy and validity diverge: the highest-accuracy configuration can produce wrong conclusions. Second, modality value is not guaranteed: text alone can yield strong performance, indicating that adding modalities can add cost without adding signal. Finally, we find that cost can be decoupled from video length when annotating short-form videos: a single $2\times8$ image grid built via simple shot-transition detection approaches full-video understanding ($κ$ within~.05), at $\sim 15\%$ of the token cost. Based on these findings, we derive guidelines that can enable cost-aware VLM annotation in CSS.

</details>


### [49] [Video Generation Models: A Survey of Post-Training and Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00812)
*Chaoyu Li,Xiaoyi Gu,Yogesh Kulkarni,Eun Woo Im,Mohammadmahdi Honarmand,Zeyu Wang,Juntong Song,Fei Du,Xilin Jiang,Kexin Zheng,Tianzhi Li,Fei Tao,Pooyan Fazli*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This survey provides the first comprehensive review of post-training and alignment techniques for video generation models, organizing approaches into four categories: supervised fine-tuning, self-training/distillation, preference/reward-based methods, and inference-time methods. It addresses unique challenges in video alignment including temporal consistency, motion-appearance coupling, and scalable reward design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While video generation has advanced in resolution and duration, pretrained models struggle with human intent following, temporal coherence, and physical/safety constraints. Video alignment faces unique challenges (error accumulation, motion-appearance coupling, limited temporal supervision) that differ from image/text generation, motivating systematic post-training strategies.

Method: The survey frames post-training as a unifying framework and distinguishes between implicit and explicit alignment based on how alignment signals are enforced. Approaches are organized into four categories: (1) supervised fine-tuning methods, (2) self-training and distillation methods, (3) preference- and reward-based methods, and (4) inference-time methods.

Result: The survey presents a coherent taxonomy of alignment approaches, reviews datasets/benchmarks/evaluation practices, and identifies open challenges including scalable reward design, long-horizon temporal consistency, stability-expressiveness trade-offs, and safety-aware generation.

Conclusion: This survey provides a structured conceptual foundation and practical guidance for advancing controllable and reliable video generation models through post-training and alignment techniques.

Abstract: Video generation has rapidly progressed from short, low-quality clips to high-resolution, long-duration sequences with complex spatiotemporal dynamics. Despite strong generative priors learned through large-scale pretraining, pretrained video models often fail to reliably follow human intent, maintain temporal coherence, or satisfy physical and safety constraints. Compared with image and text generation, alignment in video generation presents unique challenges, including error accumulation over time, motion-appearance coupling, multi-objective trade-offs, and limited supervision for temporal properties. These challenges motivate systematic post-training strategies that adapt pretrained models without retraining them from scratch. In this survey, we present the first comprehensive review of post-training and alignment in video generation models. We frame post-training as a unifying framework and distinguish between implicit alignment and explicit alignment based on how alignment signals are enforced. From this perspective, we organize existing approaches into four broad categories: supervised fine-tuning methods, self-training and distillation methods, preference- and reward-based methods, and inference-time methods. This taxonomy provides a coherent view of how alignment signals shape model behavior across both training and deployment. Beyond methodological advances, we review commonly used datasets, benchmarks, and evaluation practices, and discuss open challenges such as scalable reward design, long-horizon temporal consistency, stability-expressiveness trade-offs, and safety-aware generation. This survey aims to provide a structured conceptual foundation and practical guidance for advancing controllable and reliable video generation models.

</details>


### [50] [Align Then Reason: A Multimodal Lip-Sync Judge for Dubbing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00825)
*Rui Liu,Bhavin Jawade,Haoqi Li,Shivam Mehta,Karan Saxena,Yinghong Lan,Cameron R. Wolfe*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ATR (Align Then Reason) is a multilingual lip-sync judge for dubbing quality control that uses only silent video and text to determine if candidate text matches speaker's lip motion in content and timing. It first establishes monotonic alignment between frame-level lip representations and phonetic units, then uses an LLM to reason over this alignment for final judgment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing visual speech recognizers and video-language models are poorly suited for dubbing quality control: even when fine-tuned to recover spoken content from lip motion, they remain largely insensitive to temporal errors. Dubbing requires a reference-free judge that can assess both content match and timing alignment using only silent video and text.

Method: ATR uses a two-stage approach: (1) Alignment stage establishes monotonic alignment between frame-level lip representations and phonetic units of candidate text, providing local evidence for each phonetic unit plus a calibrated global alignment score; (2) Reasoning stage feeds this alignment information to an LLM enabling it to reason jointly about content and timing for final judgment.

Result: On a seven-language benchmark, ATR improves mean AUC over Qwen3.5 SFT baselines by 59.4%, 50.2%, and 50.8% with 2B, 4B, and 9B reasoners. Gains generalize across LLM families (45.9% for LLaMA-3.1-8B, 46.6% for Mistral-7B) and transfer to three unseen MuAViC languages. On downstream tasks: dub-line reranking achieves 52.0% improvement over best lip-reading baseline; script-to-clip assignment achieves 17.7% improvement.

Conclusion: ATR successfully addresses the temporal sensitivity gap in visual speech recognition for dubbing quality control. By explicitly aligning lip representations with phonetic units before reasoning, the method achieves substantial improvements across multiple languages, LLM families, and downstream tasks, demonstrating strong generalization to unseen languages and real-world dubbing scenarios.

Abstract: Dubbing quality control requires a reference-free judge that can determine whether a candidate text line matches a speaker's visible articulation in both content and timing, using only silent video and text because dubbed audio may not yet exist. Existing visual speech recognizers and video-language models are poorly suited to this setting: even when fine-tuned to recover spoken content from lip motion, they remain largely insensitive to temporal errors. We introduce $\textit{Align Then Reason}$ (ATR), a multilingual lip-sync judge that first establishes a monotonic alignment between frame-level lip representations and the phonetic units of the candidate line, then reasons over this alignment to make the final judgment. An alignment scorer provides the LLM with both local evidence for each phonetic unit and a calibrated global alignment score, enabling it to reason jointly about content and timing. On a seven-language benchmark, our method improves mean AUC over the corresponding Qwen3.5 SFT baselines by 59.4%, 50.2%, and 50.8% with 2B, 4B, and 9B reasoners, respectively. The gains generalize across LLM families, reaching mean AUC improvements of 45.9% and 46.6% over the best baseline for LLaMA-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, respectively. They also transfer across datasets to three unseen MuAViC languages. Furthermore, we evaluate on two downstream tasks built from real dubbing lines. On dub-line reranking, ATR-9B outperforms the best lip-reading baseline by 52.0%, while on script-to-clip assignment, ATR-9B improves over the best lip-reading baseline by 17.7%.

</details>


### [51] [Geometric Similarity in VLM Low-Level Vision Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00848)
*Shao-Jun Xia,Huixin Zhang,Zhen Lei,Anlan Sun,Yuner Zhang,Xiaoyang Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: GeoSim is a unified four-level framework for analyzing how vision-language models (VLMs) organize hidden-layer representations across 24 low-level tasks spanning 5 categories. It examines both autoregressive models and diffusion transformers to understand their geometric organization for pixel-level perception and latent transferability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The field lacks understanding of how VLMs organize hidden-layer representations and whether structurally distinct paradigms (AR models vs DiTs) share a common geometric organization for pixel-level perception. This shared organization is crucial for building transferable, unified restoration VLMs and adapters.

Method: The authors propose GeoSim, a four-level framework that analyzes task-conditioned representations from: (1) global similarity, (2) local geometry, (3) sparse feature decomposition, and (4) topological verification perspectives. The framework applies to hidden states in AR models and feature maps in DiTs across same- and cross-task/model settings.

Result: The study reveals organizing principles of low-level visual representations while exposing their limits in cross-task and cross-model agreement across 24 low-level tasks spanning 5 categories.

Conclusion: GeoSim provides an interpretability lens for probing latent transferability in low-level vision and diagnosing model limitations in task- or model-specific scenarios, serving as a foundation for building unified restoration VLMs.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as powerful candidates for universal vision backbones, with representative architectures including autoregressive (AR) models and diffusion transformers (DiTs). Yet, adapting them efficiently for all-in-one low-level image restoration remains a challenge. Crucially, the field lacks an understanding of how VLMs organize hidden-layer representations and whether these structurally distinct paradigms share a common geometric organization for pixel-level perception. Such shared organization is a prerequisite for building highly transferable, unified restoration VLMs and adapters. In this paper, we systematically investigate representational similarity across 24 low-level tasks spanning 5 categories. We propose GeoSim, a unified four-level framework that analyzes task-conditioned representations from global similarity, local geometry, sparse feature decomposition, and topological verification perspectives. Our formulation applies to the analysis of hidden states in AR models and feature maps in DiTs across same- and cross-task/model settings. Our results reveal the organizing principles of low-level visual representations while exposing their limits in cross-task and cross-model agreement. Ultimately, GeoSim provides an interpretability lens for probing latent transferability in low-level vision and diagnosing model limitations in task- or model-specific scenarios.

</details>


### [52] [SmoothOperator: Enhancing Representations for Fine-grained Open-set Recognition via Modulated Label Smoothing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00851)
*Thiru Thillai Nadarasar Bahavan,Yu Xia,Sachith Seneviratne,Saman Halgamuge*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses Open Set Recognition (OSR), where models must classify known classes while rejecting unknown classes. The authors identify that label smoothing in spherical representation learning applies a fixed coefficient to all samples, and propose SmoothOperator (SmoothOP), which dynamically sets the smoothing coefficient based on each sample's "prominence" - an embedding-space measure of how well a sample's class stands out against competing classes. This plug-in method integrates with existing spherical representation learning methods with minimal overhead, achieving up to 4.7% improvement on the Semantic Shift Benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open Set Recognition aims to enable models to reject samples from unseen classes while accurately classifying known classes. A key challenge is the inability to model the unbounded distribution of unknown classes during training. Recent spherical representation learning methods have shown strong results, with label smoothing identified as a key driver of success. However, label smoothing applies the same coefficient to every training sample regardless of how well each sample is already embedded, which is suboptimal.

Method: The authors first analyze spherical representation learning objectives used in OSR and show they share a single alignment-uniformity structure where labels enter only through the alignment term. Label smoothing acts as an alignment dial, and a fixed coefficient sets this dial to the same value for every sample. They propose SmoothOperator (SmoothOP), a plug-in method that sets the smoothing coefficient of each sample from its "prominence" - an embedding-space signal measuring how clearly the sample's own class stands out against its strongest competing class. SmoothOP assigns strong smoothing to samples with high prominence (reducing their alignment and relaxing their pull), while weak smoothing to low-prominence samples. The method integrates into four existing spherical representation learning methods at minimal training overhead.

Result: On the Semantic Shift Benchmark, SmoothOP-augmented variants generally outperform their base objectives across datasets, degrees of semantic shift, and OSR post-processors, with gains of up to 4.7% in AUROC, OSCR, and closed-set accuracy.

Conclusion: The proposed SmoothOP provides a simple yet effective way to adapt label smoothing per-sample based on embedding-space characteristics. By using "prominence" to dynamically adjust the smoothing coefficient, the method achieves consistent improvements across various settings without major architectural changes, demonstrating the importance of sample-specific treatment in spherical representation learning for OSR.

Abstract: Open Set Recognition (OSR) aims to enable models to accurately classify known classes while rejecting samples from unseen classes. A key challenge in OSR lies in the inability to model the unbounded distribution of unknown classes during training, often leading to the misclassification of samples from these classes. Rather than modeling unknowns, recent work shapes the feature space so that known classes are compact and well separated, and spherical representation learning methods have achieved strong results this way. Label smoothing has been identified as one of the key drivers of this success, yet it applies the same coefficient to every training sample, regardless of how well each sample is already embedded. We show that the spherical representation learning objectives used in OSR share a single alignment--uniformity structure in which labels enter only through the alignment term. Label smoothing therefore acts as an alignment dial, and a fixed coefficient sets this dial to the same value for every sample. We propose a plug-in, SmoothOperator (SmoothOP), which sets the smoothing coefficient of each sample from its \textbf{prominence}, an embedding-space signal measuring how clearly the sample's own class stands out against its strongest competing class. Our method integrates into four existing spherical representation learning methods at minimal training overhead. SmoothOP assigns strong smoothing to samples with high prominence, which reduces their alignment and relaxes their pull. On the Semantic Shift Benchmark, SmoothOP-augmented variants generally outperform their base objectives across datasets, degrees of semantic shift, and OSR post-processors, with gains of up to 4.7\% in AUROC, OSCR, and closed-set accuracy.

</details>


### [53] [Lang3DSeg: Annotation-Free Open-Vocabulary 3D Segmentation with Point Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00855)
*Cigdem Kokenoz,Amir Salarpour,Alkim Domeke,Christopher Salas,Pedram MohajerAnsari,Long Cheng,Mert D. Pesé,Bing Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Lang3DSeg is a point transformer-based method for open-vocabulary 3D LiDAR semantic segmentation that achieves state-of-the-art results (52.8% mIoU on nuScenes, 41.4% on SemanticKITTI) among annotation-free methods by addressing depth ambiguity in 2D-to-3D label projection through class-priority masking and depth gap truncation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Supervised LiDAR segmentation requires costly manual annotation and is limited to closed taxonomies. Existing open-vocabulary methods rely on voxel-based sparse convolutions, while point transformers have been limited to indoor environments with dense 3D data.

Method: Lang3DSeg uses a point transformer as the backbone for outdoor LiDAR segmentation, trained from scratch without geometric pre-training. It addresses 2D-to-3D projection noise (depth ambiguity) through: (1) class-priority rule for composite mask generation, and (2) truncating each projected instance at the first gap in its depth distribution.

Result: Achieves 52.8% mIoU on nuScenes validation and 41.4% on SemanticKITTI, the highest among published annotation-free methods. Inference runs in real-time on single LiDAR sweeps without requiring vision-language models at runtime.

Conclusion: Point transformers can serve as effective backbones for outdoor LiDAR open-vocabulary segmentation. The proposed depth ambiguity correction methods (class-priority rule and depth gap truncation) significantly improve projection quality. The system achieves competitive performance without any manual annotation while enabling real-time inference.

Abstract: Accurate 3D semantic perception is critical for safe autonomous navigation. However, supervised LiDAR segmentation remains tied to closed taxonomies and to the cost of point-wise manual annotation. Open-vocabulary methods avoid that cost by projecting the output of 2D vision-language models onto LiDAR and distilling it into a 3D network. These methods rely almost exclusively on voxel-based sparse convolutions, and point transformers have so far been limited to indoor environments, where 3D data is dense and bounded. We present Lang3DSeg, which establishes a point transformer as the backbone for annotation-free open-vocabulary segmentation of outdoor 3D LiDAR, and is trained from scratch without geometric pre-training. This training paradigm necessitates addressing the inherent noise in 2D-to-3D label projections; specifically, naive projection often suffers from depth ambiguity, where points behind an object are erroneously assigned its semantic label. We therefore composite masks using an explicit class-priority rule and truncate each projected instance at the first gap in its depth distribution, correcting the projection error directly rather than averaging it over registered sequences. Lang3DSeg achieves 52.8% mIoU on nuScenes validation and 41.4% on SemanticKITTI, the highest among published annotation-free methods on both benchmarks. Every 3D semantic segmentation is on a single LiDAR sweep, and inference operates in real-time without running vision-language models.

</details>


### [54] [CtrlWAM: Controllable World Action Models with Aligned Intent and Foresight](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00859)
*Chensheng Peng,Wenhao Ding,Ran Tian,Zewei Zhou,Jef Packer,Maximilian Igl,Peter Karkus,Yan Wang,Masayoshi Tomizuka,Boris Ivanovic,Marco Pavone,Yuxiao Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CtrlWAM addresses a fundamental mismatch in World Action Model training where perturbed actions should produce counterfactual visual futures, but standard training keeps noised video tied to ground truth. The method executes perturbed actions in a simulator and pairs them with noised visual consequences, using warped video-action noise schedules to maintain visual layout responsiveness as action predictions evolve.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard WAM training adds noise to actions and video simultaneously, but this creates a mismatch: perturbed actions imply counterfactual future visual while noised video remains tied to GT recording. In low-noise regimes, scene geometry and dynamic behavior remain visible from noisy future frames despite added noise, reducing model controllability.

Method: 1) Execute perturbed actions in a simulator and pair them with their noised visual consequences for joint WAM learning. 2) Introduce warped video-action noise schedules that keep visual layout responsive as action predictions evolve. 3) Extend action interface from ego-only control to variable number of agent streams for unified multi-agent future prediction.

Result: Driving experiments: more accurate action forecasts, closer agreement between generated video and actions, better command following. Robotics experiments: stronger motion fidelity and controllability. Matched controls support benefit of off-path renders for command following and manipulation fidelity.

Conclusion: CtrlWAM provides a more controllable world action model by addressing the noise mismatch problem, enabling accurate action forecasting, better video-action alignment, and multi-agent prediction through simulation-based training with adapted noise schedules.

Abstract: World action models (WAMs) jointly predict actions (intent) and visual future (foresight). Standard training adds noise to recorded actions and video simultaneously, but such training paradigms introduce a mismatch: perturbed actions imply counterfactual future visual, while the noised video remains tied to the GT recording. In low-noise regime, the scene geometry and even the dynamic behavior remain clearly visible from the noisy future frames despite the added noise. We present CtrlWAM, which executes perturbed actions in a simulator and pairs them with their noised visual consequences for joint WAM learning. To accommodate the different denoising requirements of video and actions, we introduce warped video--action noise schedules that aim to keep visual layout responsive as action predictions evolve. We further extend the action interface from ego-only control to a variable number of agent streams, allowing a unified model to represent predicted or commanded futures for multiple agents. Driving experiments show more accurate action forecasts, closer agreement between generated video and actions, and better following of supplied commands; robotics experiments show stronger motion fidelity and controllability. Matched controls support the benefit of off-path renders for command following and manipulation fidelity. Together, these findings contribute to a more controllable world action model. Project page: https://ctrl-wam.github.io/

</details>


### [55] [Machine Translation for Sign Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00881)
*Ozge Mercanoglu Sincan,Anton Pelykh,Edward Fish,Harry Walsh,JianHe Low,Karahan Sahin,Oline Ranum,Sobhan Asasi,Steven Emery,Richard Bowden*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A comprehensive review of sign language machine translation, covering the evolution from isolated sign recognition to end-to-end translation systems, technical advances in pose estimation and transformers, and ongoing challenges in datasets, evaluation metrics, and linguistic structure capture. Emphasizes ethical considerations and the need for interdisciplinary collaboration with deaf communities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sign language machine translation has made substantial progress but faces unique challenges: limited datasets compared to spoken languages, inadequate evaluation metrics, and the need to capture the simultaneous, multi-layered, and three-dimensional structure of sign languages. The field requires balancing technical advances with stakeholder considerations.

Method: Comprehensive review drawing on interdisciplinary perspectives spanning computer vision, sign language linguistics, and deaf studies. The authors examine linguistic properties that make sign languages computationally unique, trace the evolution of recognition, translation, and production systems, and analyze technical challenges while addressing ethical considerations around data governance, community involvement, and appropriate use.

Result: The review identifies key advances in pose estimation, transformer architectures, and large-scale dataset collection. It highlights ongoing challenges including limited datasets, inadequate evaluation metrics, and the complexity of modeling sign language structure. The analysis emphasizes the importance of ethical considerations and sustained collaboration across computer vision, sign language linguistics, deaf studies, and with deaf communities.

Conclusion: Continued progress in sign language machine translation requires sustained collaboration across multiple disciplines (computer vision, sign language linguistics, deaf studies) and with deaf communities. The field must balance technical advancement with ethical considerations including data governance and community involvement.

Abstract: Sign language machine translation has progressed substantially over the past decade, evolving from isolated sign recognition to end-to-end translation systems. Advances in pose estimation, transformer architectures, and large-scale dataset collection have driven progress, yet challenges remain. Datasets are limited compared to spoken-language resources; evaluation metrics inadequately capture the linguistic quality of output; and models must capture the simultaneous, multi-layered, and three-dimensional structure of sign languages. This manuscript provides a comprehensive review that seeks to balance technical challenges with stakeholder considerations. We examine the linguistic properties that make sign languages computationally unique, trace the evolution of recognition, translation, and production systems, and analyze ongoing technical challenges. Crucially, we address ethical considerations around data governance, community involvement, and appropriate use. Drawing on interdisciplinary perspectives spanning computer vision, sign language linguistics, and deaf studies, our analysis emphasizes that continued progress requires sustained collaboration across these fields and with deaf communities.

</details>


### [56] [EyeTAG: Eye Trajectory-Aware Gaze Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00922)
*Jungmin Lee,Niamat Ullah,Yoseob Han*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: EyeTAG proposes a causal multi-frame gaze estimation framework that uses an explicit first-order gaze prior by differentiating recent predictions to create a kinematic token representing gaze trajectory. This token is subject-invariant and helps reduce jitter and improve accuracy in gaze estimation under natural head-eye motion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-frame gaze estimation methods suffer from output jitter due to independent frame processing. Multi-frame methods reduce jitter but learn motion implicitly within appearance features, never treating gaze trajectory as an explicit variable. There was a need for a method that explicitly models gaze motion dynamics.

Method: EyeTAG is built around an explicit first-order gaze prior. At each time step, it differentiates its own recent predictions and feeds the resulting trajectory back as a compact kinematic token. This differencing is translation-invariant in gaze space, making the token subject-invariant (carrying motion rather than personal gaze offsets). Visual evidence comes from face and eye streams fused via cross-attention and a causal Transformer decoder.

Result: EyeTAG reduces mean angular error by about 1.0° on Gaze360 dataset and performs on par with the strongest baseline on EVE (2.56° vs. 2.58°). Ablations show that the differential formulation removes systematic saccade bias that persists even with an absolute gaze-history prior.

Conclusion: The explicit differential gaze prior in EyeTAG effectively addresses jitter and saccade bias problems in gaze estimation. The translation-invariant kinematic token provides subject-invariant motion information, leading to improved accuracy across datasets.

Abstract: Gaze estimation under natural head-eye motion underpins applications from driver monitoring to human-computer interaction. Single-frame methods predict each frame independently, so consecutive outputs fluctuate as jitter. Multi-frame methods reduce this, but they learn motion implicitly inside appearance features, so the gaze trajectory is never an explicit variable. We propose EyeTAG (Eye Trajectory-Aware Gaze Estimation), a causal multi-frame framework built around an explicit first-order gaze prior: at each step it differentiates its own recent predictions and feeds the resulting trajectory back as a compact kinematic token. Because differencing is translation-invariant in gaze space, this token carries subject-invariant motion rather than personal gaze offsets. Face and eye streams supply visual evidence, fused by cross-attention and a causal Transformer decoder. EyeTAG reduces the mean angular error by about 1.0$^\circ$ on Gaze360 and performs on par with the strongest baseline on EVE (2.56$^\circ$ vs. 2.58$^\circ$). Within-model ablations, which keep the encoder and the rest of the architecture fixed and vary only the gaze history, show that the differential formulation, rather than temporal context alone, removes the systematic saccade bias that persists even with an absolute gaze-history prior. Our code is available at https://github.com/peter8366/EyeTAG.

</details>


### [57] [Joint Branch-Space Transform Coding for Diffusion Activation Quantization with Classifier-Free Guidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00930)
*Mingrun Jiang,Yuejia Liu,Zishan Shao,Ting Jiang,Qinsi Wang,Hancheng Ye,Yixiao Wang,Rui-Feng Wang,Kangning Cui,Yixuan Chen,Fan Yang,Xiang Cheng,Hai Li,Yiran Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses post-training quantization (PTQ) for diffusion models with Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG). The authors identify that existing methods don't exploit cross-activation structure between conditional and unconditional branches. They propose branch-space transform coding, which rotates matched CFG branches using a 2x2 orthogonal matrix, and further develop GCBT (Guidance-Correlation Branch Transform) that jointly incorporates CFG guidance direction and cross-branch second moments. The method achieves statistically significant fidelity gains while leaving the host quantization pipeline unchanged.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current diffusion PTQ methods treat conditional and unconditional activations independently, leaving cross-activation structure unexploited. The authors discovered that matched CFG activations form a strongly correlated 2D source, and the choice of branch coding basis materially affects quantization fidelity under a fixed bit budget.

Method: The authors propose branch-space transform coding, which rotates matched CFG branches via an offline-derived 2x2 orthogonal matrix. They further derive GCBT, which jointly incorporates the CFG guidance direction and cross-branch second moments. GCBT admits a closed-form per-layer solution without gradient optimization or angle search under an equal-rate quantization-noise surrogate.

Result: Applied on top of existing diffusion PTQ methods, GCBT yields statistically significant fidelity gains in most evaluated comparisons with no statistically significant degradation, while leaving the underlying host quantization pipeline unchanged.

Conclusion: The cross-activation structure between conditional and unconditional branches in CFG can be exploited through branch-space transform coding to improve quantization fidelity. GCBT provides a practical solution with closed-form optimization, achieving consistent improvements without modifying the host quantization pipeline.

Abstract: Post-training quantization for diffusion models increasingly exploits timestep, feature, and layer structure. While recent work has begun incorporating CFG structure into diffusion quantization, activation quantization still operates independently across conditional and unconditional coordinates, leaving cross-activation structure unexploited. We show that matched CFG activations form a strongly correlated two-dimensional source and that, under a fixed bit budget, the choice of branch coding basis materially affects quantization fidelity. Motivated by this observation, we introduce branch-space transform coding, which rotates matched CFG branches via an offline derived 2x2 orthogonal matrix, requiring minimal modifications to model parameters or the quantization pipeline. We further derive the Guidance-Correlation Branch Transform (GCBT), which jointly incorporates the CFG guidance direction and cross-branch second moments. Under an equal-rate quantization-noise surrogate, GCBT admits a closed-form per-layer solution without gradient optimization or angle search. Applied on top of existing diffusion PTQ methods, GCBT yields statistically significant fidelity gains in most evaluated comparisons with no statistically significant degradation, while leaving the underlying host quantization pipeline unchanged.

</details>


### [58] [A Matched-Budget Audit Framework for Recaptioned Image-Text Supervision Distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00952)
*Giyeong Oh,Junghun Park,Yuhan Bae,Youngjae Yu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces a matched-budget audit framework for evaluating recaptioned image-text corpora used in text-to-image (T2I) training. The framework profiles supervision distributions across five axes at a fixed text budget (B=64), using controllable basic units (CBU) as the common claim unit. Experiments across seven paired comparisons on five public corpora reveal significant improvements (+3.39 to +6.36 CBU per caption) in cross-corpus pairs and identify a long-vs-dense frontier on CC12M.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current methods for auditing recaptioned corpora rely on length-correlated proxies that miss caption-register artifacts, and downstream T2I benchmarks entangle corpus evaluation with training choices, making it difficult to assess supervision distributions at corpus scale.

Method: The authors propose a reusable matched-budget audit framework that reports a five-axis profile (prompt-side coverage, image-conditioned faithfulness, caption-surface health) at a fixed text budget of B=64 tokens. They instantiate this framework on seven paired comparisons across five public source corpora, using Qwen and Gemma as judges.

Result: Across four cross-corpus pairs, the released surface raises supported CBU per caption by +3.39 to +6.36 under both Qwen and Gemma judges. On CC12M, the framework exposes a long-vs-dense frontier consistent across both judges and four budgets. The audited multi-source recap corpus (~490M) and audit-artifact bundle are released.

Conclusion: The proposed audit framework enables systematic evaluation of recaptioned supervision distributions, revealing that denser captions with proper register improve CBU support. The framework provides a reusable tool for corpus-scale auditing of text-to-image training data.

Abstract: Recaptioned image-text corpora are now standard for text-to-image (T2I) training, with vision--language model (VLM) captioners replacing sparse alt-text by dense descriptions. A recaptioned corpus is a supervision distribution induced by a documented captioning policy ($π$), captioner ($V_c$), and source corpus ($C$). Length-correlated proxies miss caption-register artifacts and downstream T2I benchmarks entangle the corpus with training choices, so this distribution is hard to audit at corpus scale. We introduce a reusable matched-budget audit framework for recaptioned supervision distributions $D_{π,V_c,C}$: at a fixed text budget of $B = 64$ it reports a five-axis profile spanning prompt-side coverage, image-conditioned faithfulness, and caption-surface health, with claimed controllable basic units (CBU) as the common claim unit. We instantiate the framework on seven paired comparisons over five public source corpora. Across the four cross-corpus pairs, the released surface raises supported CBU per caption by $+3.39$ to $+6.36$ under both Qwen and Gemma Judges, and on CC12M the same framework exposes a long-vs-dense frontier that is consistent across both judges and four budgets. We release the audited multi-source recap corpus ($\approx$ 490M) together with the audit-artifact bundle.

</details>


### [59] [Two Clocks in Diffusion MLLMs: When Answers Stabilize Before Rationales Unfold](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00953)
*Keuntae Kim,Yong Suk Choi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates the temporal dynamics between answer stabilization and rationale generation in masked diffusion Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). The key finding is that answer candidates often stabilize before the rationale is fully generated, with 89.4-98.1% of the rationale-side canvas remaining unwritten at stabilization in single-block EOS-suppressed conditions. The study examines how block length, EOS prompting, and visual inputs affect this timing and overall accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses a fundamental issue in masked diffusion MLLMs: when exactly does an answer "stabilize" relative to when its supporting rationale is generated? Understanding this temporal relationship is crucial for improving model performance and understanding the generation process in these increasingly important multimodal models.

Method: The researchers conducted experiments across three visual question-answering benchmarks using LaViDa and Nemotron models. They compared: (1) single-block vs. varying block lengths (128 to 8), (2) EOS-suppressed vs. EOS-enabled prompting, and (3) matched-canvas image ablations to separate visual sensitivity from answer stabilization. They decomposed changes into coverage (whether the answer appears) and conditional accuracy (accuracy given the answer appears).

Result: Key findings include: (1) 89.4-98.1% of rationale canvas remains unwritten at stabilization in single-block EOS-suppressed runs; (2) reducing block length from 128 to 8 changes this fraction from 89.4% to 1.7%; (3) EOS-enabled prompting improves Nemotron's accuracy by 15.0 and 19.5 percentage points on M3CoT and ScienceQA but reduces LaViDa/V*Bench accuracy by 11.0 points; (4) coverage changes consistently dominate over conditional accuracy changes in explaining prompting differences.

Conclusion: The study successfully distinguishes three key metrics: answer stabilization, rationale unfolding, and visual sensitivity. Coverage is identified as the dominant component driving prompting differences, rather than conditional accuracy. These measurements provide a framework for understanding and improving the generation process in masked diffusion MLLMs.

Abstract: An answer candidate in a masked diffusion MLLM can stabilize while its rationale is still unfolding. We distinguish retrospective stabilization of the logged candidate from token commitment, and examine these two clocks relative to rationale generation. Analyzing our results across three visual question-answering benchmarks, we find that 89.4-98.1% of the rationale-side canvas remains unwritten at stabilization in single-block, EOS-suppressed LaViDa runs. On V*Bench, reducing block length from 128 to 8 changes this fraction from 89.4% to 1.7%, together with answer coverage and the eligible observation window. Under EOS-enabled prompting, direct instructions improve Nemotron's overall accuracy by 15.0 and 19.5 percentage points on M3CoT and ScienceQA, but reduce LaViDa/V*Bench accuracy by 11.0 points. A symmetric decomposition associates the larger absolute component of each change with coverage rather than conditional accuracy. Matched-canvas image ablations measure visual sensitivity alongside answer stabilization, separating the two temporal readouts. Together, these measurements distinguish answer stabilization, rationale unfolding, and visual sensitivity, and identify coverage as the larger component of the prompting differences.

</details>


### [60] [Video-Index: A Curated Meta-Benchmark for Video Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00960)
*Enxin Song,Yinuo Xu,Shusheng Yang,Wenhao Chai,Jiatao Gu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces the "attack pyramid" framework to audit 115 video benchmarks for shortcut vulnerabilities, revealing that models can achieve high accuracy without actually viewing video frames. The authors release Video-Index, a curated dataset of 840 verified difficult items across 4 capability groups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Video benchmarks claim to measure video understanding capabilities, but models can exploit shortcuts in answer options, question text, or partial visual evidence rather than true video comprehension. The authors aim to systematically audit these vulnerabilities.

Method: The authors propose an "attack pyramid" with five levels of increasing access to benchmark items: (1) never seeing frames, (2) seeing answer options only, (3) seeing question text only, (4) seeing partial visual evidence, and (5) full access. They audit 115 video benchmarks, screen 505,518 QA pairs, and use agents to turn evaluation requests into specifications with a red-team gate for reproducible benchmarks.

Result: On 35 benchmarks, attackers that never see frames approach full-video accuracy. On 51 benchmarks with temporal probes, shuffled frames retain 96% median accuracy. Near-duplicate questions comprise at least half of items in 63 benchmarks. Claude Opus 5 outperforms all open-source models by over 37 percentage points, with agent tools adding ~20 percentage points, but all systems still have room for improvement.

Conclusion: Current video benchmarks have significant shortcut vulnerabilities where models can achieve high accuracy without genuine video understanding. The released Video-Index dataset (210 hardest items in each of 4 capability groups, 840 items from 76 sources) provides a more robust evaluation benchmark, though even the best systems show substantial room for improvement in efficiency and accuracy.

Abstract: A video benchmark should reward the capability it claims to measure, yet models can exploit answer options, question text, or partial visual evidence. We introduce the attack pyramid, five levels of shortcut attacks with increasing access to each item, and audit 115 video benchmarks with it. On 35 benchmarks, attackers that never see a frame approach full-video accuracy. On 51 benchmarks with temporal probes, shuffled frames keep a median 96% of full-video accuracy. Near-duplicate questions make up at least half the items in 63 benchmarks. We screen 505,518 question-answer pairs from 112 of them into an audited pool. Agents turn evaluation requests into specifications, and a deterministic selector with a red-team gate composes reproducible benchmarks. We release Video-Index, the 210 hardest verified items under these attacks in each of four capability groups, 840 items from 76 sources. With the same fixed input, Claude Opus 5 outscores every open-source model by over 37 percentage points, and agent tools add about 20 more, yet all systems leave room to improve efficiency and accuracy. Blog: https://www.enxinsong.com/blog/video-index/ GitHub: https://github.com/Espere-1119-Song/Video-Index Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Video-Index/Video-Index

</details>


### [61] [RelationVGGT: Visual Geometry Transformers for 3D Spatial Relation Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00970)
*Minsu Kim,Jaesung Choe,Jiwoo Lee,Yu-Chiang Frank Wang,Seon Joo Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces RelationVGGT, a novel feed-forward framework for 3D spatial relation segmentation that segments target objects given a visual subject and textual relational query without requiring category names, per-scene optimization, or known camera poses. The method combines semantic features from visual foundation models with geometry-aware representations from 3D geometry foundation models, using a relation transformer for cross-view prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing 3D reconstruction and semantic scene understanding methods remain confined to object-centric perception, neglecting spatial relations between objects. The authors aim to move beyond this limitation by formulating a new task that understands spatial relationships between objects in a feed-forward, pose-free multi-view setting.

Method: RelationVGGT integrates: (1) semantic features from a visual foundation model, (2) geometry-aware representations from a 3D geometry foundation model, and (3) a relation transformer for subject-conditioned, cross-view relation prediction. The approach requires neither per-scene optimization nor known camera poses. Additionally, an automated annotation pipeline was built using ScanNet++ with VLMs and LLMs for scalable training data generation.

Result: The paper proposes a new task formulation and framework for spatial relation segmentation in 3D scenes. The method achieves cross-view relation prediction without requiring category names, per-scene optimization, or known camera poses.

Conclusion: This work bridges the gap between object-centric perception and spatial relation understanding in 3D scenes by proposing a novel feed-forward framework that leverages both visual and geometric foundation models. The automated annotation pipeline enables scalable training data generation for this new task.

Abstract: Recent advances in 3D reconstruction have progressed from per-scene optimization to feed-forward inference, and semantic scene understanding has followed suit -- yet existing methods remain confined to object-centric perception, neglecting spatial relations between objects. We formulate 3D spatial relation segmentation in a feed-forward, pose-free multi-view setting: given a visually specified subject and a relational text query, the model segments the target across views without receiving its category name. To this end, we propose RelationVGGT, a novel feed-forward framework that integrates semantic features from a visual foundation model with geometry-aware representations from a 3D geometry foundation model and leverages a relation transformer for subject-conditioned, cross-view relation prediction -- requiring neither per-scene optimization nor known camera poses. We additionally provide a fully automated annotation pipeline built on ScanNet++ with VLMs and LLMs, enabling scalable training data generation for this new task.

</details>


### [62] [Concept Driven Domain Adaptation: Finding an Abstract Needle in a Haystack](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00973)
*Haiming Zhao,Tai Wang,Kun Zhang,Xicheng Peng,Zhiyang Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses concept-to-example video retrieval, where science teachers search for documentary clips by querying abstract scientific concepts rather than observable visual events. The authors propose Concept-Driven Domain Adaptation (CDDA), a three-stage framework that adapts two-tower vision-language models to bridge the abstraction gap between curriculum concepts and concrete visual evidence in documentaries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing language-based video moment retrieval methods assume queries describe observable events. However, instructional search requires retrieving concrete visual phenomena that instantiate underlying scientific principles - an abstract-needle-in-a-haystack problem that current methods cannot handle effectively.

Method: CDDA uses a three-stage approach: (1) Structure textual embedding space with textbook and teacher-handbook example-concept pairs; (2) Transfer concept-aware geometry to documentary visuals under a frozen visual encoder; (3) Jointly adapt both encoders with sparse visual concept supervision. From a geometric perspective, this staged alignment reduces text-concept and vision-concept angular gaps while preserving pretrained concrete image description alignment.

Result: On a curated middle-school physics retrieval benchmark, CDDA achieves stronger pedagogically-oriented concept retrieval than several competitive multimodal baselines, including Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B, while maintaining concrete image-text matching after adaptation.

Conclusion: The abstraction gap between curriculum concepts and visual evidence can be bridged through staged domain adaptation that treats concepts as intermediate semantic anchors. This approach enables vision-language models to support instructional search use cases in science education.

Abstract: Science teachers frequently search for documentary excerpts not by describing what appears on screen, but by querying the abstract concepts they intend to teach. This use case exposes a limitation of existing language-based video moment retrieval methods, which typically assume that queries describe observable events, whereas instructional search requires retrieving concrete visual phenomena that instantiate an underlying scientific principle. We study this setting as concept-to-example video retrieval, an abstract-needle-in-a-haystack problem where compact curriculum concepts must be grounded in temporally sparse documentary evidence. To bridge this abstraction gap, we propose Concept-Driven Domain Adaptation (CDDA), a three-stage framework for adapting two-tower vision-language models to concept-level retrieval. CDDA treats concepts as intermediate semantic anchors: it first structures the textual embedding space with textbook and teacher-handbook example-concept pairs, then transfers this concept-aware geometry to documentary visuals under a frozen visual encoder, and finally jointly adapts both encoders with sparse visual concept supervision. From a geometric perspective, this staged alignment reduces text-concept and vision-concept angular gaps, thereby encouraging concept-level adaptation while preserving the pretrained model's concrete image description alignment. On a curated middle-school physics retrieval benchmark, CDDA achieves stronger pedagogically oriented concept retrieval than several competitive multimodal baselines, including Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B, while maintaining concrete image-text matching after adaptation.

</details>


### [63] [VIEScore2: Unified Image Evaluation with Spatially Grounded Explanations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00994)
*Xianda Du,Max Ku,Weiming Ren,Zhi Rui Tam,Chunlin Ren,Ping Nie,Min-Hung Chen,Wenhu Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VIEScore2 is a unified image generation and editing evaluator that predicts both quality scores and defect locations in a single model pass using a text-native grid representation. It outperforms zero-shot general-purpose VLMs and specialized spatial evaluators on multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing synthetic image evaluators only provide scalar quality scores without identifying which image regions support the score, limiting interpretability and verifiability.

Method: VIEScore2 represents images as N×N grids and jointly predicts quality scores and defect locations. Trained on 38K examples with score-only, localization-only, and joint supervision. Uses GRPO with rewards combining cell-level Dice overlap, score accuracy, and output-format validity. Includes a parameter-free parser for readable explanations.

Result: VIEScore2 achieves overall-score SRCC of 0.601 vs 0.491 for Gemini-3-Flash. For defect localization, it outperforms general-purpose VLMs and specialized spatial evaluators on 3/6 benchmarks in per-image grid IoU and ranks top-3 on 5 benchmarks.

Conclusion: VIEScore2 demonstrates that unified quality and localization evaluation is achievable through grid-based representation, outperforming both specialized spatial evaluators and general-purpose VLMs across multiple benchmarks, including datasets outside its training distribution.

Abstract: Existing synthetic image evaluators typically provide only a scalar quality score and do not identify the image regions that support it. We introduce VIEScore2, a unified evaluator for image generation and editing tasks with optional conditioning images. VIEScore2 represents an image as an N x N grid and jointly predicts quality scores and defect locations in a single model pass. Its text-native grid representation provides a common interface for heterogeneous spatial supervision and enables directly verifiable post-training objectives. We train on 38K examples spanning score-only, localization-only, and joint supervision across generation and editing tasks. Starting from supervised fine-tuning, we further apply GRPO to improve defect localization using rewards that combine cell-level Dice overlap, score accuracy, and output-format validity. A parameter-free parser converts the structured predictions into readable explanations. On the primary suite, VIEScore2 achieves an overall-score SRCC of 0.601, compared with 0.491 for Gemini-3-Flash, the strongest zero-shot general-purpose VLM baseline under matched inputs. For defect localization, VIEScore2 outperforms both general-purpose VLMs and specialized spatial evaluators on three of six benchmarks in per-image grid IoU and ranks among the top three on five, including datasets beyond its training sources.

</details>


### [64] [VASC: Value-Aware Sparse Attention with Cross-Layer Memory for Efficient 3D Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01013)
*Junyi Wu,Fanqing Kong,Leyang Chen,Shaoqiu Zhang,Yulun Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VASC is a training-free sparse attention method for 3D vision models that combines value-aware block selection and execution-aware cross-layer memory to address quadratic attention complexity and value redundancy issues in models like VGGT.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Feed-forward 3D vision models (e.g., VGGT) have quadratic global attention making long sequences expensive, while existing sparse methods may favor highly attended but value-redundant regions.

Method: VASC integrates two components: (1) Value-aware block selection using pooled query-key relevance combined with neighboring value contrast to reduce redundancy while preserving query-relevant and distinctive content; (2) Execution-aware cross-layer memory that tracks unserved demand across layers and updates based on actual execution, enabling previously underserved blocks to compete under fixed computation budget.

Result: Experiments on 7Scenes and NeuralRGB-D with VGGT and π³ show improved pose estimation and reconstruction quality compared with FasterVGGT, with up to 2.29× faster inference than dense VGGT.

Conclusion: VASC provides an effective training-free solution for sparse attention in 3D vision models, achieving a good balance between efficiency and accuracy.

Abstract: Feed-forward 3D vision models such as VGGT have achieved remarkable progress, unifying camera estimation and dense scene reconstruction in a single pass. However, their quadratic global attention makes long image sequences expensive, while existing sparse methods may favor highly attended yet value-redundant regions. To address these limitations, we introduce VASC, a training-free sparse attention method combining value-aware block selection and execution-aware cross-layer memory. Our value-aware block selection integrates pooled query--key relevance with neighboring value contrast, reducing redundancy while preserving query-relevant and distinctive content. Cross-layer memory tracks unserved demand across layers and updates this state according to actual execution, enabling previously underserved blocks to compete under a fixed computation budget. Experiments on 7Scenes and NeuralRGB-D with VGGT and $π^3$ demonstrate improved pose estimation and reconstruction quality compared with FasterVGGT, together with up to $2.29\times$ faster inference than dense VGGT. Code is available at https://github.com/kosakayamahoo-design/VASC.

</details>


### [65] [FutureWorlds: Learning Robotic World Models from Alternative Futures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01019)
*Hao Wu,Shengju Qian,Weiyan Wang,Fan Xu,Fan Zhang,Yuanpeng He,Qingsong Wen,Yuxuan Liang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FutureWorlds is a framework for robotic world models that unifies candidate construction via diverse beam search, history maintenance via candidate-specific bounded memory, and learning via MemSPO. It achieves 9-21% LPIPS improvement across three benchmarks while improving motion prediction and object consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Robotic world models face two key challenges: (1) similar candidate predictions limit informative quality comparisons, and (2) diverging trajectories require persistent maintenance of individual histories. Existing approaches struggle to turn alternative predictions into useful learning signals.

Method: FutureWorlds employs a multimodal discrete autoregressive model with diverse beam search for candidate construction, candidate-specific bounded memory for history preservation, and MemSPO (Memory-Conditioned Search-Guided Policy Optimization) that converts video trajectory rewards into group-relative advantages for world model optimization.

Result: On RT-1, BridgeV2, and RoboCasa datasets, FutureWorlds reduces LPIPS for 32-frame predictions by 14.78%, 20.84%, and 9.12% respectively relative to strongest baselines. With only 200 MemSPO updates, the method improves generation quality and supports prediction beyond training horizon. Gains extend beyond visual quality to more accurate motion prediction (optical-flow evaluation) and more consistent object states (memory ablations).

Conclusion: FutureWorlds successfully addresses key challenges in robotic world models through unified candidate construction and history maintenance. The framework achieves significant improvements in visual quality (14.78-20.84% LPIPS reduction) across multiple benchmarks, with gains extending to motion prediction and object consistency. MemSPO enables efficient optimization with only 200 updates, demonstrating practical applicability for real-world robotic tasks.

Abstract: Robotic world models predict action-conditioned future scenes, providing a foundation for understanding action outcomes. However, turning alternative predictions into useful learning signals remains challenging: similar candidates limit informative quality comparisons, while diverging trajectories require persistent maintenance of their individual histories. We introduce FutureWorlds, a framework that unifies candidate construction, history maintenance, and learning from relative quality. Built on a multimodal discrete autoregressive model, FutureWorlds uses diverse beam search during reinforcement learning to construct candidate futures that balance confidence and diversity. Candidate-specific bounded memory preserves scene states and ensures that generation and policy scoring use matching histories. We further propose MemSPO (Memory-Conditioned Search-Guided Policy Optimization), which converts video trajectory rewards into group-relative advantages to optimize the world model. On RT-1, BridgeV2, and RoboCasa, FutureWorlds reduces LPIPS for 32-frame predictions by 14.78%, 20.84%, and 9.12%, respectively, relative to the strongest baseline on each dataset. Under fixed evaluation configurations, only 200 MemSPO updates further improve generation quality and support continued prediction beyond the training horizon. Memory ablations, decoding sensitivity analysis, and optical-flow evaluation show that these gains extend beyond visual quality to more accurate motion prediction and more consistent object states. Project page and code: https://github.com/Alexander-wu/FutureWorlds.

</details>


### [66] [Towards Automatic Video Annotation with ASH: Zero-Shot Open-Vocabulary Multi-Object Tracking and Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01022)
*Arash Rocky,Q. M. Jonathan Wu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces SAM3-ASH, a training-free video instance segmentation pipeline that enables fully automated tracking annotation of arbitrary video through two novel contributions: Generalized Presence Token (GPT) for simultaneous multi-prompt processing, and Annotation and Segmentation Handler (ASH) for arbitrary-length video processing via overlapping temporal chunks with IoU-based identity matching.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Memory-attention-based VIS methods face two key limitations: substantial memory requirements confine them to short video clips, and their single-prompt inference design makes multi-category open-vocabulary tracking computationally prohibitive.

Method: Two contributions: (1) GPT reformulates SAM3's inference pipeline to process N text prompts simultaneously via virtual prompt batching, reducing image encoding cost from O(N) to O(1) without modifying learned components. (2) ASH extends any memory-attention VIS tracker to arbitrary-length sequences through overlapping temporal chunks with IoU-based inter-chunk identity matching, requiring no dataset-specific training.

Result: SAM3-ASH achieves state-of-the-art HOTA on MOTS20 under fully zero-shot conditions and remains competitive with trained specialists across seven additional benchmarks, while peak GPU memory consumption stays below 25 GB.

Conclusion: The method establishes a practical baseline for scalable, training-free automated video annotation, balancing strong performance with computational efficiency.

Abstract: Memory-attention-based Video Instance Segmentation (VIS) methods have demonstrated strong zero-shot tracking capability, yet their substantial memory requirements confine them to short video clips and their single-prompt inference design makes multi-category open-vocabulary tracking computationally prohibitive. This work introduces two contributions toward fully automated tracking annotation of arbitrary video. The Generalized Presence Token (GPT) reformulates SAM3's inference pipeline to process N text prompts simultaneously via virtual prompt batching, reducing image encoding cost from O(N) to O(1) with no modifications to any learned component. The Annotation and Segmentation Handler (ASH) extends any memory-attention VIS tracker to sequences of arbitrary length through overlapping temporal chunks with IoU-based inter-chunk identity matching, requiring no dataset-specific training. Instantiated on SAM3, the resulting pipeline -- SAM3-ASH -- achieves state-of-the-art HOTA on MOTS20 under fully zero-shot conditions and remains competitive with trained specialists across seven additional benchmarks, while peak GPU memory consumption stays below 25 GB, establishing a practical baseline for scalable, training-free automated video annotation.

</details>


### [67] [Bootstrapping Video Interaction Generation with Synthetic State Transitions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01039)
*Jiho Jang,Jinyoung Kim,Nojun Kwak,Kyungjune Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A framework for generating scalable synthetic datasets of controllable physical interactions for video generation models, using a structured taxonomy and image editing models to create start/end state anchors, with a novel State-Guided Sampling (SGS) technique to mitigate generation artifacts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current video generative models struggle to portray plausible physical interactions and resulting state transitions, which is a critical bottleneck for robotics and VR/AR applications.

Method: 1) Leverage structured taxonomy and image editing models to create explicit 'start' and 'end' state images as visual anchors. 2) Propose State-Guided Sampling (SGS), a novel sampling technique to mitigate artifacts in conditional generation. 3) Develop automated evaluation system aligned with human judgments.

Result: Fine-tuning a base model on the generated dataset significantly enhances its ability to generate plausible physical interactions.

Conclusion: The proposed framework successfully creates high-quality synthetic interaction data that improves video generation models' capability to depict physical interactions and state transitions.

Abstract: While recent video generative models can synthesize high-fidelity videos, they struggle to portray plausible physical interactions and the resulting state transitions, a critical bottleneck for applications in robotics and VR/AR. To address this, we introduce a framework to generate a scalable synthetic dataset of controllable interactions. Our pipeline leverages a structured taxonomy and state-of-the-art image editing models to create explicit `start' and `end' state images, which serve as visual anchors for the interaction. To generate a seamless video utilizing these anchors, we propose State-Guided Sampling (SGS), a novel sampling technique that mitigates artifacts common in naive conditional generation. Furthermore, we develop and validate a new automated evaluation system that aligns with human judgments to ensure data quality. Experiments show that fine-tuning a base model on our dataset significantly enhances its ability to generate plausible interactions.

</details>


### [68] [Towards Subject Consistency over Dynamic Subject Sets in Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01052)
*Tongcheng Zhang,Jun Zhu,Jianfei Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces DynSC-Eval, a dynamic evaluation framework for subject consistency in long video generation. It tracks subjects throughout their visible lifespans and measures consistency using six complementary metrics. The framework is validated through synthetic experiments and applied to post-training (DiffusionNFT) for autonomous driving, achieving significant reductions in inconsistency metrics across multiple models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current video generation evaluation uses static subject sets, which fails to capture subject consistency issues in longer videos. Existing metrics cannot adequately measure dynamic subject consistency across varying durations (5s, 15s, 60s), necessitating a new evaluation framework that tracks subjects dynamically throughout their visible lifespans.

Method: 1) Developed DynSC-Eval framework with dynamic subject tracking and six complementary object-level metrics for measuring local continuity and global identity preservation. 2) Designed synthetic experiments with injected inconsistency events to validate sensitivity. 3) Applied DynSC-Eval rewards to DiffusionNFT post-training in autonomous driving testbed. 4) Extended generation to 10s and 30s using curriculum learning.

Result: On 5s generation: 13.82% average reduction in six inconsistency metrics for Wan-2.1-1.3B, 5.66% for SANA-2B, with improvements also on ReSim I2V model. Curriculum learning enabled effective 10s and 30s generation while preserving other capabilities. DynSC-Eval revealed substantial subject consistency differences that existing metrics obscure.

Conclusion: DynSC-Eval provides a more sensitive and comprehensive evaluation of subject consistency in video generation compared to conventional metrics. The framework enables both better evaluation and effective optimization through post-training, demonstrating its utility across different video durations and model architectures.

Abstract: We argue that as video generation extends to longer durations, subject consistency should be evaluated over \textit{dynamic subject sets}. We therefore introduce \textbf{DynSC-Eval}, an evaluation framework that dynamically tracks eligible subjects throughout their visible lifespans and measures local continuity and global identity preservation using six complementary object-level metrics, with explicit detection of inconsistency events. To validate its effectiveness, we design synthetic experiments that actively inject inconsistency events, demonstrating both the sensitivity of DynSC-Eval and the limitations of existing metrics. Evaluations of diverse models on 5s, 15s, and 60s video generation further reveal substantial subject consistency differences that are obscured by conventional metrics. Beyond evaluation, we construct rewards from DynSC-Eval and apply DiffusionNFT post-training in an autonomous-driving testbed. On 5s generation, our approach reduces the six inconsistency metrics by an average of 13.82\% for Wan-2.1-1.3B and 5.66\% for SANA-2B, with improvements also observed on the I2V model ReSim. Qualitative comparisons further demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. We then extend generation to 10s and 30s through curriculum learning and show that consistency optimization remains effective while largely preserving other capabilities.

</details>


### [69] [HierGF: Hierarchical Gaussian Fields via Geometry-perception Message Passing for Sparse-view 3D Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01056)
*Bi'an Du,Zhimin Zhang,Daizong Liu,Baoquan Chen,Wei Hu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes Hierarchical Gaussian Fields (HierGF), a novel sparse-view 3D reconstruction method that addresses limited view coverage by transforming coarse 3D geometry and 2D generative priors into structured pseudo-supervision, using a learnable confidence network and geometric densification module to enhance multi-view consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sparse view 3D reconstruction is important for AR/VR, cultural heritage digitization, and robotics but faces two major challenges: 1) Too few images for matching and multi-view consistency, 2) Insufficient view coverage leading to missing object structure in under-sampled regions. Existing methods rely on limited reprojection errors and regularization terms, prone to overfitting and inconsistent appearances, with heuristic density control lacking reliable guidance.

Method: HierGF uses a hierarchical geometry-perception perspective with three key components: 1) Two-stage geometry-perception backbone network that converts coarse 3D geometric information and 2D generative priors into structured pseudo-supervision beyond fixed priors; 2) Learnable confidence network to guide gradients toward cross-view consistent content; 3) Geometrically consistent densification module to improve reconstruction of multi-view alignment and under-sampled regions.

Result: The method enhances multi-view consistency with very few input views, providing reliable guidance for geometrically under-sampled regions and addressing issues of blurring and structural holes that plagued previous approaches.

Conclusion: By revisiting sparse-view reconstruction from a hierarchical geometry-perception perspective and converting limited observations into self-generated supervision, HierGF successfully addresses the fundamental limitations of sparse-view 3D reconstruction, offering improved multi-view consistency and structural completeness.

Abstract: Sparse view 3D reconstruction is an important and common scenario in multimedia applications, such as augmented reality/virtual reality (AR/VR) content creation, cultural heritage digitization, and certain robotic applications, where only a limited number of randomly captured views may be available. However, sparse views contain only limited 3D information, posing two major challenges:1) too few images are available for matching, making it difficult to build multi-view consistency; 2) insufficient view coverage leads to a lack of information in under-sampled regions, resulting in missing parts of object structure.
