Abstract: Public-service recommendations require evidence that matches the requested service, scope, and date. Yet treating every missing detail as decisive can withhold useful recommendations. We introduce EviGraph, which distinguishes critical decision requirements from information that can remain unresolved. A language agent links these requirements to evidence in a temporal knowledge graph, while a deterministic checker establishes whether a recommendation is supported. Evaluation on a bilingual Hong Kong public-service benchmark with executable policy references shows that this distinction reduces unnecessary abstention. Additional verification, however, can withdraw supported recommendations without improving decision quality. These findings suggest that reliable evidence-based navigation depends on specifying what must be established for a decision, rather than simply adding more verification.

</details>


### [92] [Build2SPARQL: A Large-Scale Text-to-SPARQL Benchmark Dataset for Building Knowledge Graph Querying](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00224)
*Wooyoung Jung*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Building automation systems are increasingly represented as semantic knowledge graphs (KGs) using ontologies such as Brick and ASHRAE 223P, creating a machine-readable substrate for artificial-intelligence applications. One promising application is translating natural-language questions into SPARQL (text-to-SPARQL), which would let building operators query these graphs through language agents, but progress is limited by the scarcity of large natural-language/SPARQL benchmarks. This paper presents Build2SPARQL, a large-scale benchmark for building KGs generated by a KG-grounded pipeline: SPARQL queries are produced and validated entirely by graph-traversal code, while large language models generate only the natural-language questions, keeping query correctness independent of model behavior. The pipeline mines six query-pattern families -- linear chains, branching, UNION, aggregation, OPTIONAL, and attribute-filtered -- and phrases each query across five vocabulary registers. Applied to 201 building KGs (180 Brick, 21 ASHRAE 223P), it yields 6,136 executable SPARQL queries and 30,680 questions. A two-rater human validation of 300 questions found 98.8% semantic fidelity, 98.8% naturalness, and 84.0% operational plausibility. A retrieval-augmented evaluation across three open-weight language models raised exact-match accuracy from 0.2-20% (zero-shot) to 56-65% (three-shot retrieved).

</details>


### [93] [Robust Is Salient: An Informed Adversary Moves the Optimal Signal onto the Salience Pole](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00233)
*Cris Huynh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: When an informed adversary shares a constrained signaling channel, the optimal signal that protects truth aligns with the "salience pole" rather than Bayesian discrimination. The adversary-robust optimum matches salience exactly on 108 confirmatory items, differing on only 2,748 out of 200,000 items—specifically where the salience-to-Bayes coordinate is undefined. As persuasion budget (β) increases, the optimal signal shifts from posterior-maximizing to margin-maximizing. Testing on 7 language models shows 30-77 items changed per model, but this shift cannot be empirically distinguished from salience due to their structural coincidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how to communicate truth when an informed adversary shares the audience and tries to persuade toward false answers. The paper investigates whether optimal signaling under adversarial conditions differs from standard Bayesian discrimination, and whether this difference can be empirically detected.

Method: The authors introduced an adversary into a forced-choice task (abstracted from the game "Deception: Murder in Hong Kong"). The adversary knows the target, observes the signal, and argues for the strongest wrong answer using a persuasion budget β. They analyzed a 200,000-item pool and tested on 7 language models across 108 items, examining how the chosen option changes under two adversary framings.

Result: The adversary-robust optimum aligns exactly with the salience pole on all 108 confirmatory items. Across 200,000 items, the two differ on only 2,748 items—lying exactly where the salience-to-Bayes coordinate is undefined. Where defined, robustness is achieved by moving from Bayesian discrimination entirely to salience. As β grows, the optimal signal shifts from posterior-maximizing to margin-maximizing; at β=0, the game reproduces the original oracle model with listener temperature τ=1. Empirically, 18.2% of the pool has an optimum that shifts under finite budget, and each item's critical budget is exact. Seven language models changed choices on 30 to 77 of 108 items under two adversary framings.

Conclusion: The structural coincidence between adversary-aware optimum and salience creates an irreducible empirical blind spot: no measurement can determine whether model responses shift toward the adversary-aware optimum or toward salience. This is a structural limit, not a null result. The diagnostic check is cheap: before evaluating adversary-awareness, verify whether the robust target coincides with a heuristic target on the evaluation items.

Abstract: When an informed adversary shares the audience of a constrained signalling channel, the signal that best protects the truth is the signal that best describes it. On 108 confirmatory items, the adversary-robust optimum aligns exactly with the salience pole from prior work. Across a 200,000-item pool, the two differ on only 2,748 items --- lying exactly where the prior salience-to-Bayes coordinate is undefined. Where defined, robustness is achieved by moving from Bayesian discrimination entirely to salience. We show this by introducing an adversary to a forced-choice task (abstracted from Deception: Murder in Hong Kong). The adversary knows the target, observes the signal, and argues for the strongest wrong answer using a persuasion budget, $β$. As $β$ grows, the optimal signal shifts from the posterior-maximizing option to the margin-maximizing one; at $β= 0$, the game reproduces the original oracle model with a listener temperature of $τ= 1$. This effect is real: 18.2 percent of the pool has an optimum that shifts under a finite budget, and each item's critical budget is exact. This coincidence structurally limits empirical evaluation. Two adversary framings change the chosen option of seven language models on 30 to 77 of 108 items against an exact no-effect rate. Yet, no measurement can determine whether this movement is toward the adversary-aware optimum or toward salience, because the two options are identical. This is a structural limit, not a null result. The diagnostic check is cheap: before evaluating adversary-awareness, verify whether the robust target coincides with a heuristic target on the evaluation items.

</details>


### [94] [Not All Experience Belongs in the Weights: Component Routing for Self-Improving GUI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01787)
*Beining Wu,Zihao Ding,Jun Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the disagreement in literature about whether self-improving GUI agents should store trajectories in model weights (via fine-tuning) or in context (via retrieval). The authors propose that the conflicting results stem from treating trajectories as atomic units when they actually contain components with different properties. They introduce component routing - splitting experience into locators, procedures, state facts, and lessons, then routing each to the appropriate destination. They also develop a predictive rule based on recurrence and state-conditionality that achieves 24/24 accuracy in predicting optimal destinations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The literature disagrees on whether self-improving GUI agents should use fine-tuning (weights) or retrieval (context) to leverage trajectories. The authors attribute this disagreement to the "unit of experience" - trajectories bundle components with different properties, so conclusions about the bundle depend on its composition.

Method: 1) Component routing: splitting experience into four components (locators, procedures, state facts, lessons) and routing each to context or weights based on empirical testing across three backbone families, two environments, and three seeds. 2) Fitting a predictive rule based on two properties (recurrence and state-conditionality) measured before training. 3) Analyzing how training and producer-consumer differences change destination value.

Result: 1) Locators and lessons perform better in weights; procedures and state facts perform better in context. 2) The rule based on recurrence and state-conditionality recovers the destination of a held-out backbone family in 24/24 cells. Two interventions move components toward the boundary. 3) Routing by the rule beats every whole-trajectory baseline and outperforms the better single destination by +3.5 points on average. Additional findings: note readout decreases after the same component is written into weights (most for items that recur most), context gains increase with information gap, weights gains decrease with policy gap.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates that trajectories are not atomic units - their components have different optimal destinations. The proposed component routing approach, guided by a simple rule based on recurrence and state-conditionality, significantly outperforms both whole-trajectory baselines and single-destination approaches. This explains the source of prior disagreements and provides a principled framework for deciding where to route different types of experience in self-improving agents.

Abstract: Self-improving GUI agents keep the trajectories they produce and return them to the agent, by fine-tuning or by retrieval into the prompt, and studies that compare the two destinations disagree. We attribute this to the unit of experience: a trajectory bundles items with different properties, so a conclusion about the bundle depends on its mix. To address this, (i) we introduce component routing, which splits the experience into locators, procedures, state facts and lessons and sends each component to the context or to the weights, compared on the same items across three backbone families, two environments and three seeds. One pool has two destinations: locators and lessons win in the weights, procedures and state facts in the context. (ii) We fit a rule in two properties measured before any training, recurrence and state-conditionality; it recovers the destination of a held-out backbone family in 24 of 24 cells, two interventions move a component toward the boundary, and routing by the rule beats every whole-trajectory baseline and, by +3.5 points on average, the better single destination of each backbone. (iii) We identify how training and producer-consumer differences change the value of the two destinations: note readout decreases after the same component is written into the weights, most for the items that recur most, context gains increase with the information gap, and weights gains decrease with the policy gap. Code and data will be released.

</details>


### [95] [Conflicting Supervision Moves Commitment, Not Capability: A 12.29σ arrangement effect that is exactly zero under a convention-agnostic score](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00234)
*Wenhui Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates how learning rate schedules act as "averaging operators" that determine which data convention (format/style) a neural network model commits to during training. The key finding is that the learning rate schedule (not just the data arrangement) critically influences which convention the model learns, and this effect is invisible to conventional exact-match benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors seek to understand what ordering of data writes into model parameters when training on problems written under two incompatible but correct conventions. They challenge the notion that learning-rate schedules are just background conditions—arguing instead that the schedule itself is the "averaging operator" that decides the answer.

Method: The researchers conducted controlled experiments with ten orderings of one corpus, fixed budget, and everything but the path held constant. They ran experiments twice under families differing only in lr_scheduler_type: (1) constant learning rate, and (2) single cosine schedule (the standard published approach).

Result: Under constant rate: interior spans 0.2221 in allocation, 11.63 contrast floors, monotone in how blocked the arrangement is. Under cosine schedule: the ten arms occupy two distinguishable states where their own resolution would allow ~10. Across twelve arms, acc_A+acc_B is constant to within 9.7% while allocation share runs 0.04 to 0.87. The 12.29-sigma arrangement switch measures exactly zero under convention-agnostic metrics. Marking the convention in the prompt collapses the switch and reaches 87.5% of the union ceiling.

Conclusion: The learning rate schedule is the key factor determining which convention the model commits to. "Order matters" and "order does not matter" are ends of one knob controlled by the schedule. Standard benchmarks cannot detect this effect because they are convention-agnostic, but explicitly marking the convention in prompts collapses the effect significantly.

Abstract: "Train a model on the same problems written under two incompatible conventions, both correct, and ask what the ordering of that data writes into the parameters. The learning-rate schedule is not a background condition for that question. It is the averaging operator, and it decides the answer. We prove a bound in which the arrangement and the schedule enter the ordering effect as separate multiplied factors: the arrangement only as a block period, the schedule only as how much weight the endpoint can place on any one moment of the run. A decaying schedule cannot put a large step size and an uncontracted remainder at the same moment; a constant one does exactly that at the last step. That decay moderates ordering effects has been reported in pretraining; the mechanism, the separation, and a controlled measurement of both halves are ours. Ten orderings of one corpus, one budget, everything but the path held fixed, run twice under families differing in lr_scheduler_type and nothing else: at a constant rate the interior spans 0.2221 in allocation, 11.63 contrast floors, monotone in how blocked the arrangement is. Under the single cosine every published arm uses, the same ten arms occupy two distinguishable states where their own resolution would allow about ten. "Order matters" and "order does not matter" are the two ends of one knob. What the path writes is which convention the model commits to, and no exact-match benchmark can see it. Across twelve arms acc_A+acc_B is constant to within 9.7% while the allocation share runs 0.04 to 0.87, so the 12.29-sigma arrangement switch this paper measures is exactly zero under a convention-agnostic metric. That conservation is quoted from the decayed family throughout, the constant-rate one being a noisier place to read it. Marking the convention in the prompt collapses the switch and reaches 87.5% of the union ceiling."

</details>


### [96] [Knowing When to Yield: Grounded Arbitration of User Corrections in Text-Based Embodied Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00282)
*Yezhou Cheng,Runjia Du,Zeming Liu,Hang Lyu,Zehua Yang,Bojun Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses how an embodied agent should respond when a human's correction may be incorrect. The authors propose "grounded correction arbitration" as a choice among accepting, rejecting, inspecting the environment, or asking the speaker for clarification. Their system GAVA uses observation-bounded evidence, legal probes, and a one-step expected-loss rule. Experiments in text-only ALFWorld show that semantic priors under declared costs support selective information gathering, though the study does not establish a general advantage of environmental value of information over clarification seeking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address a fundamental challenge in human-robot interaction: when a person corrects an embodied agent's understanding, the agent must decide whether to trust the correction or investigate further. The key insight is that corrections may be wrong (due to human error, miscommunication, or different perspectives), so agents need a systematic approach to arbitrate between accepting corrections and gathering additional information.

Method: The authors implement GAVA (Grounded Arbitration for Visual Assistance) with three key components: (1) observation-bounded evidence - constraining evidence to what the agent can directly observe; (2) legal probes - allowable information-gathering actions; and (3) a one-step expected-loss rule for decision-making. The method was evaluated in text-only ALFWorld environments with 162 checkpoints producing 972 paired true/false interventions. They tested an exploratory training-only object-location prior and compared against baselines including always verify, uniform GAVA, and calibrated no-VOI comparisons.

Result: With complete local inspections, GAVA achieves 100% correction accuracy, establishing an "evidence contract." In same-episode execution, GAVA reduces interaction cost compared to always verify but ties a cost threshold under a perfect speaker. An exploratory training-only object-location prior lowers interaction and declared joint cost on 340 unseen scenarios by 0.490 and 0.420 relative to uniform GAVA. On 77 non-overlapping seen checkpoints (308 scenarios), gains replicate at 0.595 and 0.517, with 95% confidence intervals excluding zero. Semantic GAVA makes 4 factual errors per cohort (98.8% and 98.7% accuracy). All methods complete every task.

Conclusion: The results support selective information gathering with semantic priors under declared costs, but do not establish a general advantage of environmental value of information over clarification seeking. The study uses normalized claims, complete symbolic observations, and controlled speakers, and explicitly evaluates neither human participants, visual input, nor physical robots.

Abstract: How should an embodied agent respond when a person's correction may be wrong? We formulate grounded correction arbitration as a choice among accepting, rejecting, inspecting the world, and asking the speaker. GAVA implements this interface with observation-bounded evidence, legal probes, and a one-step expected-loss rule. In text-only ALFWorld, 162 checkpoints produce 972 paired true and false interventions. Complete local inspections give GAVA and always verify 100 percent correction accuracy, establishing the evidence contract rather than a comparative advantage. In same-episode execution, GAVA reduces interaction cost against always verify but ties a cost threshold under a perfect speaker. An exploratory training-only object-location prior lowers interaction and declared joint cost on 340 unseen scenarios by 0.490 and 0.420 relative to uniform GAVA. After freezing the policy, costs, baselines, and multiplicity plan, the gains replicate on 77 non-overlapping seen checkpoints, covering 308 scenarios: 0.595 and 0.517, with both 95 percent checkpoint-bootstrap confidence intervals excluding zero. Joint cost also improves over an identical-prior fixed policy, while the matched calibrated no-VOI comparison remains inconclusive. Semantic GAVA makes four factual errors in each cohort, corresponding to 98.8 percent and 98.7 percent accuracy, and all methods complete every task. Results support selective information gathering with semantic priors under declared costs, but do not establish a general advantage of environmental value of information over clarification. The study uses normalized claims, complete symbolic observations, and controlled speakers; it evaluates neither human participants, visual input, nor physical robots.

</details>


### [97] [Rules to Tools: Executable Checks for LLM Agents in Scientific Computing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00313)
*Jingjie Ning,Guojiang Zhao,Chen Xu,Shanshan Zhong,Xiaochuan Li,Ji Zeng,Guolin Ke*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Rules to Tools (R2T) provides executable checks to scientific coding agents instead of just text descriptions of requirements. Experiments across multiple cohorts show tools achieve slightly better repair success (29/30 vs 26/30 in main cohort) but with tradeoffs in CPU usage and agent-side output savings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scientific coding agents need to assess programs they revise when receiving equations, boundary conditions, and output requirements. The paper investigates whether providing executable checks (tools) versus text descriptions improves repair outcomes.

Method: Matched repair groups were compared: text group receives written requirements, tool group receives callable implementations of checks. Experiments across multiple cohorts with different task IDs and configurations measured complete repair rates, model output, CPU usage, and agent-side costs.

Result: Tool group shows marginal improvement: 29/30 vs 26/30 in main cohort, 15/16 vs 13/16 in eight-ID cohort. One task favors text (37), three favor tools (17, 77, 11). Larger shared-definition cohort ties at 13/24. PDE comparison: 24/24 (tools) vs 23/24 (text), with 31.2% lower reported model output for checks. Public CPU use rises in both task-ID cohorts.

Conclusion: Results are task-dependent; prepared checks provide modest improvement in repair success but increase computational costs. The advantage varies significantly across task types, with some tasks favoring text and others favoring tools. Tradeoffs exist between repair success rates and computational efficiency.

Abstract: Scientific coding agents receive equations, boundary conditions, and output requirements in writing, then must assess the programs they revise. Rules to Tools (R2T) supplies prepared executable checks of public scientific requirements. Matched SciCode repair groups share written checks, starting programs, model, and budgets; the tool group receives a callable implementation. Across two task-ID cohorts, complete repair is 26/30 with text and 29/30 with the prepared checks. Three task IDs favor tools, one favors text, and eleven tie. The eight-ID cohort scores 13/16 versus 15/16, with a task-cluster bootstrap 95% interval of [-12.5, 43.75] percentage points for the difference. The larger shared-definition SciCode cohort ties at 13/24 per group. Five development-exposed tasks with alternate starting programs score 3/10 versus 7/10. The tool group favors tasks 17, 77, and 11; initial checks flag task 17 and report no violation for tasks 77 and 11. Task 37 favors text and has no initial reported violation. A fresh source-through-Python arm also reaches 15/16, matching the dedicated command's aggregate. In a matched PDE comparison, detailed text scores 23/24 and checks score 24/24, with 31.2% lower reported model output for checks. Agent-side output savings vary by cohort, while public CPU use rises in both task-ID cohorts. These results measure task-dependent repair outcomes and agent-side costs with prepared checks.

</details>


### [98] [Predictive Credit: Measuring What Scientific Explanations Add to Experimental Forecasts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00314)
*Jingjie Ning,Xueqi Li,Yibo Kong,Dongting Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a protocol to measure "predictive credit" for research agents—essentially evaluating whether AI agents can explain planned experiments and make accurate predictions. The study tests this across 336 controlled learning scenarios, 12 Tox21 endpoints, and 24 OpenML tasks, using various DeepSeek models. Results were largely inconclusive or negative, with most pre-registered tests failing to meet their criteria, though some limited positive effects were observed with specific model configurations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The researchers aim to establish a methodology for measuring predictive credit in research-agent benchmarks and scientific forecasting contexts. They want to determine whether matched explanations (vs. simple descriptions) can improve predictive accuracy in AI systems that explain planned experiments.

Method: The study uses paired forecasts sharing an intervention, forecaster, and outcome while varying description, matched explanation, and donor context. Five tracking checks measure commitment, delivery, predictive gain, alignment, and known-signal uptake. Experiments span three domains: 336 prospective states in controlled learning, 12 Tox21 endpoints, and 24 OpenML tasks. Multiple DeepSeek models (V4 Pro, V4 Flash) are tested.

Result: Most pre-registered tests failed to meet their criteria. Tox21's ROC AUC interval-score harm test was unmet (D-M = -0.0026). OpenML's joint formation, point-equivalence, and repeatability rule was unmet. Matched point-accuracy gains over description remained unconfirmed. However, DeepSeek V4 Pro with matched and donor cards reduced secondary Tox21 drift by 64.5% and 59.1%. A researcher-authored mechanism positive control lowered point MAE by 2.60 percentage points versus description.

Conclusion: The proposed protocol can measure predictive credit for research-agent benchmarks and scientific forecasting. However, natural-explanation credit remained unconfirmed at the tested donor resolutions. The methodology shows promise but requires further validation with different donor resolutions and model configurations.

Abstract: Research agents explain planned experiments. We measure predictive credit with paired forecasts sharing an intervention, forecaster, and outcome while varying description, matched explanation, and donor context. Five checks track commitment, delivery, predictive gain, alignment, and known-signal uptake. Across 336 prospective states in controlled learning, 12 Tox21 endpoints, and 24 OpenML tasks, v5's frozen credit decision was inconclusive. Tox21's preregistered ROC AUC interval-score harm test was unmet ($D-M=-.0026$, 95 percent interval [$-.0174$, .0104]); OpenML's joint formation, point-equivalence, and repeatability rule was unmet. Matched point-accuracy gains over description remained unconfirmed, and Tox21/OpenML seed-donor intervals spanned zero. Under requested DeepSeek V4 Pro, matched and donor cards reduced secondary Tox21 drift by 64.5 and 59.1 percent. A DeepSeek V4 Flash replay raised matched point MAE from .01823 to .02020 and missed matched-donor interval-score equivalence. OpenML full-card assignment widened nominal 80 percent intervals by 21 percent, with 49.3 percent coverage versus 51.4 percent for description and content in 66/144 cards. Direct-text Flash delivered all 144 notes without detectable matched point-accuracy gain. A researcher-authored mechanism positive control lowered point MAE by 2.60 percentage points versus description. The protocol measures predictive credit for research-agent benchmarks and scientific forecasting; natural-explanation credit remained unconfirmed at the tested donor resolutions.

</details>


### [99] [ContractRL: Shielded Group-Relative Policy Optimization for Auditable Tool-Call Repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00328)
*Miaobo Hu,Shuhao Hu,Xiaobo Guo,Xin Wang,Bokun Wang,Yina Sa,Daren Zha,Jun Xiao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ContractRL is a contract-constrained sequential repair protocol that models verifier-guided JSON repair as a bounded decision process, achieving higher semantic success (0.9362) with fewer generated tokens (34.4) compared to Patch-SFT (0.9076, 44.9 tokens) and full regeneration (0.9148, 137.2 tokens).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Structured tool calls often fail after only a small number of fields violate a schema or execution contract. Regenerating the complete object enlarges the action surface and makes repeated repair difficult to audit.

Method: ContractRL models JSON repair as a bounded decision process where at each step the policy observes: candidate, typed verifier feedback, JSON Pointer, immutable repair history, and remaining budget. A contract-derived action mask filters malformed or prohibited RFC-6902 operations before a deterministic validator performs the transition. The method uses a contract-constrained group-relative objective for patch, retry, and abstention decisions while keeping canonical targets and semantic labels outside the online state until trace freeze.

Result: Under identical verifier information, ContractRL attains 0.9362 semantic success with 34.4 generated tokens, compared with 0.9076 and 44.9 tokens for Patch-SFT and 0.9148 and 137.2 tokens for full regeneration over 192 cases per seed and five seeds. Policy optimization improves semantic success from 0.9186 for supervised ContractRL to 0.9375. A separate three-seed paired evaluation against Patch-SFT yields a semantic difference of +0.0396 (95% CI [+0.0137,+0.0662], p=0.0039).

Conclusion: ContractRL significantly outperforms Patch-SFT and full regeneration approaches in semantic success while using fewer tokens. Feedback, action-mask, budget, and schema-shift analyses connect these gains to localized correction, while adversarial and multi-turn evaluations characterize the remaining failure modes.

Abstract: Structured tool calls often fail after only a small number of fields violate a schema or an execution contract. Regenerating the complete object enlarges the action surface and makes repeated repair difficult to audit. We introduce ContractRL, a contract-constrained sequential repair protocol that models verifier-guided JSON repair as a bounded decision process. At each step the policy observes the candidate, typed verifier feedback, JSON Pointer, immutable repair history, and remaining budget; a contract-derived action mask filters malformed or prohibited RFC-6902 operations before a deterministic validator performs the transition. We specify a contract-constrained group-relative objective for patch, retry, and abstention decisions while keeping canonical targets and semantic labels outside the online state until trace freeze. Under identical verifier information, ContractRL attains 0.9362 semantic success with 34.4 generated tokens, compared with 0.9076 and 44.9 tokens for Patch-SFT and 0.9148 and 137.2 tokens for full regeneration over 192 cases per seed and five seeds. Policy optimization improves semantic success from 0.9186 for supervised ContractRL to 0.9375. A separate three-seed paired evaluation against Patch-SFT yields a semantic difference of +0.0396 (95% CI $[+0.0137,+0.0662], p=0.0039$). Feedback, action-mask, budget, and schema-shift analyses connect these gains to localized correction, while adversarial and multi-turn evaluations characterize the remaining failure modes.

</details>


### [100] [Mathematical Transfer in LLMs Follows Reasoning Approach More Than Topic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00331)
*Sajad Goudarzi,Samaneh Zamanifard,Seyed Amin Seyed Haeri,Moloud Nasiri,Hamed Rahimian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether organizing mathematical training data for LLMs by topic or by reasoning approach produces better transfer learning. Using two counterbalanced designs across probability/combinatorics and number theory/geometry with various reasoning methods, the authors find that same-approach (SA) training consistently outperforms same-topic (ST) training in all 40 model-target comparisons, with advantages of 8.2-16.2 percentage points in the first design and 12.0-16.0 in the second.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to determine the optimal organizing principle for selecting mathematical training data for LLMs. While topic-based organization (probability examples for probability targets) is intuitive, the authors propose that reasoning approach (worked solutions sharing solution methods) might be more effective for transfer learning, even across different mathematical domains.

Method: The authors conducted two counterbalanced 2×2 designs: (1) probability and combinatorics crossed with invariant reasoning and double counting (2,000 problems), and (2) number theory and geometry crossed with complement and pigeonhole reasoning (800 problems). Every cell served as the held-out target in turn, with same-approach (SA) sources sharing the target's method but different topic, and same-topic (ST) sources sharing the topic but different method. Five base models and three training seeds were tested per design, yielding 40 seed-pooled model-target comparisons.

Result: SA outperforms ST in all 40 seed-pooled model-target comparisons. Model-level advantages ranged from 8.2 to 16.2 percentage points in the primary design (mean: 10.8) and from 12.0 to 16.0 in the second design (mean: 14.3). All ten model-level 95% confidence intervals excluded zero. Notably, ST sources were more similar to targets under embedding and lexical measures, meaning the SA advantage runs opposite to measured statement-level resemblance.

Conclusion: Reasoning approach is a more effective matching criterion than topic for mathematical transfer across the evaluated topic-approach combinations. This suggests that LLMs benefit more from learning solution methods that can generalize across domains than from domain-specific practice, even when the surface-level similarity (topic) appears higher for same-topic training.

Abstract: When selecting mathematical training data for LLMs, a natural organizing principle is topic: probability examples for probability targets. An alternative is reasoning approach: worked solutions that share a solution method with the target, even when the mathematical domain differs. We ask which relation produces greater transfer after fine-tuning. We evaluate two counterbalanced $2\times2$ designs: probability and combinatorics crossed with invariant reasoning and double counting (2,000 problems), and number theory and geometry crossed with complement and pigeonhole reasoning (800 problems). In each design, every cell serves as the held-out target in turn: same-approach (SA) sources share the target's method but change the topic, while same-topic (ST) sources share the topic but change the method. Every source appears once in each role, so additive source-quality effects cancel from the equally weighted aggregate contrast. Across five base models and three training seeds per design, SA outperforms ST in all 40 seed-pooled model--target comparisons. Model-level advantages range from 8.2 to 16.2 percentage points in the primary design (mean: 10.8) and from 12.0 to 16.0 in the second design (mean: 14.3); all ten model-level 95% confidence intervals exclude zero. In both designs, ST sources are more similar to targets under embedding and lexical measures, so the SA advantage runs opposite to the measured ordering of statement-level resemblance. These findings identify reasoning approach as a more effective matching criterion than topic for mathematical transfer across the evaluated topic--approach combinations.

</details>


### [101] [Fault-Tolerant Budget Conservation in Distributed Multi-Agent Delegation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00349)
*Genliang Zhu,Chu Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a formal framework for fault-tolerant budget conservation in distributed multi-agent AI systems. It addresses overspending problems in delegation scenarios where workers may fail, messages may be lost or duplicated, or network partitions may occur. The solution uses exclusive escrow credits that move through a delegation DAG, with operation reservations bound to lineage, epoch, and other parameters. The mechanism is proven to preserve budget bounds across crash, retry, duplicate, partition, join, and late-completion schedules.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Resource limits are becoming critical for AI agents that delegate work across concurrent and failure-prone workers. Existing mechanisms like parent-child allocation constraints, affine objects, and distributed escrow fail to prevent overspend in various failure scenarios including lost replies, effects completing after timeout, message repeats, branch partitions, and DAG joins aliasing one lineage. This gap necessitates a formal approach to budget conservation under fault conditions.

Method: The paper formalizes fault-tolerant budget conservation using quantized resource vectors represented by exclusive escrow credits moving through a delegation DAG. Before dispatch, a branch converts credit into an operation reservation bound to lineage, epoch, normalized effect, maximum charge, receiver, and idempotency key. Signed dispatch permits with quarantine are persisted, and gateway verification occurs before first acceptance. Uncertain effects remain charged until authenticated settlement, fenced authoritative no-effect proof, or permanent retirement. The approach is evaluated using bounded TLA+ model checking, an independent JavaScript explorer, and crash-injected SQLite experiments.

Result: The paper proves several key properties: ownership partition, ledger and effect conservation, descendant non-amplification, at-most-once settlement, late-completion safety, and partition confinement under explicit mediation, durability, authentication, normalization, and gateway assumptions. An indistinguishability result shows that partition-local availability requires exclusive preallocation. Experimental results across evaluated crash, retry, duplicate, partition, join, and late-completion schedules demonstrate that the mechanism preserves the issued budget bound.

Conclusion: The proposed mechanism successfully preserves budget conservation across diverse failure scenarios in distributed multi-agent delegation. The combination of formal verification (TLA+), independent exploration (JavaScript), and empirical testing (SQLite with crash injection) provides strong evidence for the approach's correctness. The indistinguishability result establishing that partition-local availability requires exclusive preallocation represents a fundamental tradeoff in distributed authorization design.

Abstract: Resource limits are becoming an authorization boundary for AI agents that delegate work across concurrent and failure-prone workers. Parent-child allocation constraints, affine objects, and distributed escrow do not by themselves prevent overspend when replies are lost, effects complete after timeout, messages repeat, branches partition, or DAG joins alias one lineage. We formalize fault-tolerant budget conservation for distributed multi-agent delegation. Budgets are quantized resource vectors represented by exclusive escrow credits that move through a delegation DAG. Before dispatch, a branch converts credit into an operation reservation bound to lineage, epoch, normalized effect, maximum charge, receiver, and idempotency key. It persists a signed dispatch permit with quarantine; the gateway verifies that permit before first acceptance. Uncertain effects remain charged until authenticated settlement, a fenced authoritative no-effect proof, or permanent retirement. We prove ownership partition, ledger and effect conservation, descendant non-amplification, at-most-once settlement, late-completion safety, and partition confinement under explicit mediation, durability, authentication, normalization, and gateway assumptions. An indistinguishability result shows that partition-local availability requires exclusive preallocation. Bounded TLA+ checking, an independent JavaScript explorer, and crash-injected two-process SQLite experiments exercise the declared scope and detect timeout-refund and historical-certificate-validation mutants. The mechanism preserves the issued budget bound across the evaluated crash, retry, duplicate, partition, join, and late-completion schedules.

</details>


### [102] [JusticeAxis: Benchmarking Legal Judgment between Rigid Rule Application and Ungrounded Discretion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00353)
*Zhengkai Tu,Mingda Zhang,Zijia Wang,Xiaoying Tang,Jimmy Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces JusticeAxis, a dataset of 256 real-world criminal cases with multimodal evidence and multiple judgments, and JusticeAgent, a multi-agent framework for legal judgment that uses skills distilled from execution trajectories under Bayesian credible bounds. The framework enables open-weight models to match commercial performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing legal judgment methods either use rigid statute matching or ungrounded discretion. Current benchmarks only score labels or rubrics, and the experience that would provide balanced judgment remains unverified. The authors seek to formalize legal judgment as a reference-anchored task tied to statute and circumstances simultaneously.

Method: The authors introduce JusticeAxis (256 cases from 18 countries with audio, image, text evidence, and three lawyer-written judgments per case) and propose JusticeAgent, a multi-agent framework with element agents for fact-establishing and a judge agent for law application. Skills are distilled from execution trajectories and admitted only under Bayesian credible bounds.

Result: Failure patterns vary with model scale: open-weight backbones drift to unsupported grounds while frontier models default to statutory answers. JusticeAgent as a plugin can carry a frozen open-weight backbone to commercial-level performance.

Conclusion: The reference-anchored formalization of legal judgment, combined with the skill-distillation approach under Bayesian credible bounds, effectively bridges the gap between rigid matching and ungrounded discretion. The framework enables simpler models to achieve commercial-level performance through experience-like skills.

Abstract: A sound judgment applies the law to established facts and weighs the circumstances in which they arose. However, existing methods swing between rigid statute matching and ungrounded discretion, benchmarks score a label or a rubric, and the experience that would supply the balance stays unverified. We formalize legal judgment as a reference-anchored task, whose object is a single decision that stays tied to the statute and to the circumstances at once. We introduce JusticeAxis, 256 real-world criminal cases from 18 countries with audio, image, and text evidence, and three lawyer-written judgments for every case: the recorded one and one for each failure. We further propose JusticeAgent, a harness whose element agents establish the facts and whose judge agent applies the law under skills carrying experience of the circumstances. Skills are distilled from execution trajectories and admitted only under Bayesian credible bounds. Experiments show that failure turns direction with scale: open-weight backbones drift to unsupported grounds, frontier models to the statutory default. We further verify that JusticeAgent, as a simple yet effective plugin, carries a frozen open-weight backbone to commercial level. Project resources are available at https://github.com/beita6969/JusticeAxis.

</details>


### [103] [What Should an Agent Remember? Disentangling Retention from Retrieval in Bounded-Memory Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00366)
*Juli Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses a critical methodological issue in evaluating persistent memory agents: confounding between retention (what information to keep) and selection (what to retrieve) decisions. The authors create a streaming-recall benchmark that separates these two factors and find that proper evaluation holding access fixed shows query-aware selection improves recall by 15.5 percentage points, while previous mixed comparisons inflated this to 68.7 points (53.2 attributable to access alone).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that memory evaluations often conflate retention and selection decisions, making it impossible to isolate the true effect of selection strategies. Previous benchmarks may have overstated improvements by changing both factors simultaneously.

Method: The authors build a streaming-recall benchmark that crosses retention and selection rules, evaluating all conditions on the same 300 seeded episodes. They hold access fixed to isolate selection effects, then compare with mixed comparisons that also change history access.

Result: Query-aware selection improves required-fact recall by 15.5 pp (95% CI: 12.8-18.2) when holding access fixed. Mixed comparisons show 68.7-point advantage with 53.2 points attributable to access. Under bounded retention, query-aware, dense, and oracle selection reach the retention ceiling. All 319 failures in bounded recency are from eviction, not ranking errors. Recall drops to 0% for distant targets. On SQuAD, retention ceiling is preserved while dense retrieval outperforms lexical retrieval.

Conclusion: Bounded-memory evaluations should hold access fixed and report retention and selection separately. This methodology prevents confounding and allows proper attribution of performance improvements to the correct mechanism.

Abstract: A persistent agent must decide both what to retain as information arrives and what to surface once a query appears, yet memory evaluations can confound these decisions by comparing methods that differ in both retention and selection. We build a streaming-recall benchmark crossing retention and selection rules and evaluate every condition on the same 300 seeded episodes. Holding access fixed, query-aware selection improves required-fact recall by 15.5 percentage points (95% CI: 12.8 to 18.2), whereas a mixed comparison that also changes history access reports a 68.7-point advantage, of which 53.2 points are attributable to access. Under bounded retention, query-aware, dense, and oracle selection reach the retention ceiling, and all 319 observed failures in the bounded recency condition are caused by eviction rather than ranking errors. Recall falls to 0% as targets recede sufficiently far into the past. Repeating the evaluation on SQuAD preserves the retention ceiling while showing that dense retrieval can outperform lexical retrieval on natural text. These results show that bounded-memory evaluations should hold access fixed and report retention and selection separately.

</details>


### [104] [When Harnesses Lose the Signal: Causal Evaluation of Recovery in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00372)
*Shuyao Xiao,Shengling Wang,Xuan Chen,Ke Chao,Ming Cui,Feifei Qian,Chaoyang Mei,Fanlin Meng,Ziming Yu,Junxi Yin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses a critical flaw in how LLM agent recovery from execution errors is evaluated—by only measuring average success, which hides the fact that recovery can either help or harm trajectories. The authors propose framing recovery as a causal decision problem and introduce the Causal Intervention Router (CIR), which selectively applies recovery based on pre-recovery information. On ALFWorld tasks with Qwen3-14B, CIR improves success from 70.33% to 73.33%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluation of recovery mechanisms in LLM agents relies solely on average task success, which obscures an important tension: the same recovery operation can either rescue a failing trajectory or disrupt one that would otherwise succeed. This averaging approach hides whether recovery is actually beneficial overall or harmful in many cases.

Method: The authors frame recovery as a causal decision problem. They compare trajectories with and without recovery from the same execution state to separate rescue effects from harm effects, and study how recovery value changes over time. They then introduce the Causal Intervention Router (CIR), a lightweight policy that uses pre-recovery information to decide when intervention is worthwhile.

Result: On long-horizon ALFWorld tasks with Qwen3-14B, CIR raises success from 70.33% to 73.33%, a gain of 3.00 percentage points. It leaves all evaluated trajectories with correct observations untouched. Additional controls demonstrate that the benefit of recovery cannot be explained solely by the new observation returned by the environment.

Conclusion: The paper provides a practical framework for evaluating recovery in LLM agents and demonstrates that selective intervention via CIR can improve success rates while preserving correct trajectories. The causal approach to understanding recovery effects is a valuable contribution to the field of LLM agent reliability.

Abstract: Large language model agents rely on external harnesses to pass information between the model and its environment and to recover from execution errors. Yet recovery is usually judged only by average task success. This hides an important tension. The same operation can rescue a failing trajectory or disrupt one that would otherwise succeed. We frame recovery as a causal decision problem. Starting from the same execution state, we compare what happens with and without recovery, separate rescue from harm, and study how the value of recovery changes over time. We then introduce the Causal Intervention Router (CIR), a lightweight policy that uses information available before recovery to decide when intervention is worthwhile. On long-horizon ALFWorld tasks with Qwen3-14B, CIR raises success from 70.33% to 73.33%, a gain of 3.00 percentage points. It leaves all evaluated trajectories with correct observations untouched. Additional controls show that the benefit of recovery cannot be explained solely by the new observation returned by the environment. These results provide a practical way to evaluate recovery and apply it selectively.

</details>


### [105] [Benchmarking Prompt Optimization of Large Language Models With Chess](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00416)
*Timothée Lesort,Alejandra López de Aberasturi Gómez,Tristan Karch,Tom Veniat,Philippe Modard,Karl Tuyls,Ludovic Denoyer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces a chess benchmark (1,118 Lichess puzzles) for studying automatic prompt optimization (APO) in frozen LLMs. The benchmark addresses key challenges in LLM evaluation: benchmark saturation, test set contamination, and expensive grading infrastructure. It combines inexpensive exact-match scoring, engine-based evaluation, and renewable puzzles with adjustable difficulty.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address critical challenges in evaluating large language models as their capabilities advance: benchmarks can saturate, public test sets risk contamination, and assessing harder tasks requires expensive infrastructure. These challenges are particularly acute in automatic prompt optimization (APO), where evaluation is repeated throughout the search process. The authors need a benchmark that is cheap, deterministic, challenging yet improvable, and renewable as models evolve.

Method: The authors built a chess benchmark from 1,118 Lichess puzzles and evaluated six APO algorithms on eight target models. They measured baseline strength, optimization response, and transferability across models and to game play. The benchmark uses exact-match scoring combined with engine-based evaluation of alternative moves.

Result: The benchmark demonstrates four key properties: (i) Challenging - even the strongest model (Gemini 3.5 Flash) solves only ~55% of puzzles; (ii) Discriminative - reveals performance gains, unchanged results, and regressions across methods and models; (iii) Renewable - fresh puzzles reduce contamination risk with adjustable difficulty; (iv) Affordable - complete study runs for ~$800.

Conclusion: Chess is a well-suited benchmark for APO due to its challenging nature, discriminative power, renewability, and affordability. It successfully connects puzzle-solving gains to short game-play rollouts within the same domain, providing a practical tool for studying prompt optimization without model weight updates.

Abstract: Evaluating large language models becomes increasingly challenging as their capabilities advance: benchmarks can saturate, public test sets risk contamination, and assessing harder tasks can require expensive grading or execution infrastructure. These challenges are amplified in automatic prompt optimization (APO), where evaluation is repeated throughout the search for better prompts. Studying APO therefore requires a benchmark that is cheap and deterministic to score, hard enough to leave room for improvement, and renewable as models evolve. We introduce a chess benchmark built from 1,118 Lichess puzzles to study APO for frozen LLMs: we optimize their prompts without updating their model weights. Chess combines inexpensive exact-match scoring, engine-based evaluation of alternative moves, and a renewable supply of problems with adjustable difficulty. Unlike evaluations that report only success on isolated test items, the benchmark also connects puzzle-solving gains to short game-play rollouts within the same domain. We use it to evaluate six APO algorithms on eight target models, measuring not only baseline strength but also how much each model responds to optimization and whether optimized prompts transfer across models and to game play. Chess is thus a well-suited benchmark for APO: it is (i) challenging, as even the strongest evaluated model, Gemini 3.5 Flash (used as the meta-model), solves only about 55\% of puzzles; (ii) discriminative, revealing gains, unchanged performance, and regressions across methods and models; (iii) renewable, with fresh puzzles to reduce contamination risk and adjustable difficulty to maintain headroom as models improve; and (iv) affordable, as the complete study runs for around \$800. We release the puzzles, optimization and evaluation code, and dataset-renewal scripts (https://github.com/imec-ailabs/Automatic-Prompt-Optimization-with-Chess).

</details>


### [106] [ActiveSaddler: Automated Curriculum Learning for Agent Harness Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00906)
*Sungho Park,Wonjoong Kim,Jue Zhang,Wook-Shin Han,Pengfei Gao,Chanyoung Park,Yongqiang Yao,Rao Fu,Elsie Nallipogu,Qingwei Lin,Victor Rühle*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ActiveSaddler introduces automated curriculum learning for LLM agent harness optimization by treating the training scenario selection as a non-stationary bandit problem. It dynamically adapts the curriculum by modeling failure patterns as arms, estimating learning progress, and balancing exploration of new failures with exploitation of known weaknesses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing harness optimization methods focus on how to update the harness but keep the training scenarios fixed. The authors recognize that as the harness evolves, the most useful scenarios for further optimization change, requiring the curriculum itself to adapt alongside the harness.

Method: ActiveSaddler models the curriculum as a non-stationary bandit with dynamically instantiated optimization targets. It: (1) Abstracts recurring failures into reusable failure-pattern arms, (2) Estimates potential learning progress from targeting each pattern, (3) Adaptively balances revisiting known weaknesses with exploring unseen scenarios for new failure patterns. Optimization outcomes continually update both discovered failure patterns and their priorities.

Result: On GAIA2 and Terminal-Bench 2.0, ActiveSaddler improves test Pass@1 by 4.4 and 7.5 percentage points respectively over the same harness optimizer using fixed scenario ordering. Ablations confirm the importance of dynamic optimization target construction, evolving utility estimation, and balancing continued optimization with new failure discovery.

Conclusion: Automated curriculum learning is established as a new crucial optimization dimension for harness optimization. The co-evolution of the curriculum with the harness enables more effective LLM agent improvement.

Abstract: Automated harness optimization can substantially improve LLM agents by iteratively updating their prompts, tool interfaces, and control logic from execution feedback. However, existing methods primarily optimize how the harness is updated while largely fixing which training scenarios generate the feedback that drives those updates. As the harness evolves, the scenarios most useful for further optimization can change, suggesting that the training curriculum itself should adapt alongside the harness. We formulate this missing dimension of harness optimization as an automated curriculum learning problem and introduce ActiveSaddler. ActiveSaddler models the evolving curriculum as a non-stationary bandit with dynamically instantiated optimization targets. It abstracts recurring failures into reusable failure-pattern arms, estimates the potential learning progress from further targeting each pattern, and adaptively balances revisiting known weaknesses with exploring unseen scenarios for new ones. Optimization outcomes continually update both the set of discovered failure patterns and their priorities, allowing the curriculum to co-evolve with the harness. Experiments on GAIA2 and Terminal-Bench 2.0 show that ActiveSaddler consistently discovers stronger harnesses, improving test Pass@1 by 4.4 and 7.5 percentage points over the same harness optimizer using a scenario order fixed before optimization, respectively. Ablations further show that these gains depend on dynamically constructing optimization targets, estimating their evolving utility, and balancing continued optimization with new failure discovery. Together, these results establish automated curriculum learning as a new crucial optimization dimension for harness optimization.

</details>


### [107] [JevSpawn: Adaptive Agentic Inference through Compositional Action Spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00437)
*Haoyang Su,Weiran Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: JevSpawn is a compositional policy that combines natural language task specifications with finite probabilistic exploration, addressing the inefficiency of token-by-token LLM agent generation and the limitation of Jev-style models requiring pre-specified fields. It uses parallel action spawning with feedback-driven branch selection, representation revision, and recovery mechanisms to enable faster, more efficient autonomous task solving.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents generate reasoning and actions token by token, which is slow and computationally expensive. Jev-style models offer fast probabilistic predictions but require finite fields specified in advance, limiting autonomous task solving where available actions must be derived from natural language and adapted through interaction.

Method: JevSpawn employs parallel action spawning coupled with feedback-driven branch selection, representation revision, and recovery from retained alternatives. It uses shared action structure and model prefixes to reduce repeated generation and context computation without additional training.

Result: Evaluations on eight benchmark tasks against seven agent baselines and a TypeSafe Jev variant show JevSpawn achieves improved task performance and faster navigation.

Conclusion: JevSpawn represents a promising approach to structured agentic inference, combining the efficiency of Jev-style models with the flexibility of natural language task specifications.

Abstract: LLM agents generate intermediate reasoning and actions token by token, making extended interactions slow and computationally expensive. Jev-style models offer fast probabilistic predictions over finite fields, but require those fields to be specified in advance. This requirement limits autonomous task solving, where the available actions must be derived from natural language instructions and adapted through interaction. We introduce JevSpawn, a compositional policy that connects natural language task specifications to finite probabilistic exploration. Parallel action spawning is coupled with feedback driven branch selection, representation revision, and recovery from retained alternatives. Shared action structure and model prefixes reduce repeated generation and context computation without additional training. Evaluations on eight benchmark tasks against seven agent baselines and a TypeSafe Jev variant establish JevSpawn as a promising approach to structured agentic inference, with improved task performance and faster navigation.

</details>


### [108] [AVSD-Scenes: A Dataset for Audio-Visual Description of Urban Scenes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01861)
*Dhanunjaya Varma Devalraju,Arshdeep Singh,Mark D. Plumbley*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Natural language descriptions can provide rich semantic representations of audio-visual urban scenes, yet datasets that jointly describe both auditory and visual information remain limited. In this paper, we introduce AVSD-Scenes, a paired audio-visual scene description dataset for urban environments. The dataset contains 12,291 audio-visual scene descriptions generated from the TAU Urban Audio-Visual Scenes dataset. To construct the dataset, we first generate audio- and visual-based descriptions using Qwen2-Audio-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B, respectively. These modality-specific descriptions are then combined using large language models, namely Qwen3-14B, Mistral-Small-3.2-24B-Instruct-2506, and Gemma-3-27B-it, to produce multimodal descriptions that capture complementary information from both modalities. We benchmark AVSD-Scenes using semantic alignment, cross-modal retrieval, scene classification, LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, and human subjective assessment. Results show that multimodal descriptions improve semantic alignment and cross-modal retrieval performance compared with modality-specific descriptions while preserving strong scene-discriminative information. The generated descriptions achieve up to 94.5% accuracy in urban scene classification, while combining audio, visual, and description embeddings further improves accuracy to 95.4%. Furthermore, the descriptions remain highly scene-discriminative even when scene labels are removed from the prompting instructions, indicating that they capture semantic information derived from the audio-visual content rather than merely reflecting label information.

</details>


### [109] [Finding the Right Fit: Model-Harness Interactions across Agent Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00917)
*Yixuan Li,Yiyun Zhou,Yao Long Teng,Fuchao Yang,Yanchen Deng,Zhiyi Lyu,Xuyu Dong,Feng Chen,Bo An*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper evaluates 66 agent system configurations (4 harnesses × 5 models + native pairings) across 3 benchmarks, revealing that model rankings reverse across harnesses, and that model-harness-task combinations must be evaluated together rather than assuming a strong model or harness works universally.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research questions whether a strong language model, harness, or their pairing remains strong when the setting changes. It addresses the common assumption that a powerful model will perform well regardless of the harness, and vice versa.

Method: Evaluated 66 configurations: four configurable harnesses (OpenHands, DeepSeek Harness, PI, and openJiuwen) paired with five models on three benchmarks (TUA-Bench, ALE-CLI, Terminal-Bench 4), plus native Codex-GPT and Claude Code-Claude pairings. Analyzed 6,204 scored trajectories to understand why fit varies.

Result: Model rankings reverse across harnesses. On Terminal-Bench 4, Claude leads GPT by 7.94 points in OpenHands but trails by 30.16 points in PI. For 4/5 models, best harness changes across benchmarks. Exception: openJiuwen gives Kimi its highest score on all three benchmarks (5.61-11.11 point margins). Vendor harness is not reliably best; higher cost doesn't reliably buy higher score. GPT scores higher under PI than DSH at <1/4 the cost. Fit depends on whether harness hands failures back in usable form: GPT does best with PI's lean scaffold, while Kimi (prone to malformed tool calls) does best in openJiuwen.

Conclusion: The model, harness, and task should be evaluated together as a system. No single model or harness is universally superior; optimal pairing depends on the specific task and model characteristics. The study releases harness adapters, evaluation code, and all trajectories for reproducibility.

Abstract: Choosing an agent system means choosing both a language model and the harness through which it acts. We ask whether a strong model, harness, or pairing stays strong when the setting changes. We evaluate 66 configurations: four configurable harnesses (OpenHands, DeepSeek Harness, PI, and openJiuwen) paired with five models on TUA-Bench, ALE-CLI, and Terminal-Bench 4, plus the native Codex-GPT and Claude Code-Claude pairings. Model rankings reverse across harnesses. On Terminal-Bench 4, Claude leads GPT by 7.94 points in OpenHands but trails it by 30.16 points in PI. For four of the five models, the best harness changes from one benchmark to another, yet some pairings hold: openJiuwen gives Kimi its highest score on all three benchmarks, by 5.61 to 11.11 points. A model's own vendor harness is not reliably its best, and higher cost does not reliably buy a higher score. On Terminal-Bench 4, GPT scores higher under PI than under DSH at less than a quarter of the cost per task. Matched trajectories suggest why fit varies. Models start almost all repairs themselves, so much depends on whether the harness hands failures back in a form the model can use. GPT does best with PI's lean scaffold, while Kimi, which often issues malformed tool calls, does best in openJiuwen. We argue that the model, the harness, and the task should be evaluated together, and we release the harness adapters, evaluation code, and all 6,204 scored trajectories at https://github.com/liyix/finding-the-right-fit and https://huggingface.co/datasets/yixuanli97/finding-the-right-fit.

</details>


### [110] [Trustworthy Data- and ML-Ops for Intelligent Transportation Systems and Logistics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01282)
*Antonio Emanuele Cinà,Giovanni Scodeller,Cecilia Caterina Pasquale,Silvia Siri,Davide Anguita,Fabio Roli,Simona Sacone,Luca Oneto*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper reviews Trustworthy DataOps and MLOps in Intelligent Transportation Systems and Logistics (ITS&L), covering their necessity, key components, tools, case studies, and methods to strengthen trust in AI systems for real-world transportation and logistics applications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid evolution of ITS&L relies heavily on Data, AI, and ML integration, requiring improved efficiency, reliability, and decision-making precision in transportation and logistics services.

Method: Comprehensive literature review identifying gaps, exploring DataOps and MLOps complexities, examining trustworthiness methods and tools for AI in ITS&L scenarios.

Result: Provides foundational understanding of DataOps and MLOps in ITS&L, charts a path for further research in developing efficient, sustainable, and trustworthy intelligent transportation and logistics systems.

Conclusion: The paper serves as a vital resource for researchers, industry practitioners, and policymakers, addressing persisting challenges and future prospects in this rapidly advancing field.

Abstract: The rapid evolution of Intelligent Transportation Systems and Logistics (ITS\&L) has become a cornerstone of the modern social economy, relying heavily on the integration of Data, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and, more specifically, Machine Learning (ML). This paper provides a comprehensive review of Trustworthy Data and Machine Learning Operations (DataOps and MLOps) in the ITS\&L domain, underscoring their importance in improving efficiency, reliability, and decision-making precision within transportation and logistics services. We begin by identifying gaps in current literature, offering clear context for our contribution. Subsequently, we explore the complexities of DataOps and MLOps, discussing their necessity, key components, available tools, practical insights, and case studies relevant to ITS\&L. Additionally, we address the critical issue of Trustworthiness in AI applications, examining methods and tools designed to strengthen confidence in AI systems - especially in real-world ITS\&L scenarios. The paper concludes with a discussion of persisting challenges and future prospects in this rapidly advancing field, aiming to serve as a vital resource for researchers, industry practitioners, and policy makers. Overall, this work not only establishes a foundational understanding of DataOps and MLOps in ITS\&L but also charts a path for further research and innovation in developing more efficient, sustainable, and trustworthy intelligent transportation and logistics systems.

</details>


### [111] [Before Agents Decide: Epistemic Action in LLM-Based Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00511)
*Yizhi Liu,Balaji Padmanabhan,Siva Viswanathan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces the concept of "epistemic actions" from cognitive science into LLM-based agent design. It argues that agents should not only make decisions but also actively improve the evidence base for decisions through three modes: acquiring missing evidence, transforming available evidence, and probing systems to generate revealing responses. The authors term this "epistemic scaffolding" - the infrastructure that enables these evidence-improving actions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation stems from a gap in current LLM agent design: existing frameworks focus on search and exploration capabilities but neglect a fundamental question - whether the evidence needed for a decision is actually ready. The authors observe that humans naturally perform "epistemic actions" (like rotating objects or comparing alternatives) before difficult decisions to improve evidence quality, yet this principle is largely absent from agent architectures.

Method: The paper is a conceptual/position paper that draws on cognitive science literature to import the concept of "epistemic actions" into the LLM agent domain. It proposes a theoretical framework distinguishing three modes of epistemic actions and introduces "epistemic scaffolding" as a design principle for agent systems.

Result: The paper establishes a conceptual framework categorizing epistemic actions into three modes: (1) acquiring missing evidence, (2) transforming available evidence (e.g., reorganizing to reveal patterns), and (3) probing systems to create revealing responses. It defines "epistemic scaffolding" as the necessary interface, tools, and environmental support to enable these actions to be performed and audited.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that agent design must shift focus from merely executing decisions to actively producing "decision-ready evidence." It argues that epistemic scaffolding is essential for building more capable and trustworthy LLM-based agents that can recognize when evidence is insufficient and take appropriate actions to improve it before committing to decisions.

Abstract: Before a difficult decision, people often act simply to understand the situation better. We turn an object to see another side, place alternatives next to each other, or change one condition and observe what happens. These actions may not complete the task, but they improve the evidence needed for the next choice. LLM-based agents can search and explore, yet agent design gives less attention to an earlier question: is the available evidence ready for the decision? Sometimes necessary evidence is missing. In other cases, the evidence is present but its form hides what matters, or the comparison needed to judge it does not yet exist. Cognitive science calls actions that improve the basis for a later choice epistemic actions. We bring this idea to LLM-based agents and distinguish three modes: acquiring missing evidence, transforming available evidence, and probing a system to create a revealing response. We use the term epistemic scaffolding for the interfaces, tools, and environments that make these actions possible and auditable. This paper argues that agent design must address how decision-ready evidence is produced.

</details>


### [112] [MCRI: A Four-Dimensional Framework for Analyzing and Evaluating Agent Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01506)
*Zongrui Yang,Li Xintong,Runchen Xu,Zhongsheng Wang,Zhedong Lin,Haoyuan Li,Jiamou Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes MCRI Framework, a four-dimensional evaluation method for skills in modular agent architectures, based on information gain and behavioral constraint. Operationalized as MCRI-Eval (LLM-based), it improves top-1 skill selection by 17.7-22.8 percentile points across three benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As agents evolve from single-tool systems into modular, composite architectures, skills become important for capability development. However, the academic community lacks structured frameworks for systematically analyzing and evaluating skills.

Method: The authors propose the four-dimensional MCRI Framework based on information gain and behavioral constraint, operationalized as MCRI-Eval - an LLM-based evaluation method. They evaluated it using 63,812 public skills from OpenClaw Skill Hub with 58,275 skill-conditioned model executions across BigCodeBench, BFCL-Fundamental, and Mind2Web.

Result: MCRI-Eval scores are positively associated with community popularity signals and achieve the highest downstream ranking agreement. Compared to strongest baselines, skills selected by MCRI-Eval advance by 17.7, 22.8, and 19.6 percentile points in downstream performance rank on BigCodeBench, BFCL-Fundamental, and Mind2Web respectively.

Conclusion: MCRI-Eval provides a useful pre-execution signal for prioritizing promising skills before costly execution-based evaluation, enabling more efficient skill selection in modular agent systems.

Abstract: As agents evolve from single-tool systems into modular, composite architectures, skills are becoming an important mechanism for capability development and distribution. However, the academic community lacks a structured framework for systematically analyzing and evaluating skills. Drawing on information gain and behavioral constraint, we propose the four-dimensional MCRI Framework and operationalize it as MCRI-Eval, a large language model-based evaluation method. We evaluate MCRI-Eval using 63,812 public skills from the OpenClaw skill Hub, with 58,275 skill-conditioned model executions across BigCodeBench, BFCL-Fundamental, and Mind2Web. MCRI-Eval scores are positively associated with community popularity signals and achieve the highest downstream ranking agreement among the evaluated methods. MCRI-Eval also improves top-1 skill selection across all three benchmarks: compared with the strongest baseline on each benchmark, the skills selected by MCRI-Eval advance by 17.7, 22.8, and 19.6 percentile points in downstream performance rank on BigCodeBench, BFCL-Fundamental, and Mind2Web, respectively. These results indicate that MCRI-Eval provides a useful pre-execution signal for prioritizing promising skills before costly execution-based evaluation.

</details>


### [113] [Ontology-Based Contextual AI Evaluations (OB-CAIE) Methodology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00529)
*Julie Krugler Hollek,Michael Zargham,Mala Kumar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OB-CAIE is an ontology-based methodology for rigorous AI evaluation that uses two ontologies (DSO for what, EPO for how) to address scientific rigor, reproducibility, and the balance between human expertise and automation. It enables traceable failure analysis within a canonical problem space.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address three critical gaps in AI evaluation: (1) lack of scientific rigor from unclear testing coverage, (2) need to balance human expertise with automation, and (3) lack of reproducibility in AI testing environments.

Method: Developed two ontologies to represent the tractable problem space: Domain-Specific Ontology (DSO) defines the "what" being tested, while Evaluation Process Ontology (EPO) defines the "how" of evaluation. The methodology allows human judgment at specific, scientifically grounded points where human feedback is irreplaceable.

Result: OB-CAIE strengthens AI evaluations by clearly defining testing parameters (addressing the first step in the scientific method). Enables failure points to be traced, visualized, and analyzed within the canonical problem space. Supports one or multiple AI evaluations within a single problem space.

Conclusion: The methodology provides a scientifically grounded framework that balances automation with human expertise, particularly in complex subject areas where human feedback is genuinely irreducible. Its key advantage is the ability to trace and analyze failure points within a reproducible evaluation framework.

Abstract: The ontology-based contextual AI evaluation (OB-CAIE) methodology was developed to address a lack of scientific rigor that arises from unclear testing coverage, to balance human expertise and automations, and to address a lack of reproducibility of AI evaluation testing environments. OB-CAIE strengthens the current state of AI evaluations by addressing the first step in the scientific method by clearly defining what will be tested. Two ontologies represent the tractable problem space in the OB-CAIE methodology: the Domain-Specific Ontology (DSO) and the Evaluation Process Ontology (EPO). The DSO is the what; the EPO is the how. An OB-CAIE problem space can be used for one or multiple AI evaluations. The OB-CAIE methodology allows for human judgment at specific points, in scientifically grounded ways, and in complex subject areas where human feedback is genuinely irreducible or machine irreplaceable. A key advantage of the OB-CAIE methodology is that failure points can be traced, visualized and analyzed within the canonical OB-CAIE methodology problem space.

</details>


### [114] [Continuous Process-Level Evaluation for Evolving Enterprise AI Agent Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01833)
*Ngoc Phuoc An Vo,Aarya Doshi,Vadim Sheinin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a continuous evaluation framework for enterprise AI agents that detects process-level behavioral drift that traditional final-output evaluation misses. The framework combines outcome-level and process-level checks, including tool selection, arguments, execution order, and database integrity evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
