Motivation: Enterprise AI agent skills evolve as tool APIs, models, and specifications change, but final-output evaluation alone can miss process-level behavioral drift - meaning the AI may still produce correct outputs but through incorrect or changed processes.

Method: The framework independently computes per-run ground truth, materializes reusable template tests, and evaluates tool selection, arguments, execution order, and database integrity through programmatic checks and a narrowly scoped LLM judge. It was applied to Revenue and Productivity variants of a Business Value Determination skill in an enterprise Value Aware Resiliency system. Evaluation covered 240 trials across two skills, two specification variants, two agent harnesses, and three models.

Result: Key findings: (1) Of 175 trials passing all applicable final numerical checks, 162 (92.6%) contained another evaluator-detected deviation; (2) Under a broader seven-check final-state definition, 151 of 164 passing runs (92.1%) still violated a trajectory check; (3) Dependency attribution reduced mean failed checks from 6.34 to 2.65 roots; (4) Specification sensitivity varied by model and harness, with exploratory bootstrap interaction intervals excluding zero for all three Revenue comparisons and one of three Productivity comparisons.

Conclusion: The framework successfully detects behavioral drift that final-output evaluation misses. Runtime-resolved templates provide reusable regression coverage across configurations. However, longitudinal validation under actual API evolution remains future work.

Abstract: Enterprise AI agent skills evolve as tool APIs, models, and specifications change, yet final-output evaluation can miss process-level behavioral drift. We present a continuous evaluation framework combining outcome-level and process-level checks, applied to Revenue and Productivity variants of a Business Value Determination skill in an enterprise Value Aware Resiliency system. The framework independently computes per-run ground truth, materializes reusable template tests, and evaluates tool selection, arguments, execution order, and database integrity through programmatic checks and a narrowly scoped LLM judge. We evaluate 240 trials across two skills, two specification variants, two agent harnesses, and three models. Of 175 trials passing all applicable final numerical checks, 162 (92.6 percent; Wilson 95 percent CI: 87.7-95.6 percent) contained another evaluator-detected deviation. Under a broader seven-check final-state definition, 151 of 164 passing runs (92.1 percent; 95 percent CI: 86.9-95.3 percent) still violated a trajectory check. Dependency attribution reduced a mean of 6.34 failed checks per run to 2.65 roots. Specification sensitivity varied by model and harness, with exploratory bootstrap interaction intervals excluding zero for all three Revenue comparisons and one of three Productivity comparisons. Runtime-resolved templates provided reusable regression coverage across the evaluated configurations; longitudinal validation under actual API evolution remains future work.

</details>


### [115] [Science or Slop?: Benchmarking and Mitigating Scientific Slop in AI-Generated Papers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00531)
*Yerim Oh,Young-Jun Lee,Jaewoo Ahn,Gunhee Kim,Dongyeop Kang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces SciSlopBench, a benchmark dataset of 390 AI-generated scientific papers paired with human-written papers, and proposes six measures to detect "scientific slop" - AI-generated papers that appear plausible individually but have broken scientific reasoning. The study also presents SciSlopHarness, a framework to reduce scientific slop through evidentiary grounding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is that AI-generated scientific papers (AI slop) are increasingly common in academia, and existing token-based AI detectors fail to detect them because while each part looks plausible, the scientific reasoning connecting parts breaks down, misleading readers. The researchers aim to benchmark these failures and develop mitigation strategies.

Method: The researchers constructed SciSlopBench with 390 AI-generated papers (mostly in computer science but spanning life, social, and natural sciences), each paired with a human-written paper matched by research problem and contribution type. They developed six measures across Structure, Argument, and Artifacts. They also proposed SciSlopHarness, a harness-level framework that guides a fixed LLM to revise slop only where experiment records support the change.

Result: The six measures identify the AI paper in each pair with 85.9% accuracy, compared with 68.7% for Binoculars. Higher scientific slop correlates with lower ICLR ratings and distinguishes rejected from accepted papers above chance from 2017-2025. SciSlopHarness reduces the remaining AI-human gap by 63% over the strongest revision baseline without requiring human reference targets.

Conclusion: AI-generated scientific papers leave fundamental traces in their global reasoning. Responsible mitigation requires strict evidentiary grounding rather than mere prose refinement. The proposed measures effectively detect scientific slop, and SciSlopHarness provides a promising approach to reduce slop while maintaining scientific integrity.

Abstract: AI-generated content, often called AI slop, is increasingly common everywhere, particularly in academia. Slop in AI-generated scientific papers, however, has more complex patterns that cannot be easily detected by existing token-based AI detectors. Each part of such a paper looks plausible while the scientific reasoning that connects the parts breaks down, which can mislead how readers assess the work. We benchmark these failures as scientific slop through six measures across Structure, Argument, and Artifacts. We construct SciSlopBench with 390 AI-generated papers, mostly in computer science but spanning the life, social, and natural sciences, each paired with a human-written paper matched by research problem and contribution type. Our measures identify the AI paper in each pair with 85.9% accuracy, compared with 68.7% for Binoculars. Higher scientific slop accompanies lower ICLR ratings and distinguishes rejected from accepted papers above chance in every year from 2017 to 2025. Reducing these patterns, however, is not as simple as directly optimizing the measures. We therefore propose SciSlopHarness, a harness-level framework that guides a fixed LLM to revise slop only where the experiment records support the change. While standard revisions leave residual slop and direct slop-aware prompting triggers reward hacking, SciSlopHarness reduces the remaining AI-human gap by 63% over the strongest revision baseline without requiring human reference targets. Overall, we demonstrate that AI-generated scientific papers leave fundamental traces in their global reasoning, and that responsible mitigation demands strict evidentiary grounding rather than mere prose refinement.

</details>


### [116] [Worse Together: How Performance Breaks Down in Multi-User Multi-Agent Teams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00583)
*Sahan Paliskara,Nattaput Namchittai,Andrew Lampinen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper studies multi-user, multi-agent AI systems where different agents act for different users sharing common resources (codebase, calendar, budget). Across 5 frontier models and 77 scenarios in 4 environments, the authors compare a single coordinator agent serving all users versus teams of individual agents. Teams consistently underperform coordinators, with complete collapse in 2 environments without communication channels, and significant gaps even with communication. The paper identifies problematic behaviors (stalling, action overriding, fabricating claims) and proposes environment-specific mitigations (team lead, procedural instructions, platform checks). The authors will release three environments as MAMUBench.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI agents increasingly handle real-world tasks and encounter other agents over shared resources (codebases, calendars, budgets), coordination failures when each agent serves different users with different goals can lead to worse outcomes than if a single agent handled everything. This problem is understudied in multi-user, multi-agent settings.

Method: Experimental comparison across five frontier models and 77 scenarios in four environments: (1) API key environment sharing compute budget, (2) clinic sharing a calendar, (3) personal assistant sharing group orders/bookings, (4) merge queue sharing release cutoff. Each scenario compares: (a) single coordinator agent serving all users, (b) team of individual agents without communication, (c) team with communication channel. Tested mitigations: team lead, explicit procedural instructions, platform check (reading peers' messages before committing).

Result: Teams deliver worse group outcomes than the coordinator in every environment. Without communication channels, teams completely collapse in two environments. Even with communication, coordination overhead creates substantial gaps (e.g., coordinator fulfills ~2x more targeted user requests in personal assistant). Distinct failure behaviors identified: stalling as teams grow, overriding each other's actions, fabricating claims. Effective mitigations found but are environment-specific: team lead, explicit procedural instructions, and platform checks.

Conclusion: Multi-user, multi-agent coordination remains a significant challenge for current frontier models. Teams of agents consistently underperform coordinated single agents due to coordination failures and problematic behaviors. Environment-specific mitigations (team lead, procedural instructions, platform checks) can help but require tailoring to specific contexts. The release of MAMUBench (74 scenarios) will enable further research in this important area.

Abstract: People are increasingly delegating tasks to AI agents, and those agents are increasingly encountering other people's agents over shared resources such as a codebase, a calendar, or a budget. When each agent acts for a different user with different goals, coordination often fails, and the group ends up worse off than if a single agent had acted for everyone. We study this multi-user, multi-agent setting across five frontier models and 77 scenarios in four environments: an API key environment in which agents share a compute budget, a clinic in which they share a calendar, a personal assistant environment in which they share a group order or booking, and a merge queue in which they share a release cutoff. In each scenario, we compare a single agent that serves every user (a coordinator) to a team in which each agent serves one user, with and without a communication channel between the agents. Teams deliver worse group outcomes than the coordinator in every environment: without a channel, they completely collapse in two environments, and even with one, coordination overhead creates substantial gaps. For example, in the personal assistant environment, the coordinator fulfills a targeted user request about twice as often as teams. We identify distinct behaviors associated with this poor group-level performance, including stalling as teams grow, overriding each other's actions, and fabricating claims. We find effective but environment-specific mitigations, such as a team lead, explicit procedural instructions, and a platform check that makes an agent read its peers' messages before committing. We will release the API key, clinic, and personal assistant environments as MAMUBench, comprising 74 scenarios for evaluating multi-user, multi-agent coordination.

</details>


### [117] [Legal Research Bench: Measuring End-to-End Reliability in Long-Horizon Legal Research Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00609)
*Katrina Drozdov,Oliver Chen,Langston Nashold,Rayan Krishnan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Legal Research Bench (LRB) is a benchmark of 413 U.S. legal research questions designed to evaluate language model agents on legal workflows. Testing 13 frontier models with search and retrieval tools, the best model (Claude Opus 4.8) achieved only 42.9% full correctness, revealing that current LLM agents remain unreliable for legal research tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Legal research is time-consuming but critical—errors can render answers unusable. While LLMs are natural fits for this retrieval-intensive workflow, reliability is paramount since missing authorities or wrong conclusions are unacceptable. This motivated the creation of a rigorous benchmark to evaluate LLM performance on real legal research tasks.

Method: LRB contains 413 expert-written open-ended U.S. legal research questions with gold answers, supporting authorities, and binary grading rubrics. The authors evaluated 13 frontier models using a harness with web search, case-law search, page parsing, and retrieval tools. They used "all-pass grading" where responses are correct only if every required criterion is satisfied AND cited authorities verify. Expert attorneys validated the LLM judge.

Result: Claude Opus 4.8 was the best performer at 42.9% fully correct. Performance varied by legal area and was lower when reconciling conflicting authorities. More tool calls, turns, or inference cost did not predict higher accuracy.

Conclusion: Current LLM agents remain far from reliable for legal research. Even the best models fail on over half of questions, with significant variation across task types. The all-pass grading methodology reveals that partial success is insufficient—every element must be correct for the answer to be usable.

Abstract: Legal research is a core and time-consuming legal workflow. Lawyers must identify controlling authority, verify that it remains valid, reconcile statutes and cases, and synthesize a grounded answer. Language model agents are a natural fit for this retrieval-intensive workflow, and automating even part of it would be valuable. But that value depends on reliability: a single missing authority, stale citation, or wrong legal conclusion can make an otherwise plausible answer unusable. We introduce \textbf{Legal Research Bench} (LRB), a benchmark of 413 open-ended U.S. legal research questions written by experts, each paired with a gold answer, supporting authorities, and a binary grading rubric. We evaluate thirteen frontier models in a harness with web search, case-law search, page parsing, and retrieval tools. We score agent responses through all-pass grading with source verification, where a response is correct only if every required criterion is satisfied and its cited authorities verify. We also validate the LLM judge against expert attorneys ensuring that benchmark scores track attorney judgment. Agents remain far from reliable: among the models we tested, the strongest, Claude Opus 4.8, is fully correct on 42.9\% of questions. Performance also varies substantially by task setting: all-pass rates differ across areas of law and are lower on questions requiring reconciliation of conflicting authorities. Across models, more turns, tool calls, and inference cost do not predict higher accuracy.

</details>


### [118] [Spatial Strategies, Not Actions: Vector-Quantized Geodesics as Tools for LLM-Driven Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00613)
*Gabriel Turinici*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a novel LLM-based agent architecture that combines geometrical tools with a LLM orchestrator for spatial understanding in grid-world environments. The approach uses geodesic trajectory collection and vector quantization for tool discovery, while the LLM handles reasoning and decision-making. When tested with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B in a 2D grid environment, this approach achieves comparable goal-reaching rates to chain-of-thought methods while reducing decision time from minutes to seconds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based agents are criticized for lacking spatial understanding and exploiting statistical text patterns rather than true spatial reasoning. This research aims to address this limitation by combining geometric tools with LLM reasoning in a hierarchical architecture.

Method: The architecture combines: (1) Geodesic trajectory collection from the environment, (2) Vector quantization to extract representative trajectory subsets, (3) LLM offline association of natural language descriptions to trajectories (making them "tools"), (4) LLM online tool selection based on current state and goal, (5) Low-level primitive actions executing the selected trajectory. The approach separates learning into two levels: tool discovery via unsupervised trajectory quantization, and reasoning/decision-making via the LLM. Tested with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B in a partially observable dynamic 2D grid environment, using a zoom tool and collision detection tool.

Result: The geometry-derived tool library paired with zoom and collision detection tools allowed a fast, non-reasoning configuration to match the goal-reaching rate of a much more costly chain-of-thought version, while reducing decision time from minutes to seconds.

Conclusion: This approach effectively addresses LLM spatial comprehension limitations by combining geometric tools with LLM orchestration. The hierarchical separation between tool discovery (unsupervised) and reasoning (LLM) enables efficient spatial reasoning with significantly reduced computational cost while maintaining performance.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) based agents are often criticized for lacking spatial understanding and mainly exploiting statistical text patterns. We investigate their spatial comprehension through an architecture combining geometrical tools with a LLM serving as a high-level orchestrator in grid-world environments. The agent first collects geodesic trajectories, which are then vector-quantized to extract a representative subset. Offline, the LLM associates a natural language description of the underlying behavioral patterns to each selected trajectory, making it a tool. Online, the LLM chooses the appropriate tool conditioned on the current state and goal. Low-level control is handled by primitive actions that execute the trajectory associated with the tool. From an agentic AI perspective, this approach separates learning into two levels: tool discovery is handled through unsupervised quantization of trajectories, while reasoning and decision-making are handled by the LLM. We test the approach in a partially observable dynamic 2D grid environment with an open vision-language model (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B). Pairing the geometry-derived tool library with an agent-centered zoom tool and a collision detection tool lets a fast, non-reasoning configuration match the goal-reaching rate of a much more costly chain-of-thought version, while cutting the cost of a decision from minutes to seconds.

</details>


### [119] [CompMat-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Computational Materials Science](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00636)
*Chenmu Zhang,Levi Felix,Jun-Jie Zhang,Xingfu Li,Xuelian Jiang,Tao Jiang,Subhendu Mishra,Xixi Qin,Boris Yakobson*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CompMat-Bench is a benchmark of 94 computational materials research tasks that evaluates AI agents without running expensive simulations by having agents prepare inputs and analyze pre-computed outputs. The benchmark tests single tasks and workflows under full or reduced guidance, achieving pass rates of 66.0-90.4% with full guidance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluating AI agents on scientific research tasks is impractical due to the time and resources required for expensive simulations. The authors needed a way to assess agents on real materials research steps without repeating costly computations.

Method: The benchmark pre-reproduces 94 research steps from published computational materials studies. Agents are evaluated on preparing inputs and analyzing outputs for these simulations. Grading uses fixed rules without LLM judges, supporting four conditions: single tasks/workflows × full/reduced guidance.

Result: With full guidance on single tasks, agents based on three LLMs achieve pass rates of 66.0-90.4% across 94 tasks. Longer workflows and reduced guidance lower pass rates, especially for weaker agents. The strongest agent only fails when long workflow combines with reduced guidance. Most failures (66.0-90.4%) are attributed to scientific errors rather than software usage errors.

Conclusion: CompMat-Bench provides a practical benchmark for comparing AI agents on materials research steps and analyzing failure modes. The key insight is that most agent failures stem from scientific errors, not technical errors, indicating the need for better scientific reasoning in AI agents.

Abstract: Evaluating AI agents on scientific research tasks is constrained by the time and resources required for the underlying experiments or calculations. In computational materials research, repeating the same expensive simulations across agents and trials can make evaluation impractical. We introduce CompMat-Bench, a benchmark of 94 tasks derived from recently published computational materials studies, each asking agents to complete a step toward achieving the study's scientific goal. We reproduce the research steps in advance and assess agents on preparing inputs and analyzing outputs for expensive simulations, so expensive simulations can be avoided during evaluation. The reproduced inputs and results serve as ground truth for grading agents with fixed rules, without an LLM judge. The benchmark supports four evaluation conditions: single tasks and workflows composed of related tasks, each with full or reduced methodological guidance. With full guidance on single tasks, agents based on three LLMs demonstrate the ability to complete individual materials research steps, with pass rates of 66.0-90.4% across 94 tasks. Both longer workflows and reduced guidance can limit agent performance, but in different ways for different agents: they lower the pass rates of the weaker agents, whereas the strongest agent falls only when a long workflow is combined with reduced guidance. Failure analysis attributes most failures to scientific errors rather than to errors in software usage. CompMat-Bench provides a basis for comparing agents on the steps of real materials research and for analyzing agent failure modes.

</details>


### [120] [Incident-Arena: Getting agents to the last nine of reliability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00648)
*Andre Fu,Malik Drabla,Leon Liu,Meji Abidoye,Marek Suppa,Lata Mishra,Adnan El Assadi,Yiyuan Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces Incident-Arena, a benchmark for evaluating AI coding agents in production incident response (agentic SRE). The benchmark consists of 20 real-world tasks deployed on ephemeral Kubernetes clusters with injected faults and load profiles. Testing frontier models across 3 application substrates reveals poor performance (below 64.3% success rate), with failures stemming from diagnosis errors, incomplete repairs, and unsafe regressions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While AI coding agents are widely used in software engineering, their capability for production incident response remains under-explored. Existing benchmarks are limited by unrealistic environments (toy repositories), non-standard framework implementations, and simple static verifiers - none of which adequately reflect real-world SRE challenges.

Method: The authors created Incident-Arena, a human-built benchmark with 20 carefully selected tasks grounded in real-world deployed open source software. Each task: (1) deploys a production application to an ephemeral Kubernetes cluster, (2) injects a fault from the config layer through underlying images, (3) applies a sustained load profile given task requirements. They developed a novel verification method using functional verifiers that hold system-level metrics stable while ensuring repairs are done safely - going beyond static checks.

Result: Agent trials averaged 2.81M tokens and 41 turns, demonstrating long-horizon reasoning. Across 20 tasks and 3 application substrates, frontier models achieved less than 64.3% success rate. Failures extended from diagnosis/localization errors, through incomplete repairs, to unsafe regressions.

Conclusion: The benchmark reveals significant gaps in current frontier models' ability to handle production incident response. The combination of realistic environments, complex fault injection, and functional verification exposes limitations in agents' diagnostic reasoning, repair completeness, and safety enforcement. This work provides a more rigorous evaluation framework for agentic SRE systems.

Abstract: AI coding agents are ubiquitous in engineering workflows amongst industry and academia. Yet, despite their use in app coding, relatively less attention has been paid to their ability to execute on production incident response. This emerging field, termed agentic site-reliability-engineering (SRE) contains benchmarks limited by (1) unrealistic environments, typically toy repositories (2) non-standard framework implementations and (3) simple static verifiers. We introduce Incident-Arena, a human-built benchmark of 20 carefully selected tasks grounded in real-world deployed open source software. Each task deploys a production application to an ephemeral Kubernetes cluster, injecting a fault from the config layer through underlying images, and a sustained load profile given the task requirements. We also present a novel verification method, going beyond static checks to functional verifiers, holding systems level metrics stable, while ensuring repairs are done safely. Agent trials run an average of 2.81M tokens and 41 turns, going beyond existing benchmarks, demonstrating agentic long horizon reasoning. Across 20 tasks and 3 application substrates, frontier models score below 64.3%, with failures extending from diagnosis/localization errors, through incomplete repairs and unsafe regressions.

</details>


### [121] [Agent Evaluation Reliability: More Tasks Won't (Always) Fix An Agent Leaderboard](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00651)
*Michael Hardy,Ruhana Azam,Anka Reuel,Mykel Kochenderfer,Sanmi Koyejo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper develops a Bayesian variance-decomposition framework to assess the reliability of LLM agent evaluations. The analysis of 22 benchmarks reveals that while fixed model-scaffold systems rank reliably (0.935-0.994), underlying model reliability is substantially lower (0.148-0.841). The study demonstrates that scaffold choice affects conclusions, more tasks cannot resolve all uncertainty, and pooling diverse benchmarks can improve reliability at lower cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agent evaluations are increasingly used to compare LLMs and inform deployment decisions, yet ranks may reflect evaluation conditions (scaffolds, tasks) rather than the models themselves. This raises questions about what conclusions current agent evaluations reliably support.

Method: Bayesian variance-decomposition framework applied to 22 benchmarks from the Holistic Agent Leaderboard and Harbor Index. The framework separates signal (performance differences relevant to the intended claim) from noise (irrelevant variation that can change rankings).

Result: Four key findings: (1) Fixed model-scaffold systems rank reliably (0.935-0.994), while underlying-model reliability is substantially lower (0.148-0.841). (2) Scaffold choice can change conclusions - inter-scaffold reliability varies substantially across evaluations. (3) More tasks cannot resolve all uncertainty - even infinitely many tasks improve model-ranking reliability by at most 0.097 when uncertainty is dominated by limited scaffold coverage. (4) Pooling diverse benchmarks can improve cross-task rankings - raising projected reliability from 0.44 to 0.75 at the same task budget and reducing cost by up to 83%.

Conclusion: Evaluation design should follow the intended claim: identify what a score or ranking should mean, diagnose what limits its reliability, and spend evaluation budget on the sources of uncertainty that matter. The distinction between ranking fixed systems versus underlying models is critical for appropriate interpretation.

Abstract: Agent evaluations are increasingly used to compare LLMs and inform deployment decisions, yet ranks can reflect not only the model but also the effects of the evaluation conditions such as the scaffolds or tasks. This makes reliability claim-dependent: an evaluation that reliably ranks deployed systems may not reliably rank underlying models. We ask which conclusions current agent evaluations reliably support and what additional evaluation would improve them. We develop a Bayesian variance-decomposition framework for sparse, imbalanced agent leaderboards and apply it to 22 benchmarks from the Holistic Agent Leaderboard and Harbor Index. The framework separates signal, performance differences relevant to the intended claim, from noise, irrelevant variation that can still change rankings. We find: (1) Reliability depends on the measurement goal. Fixed model-scaffold systems are ranked reliably (0.935-0.994), while underlying-model reliability is substantially lower (0.148-0.841). (2) Scaffold choice can change conclusions. Inter-scaffold reliability measures whether scaffolds preserve model rankings, showing that scaffold effects vary substantially across evaluations. (3) More tasks cannot resolve all uncertainty. Even infinitely many similarly constructed tasks improve model-ranking reliability of a benchmark by at most 0.097 when uncertainty is dominated by limited scaffold coverage. (4) Pooling diverse benchmarks can improve cross-task rankings at lower cost. For rankings across diverse agentic tasks, pooling benchmarks raises projected reliability from 0.44 to 0.75 at the same task budget and can reduce projected cost by up to 83\%. Evaluation design should follow the intended claim: identify what a score or ranking should mean, diagnose what limits its reliability, and spend evaluation budget on the sources of uncertainty that matter.

</details>


### [122] [When More Data Is Not Enough: The Context-Sufficiency Frontier in Generative AI Personalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00654)
*Merieme Askour,Ayoub Merimi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces a "context sufficiency theory" for generative AI personalization, arguing that the relevance of context matters more than its volume. Through experiments at a home-furnishing retailer, the authors identify four states of context (insufficiency, sufficiency, saturation, interference) and propose the Context-Sufficiency Frontier to find the minimal relevant context set.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The problem stems from generative AI's ability to supply dynamic situational context at response time. While this flexibility is powerful, the authors observed that more context is not always better—irrelevant context can actually harm personalization quality. This creates a need to understand the optimal amount and type of context to provide.

Method: The authors developed a theoretical framework (context sufficiency theory) and tested it via a full-factorial experiment with a generative recommender system at a large home-furnishing retailer.

Result: Relevant context improved appropriateness ratings, while irrelevant context reduced appropriateness and destabilized retrieval. This validated the theory that context relevance matters more than context volume.

Conclusion: The framework shifts personalization paradigm from "more context is better" to identifying what the interaction actually requires and enforcing constraints throughout the service process. The Context-Sufficiency Frontier helps locate the minimal relevant context set.

Abstract: Personalization has long relied on customer data to infer what an individual is likely to value. We call this customer evidence: the customer's historical behavior and preferences. Generative AI extends personalization by allowing providers to supply changing situational information at the moment a response is produced, without encoding every condition in advance. We define this provider-side context as information about what is possible, permitted, or advisable now. This flexibility creates a new problem: once context becomes easy to supply, more is not necessarily better. We develop a theory of context sufficiency in which the relevance of context to the customer's current intent matters more than its volume. The theory identifies four states, insufficiency, sufficiency, saturation, and interference, and introduces the Context-Sufficiency Frontier to locate the minimal relevant set. In a full-factorial experiment with a generative recommender at a large home-furnishing retailer, relevant context improved appropriateness, while irrelevant context reduced it and destabilized retrieval. The framework shifts personalization from supplying more context toward identifying what the current interaction actually requires and enforcing constraints throughout the service process.

</details>


### [123] [Backdoor Containment via Expert Quarantine and Shutdown in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00663)
*Jianwei Li,Min-Seon Kim,Jung-Eun Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces "Quarantined Expert Shutdown" (QES), a novel backdoor defense strategy for LLMs that allows backdoor formation during training but routes it into a designated quarantined component that can be disabled at deployment. The method uses MoE-like architecture with LoRA branches and auxiliary routing objectives, reducing attack success rate from 100% to 0-10% while preserving model utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing backdoor defenses either suppress backdoor learning or learn then purify. This paper proposes a third strategy: "learn, but channel" - allowing backdoor formation but routing it into a quarantined component that can be disabled at deployment time through a single constant-time operation.

Method: QES augments a Transformer-based LLM with routed expert-specific LoRA branches and lightweight routers. It uses auxiliary routing objectives to attract trigger-conditioned behavior into a designated expert while preserving benign capability elsewhere. At deployment, mitigation involves simply zeroing the quarantined expert's routing weight.

Result: The method reduces attack success rate (ASR) from 100% to 0-10% across two tasks, three attacks, and four model families, while downstream utility is often preserved or only modestly affected.

Conclusion: The "learn, but channel" strategy represents a previously unexplored regime for backdoor containment in generative LLMs, offering a computationally efficient containment approach that requires no trigger screening or further model weight updates at deployment.

Abstract: Backdoored large language models (LLMs) can behave normally on benign inputs while producing attacker-specified outputs under hidden triggers. Existing defenses span four stages--prior-training, in-training, post-training, and inference-time--and share one of two underlying strategies: either suppress backdoor learning (by filtering poisoned data or interrupting its acquisition during optimization) or learn, then purify (by repairing model weights or gating inputs after a fully backdoored model has formed). We propose a third strategy, learn, but channel: allow backdoor formation during training but route it into a designated, quarantined component that can be disabled at deployment. To this end, we propose Quarantined Expert Shutdown QES, a computationally efficient containment strategy built in a regularization-steered MoE-like setting. Specifically, given a poisoned dataset, QES augments a Transformer-based language model with routed expert-specific LoRA branches and lightweight routers, and uses auxiliary routing objectives to attract trigger-conditioned behavior into a designated expert while preserving benign capability elsewhere. At deployment, mitigation reduces to a single constant-time operation: zeroing the quarantined expert's routing weight, without trigger screening or further updating model weights. Empirically, our methods reduce the attack success rate ASR from 100% to 0-10% on most settings across two tasks, three attacks, and four model families, while downstream utility is often preserved or only modestly affected. These results establish learn, but channel as a previously unexplored regime for backdoor containment in generative LLMs.

</details>


### [124] [A Simple Doxastic Deontic Logic for Norm-Guided Decision Making](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00668)
*Thorsten Engesser,Agata Ciabattoni*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces a doxastic deontic logic framework for autonomous systems to make decisions under conflicting norms and unreliable information. It combines Chellas' Minimal Deontic Logic with multi-agent KD45 belief systems, defining a norm compliance optimization problem that distinguishes subjective (belief-based) from objective (fact-based) optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous systems face fundamental challenges when making decisions: norms may conflict, information may be incomplete or unreliable, and agents must act despite uncertainty about both facts and the norms themselves. Existing deontic logics lack the ability to handle these doxastic (belief) aspects alongside normative reasoning.

Method: The authors develop a classically reducible fragment of Chellas' Minimal Deontic Logic, extended with explicit conditional norms and combined with multi-agent KD45 (a belief logic allowing agents to have beliefs about beliefs). This enables norms to depend on agents' beliefs about both facts and other norms. They then formalize the Doxastic Norm Compliance Optimization Problem and analyze two variants: subjective optimization (minimizing violations relative to the agent's beliefs) and objective optimization (minimizing violations relative to actual facts).

Result: The paper provides conditions under which (i) subjective and objective optimization coincide, and (ii) optimal decision-making can be efficiently computed via reduction to weighted partial MaxSAT in polynomial time.

Conclusion: This work bridges deontic logic, belief logic, and optimization theory, providing a formal framework for normatively constrained autonomous decision-making under uncertainty. The polynomial-time reduction to MaxSAT enables practical implementation for real-world autonomous systems.

Abstract: Making decisions despite conflicting norms and incomplete or unreliable information is a fundamental challenge for autonomous systems. We introduce a simple doxastic deontic logic for this setting: a classically reducible fragment of Chellas' Minimal Deontic Logic, extended with explicit conditional norms and combined with multi-agent KD45, so that norms can depend on agents' beliefs about both facts and norms. On this logic we define the Doxastic Norm Compliance Optimization Problem, where an agent chooses a decision minimizing weighted norm violations. We distinguish subjective optimization (relative to the agent's beliefs) from objective optimization (relative to the actual facts). We give conditions under which (i) the two coincide and (ii) optimal decision-making can be reduced to weighted partial MaxSAT in polynomial time.

</details>


### [125] [Ontology-Grounded, Reasoner-Verified Benchmarks for Evaluating LLM Reasoning in Scientific AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00682)
*Nishtha N. Vaidya,Stephan Grimm,Thomas Hubauer,Thomas A. Runkler*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents an automated pipeline for generating ontology-grounded multiple-choice question (MCQ) benchmarks from OWL 2 ontologies to evaluate logical reasoning in large language models (LLMs). The method creates correct answers directly from ontology axioms and generates distractors by perturbing class expressions, with incorrectness verified by OWL reasoners. The pipeline was evaluated on three ontologies (Pizza, PMDco, DOID) producing 17,819 MCQs, with six LLMs achieving 41.1-76.8% accuracy, demonstrating the benchmarks are challenging and discriminative.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation stems from critical gaps in evaluating LLMs for scientific AI applications: (1) LLMs increasingly power scientific AI systems requiring logical reasoning (biomedical QA, materials informatics), but they often produce factual inaccuracies; (2) Current evaluation benchmarks have scalability issues - manual dataset construction doesn't scale, and LLM-based generation risks embedding the very flaws being measured; (3) High-quality benchmarks require both correct and incorrect examples grounded in explicit, formally verifiable background knowledge using standard reasoners.

Method: The proposed pipeline works as follows: (1) Generate correct answers by design - directly grounded in the ontology axioms; (2) Generate distractors by perturbing the right-hand-side class expressions of class definition axioms; (3) Formally verify incorrectness of distractors using an OWL reasoner via entailment checks; (4) Distractors span four semantic categories: class unsatisfiability, equivalentTo violations, subsumption violations, and weakened subsumptions; (5) Evaluate natural language quality using LLM judges for fluency and similarity metrics between correct answers and distractors.

Result: The pipeline was evaluated on three diverse ontologies: Pizza (small, academic), PMDco (complex, materials science), and DOID (large, biomedical), generating 112, 2,491, and 15,216 MCQs respectively (total: 17,819). Natural language quality: mean LLM judge scores of 4.02, 4.36, and 3.36 out of 5 for fluency; correct-answer-to-distractor similarity above 0.8. Six LLMs evaluated zero-shot achieved 41.1-76.8% accuracy, well above the 25% random-guessing baseline, indicating the benchmarks are challenging and discriminative.

Conclusion: This work represents a significant step toward more reliable benchmarks for assessing logical reasoning in scientific AI. The key contributions include: (1) A scalable, automated pipeline for generating high-quality MCQ benchmarks from any sufficiently axiomatized OWL 2 ontology; (2) Formal verification of both correct and incorrect answers using OWL reasoners; (3) Diagnostic evaluation capability through four semantic categories of distractors; (4) Empirical validation showing benchmarks are challenging but solvable, with LLMs achieving above-chance performance but significant room for improvement. The approach addresses the critical need for robust evaluation of logical reasoning in scientific LLM applications.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly underpin scientific AI applications that reason over structured knowledge, from biomedical question answering to materials informatics. However, their logical reasoning often falls short, producing factual inaccuracies unacceptable in these settings. Reliable evaluation remains challenging: manual dataset construction scales poorly, and LLM-based generation risks embedding the very flaws it aims to measure. High-quality benchmarks must ground both correct and incorrect labelled examples in explicit background knowledge, formally verifiable by a standard reasoner. We propose a pipeline that automatically generates ontology-grounded multiple-choice question (MCQ) benchmarks from any sufficiently axiomatised OWL 2 ontology, with correct answers grounded in the ontology by design. Distractors are generated by perturbing the right-hand-side class expressions of class definition axioms, and their incorrectness is formally verified by an OWL reasoner via entailment checks. We evaluate the pipeline on three ontologies: Pizza (small, academic), PMDco (complex, materials science), and DOID (large, biomedical), generating 112, 2,491, and 15,216 MCQs respectively. Distractors span four semantic categories from class unsatisfiability to weakened subsumptions, enabling diagnostic evaluation of specific reasoning failures. Items meet natural language quality standards: mean LLM judge scores of 4.02, 4.36, and 3.36 out of 5 confirm fluency, and correct-answer-to-distractor similarity above 0.8 shows that wrong options cannot be dismissed on surface form alone. Six LLMs evaluated zero-shot achieve 41.1-76.8% accuracy, well above the 25% random-guessing baseline, indicating the benchmarks are challenging and discriminative. This work is a step towards more reliable benchmarks for assessing logical reasoning in scientific AI.

</details>


### [126] [Backdoor Purification for LoRA-Tuned LLMs via Null-Space Projection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00685)
*Jianwei Li,Jung-Eun Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a novel method to purify LoRA-tuned LLMs from backdoor attacks without relying on strong assumptions (trigger knowledge, clean references, or retraining). The approach uses null-space projection to remove backdoor directions while preserving both base model capabilities and downstream task adaptation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid adoption of LLMs and PEFT methods has increased backdoor attack risks. Existing purification methods have limitations: they require prior knowledge of triggers, access to clean references, or aggressive retraining, and lack comprehensive evaluations. These constraints limit practical applicability.

Method: The method involves: (1) extracting high-fidelity backdoor directions through careful data curation and feature approximation; (2) constructing orthogonal null spaces in both input and output channels for each layer or head; (3) projecting LoRA updates onto these null spaces. The approach scales from single-layer text classification to full-parameter LLM in generative tasks through ablation studies.

Result: The null-space projection method reduces attack success rate (ASR) from nearly 100% to less than 10%, while preserving the base model's benign performance and the adapter's learned abilities during downstream task adaptation.

Conclusion: The proposed null-space projection approach effectively purifies LoRA-tuned LLMs without requiring prior knowledge of triggers, clean references, or post-hoc retraining. This method provides a practical solution for defending against backdoor attacks in parameter-efficient fine-tuned LLMs.

Abstract: With the rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods, the risk of backdoor attacks has become more severe. Existing backdoor purification methods typically rely on at least one of the strong assumptions, such as prior knowledge of triggers, access to clean references, or aggressive retraining, and they often lack comprehensive evaluations. These constraints substantially limit their practical applicability. To overcome these challenges, our work proposes purifying LoRA-tuned LLMs without these assumptions and even without post-hoc retraining of the suspect parameters. Our objective is to significantly reduce the attack success rates (ASR) while preserving both (i) the base model's general capabilities and (ii) the new downstream skills learned through the adapter. Through a series of ablation studies, we progressively scale our approach from a single layer in a text classification setting to a full-parameter LLM in the generative task. Through careful data curation and feature approximation, we extract high-fidelity backdoor directions and, for each layer or head, construct orthogonal null spaces in both the input and output channels, onto which the LoRA updates are projected. Empirically, our null-space projection method reduces the ASR from nearly 100% to less than 10%, while preserving the base model's benign performance and the adapter's learned abilities during downstream task adaptation.

</details>


### [127] [R-GroundBench: A Diagnostic Benchmark for R-Group Groundingin Markush Molecular Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00700)
*Xin Wang,Zichuan Ying,Xinna Lin,Junqi Zhang,Hanyi Xiong,Tianyu Gao,Hairong Zhang,Qixiang Hua,Botian Shi,Zhenhailong Wang,Kaicheng Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: R-GroundBench is a diagnostic benchmark for evaluating AI models' ability to reason over Markush structures (chemical molecular families with variable R-group placeholders). It features multiple-choice VQA tracks with controlled difficulty and an open-ended Generation track. Results reveal substantial performance gaps: models achieve >90% on Easy VQA but only 56-66% on Hard VQA, while chemical-domain VLMs achieve merely 25.7-46.2% on Hard VQA. Generation exact match remains below 20% (below 8% with visual input).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing molecule-language benchmarks focus on fully specified molecules, leaving R-group grounding (linking variable R-groups to actual molecular substituents) largely unevaluated. Markush structures are ubiquitous in pharmaceutical patents but current AI systems lack reliable grounding and execution for Markush editing.

Method: Built R-GroundBench from real patent Markush structures with two tracks: (1) Multiple-Choice VQA track with controlled difficulty and modality splits, and (2) Open-ended Generation track. Tested various models including chemical-domain VLMs.

Result: Easy VQA: >90% accuracy. Hard VQA: 56-66% (when shortcuts controlled). Chemical-domain VLMs: 25.7-46.2% on Hard VQA. Generation Exact Match: <20% for most models, <8% when visual input required.

Conclusion: Current AI systems lack reliable grounding and execution for Markush editing. There is a substantial gap between recognition and molecular grounding, highlighting significant challenges for AI-driven scientific discovery in pharmaceutical patent analysis.

Abstract: Recent advances in AI for scientific discovery enable molecular understandingand design, yet reasoning over incomplete chemical representations remainsunclear.Markush structures, which encode molecular families through variable R-groupplaceholders (\textit{R\textsubscript{1}}, \textit{R\textsubscript{2}}, \textit{X}, etc.), are ubiquitous in pharmaceutical patents and requiregrounding across molecular, textual, and chemical information.However, existing molecule-language benchmarks focus on fully specifiedmolecules, leaving R-group grounding largely unevaluated.We introduce R-GroundBench:, a diagnostic benchmark built from real patent Markushstructures, featuring a Multiple-Choice (VQA) track with controlled difficultyand modality splits, and an open-ended Generation track.Our results reveal a substantial gap between recognition andmolecular grounding.While models achieve over 90\% accuracy on Easy VQA, performance drops to56--66\% on Hard VQA when shortcuts are controlled.Chemical-domain VLMs also remain unreliable, achieving only 25.7--46.2\% on HardVQA despite domain-specific pretraining.Moreover, Generation Exact Match remains below 20\% for most models and below8\% when visual input is required.These findings reveal that current AI systems lack reliable grounding andexecution for Markush editing, highlighting challenges for AI-drivenscientific discovery.

</details>


### [128] [Meta-Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Fast Adaptation of Interactive Policies with Applications to Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00705)
*Huiwen Yan,Kyriakos G. Vamvoudakis,Mushuang Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a meta-multi-agent reinforcement learning (meta-MARL) framework that enables rapid adaptation of interactive policies across different multi-agent scenarios modeled as Markov games. It introduces the concept of meta-NE (meta Nash Equilibrium) and provides theoretical guarantees for the gradient-play-based algorithm.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing meta-RL approaches focus on single-agent systems, but extending them to multi-agent systems is challenging because tasks involve both environmental factors and agents' strategic interactions. This work addresses the need for fast adaptation of interactive policies in multi-agent systems.

Method: 1) Model MARL problems as Markov games (MGs)
2) Develop a meta-MARL framework for rapid policy adaptation across a distribution of MGs
3) Define meta-NE as the solution concept
4) Establish sufficient conditions for equivalence between meta-NE and stationary points of gradient-play-based meta-MARL algorithm

Result: The proposed meta-MARL method achieves faster adaptation than pretrained MARL baselines on autonomous-driving tasks, validating the framework's effectiveness.

Conclusion: The meta-MARL framework successfully enables fast adaptation of interactive policies in multi-agent systems, with theoretical guarantees and empirical validation in autonomous driving scenarios.

Abstract: This paper develops a meta-multi-agent reinforcement learning (meta-MARL) framework to enable fast adaptation of interactive policies in a multi-agent system (MAS). Meta-reinforcement learning (meta-RL) enables agents to rapidly adapt to new tasks/environments using a bi-level optimization mechanism. However, existing meta-RL generally focuses on single-agent systems. Extending these frameworks and algorithms to multi-agent systems poses additional challenges, as tasks are characterized by not only the environment but also agents' strategic interactions. To address these challenges, we model multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) problems as Markov games (MGs) and develop a meta-MARL framework for rapid interactive policy adaptation across a distribution of MGs. A new concept, called meta-NE, is defined to describe the desired solution concept in a meta-MARL problem. Sufficient conditions for the equivalence between a meta-NE and a stationary point of the gradient-play-based meta-MARL algorithm are established. Our evaluation on autonomous-driving tasks demonstrates that the proposed meta-MARL method achieves faster adaptation than pretrained MARL baselines, validating the effectiveness of our framework.

</details>


### [129] [ReLiveGym: Evaluating Long-Lived Agents over Weeks of Replayed Reality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00710)
*Xisen Jin,Jingheng Li,Zhenglun Chen,Junyi Du,Xiang Ren*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ReLiveGym is a diagnostic evaluation environment for long-lived LLM agents that operate unattended for days/weeks, acting sparsely over simulated weeks of real-world news, market, and social-media streams. The study evaluates 8 base language models across tasks with varying time sensitivity, reasoning intensity, and recurrence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing long-horizon agent work assumes static environments, but real-world deployment requires agents to operate unattended for extended periods, act at the right timing, and adapt to dynamically changing environments over time. This gap necessitated a new evaluation framework.

Method: The authors introduce ReLiveGym, a diagnostic environment that simulates weeks of chronologically replayed real-world data streams (news, market, social media). They evaluate 8 base language models across diverse tasks with varying time sensitivity, reasoning intensity, and recurrence. They also evaluate continuous learning from hindsight feedback.

Result: Action timing mechanism is a critical harness-design axis for long-lived tasks; optimal design varies across tasks and sometimes model choices. Continuous learning from hindsight feedback improves performance and addresses failure modes observed in these long-lived tasks.

Conclusion: Model choice, action timing mechanism, and use of feedback are important considerations in designing long-lived LLM agents. The study provides a valuable diagnostic tool for evaluating agents in temporally dynamic, long-horizon scenarios.

Abstract: As large language model (LLM) agents become widely adopted, they are increasingly deployed for tasks that require persistent monitoring or recurring actions (e.g., market analysis). These agents are expected to operate unattended for days or weeks, act at the right timing, and adapt to the dynamic environment over time. These challenges are not fully captured in the existing long-horizon agent work, as they often consider a static environment that is not temporally changing. We introduce ReLiveGym, a diagnostic evaluation environment of long-lived tasks in which agents act sparsely over simulated weeks of chronologically replayed real-world news, market, and social-media streams. The tasks span diverse levels of time sensitivity, reasoning intensity, and recurrence. Across eight base language models, we investigate how model choice and harness design affect agent performance on such long-lived tasks. Our results show that how agents determine when to act arises as an important harness-design axis for long-lived tasks; and that the optimal design varies across tasks and sometimes model choices as well. We also evaluate how continuous learning from hindsight feedback affects performance and addresses failure modes observed in these long-lived tasks. These findings indicate model choice, action timing mechanism, and use of feedback as important considerations in the design of long-lived agents. Code: https://github.com/SaharaLabsAI/ReLiveGym

</details>


### [130] [Robust Nash Alignment under Preference Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00715)
*Shihab Ahmed,Debamita Ghosh,David Tang,Yudan Wang,Alvaro Velasquez,Yue Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes Robust Nash Alignment, a game-theoretic framework for training AI systems to perform well under uncertain human preferences. It addresses the brittleness of existing alignment methods that optimize against a single preference model by formulating a robust optimization problem that guarantees worst-case performance against any preference kernel within an uncertainty set.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Preference-based alignment methods typically optimize against a single preference model, making them brittle when pairwise preferences are uncertain—noisy, heterogeneous, or shift after deployment. The authors aim to address this limitation by developing a framework that provides certified lower bounds on worst-case performance when preferences are uncertain.

Method: The authors formulate a robust optimization problem where a major learner seeks a policy with large worst-case win rate against both an adversarial competitor and any preference kernel in an ambiguity set around nominal preferences. They introduce a four-player primal-dual proxy game (leader policy, follower policy, adversarial kernel, and dual variable) and develop a single-loop optimistic mirror descent-ascent algorithm. The proxy lower-bounds the truncated hard-constrained objective, with an exactness condition under which it recovers the robust objective.

Result: The proxy always lower-bounds the truncated hard-constrained objective with a quantifiable gap. The algorithm achieves O(1/√T) average-iteration convergence for the proxy-game duality gap, yielding a near-optimal robust policy. Experiments on controlled tabular games and LLM alignment with uncertain preferences validate the convergence theory and show improved performance over nominal baselines.

Conclusion: The Robust Nash Alignment framework provides a principled approach for aligning AI systems to uncertain human preferences, with theoretical guarantees on worst-case performance. The game-theoretic formulation and optimistic mirror descent algorithm offer a computationally tractable solution with provable convergence, demonstrated empirically to outperform nominal alignment methods.

Abstract: Preference-based alignment methods typically optimize against a single preference model, and can therefore be brittle when pairwise preferences are uncertain: noisy, heterogeneous, or shift after deployment. To address these issues, we propose Robust Nash Alignment, a game-theoretic framework for alignment to uncertain pairwise preferences. Our formulation has a major learner seeking a policy with a large worst-case win rate against both an adversarial competitor and any preference kernel lying in an ambiguity set around a nominal preference. When the ambiguity set captures the uncertainty in preferences, the resulting robust objective of the game directly yields a certified lower bound on worst-case performance. However, we note this problem is computationally challenging to optimize, and to address this, we introduce a four-player primal-dual proxy game involving the leader policy, follower policy, adversarial kernel, and dual variable, and develop a single-loop optimistic mirror descent-ascent algorithm for it. We show that the proxy always lower-bounds the truncated hard-constrained objective, quantify the proxy-to-hard gap, and characterize an exactness condition under which the proxy recovers the robust objective. We then prove an \(\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{T})\) average-iteration convergence for the proxy-game duality gap, which implies a near-optimal robust policy for the original robust objective. Experiments on controlled tabular games and LLM alignment with uncertain preference further validate the convergence theory and show improved performance over nominal baselines.

</details>


### [131] [Enterprise Representation Simplification (ERS): Reducing Representational Complexity for Enterprise AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00791)
*Terry Dorsey,Kevin Huggins*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces Enterprise Representation Simplification (ERS) as a framework for reducing unnecessary complexity in enterprise information representations while preserving essential information. It also proposes Enterprise Representation Complexity (ERC), a representation-neutral model with four dimensions (Objects, Interactions, Behaviors, Supporting Sources) for comparing complexity across different representation states. The paper explores two consequences: an economic model for lifecycle costs and the impact of reduced complexity on AI system reasoning accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise information artifacts accumulate over time, creating representational complexity that must be maintained by enterprises and interpreted by both human consumers and AI systems. This growing complexity creates challenges for maintenance, governance, and AI interpretation, necessitating a systematic approach to understanding and reducing representational complexity.

Method: The paper develops a conceptual framework (ERC) with four dimensions: Representation Objects, Interactions, Behaviors, and Supporting Sources. ERC is defined at both representation and task levels to enable comparison between different representational states. An economic model is proposed to distinguish recurring global costs, recurring task-level costs, and one-time transformation costs over a defined time horizon.

Result: The paper establishes that: (1) representational structures create lifecycle obligations across maintenance, governance, dependencies, change, enhancement, and operation; (2) reductions in task-level ERC reduce the representational extent an AI system must identify, relate, and interpret; (3) evidence from Text-to-SQL research shows that reduced schema and reasoning complexity can improve reasoning accuracy.

Conclusion: ERC serves as a framework of measurable architectural variables for comparing representational alternatives, transformation effects, economic outcomes, and AI reasoning performance—not as a universal complexity, performance, or cost metric. The framework enables distinguishing architectural simplification from retrieval optimization and provides a foundation for evaluating enterprise representation decisions.

Abstract: Enterprise information is represented through artifacts shaped by applications, projects, technologies, organizational boundaries, and local requirements. These structures accumulate over time, creating representational complexity that must be maintained by the enterprise and interpreted by information consumers and AI systems. This paper introduces Enterprise Representation Simplification (ERS) as reducing unnecessary representational complexity while preserving required information within a defined scope, and Enterprise Representation Complexity (ERC), a representation-neutral model for comparing complexity across representation states.
  ERC characterizes representational extent through four dimensions: Representation Objects, Interactions, Behaviors, and Supporting Sources. Objects, Interactions, and Behaviors form dependent categories, while Supporting Sources characterize representation exposure. ERC is defined at representation and task levels, enabling comparison and distinguishing architectural simplification from retrieval optimization.
  The paper develops two consequences of ERS. First, representational structures create lifecycle obligations for maintenance, governance, dependencies, change, enhancement, and operation. An economic model distinguishes recurring global representation cost, recurring task-level cost, and one-time transformation cost, enabling evaluation over a defined time horizon. Second, reductions in task-level ERC reduce the representational extent an AI system must identify, relate, and interpret. Text-to-SQL research provides evidence that reduced schema and reasoning complexity can improve reasoning accuracy.
  ERC is not a universal complexity, performance, or cost metric. It provides measurable architectural variables for comparing representational alternatives, transformation effects, economic outcomes, and AI reasoning performance.

</details>


### [132] [Sapien: A Stateful Policy Engine for Autonomous AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00797)
*Corinn Tiffany,Wen Zhang,Eugene Bagdasarian,Lillian Tsai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Sapien is a policy engine for enforcing stateful contextual policies on AI agents to prevent rogue actions in multi-step tasks. It uses regular expressions extended with stateful predicates, deferred policy generation, and scoped semantic checks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing contextual security defenses cannot handle multi-step tasks where action validity depends on what the agent has already done and learned. Current approaches lack the ability to specify permitted tool-call sequences in a stateful manner.

Method: Sapien specifies permitted tool-call sequences using: (1) regular expressions extended with stateful predicates, (2) deferred policy generation, and (3) scoped semantic checks. This allows the policy to adapt based on the agent's execution history and learned information.

Result: Sapien maintains high utility—within a few percent of an unconstrained agent. When the agent is fully hijacked, Sapien's policies block 93-95% of attacks on AgentDojo and 62-85% on Toolathlon, which is twice as effective as tool allowlists on long-horizon tasks.

Conclusion: Sapien effectively balances security and utility by enforcing stateful contextual policies. It significantly reduces attack surface while preserving most of the agent's functionality, outperforming simple tool allowlist approaches.

Abstract: Contextual security defenses prevent AI agents from taking rogue actions by synthesizing a task-specific policy and enforcing it on the agent's tool calls. In multi-step tasks, however, which actions are valid often depends on what the agent has already done and learned. We present Sapien, a policy engine for enforcing stateful contextual policies. A Sapien policy specifies permitted tool-call sequences using a regular expression extended with stateful predicates, deferred policy generation, and scoped semantic checks. We show that Sapien stays within a few percent of an unconstrained agent's utility. Even if the agent is fully hijacked, Sapien's policies rule out 93-95% of attacks on AgentDojo and 62-85% on Toolathlon (twice as many as tool allowlists on long-horizon tasks).

</details>


### [133] [Kepler: Auditable World Models for ARC-AGI-3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00834)
*Wensen Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Kepler is an open-source evaluation harness for ARC-AGI-3 that uses executable world models to represent and validate agent hypotheses. Under a frozen Claude Opus 5 configuration, it achieved 100.00 RHAE on all 25 public games with no per-game model selection, using 858M tokens at $777.72 cost. The study reveals three evaluation failures and shows that public-set score has limited discriminative value.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ARC-AGI-3 evaluates agents in interactive environments where rules and objectives must be inferred from observation. The authors aim to create a robust evaluation harness that can properly assess agent capabilities without common pitfalls like source-code leakage or harness reconstruction.

Method: Kepler represents hypotheses as executable world models and validates them through retrospective transition checks and conditional prediction checks. The evaluation uses a single frozen Claude Opus 5 configuration without per-game model selection or score-conditioned reruns.

Result: Achieved 100.00 RHAE on all 25 public games. 181 of 183 completed levels used no more actions than median-human baseline. 8,256 environment actions used (7,292 in scored levels). 858.0 million tokens processed, 97.37% cache reads, $777.72 cost. Three evaluation failures identified: source-code leakage, harness reconstruction, and autonomous repair masking broken planner. 48 of 50 game-model cells reached 100%.

Conclusion: Public-set score alone has limited discriminative value. The results motivate first-attempt, cost-conditioned, and verification-aware reporting for fair agent evaluation. Animation frames contain task-relevant information absent from settled text grids.

Abstract: ARC-AGI-3 evaluates agents in interactive environments whose rules and objectives must be inferred from observation. We present Kepler, an open-source harness that represents hypotheses as executable world models and validates them through retrospective transition checks and conditional prediction checks. Under one frozen Claude Opus 5 configuration, Kepler obtained a server-verified 100.00 RHAE on all 25 public games, with no per-game model selection or score-conditioned reruns. On 181 of 183 completed levels, the final Opus attempt used no more actions than the corresponding median-human baseline. The retained board runs used 8,256 environment actions, of which 7,292 occurred in scored levels. Retained local provider-session records yield 858.0 million tokens, 97.37% cache reads, and a \$777.72 cost at September 1, 2026 API list-equivalent rates. We also report three evaluation failures: source-code leakage that produced an invalid perfect run, agents reconstructing a removed harness in a control condition, and autonomous repair masking a broken planner. A single-game observation case study showed that animation frames contained task-relevant information absent from settled text grids. Across the final Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol boards, 48 of 50 game-model cells reached 100. These results indicate that public-set score alone has limited discriminative value and motivate first-attempt, cost-conditioned, and verification-aware reporting.

</details>


### [134] [Learning Multiple Timescales for Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00849)
*Pedro Robles Dutenhefner,Dikshant Shehmar,Wagner Meira,Marlos C. Machado*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL) for long-horizon tasks. The key insight is that temporal abstraction (treating k steps as one transition) can restore value signals across long distances, but no single k works optimally for all state-goal distances. The proposed GITA method conditions a value function on k and aggregates advantage-weighted supervision across multiple k values, retaining both local resolution and long-range signal without committing to a single temporal abstraction level.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline GCRL struggles with long-horizon tasks because discounting shrinks value differences between distant states below function approximation error, eliminating the signal needed to rank states. While temporal abstraction (k-step transitions) can restore this signal, fixed k values create a trade-off: large k preserves long-range differences but collapses nearby distinctions, while small k does the reverse. This fundamental trade-off needed a solution that doesn't require choosing a single k.

Method: Generalized Implicit Temporal Abstraction (GITA) conditions a single value function on the temporal abstraction parameter k. Instead of selecting a single k, GITA trains one policy by aggregating advantage-weighted supervision across multiple k values, where scales assigning larger positive advantages to state-goal pairs contribute more strongly to updates. This approach retains both local resolution and long-range signal without committing to a fixed k.

Result: On OGBench, GITA outperforms a broad range of offline GCRL baselines. It raises average success rate across all tasks by 25 percentage points (73% relative improvement) over HIQL, and by 7 percentage points (14% relative) over the strongest fixed-k method OTA.

Conclusion: GITA successfully addresses the temporal abstraction trade-off in offline GCRL by leveraging multiple k values simultaneously. The significant improvements over both HIQL and OTA demonstrate that aggregating advantage-weighted supervision across multiple temporal abstraction levels is a promising approach for long-horizon goal-conditioned tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results on the OGBench benchmark.

Abstract: Existing approaches to offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL) struggle with long-horizon tasks. Discounting shrinks value differences between distant states until they fall below the function approximation error, leaving the agent with no signal for ranking states. Temporal abstraction, which treats k environment steps as a single transition, restores this signal at long range, but no single fixed k suits all state-goal distances: large k preserves value differences across long temporal distances while collapsing distinctions between nearby states, and small k does the reverse. We make this trade-off explicit and introduce Generalized Implicit Temporal Abstraction (GITA), which conditions a single value function on k. GITA trains one policy by aggregating advantage-weighted supervision across multiple k values, so scales assigning larger positive advantages to a state-goal pair contribute more strongly to its update. GITA does not need to choose between local resolution and long-range signal; it retains both without committing to a single k. On OGBench, GITA outperforms a broad range of offline GCRL baselines, raising average success rate across all tasks by 25 percentage points (73% relative improvement) over HIQL. It also improves over the strongest fixed-k method, OTA, by 7 percentage points (14% relative).

</details>


### [135] [An Educator-Guided LLM Pedagogical Agent for Scaffolded Feedback in Conceptual Database Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00870)
*Sara Riazi,Pedram Rooshenas*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An LLM-based pedagogical agent provides scaffolded feedback for database design (ER diagrams) through a four-stage workflow, with hidden diagnosis separated from controlled feedback disclosure. Evaluation across 383 episodes showed 71.1% of student revisions incorporated the diagnostic targets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Provide effective, scaffolded feedback in database design education by grounding responses in multiple sources (student work, requirements, rubrics, resources) while controlling how and when feedback is disclosed to students.

Method: Four-stage workflow architecture: (1) concept checks, (2) guided application, (3) low-detail feedback, (4) localized clarification. Separates hidden diagnostic layer from student-facing feedback control. Deployed across three ERD environments with 383 feedback episodes; mixed-methods evaluation combining quantitative change tracking and qualitative survey analysis.

Result: 71.1% of observed target-level changes fully or partially incorporated the hidden diagnostic target, including many after early stages. Staged disclosure sometimes withheld inaccurate details, supported selective uptake, and allowed later recovery. Survey favored delayed disclosure and student agency but noted indirectness and repetition.

Conclusion: Staged feedback disclosure in LLM pedagogical agents can effectively support student learning in conceptual database design, though trade-offs exist between feedback indirectness and student agency. The architecture shows promise for scaffolding in educational AI systems.

Abstract: We present an educator-guided LLM pedagogical agent for scaffolded feedback in conceptual database design. Integrated into an entity--relationship diagram (ERD) editor, the system grounds feedback in the student artifact, assignment requirements, educator-authored rubrics, and instructional resources. Its architecture separates hidden, artifact-grounded diagnosis from the workflow that controls the form and disclosure level of student-facing support.
  We instantiate the architecture as a four-stage workflow progressing from concept checks and guided application to low-detail feedback and localized clarification. Each feedback request creates a stateful episode linked to versioned ERD states. In a deployment spanning three ERD environments and 383 feedback episodes, 71.1\% of observed target-level changes fully or partially incorporated the hidden diagnostic target, including many after Stages~1--2. Qualitative analysis showed that staged disclosure sometimes withheld inaccurate details, supported selective uptake, or allowed later recovery, though some errors still shaped revisions. Survey responses from a self-selected sample favored delayed disclosure and student agency but noted indirectness and repetition.

</details>


### [136] [MemFit: Efficient Long-Term Agentic Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00872)
*Mitchell Piehl,Muchao Ye*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemFit is a long-term memory system for conversational agents that reduces memory operation costs and latency by using LLM-free insertion (appending turns verbatim), segment summaries for indexing, and multi-path retrieval combining lexical and semantic signals with cross-encoder reranking over caption-augmented episodes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current memory systems for LLMs rely on expensive LLM agents to organize and consolidate memory, resulting in costly and inefficient write operations. These systems either require costly LLM calls for memory construction or discard surface-level details through compression.
