Method: MemFit uses three key strategies: (1) Append-only store with LLM-free insertion storing each turn verbatim with near-instantaneous indexing using segment summaries; (2) LLM-free multi-path retrieval combining lexical and semantic signals; (3) Cross-encoder reranking over caption-augmented episodes for both textual and multimodal settings.

Result: MemFit achieves state-of-the-art performance on three widely used benchmarks (LoCoMo, MemGallery, and LongMemEval-S) while reducing memory construction time and cost several-fold.

Conclusion: MemFit provides a scalable and efficient solution for persistent agentic memory, significantly reducing cost and latency compared to existing systems while maintaining or improving retrieval accuracy.

Abstract: Long-term memory systems for large language models (LLMs) have gained popularity for extending reasoning capabilities across applications. Current memory systems rely on LLM agents to organize and consolidate memory, resulting in costly, inefficient write operations. To address this limitation, we propose MemFit, a long-term memory system for conversational agents that reduces the cost and latency of memory operations. Unlike existing systems that rely on expensive LLM calls for memory construction or discard surface-level details through compression, MemFit stores each turn verbatim in an append-only store with near-instantaneous, LLM-free insertion, indexing turns with segment summaries rather than replacing them. Additionally, MemFit uses an LLM-free, multi-path retrieval strategy that combines lexical and semantic signals with cross-encoder reranking over caption- augmented episodes in both textual and multimodal settings. Empirical results on three widely used benchmarks, LoCoMo, MemGallery, and LongMemEval-S, show that MemFit achieves state-of-the-art performance while reducing memory construction time and cost several-fold, providing a scalable and efficient solution for persistent agentic memory.

</details>


### [137] [OR for AI That Does OR: Routing LLMs up the Escalator inside the OSCAR Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00912)
*Jinzhi Bu,Haixin Tang,Huanan Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OSCAR is an LLM-based framework that uses a certified offline Simulator to verify and improve optimization models generated by LLMs. It treats model improvement as sequential decision-making, achieving 95-100% accuracy on benchmarks while costing 3-6x less than commercial LLMs like Codex and Claude Code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs can translate business descriptions into optimization models, but may produce incorrect formulations (misrepresenting constraints/objectives) or miss better solutions even when feasible. Organizations need accurate, low-cost, locally-deployable solutions for repeated optimization modeling tasks.

Method: OSCAR uses: (1) an offline Simulator certified against labeled decision examples to compare candidate models; (2) continues searching beyond feasibility to find better solutions; (3) models search as sequential decisions under unobserved difficulty (which LLMs to call, when to stop). Provides cost-ordered escalation for known-prior settings and prior-free competitive guarantees for general menus.

Result: On five benchmark problems: OSCAR achieves 95-100% accuracy using two small open-weight LLMs (single-attempt accuracies 29% and 48%). Compared to Codex and Claude Code, OSCAR costs 3.1x and 5.8x less respectively. Supports both local (single GPU) and cloud deployment.

Conclusion: Organizations should maintain labeled decision examples of feasible/infeasible decisions to clarify operating rules. OSCAR follows these labels when LLM interpretations conflict. Its simple operating rules and adjustable settings help adapt to changing LLM capabilities and prices.

Abstract: Large language models can translate business descriptions into optimization models, but executable code may misrepresent constraints or objectives. A solver can then return an optimal solution to the wrong problem. Even when the solution satisfies the intended operating rules, a better plan may exist. For organizations that repeatedly use optimization modeling, an LLM-based framework should produce accurate formulations at low cost and, ideally, run locally. We study how to verify improvements and allocate attempts across LLMs that differ in price and capability. We develop OSCAR (Optimization modeling by Simulator, Coder, And Reviewer), which uses an offline Simulator certified against labeled decision examples to compare candidates and continues searching beyond feasibility. We model the search for the next certified improvement as sequential decisions under unobserved difficulty: which LLMs to call and when to stop. In a simplified known-prior setting, we give conditions under which cost-ordered escalation is optimal. For general menus, we derive a prior-free competitive guarantee. On five benchmark problems, OSCAR achieves 95% to 100% accuracy at the reported settings using two small open-weight LLMs, each deployable locally on a single GPU. Their single-attempt accuracies average 29% and 48%. In five runs per problem, Codex and Claude Code incur average token costs 3.1 and 5.8 times OSCAR's, respectively. OSCAR supports open-weight models locally or in the cloud, depending on budget and confidentiality requirements. Firms should maintain labeled decision examples of feasible and infeasible decisions to clarify plain-language operating rules. OSCAR follows these labels when an LLM's interpretation conflicts with them. As LLM capabilities and prices change, OSCAR's simple operating rules and adjustable settings help firms adapt their model choices and benefit from these advances.

</details>


### [138] [ABDA-NL: A Natural-Language Scenario Explorer for Argument-Based Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00947)
*Shawn Bowers,Martin Caminada,Haoyang Liu,Bertram Ludäscher*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ABDA-NL is a natural-language interface for ABDA (Argument-Based Discussion system) that allows users to interact with argument-based reasoning through plain English, visualize discussion games, explore what-if scenarios, and query reference documents, with an LLM bridging human language and formal argumentation formalism.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To make argument-based reasoning systems more accessible to users by providing a natural language interface that allows non-technical users to understand, explore, and interact with formal argumentation frameworks without needing to understand the underlying formalisms.

Method: The system uses a large language model as an intermediary to translate between natural language and formal representations. The LLM answers questions from documents and current scenario state, and translates plain-English edits into candidate formal statements. All proposals are validated by the deterministic ABDA engine and confirmed by the user before execution.

Result: Users can view accepted/rejected/undecided conclusions, interactively explore the grounded discussion game to understand why outcomes occurred, explore what-if scenarios by suspending assumptions/rules or changing preferences, ask questions answered from reference documents, and author new facts, assumptions, and rules in plain English.

Conclusion: ABDA-NL successfully bridges the gap between formal argumentation systems and human users by combining LLMs with a deterministic reasoning engine, ensuring both accessibility and correctness through user validation of all proposals.

Abstract: ABDA-NL adds a natural-language interface to ABDA, a system for argument-based discussion using ASPIC- knowledge bases under grounded semantics. Users see which conclusions are accepted, rejected, or undecided, open an interactive rendering of the grounded discussion game to learn why, explore what-if alternatives by suspending assumptions and rules or changing preferences, ask questions that are answered from a scenario's reference documents, and author new facts, assumptions, and rules in plain English. A large language model provides the bridge between language and formalism: it answers questions from the documents and the current state of the scenario, and it translates plain-English edits into candidate formal statements. The deterministic ABDA engine remains the sole source of arguments, attacks, and acceptance labels, and every proposal of the model is validated and confirmed by the user before it takes effect.

</details>


### [139] [PG-SFT: Balancing Capability Acquisition and Retention in Offline Agent Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00949)
*Ronghua Li,Zi Liang,Zhishan Li,Shinan Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Standard SFT on offline agent trajectories harms base model capabilities (reasoning, tool calling, code generation) while improving target task performance. PG-SFT uses turn-level information gain to adjust supervision strength, achieving better trade-off between acquiring new skills and preserving existing ones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard SFT forces models to imitate reasoning and actions token-by-token, which damages other capabilities of the base model. The authors seek to balance acquiring new capabilities while preserving existing ones during agent trace SFT.

Method: Proposed Privilege-Guided SFT (PG-SFT) leverages turn-level information gain of agent trajectories as an indicator to adaptively adjust supervision strength. Compared baselines include standard SFT, KL penalty for constraining distributional drift, and limiting update magnitude.

Result: Standard SFT improves target benchmarks but lowers non-target benchmark scores. KL penalty and update magnitude limiting did not avoid regression. PG-SFT substantially reduces distributional drift and broad capability degradation while maintaining a favorable trade-off, at the cost of slight degradation in target-task performance.

Conclusion: Balancing acquisition-retention trade-off depends not only on anchoring the model to base behavior, but also on where and how strongly supervision should depart from that behavior.

Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on offline agent trajectories is the standard approach for training specialized tool-using agents, but forcing models to imitate reasoning and actions token by token may harm other capabilities (e.g., general reasoning, tool calling, code generation) of the base model. In this work, we focus on studying \emph{how to better balance the trade-off between acquiring new capabilities and preserving existing ones during agent trace SFT}. By comparing several baselines in our setup, standard SFT improves the target benchmark while lowering several non-target benchmark scores; meanwhile, simply constraining distributional drift using KL penalty or limiting the update magnitude did not avoid this regression trend. Motivated by recent token-wise adaptive learning objectives, this work proposes \textbf{Privilege-Guided SFT (PG-SFT)} to leverage turn-level information gain of agent trajectories as an indicator to adjust supervision strength. PG-SFT yields a more favorable observed trade-off on the evaluated benchmarks, substantially reducing distributional drift and broad capability degradation at the cost of slight degradation in target-task performance. Our findings suggest that balancing the acquisition--retention trade-off depends not only on whether the model is anchored to its base behavior, but also on where and how strongly supervision should depart from that behavior.}

</details>


### [140] [Cybernetic and Epistemic: A Missing Vocabulary for Trustworthy Agentic Delegation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00961)
*Jérémie Lumbroso*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the shift from code writing to AI supervision in CS education, identifying a critical vocabulary gap between "cybernetic" language (coordinating action) and "epistemic" language (coordinating understanding). The authors argue that current AI oversight systems fail by accepting "explanation-shaped output calibrated for approval rather than truth" — essentially rubber-stamping. They propose a governance criterion: every consequential AI choice should carry the condition under which it would have gone otherwise, testable by third parties. They introduce a "two-part reconstruction test" and a deliberation-recording convention (ORRCF) to make this operational.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The bottleneck in AI-assisted code generation has shifted from writing code to supervising AI systems. However, the field lacks a working distinction between two functions language serves in delegation: coordinating action (cybernetic) versus coordinating understanding (epistemic). Current oversight mechanisms only check whether output was approved, which can be satisfied by rubber-stamping, rather than requiring accountable reasoning.

Method: The authors present three delegation episodes (illustrations, not controlled evidence), one public record where a recommendation was withdrawn on its own stated terms, and one failure case illustrating oversight requiring no reasons. They propose a governance criterion and operationalize it via a two-part reconstruction test and ORRCF convention.

Result: The paper proposes: (1) A governance criterion requiring every consequential choice to carry its counterfactual condition (what would have gone otherwise) in a testable form; (2) A two-part reconstruction test scoring delegation records by whether a second reader can predict agent behavior under perturbation; (3) ORRCF convention making the counterfactual condition a required component of recorded choices.

Conclusion: Without requiring counterfactual conditions, third parties cannot distinguish genuine decisions from rubber stamps. The proposed criterion and ORRCF convention provide an operational framework for epistemic oversight that makes AI reasoning retrievable and checkable, moving beyond mere approval-checking to genuine accountability.

Abstract: As code generation is increasingly delegated to AI systems, the bottleneck is shifting from writing code to supervising the systems that write it --- a shift CS-education researchers have begun to name. This shift exposes a vocabulary gap: the field asks for "human oversight" without a working distinction between the two things language does in a delegation channel --- coordinate action (cybernetic: words succeed when the world comes to match them) and coordinate understanding (epistemic: they succeed when they answer to the world and a hearer can check that they do). The failure this names is not cybernetic language but epistemic-form language doing cybernetic work: explanation-shaped output calibrated for approval rather than truth. Oversight that checks only whether an output was approved is satisfiable by rubber-stamping; oversight that holds an agent accountable requires the reasoning behind its work be retrievable and checkable. We present three delegation episodes --- illustrations, not controlled evidence --- in which epistemic engagement proved practicable while remaining auditable, one public record where a recommendation was withdrawn on its own stated terms, and one failure case illustrating oversight that requires no reasons for its discretionary choices. We propose a criterion for agentic-system governance, alongside existing technical trust properties: every consequential choice should carry the condition under which it would have gone otherwise, in a form a third party can test. Without such a condition, a third party cannot distinguish a decision from a rubber stamp. We give the criterion an operational form --- a two-part reconstruction test scoring a delegation record by whether a second reader can predict what the agent does under a perturbation --- and a deliberation-recording convention, ORRCF, that makes the condition a required component of every recorded choice.

</details>


### [141] [VeriHarness: Scaling Agentic Verification for Long-Horizon Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00972)
*Caiqi Zhang,Rujun Han,Zifeng Wang,Zoey CuiZhu,Nigel Collier,Tomas Pfister,Chen-Yu Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VeriHarness is an agentic verification framework that strengthens LLM output verification for complex, long-horizon tasks by transforming the base model into an interactive verifier with workspace, evidence tools, and reusable skills. It uses disagreement resolution and consensus challenging mechanisms to identify correct claims and detect hidden errors, achieving significant performance gains across multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM agents handle increasingly complex, long-horizon tasks, verifying their outputs becomes challenging, especially without reference answers or grading rubrics at test time. While repeated sampling yields multiple rollouts with complementary correct claims, there lacks a reliable verification mechanism to determine which claims to trust.

Method: VeriHarness transforms the underlying LLM into an agentic verifier by providing: (1) a workspace for evidence gathering, (2) evidence tools for environmental verification, and (3) reusable verification skills. It employs two key mechanisms: (a) Disagreement Resolver - checks competing claims against environmental evidence, and (b) Consensus Challenger - tests shared claims and searches for omitted requirements. Findings guide final artifact selection and revision.

Result: Across five long-horizon workspace benchmarks and two frontier models (Gemini 3.5 Flash and Claude Opus 4.8), VeriHarness achieves the highest selection scores among evaluated baselines. Evidence-backed revision further improves average performance, with gains over single rollout of 6.2 points (Gemini 3.5 Flash) and 6.4 points (Claude Opus 4.8). Verification skills can self-improve from failure feedback.

Conclusion: VeriHarness represents a novel and critical approach for scaling long-horizon agentic verification. The framework demonstrates that verification skills can self-improve from failure feedback, providing a scalable solution for complex agentic tasks. The release of ~26,000 rollouts across all benchmarks supports future research in this direction.

Abstract: As LLM agents undertake increasingly complex, long-horizon tasks, verifying their outputs becomes increasingly challenging. We study how verification capability can be strengthened with a fixed base model, without access to reference answers or grading rubrics at test time. Repeated sampling yields multiple rollouts that can contain complementary correct claims, but we need a reliable verification mechanism to determine which claims to trust. We first find that disagreement often exposes correct alternatives, while consensus can conceal errors. These observations motivate VeriHarness, which turns the underlying LLM a generator uses into an agentic verifier by giving it a workspace, evidence tools, and reusable verification skills. A disagreement resolver checks competing claims against environmental evidence, while a consensus challenger tests shared claims and searches for omitted requirements. Their findings guide the selection and revision of the final artifact. Across five long-horizon workspace benchmarks and two frontier models, VeriHarness achieves the highest selection scores among the evaluated baselines. Evidence-backed revision further improves average performance, bringing gains over a single rollout to 6.2 points with Gemini 3.5 Flash and 6.4 points with Claude Opus 4.8. We further show that verification skills can self-improve from failure feedback, demonstrating VeriHarness as a novel and critical approach for scaling long-horizon agentic verification. We release the full pool of approximately 26,000 rollouts across all five benchmarks and both models, produced at a cost of over $100,000, to support future research on agentic verification.

</details>


### [142] [RISED: RubrIcs for agentic multi-environment Selection and sElf-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00979)
*Jingtan Wang,Sirajul Salekin,Young mok Jung,Javier Movellan,Bryan Kian Hsiang Low,Manjot Bilkhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RISED is a method for training LLM agents across diverse interactive environments using rubric-based feedback. It addresses limitations of scalar rewards by using an LLM judge to tag rollouts with rubrics, enabling cross-environment data selection and policy supervision through self-distillation and failure mode avoidance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-environment RL training approaches have two key limitations: (1) they allocate training at environment level without considering cross-environment relationships, and (2) scalar rewards provide no within-group contrast when rollouts have identical outcomes (all-success or all-failure). This limits learning from cross-environment relationships and wastes potentially useful behavioral data.

Method: RISED uses rubric-based feedback to guide learning in three ways: (1) An LLM judge tags each rollout with predefined rubrics shared across environments; (2) Rubric profiles guide online data selection to align with desired behavioral composition while limiting overlap; (3) Positive rubrics provide token-level supervision via on-policy self-distillation teacher, while negative rubrics guide subsequent rollout generation away from failure modes.

Result: RISED achieves the highest mean pass rate across environments and ranks first or second in every individual environment across different model backbones. Rubric-based analysis can characterize behavioral changes accompanying these gains.

Conclusion: Using richer textual feedback (rubrics) instead of solely relying on scalar rewards enables more effective multi-environment LLM agent training. The rubric-based approach successfully addresses cross-environment relationship learning and within-group reward contrast issues, demonstrating superior performance across diverse environments.

Abstract: Training a single LLM agent jointly across diverse interactive environments has attracted increasing attention as a route to generalist agents. Existing curriculum and data-selection strategies often allocate training at the environment level or prioritize local reward-based signals, without explicitly considering relationships between current rollouts across environments for prompt-group selection. Meanwhile, as environments are learned at different rates, all-failure and all-success rollout groups can coexist within a batch, leaving those data without group-relative reward signals. Both challenges highlight limitations of relying solely on scalar rewards in multi-environment RL: they provide limited information about cross-environment relationships and no within-group reward contrast when rewards are identical. This motivates richer textual feedback, such as rubrics describing rollout behaviours, to guide learning. Beyond rubrics' usage as reward, we repurpose rubrics to guide both online data selection and policy supervision. An LLM judge tags each rollout using a predefined rubric vocabulary shared across environments. The resulting profiles guide the selection of data that aligns with the overall behavioural composition of the mixed-environment batch while limiting overlap with already-selected data. Available positive rubrics (describing desired behaviours) provide privileged context for an on-policy self-distillation teacher, supplying additional token-level supervision, while negative rubrics (describing undesired behaviours) guide subsequent rollout generation away from recurring failure modes. Together, these components form RISED. Across model backbones, RISED achieves the highest mean pass rate across environments and ranks first or second in every individual environment. Rubric-based analysis of RISED can further characterize the behavioural changes accompanying these gains.

</details>


### [143] [Evaluating LLM-Generated Preference Distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01000)
*Fan Huang,Minsuk Kim,C. Tyler Diggans,Filippo Radicchi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether Large Language Models can reliably serve as probabilistic generators for simulating human preferences across three domains (air travel, restaurants, consumer products). The study examines nine open-weight models and finds that while models show self-coherence (stable outcomes under repeated sampling), there is substantial disagreement across different models, challenging the assumption that LLMs can be used as stand-ins for survey respondents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The use of LLMs as probabilistic generators for simulation, synthetic data generation, and decision support is increasing, yet the structure and reliability of the distributions they produce remain understudied. The researchers aim to fill this gap by systematically analyzing LLM-generated preference distributions.

Method: The researchers systematically analyzed LLM-generated distributions of preferences across three choice domains (air travel, restaurants, consumer products). They tested nine open-weight models under various conditions including temperature changes, greedy decoding, and perturbations of prompt and ordering to assess robustness.

Result: All models exhibited self-coherence with most probable outcomes stabilizing rapidly under repeated sampling. However, substantial discordance was observed across both model families and scales, with little consensus even among their most probable outcomes. These patterns were robust across nine open-weight models, three choice domains, and held under temperature changes, greedy decoding, and perturbations of prompt and ordering.

Conclusion: The choice of model influences outcomes more than the wording of the prompt, challenging the common assumption that sufficiently capable LLMs produce similar preference distributions when used as stand-ins for survey respondents. This has significant implications for using LLMs in simulation and synthetic data generation contexts.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as probabilistic generators for simulation, synthetic data generation, and decision support in settings where real-world data are unavailable. Yet, the structure and reliability of the distributions they produce remain understudied. Here, we systematically analyze LLM-generated distributions of preferences for air travel, restaurants, and consumer products. Encouragingly, all models considered in our analysis exhibit self-coherence, with the most probable outcomes stabilizing rapidly under repeated sampling. At the same time, we observe substantial discordance across both model families and scales, with little consensus even among their most probable outcomes. These patterns hold across nine open-weight models, three choice domains, and show robustness under temperature changes, greedy decoding, and perturbations of prompt and ordering. Our findings indicate that outcomes are influenced more by the choice of model than by the wording of the prompt, challenging the common assumption that sufficiently capable LLMs produce similar preference distributions when used as stand-ins for survey respondents.

</details>


### [144] [Calibration-risk routing for controlled world-model adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01001)
*Yifan Zhang,Liang Zheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) faces a simulator-to-target shift problem where correcting the simulator or fitting the target directly can fail under limited target data. The Model-Corrected World Model (MC-WM) addresses this by separating initial target data into disjoint fit, selection, and calibration partitions, deploying the family with lower standardized calibration risk using a learned confidence signal and deterministic validity predicates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MBRL can exploit simulated experience, but a simulator-to-target shift creates a model-selection problem: correcting the simulator and fitting the target directly can each fail under limited target data. This requires a method to select the best model family when target data is limited.

Method: MC-WM separates initial target data into disjoint fit, selection, and calibration partitions. It uses a learned confidence signal and deterministic validity predicates to weight one-step imagined policy updates without rewriting physical rewards. The model family with lower standardized calibration risk is deployed.

Result: Evaluated 540 unique reported run cells across three controlled Multi-Joint dynamics with Contact (MuJoCo) shifts; one exact-routing cell was repeated after a pre-deployment artifact gate, giving 541 completed executions.

Conclusion: The MC-WM method successfully addresses the model-selection problem in MBRL under simulator-to-target shift by using standardized calibration risk for model family selection and deployment.

Abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) can exploit simulated experience, but a simulator-to-target shift creates a model-selection problem: correcting the simulator and fitting the target directly can each fail under limited target data. We introduce the Model-Corrected World Model (MC-WM), which separates initial target data into disjoint fit, selection, and calibration partitions and deploys the family with lower standardized calibration risk. A learned confidence signal and deterministic validity predicates weight one-step imagined policy updates without rewriting physical rewards. We evaluate 540 unique reported run cells across three controlled Multi-Joint dynamics with Contact (MuJoCo) shifts; one exact-routing cell was repeated after a pre-deployment artifact gate, giving 541 completed executions.

</details>


### [145] [What Can Analogy Tell Us About Artificial Consciousness?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01002)
*Keith J. Holyoak,Martin M. Monti*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a causal framework for evaluating whether non-human animals or artificial intelligence systems possess consciousness, based on analogical reasoning. The framework distinguishes between similarities in causal factors (which generate consciousness) versus similarities in behavioral or cognitive effects (which are downstream). It argues that behavioral similarity alone provides limited evidence for AI consciousness because the relevant causal mechanisms remain poorly understood.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address the fundamental question of who or what is conscious, particularly in light of advances in AI that have made the possibility of conscious machines a pressing issue. The challenge is that subjective experience is only directly accessible through first-person observation, making analogies necessary for inferring consciousness in other entities.

Method: The paper develops a causal framework that weights source-target similarity by causal relevance. This framework allows for: (1) unknown causes of consciousness, (2) disabling differences (factors that prevent consciousness despite superficial similarities), and (3) alternative routes to consciousness (different causal paths to similar outcomes).

Result: Applied to biological systems, the framework explains why analogical support for consciousness generally weakens with increasing causal distance from humans. Applied to contemporary AI, it shows that behavioral similarity provides only limited evidence for consciousness because the relevant causal correspondences remain poorly established. The framework also identifies what evidence would be needed to strengthen claims of artificial consciousness.

Conclusion: The causal framework provides a systematic way to evaluate evidential analogies for consciousness. It clarifies that behavioral arguments alone are insufficient for establishing AI consciousness; what is needed is evidence about causal mechanisms. The framework offers a roadmap for what kinds of evidence would be more compelling - specifically, evidence about the causal factors underlying consciousness rather than just behavioral outputs.

Abstract: Who or what is conscious? Because subjective experience is directly accessible only in the first person, judgments about consciousness in other entities depend partly on analogy. Historically, such inferences have focused on nonhuman animals, but advances in artificial intelligence have raised the possibility of conscious AI. Here we develop a causal framework for evaluating such evidential analogies. The key distinction is between similarities in factors plausibly involved in generating consciousness and similarities in downstream behavioural or cognitive effects. Our framework weights source-target similarity by causal relevance while allowing for unknown causes, disabling differences and alternative routes to consciousness. Applied to biological systems, it explains why analogical support generally weakens with increasing causal distance from humans. Applied to contemporary AI, it suggests that behavioural similarity provides only limited evidence for consciousness because relevant causal correspondences remain poorly established. The framework also clarifies what evidence would strengthen claims of artificial consciousness.

</details>


### [146] [Beyond Answer Confidence: A Controlled Audit of Self-Knowledge in a Black-Box Decision Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01006)
*Sharath M Shankaranarayana,Davor Runje,Jan Jannink*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether calibration (making probability outputs match actual frequencies) is sufficient for decision models to recognize when they lack knowledge. The authors audit Jev, a decision model, across 15+ datasets and 6 task families, finding that while confidence is calibrated on familiar tasks, it fails as an indicator of missing knowledge—assigning high confidence (up to 0.80) when given no answer-relevant information, and exceeding accuracy by 0.21-0.33 on out-of-distribution news. Targeted yes/no questions ("Does the model know the answer?") perform better (AUROC 0.91-1.00) but can exploit surface cues. The key insight is that black-box knowledge audits require explicit controls for surface features.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Calibration makes probability outputs useful on average, but it doesn't establish whether low confidence reflects genuine uncertainty (chance) or missing knowledge (model doesn't know what it doesn't know). The authors seek to audit this distinction—a critical issue for deploying decision models in real-world settings where knowing the limits of one's knowledge is as important as being accurate.

Method: The authors audited Jev (a decision model) using over 15 public datasets and 6 generated task families, employing paired interventions that vary information supplied for a fixed item. They compared confidence scores against accuracy, tested recalibration on historical data, and evaluated targeted yes/no questions as alternative knowledge indicators.

Result: Confidence is calibrated on familiar closed-choice tasks but fails as an indicator of missing knowledge: with no answer-relevant information, Jev assigns up to 0.80 confidence to a salient option. On news beyond its knowledge boundary, confidence exceeds accuracy by 0.21-0.33, and recalibration doesn't close this gap. Targeted yes/no questions perform better: AUROC 1.00 for detecting settled outcomes, 0.95 for evidence sufficiency (vs. 0.85 for confidence). Asking "does it know the answer?" detects fabricated entities and post-boundary news (0.91 AUROC), but with realistic names or dates removed, this advantage disappears—suggesting the model exploits surface cues rather than genuine knowledge.

Conclusion: Calibration alone is insufficient for detecting knowledge boundaries in decision models. Black-box knowledge audits need explicit controls for surface cues (like entity names or dates) because models may appear to know by exploiting spurious patterns. The "do you know?" interrogation approach is more effective than confidence scores but is not a complete solution.

Abstract: Decision models return probabilities intended for routing, abstention and automated action. Calibration makes those probabilities useful on average, but does not establish whether low confidence reflects chance or missing knowledge, nor whether confidence falls when a model moves beyond what it knows. We audit this distinction in Jev, a decision model, with over 15 public datasets and 6 generated task families, with paired interventions that vary the information supplied for a fixed item. Jev's confidence is calibrated on familiar closed-choice tasks but fails as an indicator of missing knowledge: with no answer-relevant information it assigns up to 0.80 to a salient option, and on news beyond an observed knowledge boundary it exceeds accuracy by 0.21--0.33, a gap that recalibration on earlier months does not close. Targeted yes/no questions give sharper readouts of the case: whether an outcome is settled (AUROC 1.00) and whether the evidence suffices (0.95, against 0.85 for confidence on the same items). Asking whether Jev knows the answer appears to flag fabricated entities and post-boundary news (0.91), but with realistic names or with dates removed it shows no advantage over answer uncertainty. Black-box knowledge audits therefore need explicit controls for surface cues. Code: https://github.com/Syntheme/beyond-answer-confidence.

</details>


### [147] [From Discovery to Decision: Finite-Budget Recoverability in LLM Voting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01014)
*Shaoang Li,Jian Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper analyzes the "discovery-to-decision gap" in voting over multiple LLM responses - the challenge of accumulating enough votes for a discovered correct answer to win under a fixed call budget. The authors derive theoretical thresholds for recoverability, characterize how candidate sets expand while reachable winners contract, and show that exact locking can save 28-30% of calls while preserving accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand and characterize the fundamental tension in test-time scaling: when multiple LLM responses are sampled, a correct answer may be discovered early but fail to win the plurality vote due to insufficient remaining votes. This creates a "discovery-to-decision gap" that limits the effectiveness of ensemble inference under fixed computational budgets.

Method: The authors use theoretical analysis deriving sharp recoverability thresholds under iid response laws, showing exact finite-horizon endpoint probabilities based on realized vote state and remaining call budget. They also conduct empirical validation on a controlled Word16 study, testing input permutation and exact locking strategies.

Result: Key findings include: (1) candidate set can only expand while reachable endpoint winners can only contract as sampling proceeds; (2) merging wrong-answer identities preserves single-call correctness but cannot improve plurality accuracy; (3) input permutation improves raw-plurality accuracy by 21.1 points with essentially unchanged single-call correctness; (4) exact locking saves 28-30% of calls at 16-call budget while preserving every fixed-budget output; (5) most discovered-but-unselected correct answers lose reachability only after discovery.

Conclusion: The paper provides a theoretical framework for understanding the discovery-to-decision gap in LLM ensemble voting. The key insight is that the conversion window - the time during which a discovered candidate can still win - is fundamentally constrained. Exact locking provides a practical method to save computational calls without losing accuracy, and the "gold-free exact locking certificate" based on singleton reachability offers a way to determine when voting can safely terminate early.

Abstract: Voting over multiple LLM responses is a common primitive in test-time scaling and ensemble inference. Collecting more responses can expand the candidate pool and increase the chance that a correct answer is discovered. Under a fixed call budget, a discovered answer still needs to accumulate enough support within the remaining calls to become the final plurality winner, creating a discovery-to-decision gap. In this work, we characterize this gap through the realized vote state and remaining call budget. We derive a sharp recoverability threshold and show that, as sampling proceeds, the observed candidate set can only expand while the set of reachable endpoint winners can only contract, inducing a candidate-level conversion window. Under a specified iid response law, the same state yields exact finite-horizon endpoint probabilities. We further show that merging wrong-answer identities preserves single-call correctness and cannot improve plurality accuracy, and that the effect of redistributing wrong-answer probability depends on the realized vote state. Singleton reachability yields a gold-free exact locking certificate. For a known answer universe, its first trigger is the earliest prefix at which all admissible continuations yield the same fixed-budget output. Empirically, most discovered-but-unselected correct answers lose reachability only after discovery. In a controlled Word16 study, input permutation improves raw-plurality accuracy by 21.1 points with essentially unchanged single-call correctness. Exact locking saves 28-30% of calls at a 16-call budget while preserving every fixed-budget output.

</details>


### [148] [Pay for the Fault, Not the Flow: Label-Free In-Flow Multi-Agent Workflow Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01017)
*Xuehang Guo,Haoyu Wang,Shengyu Chen,Zach Chen,Wei Cheng,Qingyun Wang,Haifeng Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: InFlowOp is a framework for optimizing multi-agent LLM workflows by pricing every decision in a label-free cost that balances agent competence against task demands and computational cost. It determines task decomposition and agent assignment bidirectionally before execution, and corrects faults with the cheapest move during execution. Braid benchmark is introduced to evaluate multi-agent coordination. Results show up to +11.97% improvement over single-agent baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Building multi-agent workflows for LLMs is challenging because: (1) deciding task decomposition granularity, agent assignment, and when to create new specialists are critical upfront decisions; (2) improving workflows is costly as fault location requires reference answers, graded outcomes, or trained assessors; (3) fixes require whole workflow re-execution, re-search, or retraining.

Method: InFlowOp uses a label-free cost function that prices every decision by weighing how well an agent's competence meets subtask demands against the agent's computational cost. Before execution, it bidirectionally determines task decomposition granularity and agent assignment following this cost. During execution, it corrects faults with the cheapest move using the same cost function. The Braid benchmark is introduced to evaluate multi-agent coordination beyond single-agent capability.

Result: Across various domains and backbones, InFlowOp outperforms single agent baselines by up to +11.97%, achieving +9.64% with in-flow optimization.

Conclusion: InFlowOp provides an effective approach for optimizing multi-agent LLM workflows through a unified cost-based framework that works both during workflow construction and execution, outperforming single-agent baselines significantly.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly construct multi-agent workflows that decompose a complex task and assign specialist agents from a pool. However, building such a workflow well remains challenging: how finely to divide the task, which agent to trust with each subtask, and when to create a new specialist are all critical decisions a workflow constructor needs to settle up front. Thus, whether each subtask succeeds remains unknown until the workflow runs. Yet, improving a workflow is costly. Locating a fault usually requires a reference answer, a graded outcome, or a trained assessor, and the fix is applied to the whole workflow through re-execution, re-search, or retraining. We propose InFlowOp, which prices every decision in one label-free cost that weighs how well an agent's competence meets what a subtask demands against how much that agent takes to run. Before execution, InFlowOp bidirectionally determines the granularity of task decomposition and agent assignment following from the cost rather than from a fixed template. During execution, InFlowOp corrects a fault with the cheapest move via the same cost that serves the workflow both as it is built and as it runs. Facing the workflow-level evaluation challenge, we introduce Braid, a benchmark whose tasks require multi-agent coordination beyond single-agent capability. Across various domains and backbones, InFlowOp outperforms single agent baselines by up to $+11.97\%$, achieving $+9.64\%$ with in-flow optimization. Our project page: https://xhguo7.github.io/InFlowOp/.

</details>


### [149] [Beyond Final Accuracy: Auditing Communication in LLM Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01042)
*Shixuan Li,Wei Yang,Peiyu Zhang,Anzhe Cheng,Heng Ping,Paul Bogdan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ICR is a controlled evaluation framework that isolates communication benefits from architectural gains and additional reasoning by measuring answer revision following independent reasoning. It reveals that similar aggregate accuracy can mask substantially different revision behaviors across communication methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-agent communication improvements leave ambiguity about whether gains come from effective communication, favorable agent architecture, or additional reasoning. Final accuracy merges corrected errors and corrupted answers into a single outcome, obscuring how communication changes decisions. Existing evaluation methods cannot disentangle these factors.

Method: ICR framework fixes initial reasoning trajectories, measures correction and preservation conditional on both agents' initial correctness, and uses a no-message revision control to quantify gains beyond additional reasoning. Applied to four reasoning benchmarks with textual and latent communication channels.

Result: Full reasoning increases correction while reducing preservation compared to transmitting answers alone across all four benchmarks. Richer messages amplify both beneficial and harmful influence. A structured verification policy shifts every channel toward greater preservation and lower correction, with effects on selectivity varying across channels and tasks.

Conclusion: Communication quality is not an intrinsic property of a channel—it depends on message content and receiver policies jointly. ICR provides a unified framework for examining selective revision, recentering evaluation on how message content and receiver policies produce benefits and harms.

Abstract: Multi-agent communication aims to help agents benefit from one another's information. Yet improvements in system performance leave a fundamental ambiguity: do they reflect effective communication, a favorable agent architecture, or simply additional reasoning? Because communication methods are commonly evaluated within the systems they were designed for, these factors are difficult to disentangle. Final accuracy further merges corrected errors and corrupted answers into a single outcome, obscuring how communication changes decisions. We introduce Independent--Communicate--Revise (ICR), a controlled framework that evaluates communication as answer revision following independent reasoning. ICR fixes initial reasoning trajectories, measures correction and preservation conditional on both agents' initial correctness, and uses a no-message revision control to quantify gains beyond additional reasoning. Across four reasoning benchmarks, our audit of textual and latent communication reveals that similar aggregate accuracy can conceal substantially different revision behaviors. Compared with transmitting answers alone, full reasoning increases correction while reducing preservation on all four benchmarks, so richer messages amplify beneficial and harmful influence alike. Receiver-policy comparisons on MedQA and GPQA-D further show that a structured verification policy shifts every channel toward greater preservation and lower correction, while its effect on selectivity varies across channels and tasks. These findings challenge treating communication quality as an intrinsic property of a channel. ICR therefore recenters evaluation on selective revision, providing a unified framework for examining how message content and receiver policies jointly produce benefits and harms.

</details>


### [150] [Empty Commitments: When Agents Promise What Their Runtime Cannot Deliver](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01045)
*Jiaqi Tang,Lan Wei,Bingyu Shen,Boyang Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces the concept of "empty commitments" in conversational agents - promises made by chatbots that cannot be fulfilled due to the agent's configuration alone (e.g., "I will remind you tomorrow"). Unlike broken promises, these are empty from the start because no tool or runtime mechanism exists to carry them out.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors identify a fundamental problem in conversational AI: agents make promises about future actions (like reminders) that they have no capability to execute. This issue exists regardless of user behavior - it's inherent to the agent's design.

Method: The paper defines empty commitments on top of existing commitment semantics, introducing: (1) three failure types, (2) an anchoring condition for identifying promises that tools could fulfill, and (3) a response-level outcome taxonomy. A measurement protocol is described using five setups that incrementally add persistence affordances, with implicit vs. stated environments.

Result: The abstract presents a conceptual framework and measurement protocol rather than experimental results. The framework provides a systematic way to identify and categorize empty commitments in conversational agents.

Conclusion: This work provides a foundation for understanding and measuring a specific type of conversational agent failure - making promises that are structurally impossible to keep due to system limitations, rather than failures that depend on subsequent user interactions.

Abstract: A chatbot that says "I will remind you tomorrow" will not run again until the user writes. We call such a promise an empty commitment: a promise of an action after the current turn that nothing in the agent's tools or runtime can carry out. Unlike a broken promise, its emptiness follows from the agent's configuration alone; no later trajectory is needed. We define empty commitments on top of commitment semantics, with three failure types, an anchoring condition for promises that a tool could make real, and a response-level outcome taxonomy. We then describe a measurement protocol: follow-up requests run in five setups that add one persistence affordance at a time, with the environment either left implicit or stated.

</details>


### [151] [Network World Models as Environments for Algorithm Design on Complex Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01048)
*Rishab Alagharu,Hongji Pu,Zeeshan Memon,Xinyuan Song,Yuntong Hu,Liang Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes an action-conditioned Network World Model that learns network diffusion dynamics under interventions to serve as a fast evaluator. It combines this with a coding agent that designs algorithms using feedback from rollouts, credit assignment, and counterfactual probes. The approach achieves comparable or superior results to baselines in 138/141 settings while enabling 14.5x speedup over Monte Carlo simulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world applications like robotics use world models to simulate environments and predict outcomes. Complex systems like networks require the same tool because intervention effects are not immediate (e.g., seeding nodes or immunizing against epidemics). The challenge is that evaluating candidate actions through simulation is computationally expensive, becoming a bottleneck when candidates are assessed over many sampled trajectories.

Method: The authors propose: (1) An action-conditioned Network World Model that learns network diffusion dynamics under interventions over time, applies each action to the network, and predicts the resulting outcome. (2) An algorithm design loop where a coding agent designs and refines executable algorithms using feedback from full rollouts, action-level credit assignment, and counterfactual probes over alternative interventions.

Result: Across eight network tasks and five diffusion models, the designed algorithms match or exceed the strongest reported baseline in 138 of 141 settings while enabling up to 14.5 times faster rollouts than Monte Carlo simulation.

Conclusion: The combination of a learned network world model with an algorithmic coding agent provides an effective framework for designing network intervention algorithms. The approach achieves strong performance across diverse tasks while significantly reducing computational cost compared to traditional simulation-based evaluation.

Abstract: World models, which simulate an environment and predict how it changes under actions, are increasingly used in real-world applications such as robotics. Complex systems call for the same tool because the effect of an action is not immediate. Seeding nodes for a campaign, or immunizing nodes against an epidemic, changes little on its own; what matters is the outcome that unfolds over the steps that follow. Designing an algorithm that selects such actions to maximize expected performance on a task is inherently iterative, and every candidate must be scored by the outcome it produces. Obtaining that outcome has relied on simulation, whose cost becomes a bottleneck when candidates are evaluated over many sampled trajectories. We propose an action-conditioned Network World Model that learns a network's diffusion dynamics under interventions over time, applies each action to the network, and predicts the outcome that follows. It serves as a fast evaluator inside an algorithm design loop in which a coding agent designs and refines executable algorithms using feedback from full rollouts, action-level credit, and counterfactual probes over alternative interventions. Across eight network tasks and five diffusion models, the designed algorithms match or exceed the strongest reported baseline in 138 of 141 settings while enabling up to 14.5 times faster rollouts than Monte Carlo simulation. Code will be released upon acceptance.

</details>


### [152] [Improving Math Reasoning through Value-guided Informative Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01080)
*Shaohuai Liu,Yuning Wu,Haoran Liu,Enzo Jia,Devin Chen,Kai Wei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: APIVIS is a training-time framework that improves mathematical reasoning in large language models by adapting finite-budget Gumbel search to chunk-level reasoning within RLVR. It combines direct and searched responses to create informative relative rewards and applies selective supervision to preserve learning signals when standard GRPO fails.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous work introduced search into RLVR rollouts to increase trajectory diversity, but diversity alone does not guarantee that the search-induced rollout policy improves upon the current policy. This gap needed to be addressed to ensure search actually enhances learning rather than just providing variety.

Method: APIVIS combines direct and searched responses within each rollout group, allowing improvements found by search to produce informative relative rewards. It applies selective supervision to search-improved tokens, preserving learning signals when uniform group rewards render GRPO ineffective. The method uses exact value-guided selection to improve expected verifier reward at each searched state, with approximate guarantees under bounded value-estimation error.

Result: APIVIS demonstrates substantial improvements over competitive search-based methods on widely recognized mathematical reasoning benchmarks across different model scales.

Conclusion: APIVIS successfully addresses the limitation that trajectory diversity alone does not ensure policy improvement. By combining direct and searched responses with selective supervision, the framework ensures that search-induced improvements actually enhance the rollout policy, validated by strong empirical results on mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved the mathematical reasoning capabilities of large language models. Recent work introduces search into RLVR rollouts to increase trajectory diversity, but diversity alone does not ensure that the search-induced rollout policy improves upon the current policy. To address this gap, we propose APIVIS, a training-time framework that adapts finite-budget Gumbel search to chunk-level mathematical reasoning. APIVIS combines direct and searched responses within each rollout group, allowing improvements found by search to produce informative relative rewards. It further applies selective supervision to search-improved tokens, preserving a learning signal when uniform group rewards render GRPO ineffective. We show that exact value-guided selection improves the expected verifier reward at each searched state and that this guarantee extends to the complete rollout policy, with a corresponding approximate guarantee under bounded value-estimation error. Experiments on widely recognized mathematical reasoning benchmarks and different model scales demonstrate substantial improvements over competitive search-based methods, validating the effectiveness of APIVIS.

</details>


### [153] [YouRA: A Persistent-State Architecture for Evidence-Traceable Autonomous Research Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01097)
*Yoonkyu Woo,Woojin Lee,Jin-Xia Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: YouRA is an architecture for stateful, evidence-traceable autonomous research that addresses the gap between manuscript claims and executed experiments in end-to-end research agents. It integrates three components: Verification State Architecture (VSA), Independent Controller, and Stateful Reflection to preserve research state, execution evidence, and failure history across research trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: End-to-end research agents can now produce complete scientific papers, but manuscript claims often diverge from executed experiments. This gap is structural because research state, failure histories, and claim-evidence alignment are not maintained as persistent, verifiable state across long-horizon pipelines.

Method: YouRA integrates three components: (1) Verification State Architecture (VSA) that tracks hypotheses, gates, and evidence pointers; (2) Independent Controller that separates control from execution and manages lifecycle, recovery, and debate/review; and (3) Stateful Reflection that logs failures as structured lessons and routes recovery through bounded repair, redesign, or reset.

Result: On MLR-Bench's predefined ten-task end-to-end subset, YouRA improves over both MLR-Agent and AI Scientist V2 on scalar Overall across all three matched backbones. An automated diagnostic using MLR-Bench's hallucination taxonomy reports intersection/union counts for four fact-based failure types, and data-provenance diagnostic shows more real-data-based outputs. Ablation study shows removing either core-state component drops performance below the full system.

Conclusion: The three components (VSA, Independent Controller, and Stateful Reflection) work together to maintain persistent, verifiable state across long-horizon research pipelines, with each component making separable contributions to the overall performance improvement.

Abstract: End-to-end research agents can now produce complete scientific papers, yet manuscript claims often diverge from executed experiments. This gap is structural: research state, failure histories, and claim-evidence alignment are not maintained as persistent, verifiable state across long-horizon pipelines. We present YouRA (Your Research Agent), an architecture for stateful, evidence-traceable autonomous research. YouRA preserves research state, execution evidence, and failure history across the research trajectory by integrating three components: a Verification State Architecture (VSA) that tracks hypotheses, gates, and evidence pointers; an Independent Controller that turns state and reflection records into lifecycle, recovery, and debate/review control while separating control from execution; and Stateful Reflection that logs failures as structured lessons and routes recovery through bounded repair, redesign, or reset. On MLR-Bench's predefined ten-task end-to-end subset, YouRA improves over both MLR-Agent and AI Scientist V2 on scalar Overall across all three matched backbones. An automated diagnostic using MLR-Bench's hallucination taxonomy reports intersection/union counts for four fact-based failure types, and data-provenance diagnostic shows more real-data-based outputs. Ablating each of the four components (the VSA, the Independent Controller, MCP tool access, and reflection-guided recovery) supports their separable contributions. Removing either core-state component drops YouRA below the full system. Code: https://github.com/PrayPrey/Your-Research-Agent.

</details>


### [154] [Beyond State-of-the-Art: Standardising Environmental Impact Metrics for AI Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01116)
*Lachlan McGinness,Dan Pagendam,Robert Offner*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the lack of standardized carbon accounting practices in the machine learning community by analyzing NeurIPS 2025 papers, defining sustainability metrics for model training efficiency, providing heuristics for estimating LLM inference carbon costs, and proposing the "Smallest Model that Achieves the Job" (SMAJ) framework to replace the traditional State-of-the-Art accuracy-focused approach.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The environmental footprint of Large Language Models (LLMs) is growing as their capabilities and ubiquity increase, yet the machine learning community lacks standardized practices for carbon accounting, and reporting of environmental impact is nearly non-existent in academic papers.

Method: The authors conducted an automated literature review of 5,285 papers accepted to NeurIPS 2025 to assess current reporting practices. They defined standardized sustainability metrics for evaluating model training efficiency and developed heuristics to estimate carbon cost of LLM inference. They also implemented these metrics in carbonbenchmark, a drop-in software solution for tracking and reporting emissions.

Result: The literature review revealed that reporting of environmental impact is nearly non-existent in NeurIPS 2025 papers. The authors created standardized sustainability metrics and a software tool (carbonbenchmark) for emissions tracking.

Conclusion: To combat the pursuit of marginal accuracy gains at disproportionate environmental costs, the authors formalize the SMAJ framework, which challenges the field to prioritize computational efficiency and environmental accountability alongside traditional SotA accuracy metrics.

Abstract: As the capabilities and ubiquity of Large Language Models (LLMs) grow, so does their environmental footprint. Despite calls for responsible AI, the machine learning community lacks standardised practices for carbon accounting. Our automated literature review of the 5,285 papers accepted to NeurIPS 2025 reveals that reporting of environmental impact is nearly non-existent. To catalyse a shift toward sustainable AI, we define standardised sustainability metrics for evaluating model training efficiency, accompanied by simple heuristics to estimate the carbon cost of LLM inference. We implement these metrics in carbonbenchmark, a drop-in software solution for tracking and reporting emissions.
  Finally, to combat the pursuit of marginal accuracy gains at disproportionate environmental costs, we formalise the `Smallest Model that Achieves the Job' (SMAJ), a framework which challenges the field to prioritise computational efficiency and environmental accountability alongside traditional `State-of-the-Art' (SotA) accuracy.

</details>


### [155] [AbsorbEvo: An Agentic Framework for Autonomous Inverse Design of Microwave Absorbers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01119)
*Zhicheng Feng,Yubo Zhao,Xuefeng Yao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AbsorbEvo is an agentic framework for autonomous inverse design of high-performance microwave absorbers that translates natural-language performance objectives into designs verified by full-wave simulations. It integrates language reasoning, physics-based prediction, and historical feedback to efficiently explore the design space.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Designing high-performance microwave absorbers requires specialized expertise in electromagnetic theory, materials science and simulation programming, and entails time-consuming optimization. There is a need for an automated system that can translate natural-language performance objectives into verified designs without requiring extensive human expertise and trial-and-error.

Method: AbsorbEvo uses a candidate evolution strategy that: (1) A large language model proposes directions and magnitudes of parameter adjustments based on task objectives and computational history; (2) Combines directed increments with global sampling to generate candidates; (3) Uses a low-cost predictive model as physics prior to rank candidates; (4) Only high-ranking designs undergo full-wave simulation; (5) Results passing physical validity checks evaluate performance and guide subsequent search; (6) Experience from training tasks is distilled into textual skills, independently validated before use in new tasks.

Result: Under identical proposal budgets on AbsorbBench-36 tasks, AbsorbEvo achieved 79.17% task success rate, versus 25.00% for generic agent and 12.50% for random search. Its mean best coverage was 0.7816, compared with 0.6434 and 0.6448 for the comparison methods.

Conclusion: By integrating language reasoning and physics-based feedback into design decisions, AbsorbEvo provides a methodological foundation for natural-language-driven autonomous inverse design of microwave absorbers. It significantly outperforms generic agents and random search in both success rate and coverage metrics.

Abstract: Designing high-performance microwave absorbers requires specialized expertise in electromagnetic theory, materials science and simulation programming, and entails time-consuming optimization. Here, we present AbsorbEvo, an agentic framework for autonomous inverse design that translates natural-language performance objectives into designs verified by full-wave simulations. Its candidate evolution strategy integrates language reasoning, physics-based prediction and historical feedback. A large language model proposes the directions and magnitudes of parameter adjustments based on task objectives and computational history. The system combines directed increments with global sampling to generate candidates and uses a low-cost predictive model as a physics prior to rank them. Only high-ranking designs undergo full-wave simulation. Results passing physical validity checks are used to evaluate performance and guide subsequent search. Experience from training tasks is further distilled into textual skills, which are independently validated before use in new tasks. Under identical proposal budgets on held-out AbsorbBench-36 tasks, AbsorbEvo achieved a task success rate of 79.17%, versus 25.00% for a generic agent and 12.50% for random search. Its mean best coverage was 0.7816, compared with 0.6434 and 0.6448, respectively. By integrating language reasoning and physics-based feedback into design decisions, AbsorbEvo provides a methodological foundation for natural-language-driven autonomous inverse design of microwave absorbers.

</details>


### [156] [CortexBridge: Cortical Alignment of EEG Montages for Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01124)
*Jiazhen Hong,Xiaotian Zhou,Zihao Ding,Kailong Wang,Yu Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CortexBridge is a lightweight adapter that enables transfer learning between EEG foundation models and arbitrary electrode montages by mapping features into a shared cortical latent space using electrode and atlas coordinates. It improved performance in 13/15 evaluations across three foundation models and five BCI datasets, with up to 13.02% accuracy gain on SSVEP classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EEG foundation models are typically pretrained with fixed channel vocabularies or limited electrode montages, making it difficult to transfer them to new datasets with different electrode layouts. This limits the practical applicability of pretrained EEG models in real-world BCI applications.

Method: CortexBridge combines EEG features with electrode coordinates and atlas coordinates to map arbitrary montages into a shared cortical latent space. It was evaluated using three frozen foundation models (EEGPT, LaBraM, CBraMod) on five BCI datasets from the Mother of All BCI Benchmarks (MOABB).

Result: CortexBridge improved performance in 13 of 15 evaluations. Average balanced accuracy gains were 0.80% for EEGPT, 0.70% for LaBraM, and 3.26% for CBraMod, with a maximum gain of 13.02% on 12-class SSVEP classification. Visualizations revealed task-dependent spatial patterns, with SSVEP showing concentrated representation in the Yeo Visual network compared to auditory P300.

Conclusion: Cortical alignment represents a learnable and anatomically grounded routing mechanism that enables transfer from heterogeneous EEG montages to pretrained foundation models, successfully bridging the gap between arbitrary electrode configurations and fixed model architectures.

Abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models are often pretrained with a fixed channel vocabulary or a limited set of montages, making transfer difficult when electrode layouts change. We propose CortexBridge, a lightweight adapter that combines EEG features with electrode and atlas coordinates to map arbitrary montages into a shared cortical latent space. Evaluated with three frozen foundation models on five brain-computer interface (BCI) datasets from the Mother of All BCI Benchmarks (MOABB), CortexBridge improves performance in 13 of 15 evaluations. The gains in balanced accuracy average 0.80% for EEGPT, 0.70% for LaBraM, and 3.26% for CBraMod, with a maximum gain of 13.02% on 12-class steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP) classification. Visualizations of the learned atlas representations reveal task-dependent spatial patterns, with SSVEP showing a more concentrated representation in the Yeo Visual network than auditory P300. These results establish cortical alignment as a learnable and anatomically grounded routing mechanism from heterogeneous EEG montages to pretrained foundation models.

</details>


### [157] [Grounding Large Language Models in DSGE Simulators for Policy Generation and Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01128)
*Aditya Dubey,Namah Gupta,Vinti Agarwal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper tests whether large language models can make economically consistent policy decisions by placing them inside six DSGE simulators. The study addresses the long-horizon credit assignment problem where policy effects may appear quarters after actions, comparing PPO (with learned value function) against GRPO (critic-free baseline) to evaluate if LLMs can learn economically meaningful policies beyond producing plausible-sounding language.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models can produce reasonable-sounding economic policy responses, but this does not guarantee their actions are consistent with actual economic dynamics. The authors seek to evaluate policy actions by their simulated economic consequences rather than by the plausibility of their language output.

Method: The researchers implemented an instruction-tuned LLM within six Snowdrop-backed DSGE simulators. At each turn, the model observes the economy and economic discourse changes, selects a bounded policy action, and receives the next simulated state with an economic reward. They created a Python interface supporting repeated rollouts, persistent shocks, state cloning, and rolling-horizon simulation. PPO was used as the primary method (with learned value function for delayed reward propagation via generalized advantage estimation), while GRPO served as a matched critic-free baseline. Experiments tested directional semantic signals, reward horizon, trajectory warm starts, cross-simulator transfer, and historically anchored pandemic and monetary-policy shocks.

Result: The abstract does not provide specific quantitative results. It focuses on the experimental methodology and framework design rather than reporting outcomes.

Conclusion: The study establishes a rigorous testing framework to evaluate whether LLM-based policy decisions produce economically valid outcomes. By using DSGE simulators with realistic economic dynamics, the research moves beyond evaluating language plausibility to assessing actual economic consistency of AI-generated policies.

Abstract: Large language models can produce economic policy responses that sound reasonable, but this does not show that their actions are consistent with economic dynamics. We test this by placing an instruction-tuned language model inside six Snowdrop-backed dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) simulators. At each turn, the model observes the economy and a change in economic discourse, selects a bounded policy action, and receives the next simulated state and an economic reward. We implement a common Python interface for repeated rollouts, persistent shocks, state cloning, and rolling-horizon simulation.
  This setting creates a long-horizon credit-assignment problem. Policy effects may appear several quarters after an action is taken. PPO has a learned value function that can propagate delayed reward to earlier tokens through generalized advantage estimation. GRPO has no learned value function and instead assigns a group-relative advantage from complete rollout returns. It therefore cannot distinguish which earlier turn caused the outcome; if every rollout receives the same return, the normalized advantage is zero. We use PPO as the primary method and GRPO as a matched critic-free baseline. The experiments also test directional semantic signals, reward horizon, trajectory warm starts, cross-simulator transfer, and historically anchored pandemic and monetary-policy shocks. The objective is to judge policy actions by their simulated economic consequences rather than by plausible language alone.

</details>


### [158] [Auditing Action Settlement in LLM Agent Environments: Order, Progress, and Replay](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01138)
*Haotian Chen,Bowen Ye,Yuning Zhang,Jingkun Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses concurrent action arbitration in LLM agent environments through a typed snapshot-settlement contract, testing five policies across exhaustive trials and scripted episodes. Key findings show random tickets outperform conservative rejection by 59 percentage points in a six-agent task, while full-state journal auditing enables precise replay and corruption detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to solve the problem of arbitrating concurrent actions in LLM agent environments where multiple proposals may each be individually valid but require systematic handling. The authors identify a need to formalize execution semantics and test properties like order sensitivity, useful progress, and replay consistency.

Method: The researchers implemented a typed snapshot-settlement contract and tested five settlement policies through: (1) 28,800 exhaustive permutation trials, (2) 2,160 scripted multistep episodes, and (3) a separate full-state journal audit with 156 checkpoints and 1,332 constructed corruptions. They tested properties including order sensitivity, useful progress, and replay consistency across different policies.

Result: Key results include: (1) Joint policies are spatially order-invariant conditional on fixed priorities; (2) Conservative rejection completes only 31.25% of agents in a six-agent doorway task versus 90.28% for random tickets (59.03 pp improvement, 95% CI: 50.00-68.06); (3) All policies preserve tested spatial constraints; (4) Priority arbitration still misses the independent small-instance optimum; (5) Full-state journal audit exactly replays 156 checkpoints and rejects all 1,332 constructed corruptions while retaining terminal anchor.

Conclusion: The evidence presented concerns execution semantics in LLM agent systems, not human realism or long-run fairness. The study reveals that simple randomization (random tickets) significantly outperforms conservative rejection policies, and while joint policies maintain spatial order-invariance, priority-based arbitration still fails to achieve optimal outcomes in independent small-instance scenarios.

Abstract: Concurrent actions in large language model (LLM) agent environments require arbitration even when each proposal is individually valid. We implement a typed snapshot-settlement contract and audit three distinct properties: order sensitivity, useful progress, and replay consistency. Five settlement policies are tested in 28,800 exhaustive permutation trials and 2,160 scripted multistep episodes. Joint policies are spatially order-invariant conditional on fixed priorities, yet conservative rejection completes only 31.25% of agents in a six-agent doorway task versus 90.28% for random tickets; the paired improvement is 59.03 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval: 50.00-68.06). All policies preserve the tested spatial constraints, and priority arbitration still misses the independent small-instance optimum. A separate full-state journal audit exactly replays 156 checkpoints and rejects 1,332 constructed corruptions with a retained terminal anchor. The evidence concerns execution semantics, not human realism or long-run fairness.

</details>


### [159] [ReSolve: Reusing Candidate Reasoning through Selective Generative Moderation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01140)
*Bangji Yang,Jiajun Fan,Hongba Ma,Xi Zhu,Weizhi Zhang,Minghao Guo,Ye Li,Hamid Palangi,Jiaxuan You*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ReSolve is a training-free inference procedure that reuses candidate reasoning through selective generative moderation, achieving higher accuracy (100/99 correct) on 130 competition-math problems than voting (91/92) while using ~47% fewer tokens than eight-sample self-consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
