Motivation: Sampling multiple solutions spends computation on intermediate deductions and unfinished arguments as well as final answers. The authors propose reusing this candidate reasoning rather than discarding it.

Method: An answer-distribution controller invokes a model to examine existing derivations when candidates disagree or lack a parseable answer, then incorporates the generated solution into a bounded loop. Selective generative moderation is applied.

Result: ReSolve obtains 100 and 99 correct answers vs. 91 and 92 for voting over four candidates. Uses 46.3-47.2% fewer tokens than eight-sample self-consistency. Ablation study shows visible derivations are crucial (accuracy drops from 100 to 93 when removed). Selective moderation reduces moderation tokens by ~54% and total tokens by 6.2%.

Conclusion: Results support candidate reasoning as reusable inference computation. However, no accuracy advantage over additional sampling or distinct benefit from specialized route instructions was established.

Abstract: Sampling multiple solutions spends computation on intermediate deductions and unfinished arguments as well as final answers. We introduce ReSolve, a training-free inference procedure that reuses this candidate reasoning through selective generative moderation. An answer-distribution controller invokes a model to examine existing derivations when candidates disagree or lack a parseable answer, then incorporates the generated solution into a bounded loop. Under Hybrid scoring on 130 competition-mathematics problems evaluated with two independently sampled candidate pools, ReSolve obtains 100 and 99 correct answers, compared with 91 and 92 for voting over the same four candidates, with no correct-to-incorrect changes relative to that vote in either pool. Eight-sample self-consistency obtains 94 and 96 correct answers while consuming substantially more tokens; ReSolve uses 46.3% and 47.2% fewer tokens in the two evaluations. A controlled ablation removes visible derivations while retaining answer keys, vote counts, and the per-state output-cap rule, reducing accuracy from 100 to 93 correct despite increasing computation. Selective and always-on Uniform moderation both solve 97 problems, while selectivity reduces moderation tokens by approximately 54% and total pipeline tokens by 6.2%. These results support candidate reasoning as reusable inference computation. They do not establish an accuracy advantage over additional sampling or a distinct benefit from specialized route instructions.

</details>


### [160] [When Does Exercise-Specific Joint Selection Help? An Audit of Evaluation and Control Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01188)
*Haotian Chen,Jingkun Yu,Yuning Zhang,Bowen Ye*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper audits a previous claim that exercise-specific joint selection improves skeleton-based exercise correctness classification. The authors find that the observed "gain" is highly sensitive to the evaluation metric used, often not statistically significant, and requires proper structural controls. The paper does not propose a new algorithm or clinical benefit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation appears to be questioning the robustness and generalizability of claims about joint selection benefits in skeleton-based exercise classification. The authors aim to determine what the "gain" from joint selection actually establishes, if anything.

Method: The authors conducted an exploratory audit using 1,057 repetitions from 10 subjects (REHAB24-6 dataset). They systematically examined: (1) evaluation aggregation methods, (2) subset structure, and (3) temporal representation. They compared manual-subset kNN against random controls with varying levels of structure matching (dimension-matched random maps, bilateral structure + trunk inclusion matched). They also tested different classifiers (RBF-SVM, logistic regression) and used sequence-order and paired-seed controls.

Result: The key findings are: (1) The manual-subset kNN gain changes drastically from 0.055 (pooled out-of-fold AUROC) to 0.020 (equal-weight within-person AUROC); both confidence intervals include zero. (2) Among 1,000 dimension-matched random maps, 14 match or exceed the manual pooled result, but 145 do when bilateral structure and trunk inclusion are matched. (3) RBF-SVM retains a positive within-person gain, while logistic regression and random-convolution comparator show negative point gains. (4) The results are sensitive to the estimand (evaluation metric) and require appropriate structural controls.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that joint-selection claims require explicit estimands and structurally appropriate controls. This exploratory audit shows why such claims need careful specification and validation. Importantly, the paper does not establish a new algorithm or clinical benefit - it is a critical analysis of methodological choices in evaluating exercise classification approaches.

Abstract: Exercise-specific joint selection can improve skeleton-based correctness classification, but what does that gain establish? We audit 1,057 repetitions from ten REHAB24-6 subjects, separating evaluation aggregation, subset structure, and temporal representation. The manual-subset kNN gain changes from 0.055 for pooled out-of-fold AUROC to 0.020 for equal-weight within-person AUROC; both paired intervals include zero. Among 1,000 dimension-matched random maps, 14 match or exceed the manual pooled result, versus 145 when bilateral structure and trunk inclusion are also matched. RBF-SVM retains a positive within-person gain, whereas logistic regression and a random-convolution comparator have negative point gains under that estimand. Sequence-order and paired-seed controls further qualify the interpretation. This exploratory audit shows why joint-selection claims require explicit estimands and structurally appropriate controls; it does not establish a new algorithm or clinical benefit.

</details>


### [161] [Federated Agent Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01195)
*Qiang Yang,Zhiqiang Kou,Xueyi Zhang,Dong-Dong Wu,Hanlin Gu,Jing Guo,Yang Liu,Di Jiang,Qian Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces Federated Agent Optimization (FAO), a novel framework for distributed LLM agents to collaboratively improve through controlled information exchange while preserving privacy. Unlike conventional federated learning that only shares model parameters, FAO addresses a broader spectrum of agent capabilities including memory, tools, rewards, skills, and structured knowledge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents increasingly operate in private environments and accumulate valuable experience (task execution, tool use, feedback, local knowledge). However, this experience cannot be directly shared across organizations due to privacy and proprietary constraints. Conventional federated learning is insufficient because it only handles model parameters, while agent capabilities extend far beyond to include memory, tools, rewards, skills, and structured knowledge.

Method: The paper formulates FAO as a multi-objective optimization problem balancing three key factors: agent utility, privacy leakage, and communication cost. The optimization space is organized across five dimensions: policy, memory, tool use, reward, and structured knowledge/skills. The framework characterizes how private experience can be abstracted, protected, aggregated, and adapted into transferable capabilities.

Result: The paper provides a unified view of how distributed agents can benefit from one another without direct experience sharing, enabling collaborative improvement while keeping raw data, complete trajectories, and private knowledge local.

Conclusion: The authors identify key challenges of FAO and outline promising directions for future research toward trustworthy federated agent systems. This work opens a new research direction bridging federated learning and multi-agent systems for LLM agents.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate in private environments and accumulate valuable experience from task execution, tool use, feedback, and local knowledge. Yet such experience is distributed across organizations and cannot be directly shared because of privacy and proprietary constraints. Conventional federated learning is insufficient for this setting, as agent capabilities extend beyond model parameters to memory, tools, rewards, skills, and structured knowledge. In this paper, we formulate \textbf{Federated Agent Optimization (FAO)}, which studies how distributed agents can collaboratively improve through controlled information exchange while keeping raw data, complete trajectories, and private knowledge local. We define FAO as a multi-objective problem balancing agent utility, privacy leakage, and communication cost, and organize its optimization space across policy, memory, tool use, reward, and structured knowledge and skills. We further characterize how private experience can be abstracted, protected, aggregated, and adapted into transferable capabilities, providing a unified view of how agents can benefit from one another without direct experience sharing. Finally, we identify the key challenges of FAO and outline several promising directions for future research toward trustworthy federated agent systems.

</details>


### [162] [Dependency-Aware Reward Shaping for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01207)
*Ziyi Chen,Yan Zhang,Jianhui Wei,Daoan Zhang,Zuozhu Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DARS is a reward shaping method for LLM training that assigns step-level credit by modeling task progress as predicates with prerequisite relations. It discounts verified predicates based on graph distance from broken prerequisites, maintains credit for independent work, and updates weights when errors are repaired. This addresses the problem where terminal rewards provide no guidance for intermediate steps in failed episodes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current reward assignment methods overlook that work built on uncorrected mistakes is wasted while independent work remains valid. With only final success/failure rewards, every step in a failed episode has zero total future reward, even when it made progress. This limits learning from valuable intermediate steps.

Method: DARS represents task progress as predicates linked by prerequisite relations. Annotators mark which predicates each step verifies, invalidates, or repairs. Verified predicates are discounted by graph distance from the nearest broken prerequisite. Independent predicates remain unaffected. Repairs update weights based on remaining errors; invalidated predicates need re-verification. A fixed potential converts annotations into signed per-step rewards. Integrates with reasoning/agentic training methods (GiGPO, ARPO/AEPO) without changing their rollout strategies or optimizers.

Result: Across five task families and models from 1.5B to 8B: improves success by up to 10 points over GiGPO on ALFWorld; raises WebShop task score and Search-R1 QA accuracy; complements AEPO on AIME24/25 with Python interpreter; exceeds OmniOPD in controlled tool-free reasoning at 1.7B and 4B. Ablations show step-level credit, dependency attenuation, and graph topology each contribute. A distilled 8B annotator matches API annotator on ALFWorld.

Conclusion: DARS provides effective step-level credit assignment for LLM reasoning and agentic training by modeling predicate dependencies. It integrates with multiple training methods, works across different model scales, and enables efficient deployment with distilled annotators. The approach significantly improves performance on diverse benchmarks.

Abstract: When training large language models with reinforcement learning, terminal rewards provide little guidance about which steps matter. Common methods for assigning step credit overlook that work built on uncorrected mistakes is wasted while independent work remains valid. With only a final success/failure reward, every step in a failed episode has zero total future reward, even when it made progress. We propose Dependency-Aware Reward Shaping (DARS), which represents task progress as predicates linked by prerequisite relations and assigns step-level credit over the dependency graph. An annotator marks which predicates each step verifies, invalidates, or repairs. Verified predicates are discounted according to graph distance from the nearest broken prerequisite, while independent predicates are unaffected. Repairs update these weights based on any errors that remain; invalidated predicates need re-verification to regain credit. A fixed potential converts these annotations into signed per-step rewards. A common reward and annotation interface allows DARS to integrate with a range of reasoning and agentic training methods, such as GiGPO and ARPO/AEPO, without changing their rollout strategies or optimizers. Across five task families and models from 1.5B to 8B, DARS improves success by up to 10 points over GiGPO trained with the same budget and harness (ALFWorld), raises the WebShop task score and Search-R1 QA accuracy, complements AEPO's entropy-based training on AIME24/25 with a Python interpreter, and exceeds OmniOPD in controlled tool-free reasoning comparisons at 1.7B and 4B. Ablations show that step-level credit, dependency attenuation, and graph topology each contribute. On ALFWorld, a distilled 8B annotator matches the API annotator, enabling DARS to run efficiently without a frontier judge. Code is available at https://github.com/JianhuiWei7/DARS.

</details>

### [163] [Reverse Item Response Theory for Sparsity-Robust Ranking in Fragmented Cancer Drug-Response Matrices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00002)
*Jung Min Kang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A novel "reverse IRT" method treats cancer types as latent subjects with resistance ability and drugs as items with evasion difficulty, applied to 242,036 drug sensitivity measurements from GDSC2. The model estimates cancer-type-level resistance and drug-level activity on a shared latent scale, outperforming simple averaging and achieving best Brier score in held-out prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pharmacogenomic drug-response analysis faces challenges with fragmented data and missing values. Traditional methods like simple averaging fail to handle missing data effectively. There was a need for a method that can recover full-data latent rankings under various missingness regimes and provide robust drug sensitivity predictions.

Method: Reverse IRT model treating cancer types as latent "subjects" with resistance ability and drugs as "items" with evasion difficulty. Validated across four missingness regimes (MCAR, cancer-biased, drug-biased). Compared with five methods using Brier score. Bootstrap confidence intervals used for stability assessment. Cross-platform PRISM replication for validation.

Result: Reverse IRT better recovers full-data latent ranking than simple averaging (Delta-rho = +0.089 to +0.095 at 60% missingness). Best Brier score in held-out prediction. 19 of 28 cancer types have stable resistant/sensitive classifications. Cross-platform PRISM shows 82% directional agreement but weak rank-order correlation (rho = 0.25).

Conclusion: The method provides methodological robustness for pharmacogenomic analysis under fragmented data, but does not provide a universal clinical resistance leaderboard. The weak cross-platform correlation indicates limitations in generalizability across different datasets.

Abstract: We introduce reverse Item Response Theory (IRT) to pharmacogenomic drug-response analysis by treating cancer types as latent "subjects" with resistance ability and drugs as "items" with evasion difficulty. Applied to 242,036 drug sensitivity measurements from the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC2) database, the model estimates cancer-type-level in-vitro resistance and drug-level broad activity on a shared latent scale. Validation across four missingness regimes demonstrates that reverse IRT better recovers the full-data latent ranking than simple averaging, with advantages of Delta-rho = +0.089 to +0.095 at 60% missingness under MCAR, cancer-biased, and drug-biased sparsity. Held-out prediction confirms IRT achieves the best Brier score among five evaluated methods. Bootstrap confidence intervals show 19 of 28 cancer types have stable resistant/sensitive classifications. Cross-platform PRISM replication shows 82% directional agreement but weak rank-order correlation (rho = 0.25), indicating the contribution is methodological robustness under fragmented evaluation, not a universal clinical resistance leaderboard.

</details>


### [164] [How Far is Adam from Natural Gradient Descent?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00004)
*Vihaan Paka-Hegde*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper analyzes Adam optimizer's geometric relationship to natural gradient descent (NGD) using a novel scale-invariant metric. The study reveals that Adam's deviation from NGD varies significantly across different loss landscapes, with higher ill-conditioning leading to greater misalignment (up to ~10³ in neural networks), though this does not prevent Adam from achieving good final optimization outcomes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Adam is a standard deep learning optimizer, but its geometric relationship to natural gradient descent (NGD) contains unresolved questions. Understanding this relationship could provide insights into why Adam works so well in practice.

Method: The study analyzes Adam's full update rule (including momentum) as a diagonal empirical Fisher approximation subject to diagonal truncation, empirical label substitution, and temporal lag. Using the scale-invariant γ(Δθ) metric, they measure Adam's geometric deviation from true NGD across four loss landscapes: well-conditioned linear regression, ill-conditioned linear regression, logistic regression, and a non-convex small neural network.

Result: Adam's geometric trajectory is context-dependent. Deviation remains low in well-conditioned settings but rises significantly under ill-conditioning, reaching misalignments of ≈10³ in the neural network. Higher geometric drift correlates with slower initial optimization but does not degrade final objective minimization—Adam consistently reaches low loss. The improved empirical Fisher (iEF) tracks more stable paths than the standard empirical Fisher (EF), which frequently oscillates or diverges.

Conclusion: Adam's practical optimization power may stem from a balance of structural approximation errors and momentum smoothing rather than close tracking of the natural gradient path.

Abstract: Adam is the standard optimizer in deep learning, yet its geometric relationship to natural gradient descent (NGD) contains unresolved questions. We study Adam's full update rule, including momentum, as a diagonal empirical Fisher approximation subject to diagonal truncation, empirical label substitution, and temporal lag. Using the scale-invariant $γ(Δθ)$ metric, we measure Adam's geometric deviation from true NGD across four loss landscapes: well-conditioned linear regression, ill-conditioned linear regression, logistic regression, and a non-convex small neural network. Adam's geometric trajectory is context-dependent. Deviation remains low in well-conditioned settings but rises significantly under ill-conditioning, reaching misalignments of $\approx 10^3$ in the neural network. Higher geometric drift correlates with slower initial optimization but does not degrade final objective minimization; Adam consistently reaches low loss. Furthermore, the improved empirical Fisher (iEF) tracks more stable paths than the standard empirical Fisher (EF), which frequently oscillates or diverges. Our results suggest Adam's practical optimization power may stem from a balance of structural approximation errors and momentum smoothing rather than close tracking of the natural gradient path.

</details>


### [165] [FourierQK: Filter Shape, Admissibility and the Leakage-Coverage Law](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00009)
*Athanasios Zeris*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates optimal filter shapes for frequency-collapse attention in character-level language modeling. Through controlled ablation on TinyShakespeare (6-layer GPT), the study identifies that bandpass filters with DC/Nyquist suppression, ~70 token bandwidth at paragraph scale, and admissible filter properties (zero-mean Mexican Hat DOG) yield the best performance (+1.15 nats over baseline). The findings show FourierQK works well for bidirectional attention (BERT-style) but not for autoregressive generation (GPT-style), requiring causal variants like MorletQK.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Frequency-collapse attention previously showed gains over standard dot-product attention by replacing Q/K dot product with bandpass-filtered inner product. This paper seeks to understand which filter shape works best and why, by systematically testing five hypotheses about filter properties.

Method: Controlled ablation study on character-level language modeling (TinyShakespeare, 6-layer GPT) testing five hypotheses: DC suppression, Nyquist suppression, bandwidth, centre frequency, and multi-scale coverage. Five specific findings were generated from this approach.

Result: Key findings: (1) DC and Nyquist components are actively harmful (val ~= 2.0); (2) optimal single-scale bandwidth is sigma ~= 2 bins at paragraph scale (~70 tokens), giving +1.15 nats gain over BASE-DOT; (3) admissible filters (zero-mean Mexican Hat DOG m=2) outperform non-admissible Gaussians; (4) bilateral FFT leakage scales with spectral coverage - narrowband filters clean, wideband leaky; (5) causal time-domain Morlet at character scale cannot beat BASE-DOT.

Conclusion: FourierQK is effective in bidirectional attention settings (encoder-style like BERT) where full-sequence context is available at both training and inference time. Autoregressive generation requires a causal spectral variant such as MorletQK (decoder-style like GPT).

Abstract: Frequency-collapse attention [Zeris, 2026e] achieves large gains over standard dot-product attention by replacing the Q/K dot product with a bandpass-filtered inner product at a learned frequency. A natural follow-up question is: which filter shape works best, and why? We test five hypotheses about filter properties -- DC suppression, Nyquist suppression, bandwidth, centre frequency, and multi-scale coverage -- using a controlled ablation on character-level language modelling (TinyShakespeare, 6-layer GPT). Our main findings are: (1) DC and Nyquist components are actively harmful (val ~= 2.0, equivalent to phase randomisation), confirming that oscillatory bandpass structure is essential, not just any low-dimensional spectral summary; (2) the optimal single-scale bandwidth is sigma ~= 2 bins centred at paragraph scale (~70 tokens), giving a clean gain of Delta = +1.15 nats over BASE-DOT; (3) admissible filters (zero-mean, Mexican Hat DOG m = 2) outperform non-admissible Gaussians at the same scale and provide partial protection against bilateral FFT leakage; (4) bilateral FFT leakage scales monotonically with spectral coverage -- narrowband filters (gap > +4) are clean, wideband filters (gap < +2) are leaky; and (5) causal time-domain Morlet at character scale cannot beat BASE-DOT (K=128 taps covers 50% of T=256 context), motivating word-level experiments in the companion MorletQK paper [Zeris, 2026f]. Together, findings (1)-(5) characterise FourierQK as effective in bidirectional attention settings (encoder-style, e.g. BERT), where full-sequence context is available at both training and inference time; autoregressive generation requires a causal spectral variant such as MorletQK [Zeris, 2026f] (decoder-style, e.g. GPT). Code available at: https://github.com/AthanasiosZeris/energy-gated-attention

</details>


### [166] [Integrating Fairness and Explainability in a Multiple Instance Reinforcement Learning System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00035)
*Bente Hinkenhuis,Seyed Sahand Mohammadi Ziabari,Ali Mohammed Mansoor Alsahag*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>

Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Predicting student performance from educational interaction data requires models that are both accurate and sufficiently transparent to support meaningful intervention, while demographic information introduces an additional risk of unfair predictions. This study investigates a multi-objective framework that combines reinforcement learning-based multiple instance learning (RL-MIL), adversarial debiasing, and preference-conditioned hypernetworks for student-at-risk prediction. MIL represents each student as a bag of weakly labeled interactions, while an RL agent selects informative instances for downstream classification. Two hypernetwork variants are evaluated to determine whether a user-defined preference scalar can continuously control the trade-off between predictive performance and Equalized Odds. The underlying RL-MIL baseline achieves strong classification performance, but both hypernetwork extensions exhibit mode collapse: changing the preference weight produces little systematic movement along the intended fairness-performance frontier. The failure is associated with objective dominance, weak gradient propagation through the conditioning mechanism, and interactions between dynamically generated parameters. The results show that fairness objectives can be incorporated into an interpretable RL-MIL pipeline, but preference conditioning alone does not guarantee controllable multi-objective behavior. Robust fair RL-MIL therefore requires explicit mechanisms for gradient balancing, objective separation, and stability analysis.

### [167] [Fast Polynomial Transcendentals for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00049)
*Robert Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates using short polynomial programs to accelerate special-function unit (SFU) operations (sigmoid, tanh, SiLU) in LLMs on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. By replacing native PyTorch implementations with degree-3 or degree-4 BF16 polynomial approximations, the authors achieve 1.19-2.19x speedups in isolated benchmarks and 0.3-8.0% improvements in end-to-end training throughput across four integration tasks, with minimal impact on training loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GPU generations scale matrix, special-function, and memory pipelines at different rates, causing kernel bottlenecks to shift as hardware evolves. FlashAttention-4 exposed this imbalance in attention on NVIDIA Blackwell. The authors hypothesize that short polynomial programs can accelerate other SFU operations beyond attention, which are computationally expensive in LLMs.

Method: The authors: (1) conducted isolated IEEE FP16 benchmarks comparing native PyTorch evaluation with packed FMA programs across L2-resident and HBM-resident working sets; (2) replaced native sigmoid, tanh, and SiLU with degree-3 or degree-4 BF16 polynomial programs in four integration tasks: dense SiLU, tanh-softcapped attention, sigmoid attention, and routed-expert SwiGLU; (3) combined analytical symmetry, target-format rounding, and packed arithmetic within consuming kernels; (4) performed same-checkpoint open-weight ablations and paired pre-training comparisons to evaluate model behavior.

Result: Isolated benchmarks showed 1.19-2.19x speedup in L2 and 1.00-1.70x in HBM. Integration task improvements: dense-SiLU improved training-step throughput by 2.7%, tanh-softcapped-attention by 2.9%, routed-expert SwiGLU by 8.0%, sigmoid-attention improved attention forward by 7.4% and complete GPU step by 0.3%. Training loss differences (polynomial minus native) at ~100B tokens ranged from -0.107 to +0.079 across four tasks.

Conclusion: Short polynomial approximations can effectively accelerate SFU operations in LLMs on modern GPU architectures like NVIDIA Blackwell, providing meaningful throughput gains with minimal training loss impact. The approach is most effective for routed-expert architectures (8.0% gain) and attention mechanisms (7.4% forward improvement). The polynomial approximations introduce negligible model quality degradation, with loss differences remaining within acceptable bounds.

Abstract: Graphics processing unit (GPU) generations scale matrix, special-function, and memory pipelines at different rates, so kernel bottlenecks move as hardware evolves. FlashAttention-4 exposed this imbalance inside attention on NVIDIA Blackwell. We test whether short polynomial programs can accelerate other special-function-unit (SFU) operations in large language models (LLMs). We first compare native PyTorch evaluation with packed fused multiply--add (FMA) programs in an isolated IEEE binary16 (FP16) sweep spanning L2-resident and high-bandwidth-memory (HBM)-resident working sets. We then replace native sigmoid, tanh, and sigmoid linear unit (SiLU) with degree-3 or degree-4 bfloat16 (BF16) programs in four GB200 integration tasks: dense SiLU, tanh-softcapped attention, sigmoid attention, and routed-expert Swish-gated linear unit (SwiGLU). The programs combine analytical symmetry, target-format rounding, and packed arithmetic inside consuming kernels. The isolated paths improve by 1.19--2.19x in L2 and 1.00--1.70x in HBM. The dense-SiLU, tanh-softcapped-attention, and routed-expert substitutions improve complete training-step throughput by 2.7\%, 2.9\%, and 8.0\%, respectively. The sigmoid-attention substitution improves complete-attention forward by 7.4\% and the complete GPU step by 0.3\%. Same-checkpoint open-weight ablations and one paired pre-training comparison per task extend the evaluation to model behavior. At common horizons near 100 billion tokens, the final smoothed training-loss differences (polynomial minus native) range from $-0.107$ to $+0.079$ across the four tasks.

</details>


### [168] [SW-KAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with Stieltjes-Wigert q-Orthogonal Polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00050)
*Amirhosein Azarpour,Seyyed Moein Kazemi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SW-KAN introduces Stieltjes-Wigert q-orthogonal polynomials on semi-infinite domain to address domain mismatch in polynomial-based KANs, with exponential-of-tanh mapping and stable three-term recurrence for efficient evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Polynomial-based KAN variants suffer from domain mismatch between unbounded real inputs and bounded orthogonal polynomial bases. Original B-spline KANs are computationally expensive. This work aims to create a more efficient and accurate KAN architecture.

Method: 1) Use Stieltjes-Wigert q-orthogonal polynomials defined on semi-infinite domain (0, ∞); 2) Introduce smooth exponential-of-tanh mapping to bridge domain gap while preserving gradients; 3) Leverage numerically stable three-term recurrence for O(N) polynomial evaluation without special-function calls; 4) Utilize log-normal weight structure and learnable q-parameter for inductive bias.

Result: SW-KAN achieves superior accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across image classification and function approximation tasks. It outperforms polynomial KAN baselines on standard benchmarks, with strong performance under resource-constrained conditions (reduced dimensionality, limited data).

Conclusion: SW-KAN is a compelling alternative for efficient function approximation and classification in resource-constrained settings, offering robust performance with remarkably few parameters due to its distinct inductive bias from log-normal weight structure and learnable q-parameter.

Abstract: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) represent a paradigmatic shift in deep learning by replacing fixed node activations with learnable univariate functions on edges, offering enhanced interpretability and parameter efficiency. While recent polynomial-based KAN variants have addressed the computational overhead of original B-spline implementations, they introduce a fundamental yet underexplored challenge: the domain mismatch between unbounded real-valued inputs and the bounded or semi-infinite support of orthogonal polynomial bases. To address this limitation, we propose the Stieltjes-Wigert Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (SW-KAN), a novel architecture that employs Stieltjes-Wigert q-orthogonal polynomials defined on the semi-infinite domain (0, infinity). We introduce a smooth exponential-of-tanh mapping that stably bridges the domain gap while preserving well-conditioned gradients, and leverage a numerically stable three-term recurrence that evaluates polynomial expansions in O(N) operations without special-function calls. Through comprehensive experiments spanning image classification and continuous function approximation, we demonstrate that SW-KAN achieves superior accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across diverse tasks. The log-normal weight structure and learnable q-parameter of Stieltjes-Wigert polynomials provide a distinct inductive bias that enables robust performance under resource-constrained conditions, including reduced feature dimensionality and limited training data. The proposed architecture not only outperforms established polynomial KAN baselines on standard benchmarks but also exhibits strong representational capacity for approximating complex multivariate functions with remarkably few parameters, making it a compelling alternative for efficient function approximation and classification in resource-constrained settings.

</details>


### [169] [Format-Aware Fusion for Fast FP4 Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00053)
*Robert Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents "format-aware fusion" to optimize 4-bit floating-point (FP4) Tensor Core acceleration in LLM training, addressing overhead issues that can negate performance gains. The approach co-designs quantization with scale domains and consumer layouts for different FP formats. Using Llama-3 8B pretraining with 160B tokens, the fastest custom route achieves 37.9K tokens/s/GPU, nearly doubling bfloat16 baseline (18.8K), while MXFP with specific optimizations reaches 37.2K tokens/s/GPU at 86.3% model FLOP utilization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: FP4 Tensor Cores can accelerate matrix multiplication, but the overhead from scale computation, operand packing, layout construction, and saved backward state can erase the performance gains. This overhead is a fundamental bottleneck preventing effective low-precision training acceleration.

Method: The authors propose format-aware fusion, which co-designs each quantization producer with its scale domain and consumer layout for native MXFP, global NVFP, and CTA-local NVFP. They evaluate on Llama-3-family 8B pretraining through 160B tokens using bfloat16 output projections and compiled cross entropy, testing multiple configurations including MXFP with row-gradient stochastic rounding and fixed-sign 32-value Hadamard weight-gradient preconditioning, and a Transformer Engine recipe with four final bfloat16 blocks.

Result: In matched same-accelerator probes: bfloat16 achieves 18.8K tokens/s/GPU, Transformer Engine NVFP reaches 27.6K tokens/s/GPU, fastest custom route achieves 37.9K tokens/s/GPU. MXFP with the specified techniques reaches 37.2K tokens/s/GPU (86.3% bfloat16 model FLOP utilization) and ends 2.11% above raw bfloat16 training-loss endpoint. The Transformer Engine recipe with four final bfloat16 blocks ends 0.87% above bfloat16 at 27.1K tokens/s/GPU. Notably, downstream rankings differ from training-loss rankings, showing FP4 outcomes depend jointly on scale contract, operand, and execution path.

Conclusion: Format-aware fusion effectively addresses FP4 overhead bottlenecks, achieving near-2x speedup over bfloat16 baseline. The key insight is that FP4 performance depends not just on numerical precision but on the joint optimization of scale contracts, operand formats, and execution paths. The trade-off between speed and accuracy varies significantly: fastest route (37.2K tokens/s) shows 2.11% higher loss, while the more accurate recipe (0.87% above bfloat16) runs at 27.1K tokens/s. Downstream task performance may not correlate with training loss, indicating the need for holistic optimization approaches.

Abstract: Four-bit floating-point (FP4) Tensor Cores accelerate matrix multiplication, but scale computation, operand packing, layout construction, and saved backward state can erase the gain. We present \emph{format-aware fusion}, which co-designs each quantization producer with its scale domain and consumer layout for native \mxfp{}, global \nvfp{}, and cooperative-thread-array-local \nvfp{}. We evaluate Llama-3-family 8B pretraining through 160 billion tokens using bfloat16 output projections and compiled cross entropy. In matched same-accelerator probes, bfloat16 and Transformer Engine \nvfp{} reach 18.8K and 27.6K tokens/s/GPU, while our fastest custom route reaches 37.9K. \mxfp{} with row-gradient stochastic rounding and fixed-sign 32-value Hadamard weight-gradient preconditioning reaches 37.2K tokens/s/GPU (86.3\% bfloat16 model FLOP utilization) and ends 2.11\% above the raw bfloat16 training-loss endpoint. A Transformer Engine recipe with four final bfloat16 blocks ends 0.87\% above bfloat16 at 27.1K tokens/s/GPU. Downstream rankings differ from training-loss rankings, showing that FP4 outcomes depend jointly on scale contract, operand, and execution path.

</details>


### [170] [Uncertainty-Aware RL-Controlled Adaptive 3D Mapping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00188)
*Alpay Ozkan,Tunc Ozan Aydin,Marc Pollefeys,Jelena Trisovic,Daniel Barath*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes an adaptive voxel-based 3D reconstruction framework that uses semantic entropy, geometric curvature, and texture richness as complexity cues for principled resolution allocation, combined with a reinforcement learning agent that learns voxel subdivision policies under a user-specified memory budget.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fixed-resolution volumetric grids are inefficient for 3D reconstruction—wasting memory in uniform regions while losing detail in complex areas. Existing adaptive methods like MAP-ADAPT require expert tuning, lack generalization to unseen objects, and provide no explicit mechanism to control memory usage.

Method: The framework refines voxels based on semantic entropy (capturing label uncertainty), geometric curvature, and texture richness as scene complexity cues. A reinforcement learning agent learns voxel subdivision policies under a user-specified target memory budget, replacing hand-tuned thresholds with a single intuitive control parameter. The result is a multi-resolution TSDF.

Result: The proposed method achieves higher geometric accuracy, better semantic consistency, and improved memory-accuracy trade-offs compared to MAP-ADAPT and fixed-resolution baselines on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

Conclusion: The approach provides an explicit, user-controlled accuracy-memory trade-off through a single intuitive parameter, achieving superior performance without relying on semantic taxonomies.

Abstract: Voxel-based volumetric mapping is fundamental to 3D reconstruction, yet fixed-resolution grids remain inherently inefficient - wasting memory in uniform regions and losing detail in complex ones. Existing adaptive methods, such as MAP-ADAPT, partially address this by varying resolution based on geometry and user-defined semantic class lists, but these heuristics require expert tuning, lack generalization to unseen objects, and provide no explicit mechanism to control memory usage. We propose an adaptive framework that refines voxels based on semantic entropy, which captures label uncertainty, together with geometric curvature and texture richness as scene complexity cues, yielding principled resolution allocation without reliance on semantic taxonomies. To make the accuracy-memory trade-off explicit and user-controlled, we further introduce a reinforcement learning agent that learns voxel subdivision policies under a user-specified target memory budget, replacing hand-tuned thresholds with a single intuitive control parameter. The resulting multi-resolution TSDF achieves higher geometric accuracy, better semantic consistency, and improved memory-accuracy trade-offs compared to MAP-ADAPT and fixed-resolution baselines on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/alpayozkan/UnRL.

</details>


### [171] ["very likely" Means "uncertain"? How LLMs Diverge from Humans in Linguistic Uncertainty Quantification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00083)
*Jinhao Duan,Zicheng Liu,Zijie Liu,Kaidi Xu,Tianlong Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates how LLMs differ from humans in verbal uncertainty quantification, and introduces METHODNAME, an optimization-based algorithm that learns optimal uncertainty profiles over verbal markers from LLM outputs to enable direct comparison of confidence semantics between humans and LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Humans naturally express uncertainty through verbal markers (e.g., "possible," "likely"), reflecting metacognitive monitoring of knowledge boundaries. However, most LLM uncertainty quantification relies on likelihood- or consistency-based signals rather than verbal markers. This study seeks to understand how LLMs diverge from humans in verbal uncertainty expression and whether verbal markers can reliably quantify LLM uncertainty.

Method: The researchers curated a corpus of human uncertainty markers from psychology and decision-science literature, then benchmarked LLMs against this corpus. They developed METHODNAME, an optimization-based algorithm that learns an optimal uncertainty profile over uncertainty markers directly from LLM outputs by fitting a marker-uncertainty mapping to best explain empirical correctness, rather than estimating uncertainty via repeated sampling.

Result: The study found that LLMs encode verbal uncertainty with numerical levels that differ substantially from those of humans. METHODNAME enables direct, marker-level comparison of confidence semantics between humans and LLMs, successfully disentangling mismatch and revealing systematic confidence disparities in verbal expressions.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates that there are significant divergences between human and LLM verbal uncertainty expressions. The proposed METHODNAME provides a novel approach to quantify and compare uncertainty semantics, revealing systematic disparities in how confidence is conveyed through verbal markers between humans and LLMs.

Abstract: Humans express uncertainty verbally via markers (e.g., "possible," "likely"), yet most LLM uncertainty quantification (UQ) relies on costing likelihood- or consistency-based signals. From a cognitive perspective, accurate verbal uncertainty reflects metacognitive monitoring, representing knowledge boundaries ("knowing that you don't know") to support regulation and information seeking. In this paper, we investigate how LLMs diverge from humans in verbal uncertainty quantification and whether verbal markers can reliably quantify LLM uncertainty. We curate a corpus of human uncertainty markers from psychology and decision-science literature and benchmark LLMs against it. We observe that LLMs encode verbal uncertainty with numerical levels that differ substantially from those of humans. We then introduce METHODNAME, a novel optimization-based algorithm that learns an optimal uncertainty profile over uncertainty markers directly from LLM outputs. By fitting a marker-uncertainty mapping to best explain empirical correctness, METHODNAME discovers how much probability mass each verbal marker should convey, rather than estimating uncertainty via repeated sampling. METHODNAME enables a direct, marker-level comparison of confidence semantics between humans and LLMs, disentangling mismatch and revealing systematic confidence disparities in verbal expressions.

</details>


### [172] [Nous: Learning and Certifying Memory Decisions Before Source Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00094)
*Pranav Singh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether belief-based agent memory must calibrate its sources before improving decisions. The key finding is that learning and certifying useful decisions can require quadratically fewer records (Θ(l⁻²)) than source calibration (Θ(l⁻⁴)), demonstrating that memory decisions can be learned and justified without fully recovering source reliability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Belief-based agent memory needs reliable decisions about current state, but evidence may be noisy, copied, or stale. The fundamental question is whether memory must first calibrate its sources before it can improve its decisions—a potentially costly requirement that this paper challenges.

Method: The authors analyze a four-model hidden Markov family, separating learning, calibration, and revision certification. They derive complexity bounds for learning Bayes decisions (Θ(l⁻²) records) versus source estimation (Θ(l⁻⁴) records), extend analysis to a broader model class, and characterize the identified interval for policy improvement under an unknown identity-plus-background report channel. They also develop a robustness extension tolerating bounded history-dependent misspecification and conditional copying. Empirical validation uses 45,000 held-out mutable-state histories and 9,000 episodes across three MiniGrid memory environments with noisy-report interfaces.

Result: Learning an unknown Bayes decision requires Θ(l⁻²) records, while certifying improvement over an incumbent takes O(l⁻²) fresh records. Fixed-precision source estimation requires Θ(l⁻⁴) records. Thus, decision learning and certification can require quadratically fewer records than source calibration. Under the identity-plus-background channel, the sharp identified interval for policy improvement was characterized with finite-sample certificates using observable witness regions. In experiments, the new certificate achieved 9/9 improvements over a constant incumbent and 4/9 over last-write-wins, compared to 0/9 for the earlier certificate.

Conclusion: The result provides a statistical account of when memory decisions can be learned and justified without recovering source reliability. This is not a universally superior memory algorithm, but rather a characterization of the conditions under which decision learning is possible with less information than full source calibration. The key insight is that direct decision learning can be more efficient than the two-step approach of first calibrating sources then making decisions.

Abstract: Belief-based agent memory needs reliable decisions about current state, yet its evidence may be noisy, copied, or stale. Must a memory calibrate its sources before it can improve its decisions? We separate learning, calibration, and revision certification. On one four-model hidden Markov family, learning an unknown Bayes decision requires Theta(l^-2) records and certifying its improvement over an informative incumbent takes O(l^-2) fresh records from the same observation law, while fixed-precision source estimation requires Theta(l^-4) as persistence l vanishes. Thus learning and certifying useful decisions can require quadratically fewer records than source calibration. A broader model class retains the decision rate and source lower bound. Under an unknown identity-plus-background report channel, we characterize the sharp identified interval for policy improvement and derive a finite-sample certificate using observable witness regions, without pure-class anchors. A robustness extension tolerates bounded history-dependent misspecification and conditional copying; split-trained witnesses apply to arbitrary history spaces with explicit power conditions. We integrate policy-bound receipts with Nous Dimensions and test 45,000 held-out mutable-state histories and 9,000 episodes in three external MiniGrid memory environments with an introduced noisy-report interface. The new certificate accepts 9/9 improvements over a constant incumbent and 4/9 over last-write-wins, versus none for the earlier certificate in MiniGrid. Strong established inference baselines remain competitive or better. The result is a statistical account of when memory decisions can be learned and justified without recovering source reliability, not a universally superior memory algorithm.

</details>


### [173] [One Mastery Threshold Does Not Fit All Knowledge Tracing Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00095)
*Xianghui Meng,Yujing Zhang,Jionghao Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates how mastery thresholds in intelligent tutoring systems interact with different knowledge tracing (KT) models. The authors evaluate six KT models across four educational datasets using 12 thresholds (0.50-0.99), measuring post-advancement performance, advancement coverage, practice burden, and disparities. They find that BKT is relatively insensitive to threshold changes while neural models become increasingly selective as thresholds rise. The same numerical threshold represents different mastery levels across model types, and the best-balanced threshold varies substantially by model and instructional setting. Stricter thresholds don't reliably reduce performance gaps and can disproportionately restrict advancement for weaker students.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tutoring systems use mastery thresholds to decide when students can advance, but the same numerical threshold can lead to very different decisions when the underlying knowledge tracing model changes. This raises concerns about threshold consistency and fairness across different KT implementations.

Method: The authors examined six KT models across four public educational datasets, evaluating 12 thresholds from 0.50 to 0.99. They measured four key metrics: post-advancement performance, advancement coverage, practice burden, and disparities across prior-performance groups. They also identified balanced thresholds under 30 predefined instructional settings.

Result: BKT is relatively insensitive to threshold changes, while neural models become much more selective as thresholds increase. The same cutoff represents different mastery levels across model types (BKT estimates latent mastery probability vs. neural models estimate probability of correct next response). In half the tested settings, neural models and BKT differed by more than 0.10 in selected thresholds. Stricter thresholds did not reliably reduce performance gaps and could disproportionately restrict advancement, with stronger-prior students advancing up to 3.26 times as often as weaker-prior students.

Conclusion: Mastery thresholds should be recalibrated when the KT model or instructional priorities change. Thresholds should be evaluated by their effects on performance, practice, advancement, and access rather than using fixed numerical values across different models.

Abstract: Tutoring systems use mastery thresholds to decide when students can stop practicing and advance, but the same numerical threshold can lead to very different decisions when the underlying knowledge tracing (KT) model changes. We examine six KT models across four public educational datasets and evaluate 12 thresholds from 0.50 to 0.99 using post-advancement performance, advancement coverage, practice burden, and disparities across prior-performance groups. We also identify thresholds that balance performance, extra practice, and advancement under 30 predefined instructional settings. Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT) is relatively insensitive to threshold changes, while neural models become much more selective as thresholds increase. This partly reflects different model outputs: BKT estimates latent mastery probability, whereas neural models estimate the probability of a correct next response, so the same cutoff does not represent the same level of mastery. The best-balanced threshold varied substantially across models and settings. In half of the tested settings, neural models and BKT differed by more than 0.10 in their selected thresholds, although this gap became smaller when greater priority was placed on reducing extra practice and allowing more students to advance. Stricter thresholds also did not reliably reduce performance gaps and could disproportionately restrict advancement, with stronger-prior students advancing up to 3.26 times as often as weaker-prior students. These results show that mastery thresholds should be recalibrated when the KT model or instructional priorities change and evaluated by their effects on performance, practice, advancement, and access.

</details>


### [174] [Uncertainty-Aware Learning from Multi-Expert Interval Targets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00102)
*Samira Alkaee Taleghan,Younghyun Koo,Andrew P. Barrett,Farnoush Banaei-Kashani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses the challenge of modeling two distinct sources of label uncertainty in machine learning: within-label imprecision (expert-reported intervals) and between-expert variation (disagreement among experts). The proposed approach preserves individual expert intervals, separates these uncertainty sources, and validates predictive uncertainty components through decomposition matching. The method demonstrates a 31% MAE reduction on sea-ice concentration data compared to hard labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods treat label uncertainty sources separately: multi-expert approaches collapse labels to consensus, interval-target methods yield single predictions, and predictive-uncertainty methods rarely validate against observed expert disagreement. This creates a gap in properly handling and validating uncertainty estimates when both within-label imprecision and between-expert variation exist.

Method: Three-component approach: (1) Harmonize heterogeneous label vocabularies into common probabilistic label space to separate encoding differences from expert judgment; (2) Retain individual label intervals and model with mixture of Beta distributions trained using proper Cramér-distance objective; (3) Decompose predictive uncertainty into within-component, between-component, and model uncertainty, then apply decomposition matching to align predictive components to label-side sources.

Result: On sea-ice concentration task, the model reduces MAE by 31% over hard labels and outperforms aggregation, interval-distribution, and interval-regression baselines.

Conclusion: The proposed approach successfully handles both within-label imprecision and between-expert variation in expert-labeled data. By preserving individual expert intervals and properly decomposing/validating predictive uncertainty components, the method achieves significant performance improvements over existing approaches on the sea-ice concentration benchmark.

Abstract: Many machine learning (ML) applications rely on expert labels, and qualified experts may provide different but plausible interpretations of the same observation. Such variation across expert labels may reflect genuine disagreement or ambiguity rather than annotation error. When individual experts additionally report intervals rather than exact values, the supervision contains two distinct sources of label uncertainty: within-label imprecision and between-expert variation. Existing methods treat these forms separately: multi-expert approaches collapse labels to a consensus, interval-target methods often yield a single prediction, and predictive-uncertainty methods rarely validate their uncertainty estimates against observed expert disagreement. To address this problem, we propose an approach that preserves individual expert intervals, separates within-label imprecision from between-expert variation, and validates the corresponding predictive uncertainty components. First, heterogeneous label vocabularies are harmonized into a common probabilistic label space, separating encoding differences from expert judgement. Second, individual label intervals are retained and modeled with a mixture of Beta distributions trained using a proper Cramér-distance objective, preserving distinct expert-reported labels. Third, we decompose predictive uncertainty into within-component, between-component, and model uncertainty, and evaluate whether these components correspond to within-label uncertainty, between-label uncertainty, and model error, respectively. Because this correspondence is not guaranteed, we introduce decomposition matching, which aligns the predictive components to their intended label-side sources. On sea-ice concentration the model reduces MAE by 31\% over hard labels and outperforms aggregation, interval-distribution, and interval-regression baselines.

</details>


### [175] [The Hidden Costs of 99% Accuracy: A Trustworthiness Audit of the Telco Customer Churn Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00118)
*Soumyadeep Roy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper audits the IBM Telco Customer Churn benchmark dataset for four trustworthiness failures: (1) pre-split SMOTE inflates churn-class F1 by 13.1 pp due to synthetic training points being nearest-neighbor interpolations of test instances; (2) TotalCharges is nearly determined by tenure × MonthlyCharges (R2=0.999), corrupting SHAP interpretations; (3) isotonic regression outperforms temperature scaling for calibration; (4) cost-optimal thresholds are 5-10× lower than F1-optimal, saving ~$77K per 1,000 customers. The authors propose a four-component reporting checklist and release reproducible code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors noticed that the IBM Telco benchmark routinely reports >95% accuracy, but accuracy/F1-centered reporting ignores potential trustworthiness failures. They aimed to audit this benchmark for common pitfalls invisible to standard metrics.

Method: The authors conducted four audits: (1) SMOTE inflation test across 10 classifiers and 15 seeds with Wilcoxon tests; (2) R2 correlation analysis of TotalCharges; (3) 15-seed calibration audit comparing isotonic regression and temperature scaling; (4) cost-sensitive threshold analysis using $50 retention offer and 24-month CLV proxy. They also replicated experiments on Iranian Telecom Churn and Bank Customer Churn datasets.

Result: Key findings: (1) ~36% of synthetic SMOTE points are nearest-neighbor interpolations of test instances, inflating F1 by 13.1 pp (p < 10^-4); (2) TotalCharges R2 = 0.999, removing it changes accuracy by <0.2 pp but SHAP ranks it 9th; (3) Isotonic regression is strongest default; temperature scaling fails on class-weighted tree ensembles with bimodal probability distributions; (4) Cost-optimal threshold is 5-10× lower than F1-optimal, saving ~$77K per 1,000 customers. F1 generalizes across domains; F2 generalizes only within telecom.

Conclusion: The authors propose a four-component reporting checklist: pipeline disclosure, redundancy diagnostic, calibration audit, and cost-sensitive thresholds. They release reproducible implementation. The paper demonstrates that high accuracy metrics can mask significant trustworthiness issues in churn prediction benchmarks.

Abstract: Customer churn prediction on the IBM Telco Customer Churn benchmark (n = 7,043) routinely reports test accuracies above 95%, with the most cited published study reporting 99.01%. We audit this benchmark for four trustworthiness failures invisible to the accuracy- and F1-centred reporting that dominates the literature. First, pre-split SMOTE inflates churn-class F1 by 13.1 percentage points across ten classifiers and fifteen seeds (Wilcoxon p < 10^-4 per classifier); the same leaky pipeline ordering paired with class weighting yields no inflation, isolating the effect to SMOTE's geometric construction. We measure the mechanism directly: approximately 36% of synthetic training points are nearest-neighbour interpolations of test-set instances. Second, the TotalCharges field is approximately determined by tenure multiplied by MonthlyCharges (R2 = 0.999); removing it changes accuracy by less than 0.2 percentage points, yet TreeSHAP ranks it ninth in mean absolute attribution - a pattern that materially corrupts SHAP-based interpretation. We propose an R2 > 0.95 pre-modelling diagnostic. Third, in a 15-seed calibration audit, isotonic regression is the strongest default; temperature scaling fails on class-weighted tree ensembles whose predicted-probability distribution is bimodal. Fourth, the cost-optimal decision threshold (under a 50 USD retention offer and 24-month CLV proxy) is approximately 5-10 times lower than the F1-optimal threshold, saving approximately 77,000 USD per 1,000 customers. We replicate F1 and F2 on Iranian Telecom Churn (within domain) and Bank Customer Churn (across domain): F1 generalises; F2 generalises only within telecom. We synthesise these findings into a four-component reporting checklist - pipeline disclosure, redundancy diagnostic, calibration audit, and cost-sensitive thresholds - and release a reproducible implementation.

</details>


### [176] [Generalized Biomedicine Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00120)
*Luyao Tang,Yingkai Yang,Hanqi Chen,Jiewei Zheng,Chaoqi Chen,Cheng Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces Generalized Biomedicine Discovery (GBD), a unified framework for addressing open-world challenges in medical imaging, including long-tailed rare diseases, subtle lesions, and hierarchical taxonomies. The proposed SCAN method follows a cognition-inspired perceptual progression to discover novel concepts while preserving known clinical knowledge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world clinical practice presents three open-world challenges: (1) long-tailed rare diseases, (2) subtle lesions dominated by normal anatomy, and (3) hierarchical taxonomies. Existing open-world paradigms assume flat, balanced label spaces, which fail to address these biomedical-specific needs. The key insight is that dominant known patterns form a visual manifold that masks subtle novelty.

Method: The paper proposes SCAN (Surprise-evoked Complementary AccommodatioN), which follows a cognition-inspired perceptual progression with three components: (1) Predictive suppression to filter expected norms, (2) Surprise-evoked salience to highlight unexpected deviations, and (3) Complementary accommodation to integrate these shifts into global representations.

Result: SCAN improves novel concept discovery while generally preserving established clinical knowledge. The method can be plugged into existing architectures to better navigate the known-unknown trade-off in medical imaging.

Conclusion: The proposed GBD framework and SCAN method provide a unified solution for biomedical discovery tasks, effectively addressing long-tail, anomaly, and taxonomy-aware discovery challenges. This work bridges the gap between generic open-world learning and practical clinical requirements.

Abstract: In real-world clinical practice, medical images face open-world shifts: (i) long-tailed rare diseases, (ii) subtle lesions dominated by normal anatomy, and (iii) hierarchical taxonomies. Yet most open-world paradigms assume flat, balanced label spaces, leaving these biomedical demands unresolved. We introduce Generalized Biomedicine Discovery (GBD) and a unified benchmark spanning long-tail, anomaly, and taxonomy-aware discovery. Our key insight is that dominant known patterns form a visual manifold that masks subtle novelty. Inspired by expert diagnosis, we propose SCAN (Surprise-evoked Complementary AccommodatioN), which follows a cognition-inspired perceptual progression: it applies predictive suppression to filter expected norms, triggers surprise-evoked salience to highlight unexpected deviations, and performs complementary accommodation to integrate these shifts into global representations. Extensive experiments show that SCAN improves novel concept discovery while generally preserving established clinical knowledge, and it plugs into existing architectures to better navigate the known-unknown trade-off in medical imaging. Code is available at https://github.com/lytang63/generalized-biomedicine-discovery.

</details>


### [177] [Classification Based on Association Rules Algorithm for Breast Cancer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00174)
*Ali Alsalama,Ahmed Kubba,Ghaith Jamjoum,Zaher Al Aghbari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a novel association rule-based data mining technique for breast cancer classification using a weighted classification approach. The method employs three core algorithms: Rule Generation, Rule Pruning, and Rule Prediction to identify frequent itemsets, create and prune association rules, and classify test data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Breast cancer is a significant contributor to female mortality worldwide with one of the highest occurrence rates among cancer types. There is a need for early breast cancer detection methods that are both effective and produce results understandable for medical professionals.

Method: The proposed approach uses three core algorithms: (1) Rule Generation - identifies frequent itemsets and creates association rules; (2) Rule Pruning - eliminates rules using specific criteria and separates them into major and minor groups based on their influence on training data; (3) Rule Prediction - applies the pruned rules to classify test data.

Result: The final prediction algorithm was tested on several testing samples to demonstrate the feasibility and performance of the approach.

Conclusion: The association rule-based classification method shows promise for breast cancer detection, offering the benefit of producing results that are readily understandable for medical professionals.

Abstract: Breast cancer is a significant contributor to female mortality across the world, displaying one of the highest oc currence rates among the various cancer types. In response to the need for early breast cancer detection, researchers have increasingly turned to association rule-based classification as a favored method. Association Rule mining is a data mining approach which offers the benefit of yielding results that are readily understandable for medical professionals. This paper introduces a novel association rule-based data mining technique for breast cancer classification based on a weighted classification approach. This implementation employs three core algorithms: Rule Generation, Rule Pruning, and Rule Prediction. Rule Generation identifies frequent itemsets and creates association rules. Rule Pruning eliminates rules using specific criteria and separates them into major and minor groups based on their influence on training data. Rule Prediction applies the pruned rules to classify test data. The final prediction algorithm was tested on several testing samples to show the feasibility and performance of the approach.

</details>


### [178] [Four Ways to Grow a Classifier and Why One of Them Cannot Learn](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00180)
*Cagri Temel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper analyzes four "growth decisions" in constructive classifiers (models that add structure during training). The author finds that three decisions each buy something specific (smaller networks, sparsity, or nothing useful), while one decision - deepening soft decision trees by adding gates - buys nothing because it leaves gradients identically zero. A fix using small random perturbation is proposed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand what each growth decision in constructive classifiers actually achieves, measured under a fixed protocol. The author identifies that one natural growth decision (deepening soft decision trees) fails to learn and seeks to diagnose why and provide a fix.

Method: The paper uses empirical evaluation with three seeds of five-fold cross-validation on three datasets (Iris, Wine, Digits). For the problematic growth decision, the author provides mathematical proof that gradients are zero, then validates experimentally. The three other growth decisions are tested: (1) fitting new hidden unit to residual error, (2) splitting leaf with largest expected error, (3) requiring statistical significance before split.

Result: 1. Deepening soft decision trees by adding gates leaves gradients zero - the added level cannot learn (loses 19.6 on Iris, 19.1 on Wine, 55.6 on Digits). Fix: small random perturbation of children.
2. Fitting new hidden unit to residual error buys smaller networks but not more accuracy; on Digits it significantly costs accuracy.
3. Splitting leaf with largest expected error buys sparsity (0.885 with 3.7 splits vs 63 for complete tree) but loses 4.3 points on harder problem.
4. Requiring statistical significance before split buys nothing - tree gets larger and less accurate.

Conclusion: Three of four growth decisions buy something specific: fitting new hidden units to residuals buys smaller networks, splitting by largest expected error buys sparsity, and requiring statistical significance buys nothing useful. The fourth decision (deepening soft decision trees) is fundamentally broken because gradients are identically zero, not just weak. The fix is simple: add small random perturbation after adding parameters and assert gradient is nonzero.

Abstract: Constructive classifiers add structure while they train: a level to a tree, a unit to a hidden layer, a split at a leaf. This paper asks what each of four such growth decisions actually buys, measured under one fixed protocol in tree-structured and constructive models, and gives an exact diagnosis and a fix for the one that buys nothing.
  The diagnosis concerns the most natural way to deepen a soft decision tree: turn every leaf into a gate whose two children inherit the parent's class distribution, so that the function is unchanged. I prove that this leaves the gradient of every new gate identically zero and, with the gate at 1/2, gives the two children identical gradients, so the added level can never learn. Unlike the symmetry that Net2Net breaks with noise or the saddle point that splitting steepest descent escapes with second-order information, first-order information here is not weak but absent. Over three seeds of five-fold cross-validation the construction loses 19.6 accuracy points on Iris, 19.1 on Wine and 55.6 on Digits against the same depth trained from scratch. The fix is a small random perturbation of the children, whose size barely matters. The practical rule is one line in a test: after adding parameters, assert that their gradient is nonzero.
  The other three decisions each buy one thing. Fitting a new hidden unit to the residual error before installing it buys a smaller network on every dataset, though not a more accurate one, and on Digits it costs accuracy significantly. Splitting the leaf with the largest expected error buys sparsity, reaching 0.885 with 3.7 splits where a complete depth-six tree uses 63, but loses 4.3 points on a harder problem. Requiring statistical significance before a node receives a more expressive split buys nothing: the tree gets larger and less accurate.
  Every number in the paper is inserted from the measurement script.

</details>


### [179] [Energy Time-Series Imputation with Differentially Private Diffusion Models via Clipping-Aware Objective Conditioning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00209)
*Huizhen Huang,Yu Li,Tao Huang,Chen Hou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a privacy-preserving diffusion model for energy time-series imputation using DP-SGD. It addresses the problem that late timesteps in cosine diffusion schedules produce large pre-clipping gradients that get clipped, reducing optimization signal. The solution uses v-prediction, static loss weighting, and diffusion-schedule-aware dynamic weighting to mitigate gradient amplification at low-SNR timesteps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reliable recovery of missing measurements is important for monitoring and analysis in energy time-series systems. However, fine-grained measurements may contain sensitive temporal information, requiring privacy protection. Existing diffusion models trained with DP-SGD suffer from gradient clipping issues at late timesteps (low SNR conditions), which reduces the retained optimization signal and degrades imputation quality.

Method: The proposed method formulates the clipping interaction as an objective optimization problem under fixed-threshold DP-SGD. It employs three key techniques: (1) v-prediction to mitigate late-timestep gradient amplification, (2) static loss weighting as a uniform-scaling control, and (3) diffusion-schedule-aware dynamic weighting for stronger attenuation before clipping. The method was evaluated on five real-world energy time-series datasets under various missing data scenarios (random point missingness, contiguous block missingness, persistent outages, and multiple missing-data severities).

Result: Under matched DP-SGD settings, the proposed method consistently improves imputation utility over the ε-prediction baseline. Gradient diagnostics reveal lower upper-tail pre-clipping gradient norms, reduced clipping fractions, and stronger attenuation at late low-SNR timesteps.

Conclusion: Clipping-aware objective conditioning is effective for privacy-preserving energy time-series imputation. The proposed approach successfully addresses the gradient clipping problem in DP-SGD training of diffusion models, providing better utility-privacy tradeoffs for sensitive energy time-series data.

Abstract: Reliable recovery of missing measurements is important for monitoring and analysis in energy time-series systems, where fine-grained measurements may contain sensitive temporal information. Diffusion models trained with differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) provide a promising framework for privacy-sensitive energy time-series imputation. Under cosine diffusion schedules, late timesteps correspond to low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions, where standard $\varepsilon$-prediction can induce large pre-clipping gradients. Such gradients are more likely to be clipped, reducing the retained optimization signal. The artificial intelligence (AI) contribution lies in formulating this objective--clipping interaction as an objective optimization problem under fixed-threshold DP-SGD and developing timestep-aware objective conditioning for diffusion-based energy time-series imputation. The method adopts $v$-prediction to mitigate late-timestep gradient amplification, uses static loss weighting as a uniform-scaling control, and introduces diffusion-schedule-aware dynamic weighting for stronger attenuation before clipping. For the engineering application, we evaluate the method on five real-world energy time-series datasets across random point missingness, contiguous block missingness, persistent outages, and multiple missing-data severities. Under matched DP-SGD settings, the proposed method consistently improves imputation utility over the $\varepsilon$-prediction baseline. Gradient diagnostics reveal lower upper-tail pre-clipping gradient norms, reduced clipping fractions, and stronger attenuation at late low-SNR timesteps, supporting the effectiveness of clipping-aware objective conditioning for energy time-series imputation.

</details>


### [180] [Useful to Whom? Sample Value Is Defined Only Relative to the Learner](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00221)
*Yangze Liu,Xiao-Long Yin,Zhongyi Han*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether the crossover boundary between easy-first and geometric coverage criteria in coreset selection is fixed or changes with the target learner. Through controlled experiments freezing selected subsets while manipulating only the training learner, the authors demonstrate that the boundary is learner-dependent, not data-fixed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core question is whether coreset selection criteria (easy-first vs geometric coverage) have a fixed crossover point determined by data, or whether this boundary changes with the target learner. Understanding this is crucial for practical deployment of coreset selection methods.

Method: Controlled experiments freezing selected subsets while manipulating only the training learner. Experiments include: (1) varying ResNet-18 width on ImageNet-100, (2) manipulating input grid/resolution, (3) stride controls, (4) testing on native-224px ImageNet-1k, and (5) swapping CNN for ViT.

Result: Doubling ResNet-18's width moves crossover from 57 to 85 samples per class. Grid enlargement shifts boundary left, with weakening effect as width increases. Removing last downsampling stride recovers the leftward shift. On ImageNet-1k, width effects are smaller and depend on the probe (LFrac flat, EL2N shifts modestly right). ViT makes coverage win throughout the measured range even with convolutional-derived subsets.

Conclusion: The crossover boundary is not fixed by data but changes with the target learner. Network structure (width, stride, architecture) can move the boundary. No universal scaling law exists. Practical implication: selection strategy's preferred budget regime must be evaluated with respect to the target learner.

Abstract: What kind of data does a model need in order to learn? Coreset selection makes this question concrete: under a budget, keep the samples most useful for training. Easy-first and geometric coverage criteria can win in different budget regimes, separated by a crossover boundary. We ask whether this boundary is fixed by the data or changes with the target learner. Controlled experiments freeze the selected subsets and manipulate only the training learner. On low-resolution ImageNet-100, doubling ResNet-18's width moves the crossover from 57 to 85 samples per class: the learner changes the relative value of the same samples. A wider sweep reveals an interaction between input grid and capacity. Enlarging the grid while retaining the same image information shifts the boundary left, and this shift weakens as width increases. Stride controls reproduce and reverse the grid effect without changing the input grid; removing only the last downsampling stride is sufficient to recover the leftward shift. Under the native-224px ImageNet-1k protocol, width effects are smaller and depend on the probe: LFrac remains nearly flat, while EL2N shifts modestly right. Swapping the convolutional learning system for a ViT makes coverage win throughout the measured range, even when the easy subsets come from the convolutional proxy. These results establish learner dependence through frozen-subset interventions and identify network structure that can move the boundary. They do not yield a universal scaling law. Their practical implication is direct: a selection strategy's preferred budget regime must be evaluated with respect to the target learner.

</details>


### [181] [Constant-Memory Recall: Learned Associations in a Fixed Matrix State](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00232)
*Samuel Larson*

Main category: cs.LG
