TL;DR: This paper investigates a small DeltaNet variant with fixed token-specific key biases for remembering 32 new key-value pairings per sequence. The model achieves 99.95% mean accuracy with 32 KiB of recurrent matrix state, and recall persists even with extended context up to 1,798 tokens. However, parameter-matched Transformer and vector baselines fail at this task, preventing fair memory-efficiency comparisons.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to study how fixed-size recurrent memory limits storage growth during inference, and to understand what makes successful recall possible - depending on the task and training. The researchers aim to test the capacity of a small DeltaNet variant for remembering new key-value pairings.

Method: The study uses a small DeltaNet variant with fixed token-specific key biases, trained to remember 32 new key-value pairings per sequence. The model has 32 KiB of recurrent matrix state. Experiments include testing recall with extended pre-query context (1,798 tokens), ablating the first memory block, and testing with 48 pairs. Parameter-matched vector and Transformer baselines are also evaluated.

Result: The DeltaNet achieves 99.95% mean accuracy across three training seeds when selecting among sequence values. Recall remains near perfect when filler extends the pre-query context to 1,798 tokens without adding pairings. Zeroing the first memory block completely removes recall capability. An exploratory 48-pair test remains near chance after one quarter of the primary training budget. Parameter-matched baselines (vector and Transformer) remain near chance even after additional training searches.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that the DeltaNet variant can successfully recall 32 key-value pairings with near-perfect accuracy, even with extended context. The first memory block is critical for recall. However, the unresolved failure of baseline models prevents a fair memory-efficiency comparison between the recurrent approach and Transformers. The capacity limit for the 48-pair task was not found within the training budget.

Abstract: Fixed-size recurrent memory limits storage growth during inference, but successful recall depends on the task and training. We study a small DeltaNet variant with fixed token-specific key biases, trained to remember 32 new key-value pairings per sequence. With 32 KiB of recurrent matrix state, it achieves 99.95% mean accuracy across three training seeds when choosing among the sequence's values. Recall remains near perfect when filler extends the pre-query context to 1,798 tokens without adding pairings. Zeroing the first memory block removes this recall. An exploratory 48-pair test remains near chance after one quarter of the primary training budget and does not locate a capacity limit. Parameter-matched vector and Transformer baselines remain near chance, including the Transformer after additional training searches. This unresolved baseline failure prevents a memory-efficiency comparison.

</details>


### [182] [How Many Categories Are Enough? Distribution-Free Certification Limits for Few-Shot Anomaly Thresholds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00236)
*Gia Huy Thai,Nguyen Thai Anh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses a critical gap in few-shot anomaly detection: the disconnect between ranking-based evaluation and deployment requirements for controlled false-alarm rates (FAR). The authors demonstrate that threshold certification for unseen categories is severely limited by resolution constraints and distribution shift, and propose the CRESS protocol to systematically assess when source evidence can support transferable reliability claims.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that few-shot anomaly detectors are evaluated using ranking metrics, but real-world deployment requires setting a specific alarm threshold with a controllable false-alarm rate. This creates a fundamental challenge: how much normal evidence is needed to reliably certify a threshold for an unseen category? This question is practically important but theoretically underexplored.

Method: The authors use a frozen DINOv2 PCA residual ranker evaluated on 15 MVTec and 12 VisA categories under four corruption types. They derive a category-count feasibility calculus for distribution-free 95% upper confidence bounds (UCB). They propose the Cross-category Reliability Estimation with Source Support (CRESS) protocol, which splits source categories into disjoint reference, proposal, and certification roles to assess threshold transferability.

Result: Key findings: (1) LOIO calibration is resolution-limited (rank values ≥ 1/(k+1)) and shift-fragile—at α=0.20, empirical FAR reaches 0.341 on Gaussian-corrupted MVTec, 1.7× the nominal level. (2) Minimum category counts needed for deterministic UCB: 14, 29, and 59 iid draws at α=0.20, 0.10, 0.05. (3) With only 3-4 certification categories, all 960 configurations return fail-closed threshold τ*=0. (4) Image-unit analyses select positive thresholds in only 36.7% to 60.3% of target cells, with bounds holding only for the selected source mixture, not for new-category marginal risk.

Conclusion: The paper establishes a quantitative feasibility boundary for threshold certification in few-shot anomaly detection. It demonstrates that source evidence can only support reliability claims under very specific conditions, and the CRESS protocol provides an estimand-aware framework for specifying when such transferability is valid. The main takeaway is that threshold transferability is far more constrained than typically assumed, requiring substantial category-level evidence and careful protocol design.

Abstract: Few-shot anomaly detectors are judged by ranking metrics, yet deployment requires an alarm threshold with a controlled false-alarm rate (FAR). We ask how much normal evidence, in images or category units, is needed to certify such a threshold for an unseen category. Using a frozen DINOv2 principal component analysis (PCA) residual ranker on 15 MVTec and 12 VisA categories under four corruption types, we show that target-only leave-one-image-out (LOIO) calibration is resolution-limited and shift-fragile: rank values cannot fall below $1/(k+1)$, and at the attainable level $α=0.20$, empirical FAR reaches 0.341 on Gaussian-corrupted MVTec at $k=4$, 1.7 times the nominal level. A category-count feasibility calculus is then derived: even with all-zero category losses and no multiplicity charged, any deterministic, uniformly valid, distribution-free 95% upper confidence bound (UCB) requires at least 14, 29, and 59 independent and identically distributed (iid) category draws at $α=0.20$, $0.10$, and $0.05$; these counts are necessary but not sufficient. The Cross-category Reliability Estimation with Source Support (CRESS) protocol splits source categories into disjoint reference, proposal, and certification roles. With only three or four certification categories, all 960 frozen configurations return the fail-closed threshold $τ^\star=0$, and the smallest category-level UCB is 0.950. Image-unit analyses of the same archive select positive thresholds in 36.7% to 60.3% of target cells; these bounds hold for the selected source mixture, not for the marginal risk of a new-category draw. The contribution is a quantitative feasibility boundary and an estimand-aware protocol specifying when source evidence can, and cannot, support a transferable reliability claim.

</details>


### [183] [Cross-Benchmark Transfer from RL on Agentic Coding Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00890)
*Sushant Mehta,Logan Ritchie,Edwin Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether reinforcement learning (RL) on expert-built agentic coding tasks can close the "last mile" gap in coding agents—where they drop requirements, test only easy cases, break existing behavior, or validate against unchecked assumptions. The authors post-train Kimi K2.7 Code (a 1T-parameter MoE model) using RL on 1,700 tasks, achieving significant improvements across six external benchmarks, with transfer demonstrated on tasks released after training data collection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coding agents frequently fail in the "last mile": they build most of a feature but drop a requirement, test only cases their implementation already handles, break behavior that was supposed to stay intact, or validate against unchecked assumptions. The authors investigate whether RL on expert-built agentic coding tasks can close this gap and whether learned capabilities transfer beyond the training distribution.

Method: Post-training Kimi K2.7 Code (1T-parameter, 32B active MoE model) using RL alone on 1,700 tasks: 1,000 repository tasks graded by hidden fail-to-pass tests and pass-to-pass tests of existing behavior, and 700 terminal tasks graded by expert-written hidden verifiers. Reward is the fraction of target checks passed, dropping to zero if any pass-to-pass test fails. One epoch of GSPO on a rank-32 LoRA adapter.

Result: Pass@1 improved on all six external benchmarks across three agent harnesses: SWE-Bench Pro (60.1→64.8), DeepSWE (31.0→43.4), Terminal-Bench 2.1 (67.4→82.0), Terminal-Bench 3 (1.4→12.1), Terminal-Bench 4 (0.0→7.6), SWE-Marathon (5.0→25.0). Median trajectories on DeepSWE and Terminal-Bench 3 are 24-35% shorter in agent steps. The trained model avoids all four failure modes on newly solved tasks.

Conclusion: RL on expert-built agentic coding tasks successfully closes the last-mile gap in coding agents. Improvements are statistically significant (p < 0.001 overall, p = 0.004 on post-training released benchmarks), demonstrating transfer beyond the training distribution. The model learns to avoid the four failure modes (dropped requirements, incomplete testing, broken existing behavior, unchecked assumptions).

Abstract: Coding agents often fail in the last mile: they build most of a feature but drop a requirement, test only the cases their implementation already handles, break behavior that was supposed to stay intact, or validate against an unchecked assumption. We ask whether reinforcement learning (RL) on expert-built agentic coding tasks closes this gap, and whether what the agent learns transfers beyond the training distribution. We post-train Kimi K2.7 Code, a 1T-parameter (32B active) open-weight mixture-of-experts model, with RL alone on 1,700 tasks: 1,000 repository tasks graded by hidden fail-to-pass tests and by pass-to-pass tests of existing behavior, and 700 terminal tasks graded by expert-written hidden verifiers. The reward is the fraction of target checks passed and drops to zero if any pass-to-pass test fails. One epoch of GSPO on a rank-32 LoRA adapter improves pass@1 on each of the six external benchmarks we evaluated, across three agent harnesses: SWE-Bench Pro (60.1 to 64.8), DeepSWE (31.0 to 43.4), Terminal-Bench 2.1 (67.4 to 82.0), Terminal-Bench 3 (1.4 to 12.1), Terminal-Bench 4 (0.0 to 7.6), and SWE-Marathon (5.0 to 25.0). Pooled over the five independent task sets (Terminal-Bench 4 revises Terminal-Bench 3), the improvement is significant (p < 0.001), and it remains significant on the three sets released after the training data was collected (p = 0.004); the model also improves under both harnesses never used in training. Median trajectories on DeepSWE and Terminal-Bench 3 are 24-35% shorter in agent steps. The base model's failed DeepSWE runs are mostly near-misses, and on the tasks the trained model newly solves, paired trajectories show it avoiding each of the four failure modes above.

</details>


### [184] [Contingent Exposure Routing for Financial AI: Outage Risk and the Cost of Indivisible Decisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00239)
*Shivam Gupta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses financial system resilience during endpoint failures (model failover). It proposes an outage-contingent routing framework using a market-impact response matrix to minimize expected squared price displacement. The authors show that shared backups can create concentration risk, while balanced fallback strategies reduce risk inversely with surviving endpoints. They develop randomized routing with conditional-expectation rounding and a swap procedure, demonstrating 6.57-10.53% risk reduction across synthetic portfolios and 3.30% on recorded API replays.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address a critical gap in financial system infrastructure: when primary endpoints fail (model failover), availability is restored but the routing of decisions changes which financial institutions share decision errors. This creates a systemic risk concern where shared backups can concentrate risk rather than diversify it. The authors aim to develop an auditable routing stress test and implementation analysis for endpoint diversification.

Method: The methodology involves: (1) Formulating outage-contingent routing through a local market-impact response matrix; (2) Analyzing expected squared price displacement as the risk metric; (3) Constructing symmetric analysis showing concentration floors with shared backups; (4) Deriving exact second moment of independent randomized routing; (5) Developing conditional-expectation rounding for finite-agent bounds; (6) Creating a swap procedure that preserves endpoint counts; (7) Empirical validation across 60 synthetic portfolio networks (11,340 scenarios) and 1,024 recorded API responses.

Result: Key results include: (1) Shared backups can leave an order-one concentration floor as primary endpoints grow; (2) Balanced fallback risk decreases inversely with surviving endpoint count; (3) Risk reduction of 6.57% for single and 10.53% for double endpoint removals at central feedback setting; (4) Held-out reduction of 3.30% (CI: 2.07-4.57%) on recorded API replay; (5) Strongly aligned errors, inferior endpoints, and indivisibility limit diversification benefits.

Conclusion: The contribution is an auditable routing stress test and implementation analysis, not an estimate of real-market crash probabilities. The paper demonstrates that endpoint diversification can reduce risk but has fundamental limits when errors are correlated, endpoints have different quality, or decisions are indivisible. The proposed methods provide practical tools for evaluating routing strategies in financial systems, though real-world deployment requires careful consideration of error correlations and endpoint heterogeneity.

Abstract: Model failover restores availability, but changes which financial institutions share decision errors. We formulate outage-contingent routing through a local market-impact response matrix and study expected squared price displacement. A symmetric construction shows that a shared backup can leave an order-one concentration floor as the number of primary endpoints grows, while balanced fallback risk decreases inversely with the surviving endpoint count. For indivisible decisions, we derive the exact second moment of independent randomized routing and an effective-exposure granularity that determines its gap from fractional allocation. Conditional-expectation rounding gives a finite-agent bound without coupled quotas; a separate swap procedure preserves endpoint counts and is assessed against dual lower bounds. Across 60 synthetic portfolio networks and 11,340 scenario evaluations, the latter reduces risk by 6.57% and 10.53% for single and double endpoint removals at the central feedback setting with independent errors. A replay of 1,024 recorded API responses on constructed rebalancing tasks gives a smaller held-out reduction of 3.30% (paired bootstrap interval 2.07--4.57%). Strongly aligned errors, inferior endpoints, and indivisibility limit diversification. The contribution is an auditable routing stress test and implementation analysis, not an estimate of real-market crash probabilities.

</details>


### [185] [Exposing the Cost of Deep Learning Audio Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01619)
*Constance Douwes,Paul Magron,Romain Serizel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a methodology to estimate the energy consumption of the development phase in deep learning projects, using data from the Grid5000 platform. The study focuses on audio projects from the Multispeech research team and finds that development phase energy costs are 3-256 times greater than training the best-performing model alone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing environmental impact studies of deep learning mainly focus on training and inference phases, overlooking the development phase which includes architecture prototyping and intensive experiments. This oversight leads to significant underestimation of the true carbon footprint of deep learning projects.

Method: The researchers proposed a methodology to estimate energy costs based on activity logs from the Grid5000 shared computing platform used by the LORIA laboratory. They conducted a case study on audio projects developed in the Multispeech research team, evaluating four projects and comparing their development phase energy costs to the training costs of reported models.

Result: The energy required for the development phase is 3 to 256 times greater than that required to train the best-performing model alone. This represents a substantial underestimation in previous carbon footprint calculations that only considered training/inference.

Conclusion: The results advocate for more systematic reporting of energy consumption across the entire life cycle of deep learning-based audio projects, not just the training phase. This comprehensive approach is essential for accurate environmental impact assessment of deep learning research.

Abstract: The environmental impact of deep learning has attracted increasing attention over the past decade. Existing studies mainly focus on the energy and carbon emissions of model training and inference, while the whole development phase is often overlooked. Yet, architecture prototyping and intensive experiments are conducted during this stage, which is highly energy-demanding. In this article, we propose a methodology to estimate these costs, based on activity logs from the Grid5000 shared computing platform used by the LORIA laboratory. As a case-study, we focus on audio projects developed in the Multispeech research team. We evaluate the overall energy cost of four projects, and we compare them to those of training the reported models. Our results show that the energy required for the development phase is 3 to 256 times greater than that required to train the best-performing model alone. These results advocate for a more systematic reporting of energy consumption across the entire life cycle of deep learning-based audio projects.

</details>


### [186] [The Null Is the Hard Part: Exact Tests for Memorization in Generative Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00251)
*Sushovan Majhi,Pramita Bagchi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper identifies critical statistical flaws in current memorization audits of generative models, which lack proper null distributions and can produce false conclusions. The authors propose two new null hypothesis methods: a permutation test for whole-model evaluation and matched controls for single-image auditing. When applied to Stable Diffusion and other models, current benchmark mitigations show much weaker effects than claimed (2/3-100% of "certified" images become undetected under various perturbations). The paper recommends the small-scale mass of the Intersection Euler Characteristic Profile as a robust scale-restricted statistic.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current memorization audits of generative models read similarity scores against arbitrary thresholds without proper null distributions, leading to incorrect conclusions. The field lacks validated statistical methods to distinguish true memorization from random similarity, and the "data-copying test" falsely flags generators that reproduce nothing when compared against its own null distribution.

Method: The authors introduce two null hypothesis approaches: (1) For whole-model evaluation, a permutation test where training and held-out images are exchangeable given model samples, exact for any statistic with random splits; (2) For single-image auditing, matched controls calibrated against resampling independent generations. They test these methods against MemBench's Stable Diffusion memorization benchmarks using various perturbations (random prompts, attention rescaling, embedding optimization) and evaluate 24 different generators.

Result: Under MemBench's rule, mitigations roughly halve Stable Diffusion's memorization. However, with false-discovery control: (a) random prompt perturbations eliminate detection in 2/3 of certified images; (b) attention rescaling eliminates 5/6; (c) embedding optimization eliminates all. The standard data-copying test falsely flags 10/24 generators. With the new permutation test, nearest-neighbor preference still fires on 7/24 models, but count restricted to near-duplicate scale on none (McNemar p=0.016). For single images, ranking among random images yields 596 false discoveries among 2,365 controls, and resampling makes the null three times too narrow. The calibrated audit certifies 36/61 MemBench images at 5% FDR, with held-out controls certified in only 0.01% of calibration splits. A calibrated maximum certifies 46 images.

Conclusion: The field's memorization auditing methods suffer from fundamental statistical flaws including missing null distributions and overly narrow confidence intervals. The authors recommend the small-scale mass of the Intersection Euler Characteristic Profile as a robust scale-restricted statistic that counts distinct images copied and can test whether two models copy the same images. Proper calibration against matched controls is essential for valid memorization detection.

Abstract: Memorization audits of generative models read similarity scores against thresholds, with no null distribution, and the conclusions they support can be wrong. By MemBench's rule, the benchmark's mitigations roughly halve Stable Diffusion's memorization; audited with false-discovery control, two thirds of the certified images are no longer detected under random prompt perturbations, five sixths under attention rescaling, and all of them under embedding optimization. The field's data-copying test, read against its own null, flags ten of twenty-four generators that reproduce nothing. We argue that for memorization the null is the hard part, and supply two. For a whole model, training and held-out images are exchangeable given its samples, and relabelling them is a permutation test, exact for any statistic when the held-out images are a random split; under it, a nearest-neighbour preference still fires on seven of those twenty-four, and a count restricted to the near-duplicate scale on none (McNemar p=0.016). For single images, the natural nulls fail twice, measurably: ranking an image among random images yields 596 false discoveries among 2,365 controls, and resampling independent generations makes the null three times too narrow. Calibrated against matched controls, the audit certifies 36 of 61 MemBench images at 5% false-discovery rate, held-out controls are certified in 0.01% of calibration splits, and on this benchmark two generations per image recover that count. A calibrated maximum, which reads occasional rather than typical copying, certifies 46. As the scale-restricted statistic we recommend the small-scale mass of the Intersection Euler Characteristic Profile, which also counts distinct images copied and tests whether two models copy the same ones.

</details>


### [187] [Sharp Oracle-Regret Tradeoffs for Projection-Free Online Convex Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00254)
*Vaneet Aggarwal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies online convex optimization when the learner can only access the feasible set through an exact linear optimization oracle. The main result establishes a dimension-free minimax expected regret of Θ(GD max{√T, T/(1+min{Q,BT})^1/4}) for convex G-Lipschitz losses with diameter D, Q total oracle calls, and B calls per round. The lower bound holds for arbitrary randomized learners, and a counted approximate-gradient method with interleaved blocks achieves the matching rate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand the fundamental limits of online convex optimization when the learner has limited access to the feasible set, specifically only through an exact linear optimization oracle. This constrained access model is practical in scenarios where querying the feasible set is expensive or restricted, and the paper aims to characterize the regret achievable under such constraints.

Method: The paper uses two main technical constructions for the lower bound: (1) universal feasibility forcing each action into the hull of the supplied ball and preceding oracle replies, and (2) a fixed-body construction coupling fresh phase directions to a shared simplex to make useful replies costly repeatedly. For the upper bound, a counted approximate-gradient method with interleaved blocks is developed to achieve the matching rate.

Result: The main result is a dimension-free minimax expected regret of Θ(GD max{√T, T/(1+min{Q,BT})^1/4}) for convex G-Lipschitz losses. This characterization captures two regimes: the standard √T regret when sufficient oracle calls are available, and a T^{3/4} rate when limited to one call per round. Special cases include T^{3/4} rate with B=1 call per round and √T regret with quadratic total budget Q = Ω(T^2). For prescribed smoothness β, the paper also provides a curvature-dependent lower bound and identifies the threshold above which the general characterization remains sharp.

Conclusion: The paper provides a complete characterization of the regret achievable in online convex optimization with limited oracle access. The Θ(GD max{√T, T/(1+min{Q,BT})^1/4}) bound is universal across dimensions and matches for both total-budget (Q) and strict per-round (B) constraints. The results show that even when all losses share a common minimizer, useful oracle replies remain costly repeatedly, highlighting the fundamental tradeoff between oracle queries and regret performance.

Abstract: We characterize the regret attainable in online convex optimization when access to the feasible set is limited to an exact linear optimization oracle. The learner is given an inscribed ball and a diameter bound and must remain feasible on every consistent instance. For convex $G$-Lipschitz losses, diameter at most $D$, a total allowance of $Q$ oracle calls, and a strict limit of $B$ calls per round, the dimension-free minimax expected regret is $Θ(GD\max\{\sqrt T,T/(1+\min\{Q,BT\})^{1/4}\})$. The lower bound applies to arbitrary randomized learners. Universal feasibility first forces each action into the hull of the supplied ball and the preceding oracle replies. A fixed-body construction then couples fresh phase directions to a shared simplex, making useful replies costly repeatedly even though all losses have a common minimizer. A counted approximate-gradient method with interleaved blocks attains the matching rate. Total-budget and strict per-round guarantees follow as special cases, including the $T^{3/4}$ rate with one call per round and the quadratic total budget needed for $\sqrt T$ regret. For prescribed smoothness $β$, an analytic construction yields a curvature-dependent lower bound and identifies the threshold above which the general characterization remains sharp.

</details>


### [188] [Verification Pulses and the Cost of Escaping Wrong Consensus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00256)
*Shivam Gupta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper analyzes how to optimally allocate a fixed verification budget to recover a population from wrong consensus in an asynchronous binary register. Using nonlinear response models, birth-death processes, and asymptotic analysis, the authors derive a critical budget window and demonstrate significant gaps between mean-field predictions and exact calculations. Empirical tests with language models reveal that calibration differences and mean prediction errors can obscure terminal consensus behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses a critical problem in distributed systems and verification: how external verification affects recovery from wrong consensus in a population, particularly when limited verification resources must be allocated strategically. The core tension is that individual verification can correct specific outputs but may fail to shift the entire population from a "basin of attraction" for a wrong consensus.

Method: The paper employs multiple methods: (1) A general nonlinear response model with minimum fuel calculation under peak verification constraints to determine basin boundary crossing; (2) Exact birth-death calculations for finite populations to compute post-pulse wrong consensus probability; (3) Asymptotic analysis identifying a critical budget window with leading term N·log(x₀/b) and O(√N) corrections; (4) An empirical experiment with 13,392 language model responses including calibration and 108 held-out trajectories.

Result: Key findings include: (1) The critical budget has a leading term N·log(x₀/b) with √N corrections from two sources—repeated verification targets and autonomous amplification after verification stops; (2) With 16 majority-updated slots and 14 initially wrong, 9 random checks cross the mean-field threshold, but 23 are needed for 95% eventual recovery in the exact model; (3) Calibration produces different fitted response regimes, but all four adjusted schedule-comparison intervals include zero; (4) A distributional audit reveals that modest mean-prediction error can conceal large underestimates of terminal consensus occupancy.

Conclusion: The results support risk-calibrated reset scheduling under a specified update contract, while explicitly separating this from distinct-target checking and unrestricted evidence broadcast. The gap between mean-field predictions and exact calculations (9 vs. 23 checks) demonstrates the practical importance of precise finite-population modeling. The language model experiments highlight challenges in applying theoretical results to real-world systems where calibration regimes differ and prediction errors can mask terminal state distributions.

Abstract: External verification can correct individual outputs while leaving a self-reinforcing population in the basin of a wrong consensus. We study how the timing and addressing of a fixed verification budget affect recovery in an asynchronous binary register. For a general nonlinear response, we derive the minimum fuel required to cross a basin boundary under a peak verification constraint. For a finite population, an exact birth--death calculation gives the probability of subsequent wrong consensus after a pulse. Our main asymptotic result identifies the critical budget window: a leading term $N\log(x_0/b)$ and a correction of order $\sqrt N$, with separate variance contributions from repeated verification targets and autonomous amplification after verification stops. The distinction is substantial: with 16 majority-updated slots and 14 initially wrong, 9 random checks cross the mean-field budget threshold, whereas 23 are required for 95% eventual recovery in the exact model. A prospectively specified experiment records 13,392 language-model responses, including calibration and 108 held-out trajectories. Calibration produces different fitted response regimes, but all four adjusted schedule-comparison intervals include zero. A distributional audit also finds that modest mean-prediction error can conceal a large underestimate of terminal consensus occupancy. The results support risk-calibrated reset scheduling under a specified update contract, while explicitly separating it from distinct-target checking and unrestricted evidence broadcast.

</details>


### [189] [Attention Manifolds: Steering or Blocking Language Models by Editing Learned B-Spline Surfaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00257)
*Naveen Mysore*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces "attention manifolds" - learned 2D B-spline surfaces that modulate value vectors in transformer attention based on query-key interactions. Applied to LLaMA 3.2 models, it reduces perplexity by 2-2.5 points with 0.3% parameter overhead and enables model steering through editable surfaces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In standard transformer attention, a source token sends the same value vector to every receiver regardless of the query. The query determines how much to attend but not what to extract, limiting the model's ability to extract query-dependent information from values.

Method: The method introduces attention manifolds: learned 2D tensor-product cubic B-spline surfaces S_d(q_d, k_d) that modulate each value dimension based on query-key interaction. Each surface is initialized to zero, preserving pretrained behavior. The surfaces are mechanically editable - inverting coefficients or setting them to -1 creates "attention walls" that block value flow.

Result: Applied to LLaMA 3.2-1B-Instruct and 3B-Instruct: (1) WikiText-2 validation perplexity reduced by 2-2.5 points with 0.3% parameter overhead; (2) 69% (1B) to 83% (3B) of 112 diverse prompts show changed greedy-decoded output; (3) 94-100% change rate on ambiguous/polysemous inputs; (4) Improves output quality by correcting factual errors, increasing precision, and adding specificity; (5) Inverting layer coefficients changes output for 9/10 prompts; (6) Attention walls can redirect harmful prompts to safer content.

Conclusion: Attention manifolds provide a geometric mechanism for model steering with minimal parameter overhead. The learned surfaces enable query-dependent value extraction, improve output quality across various tasks, and offer a promising approach to safety-oriented model manipulation through editable attention modulation.

Abstract: In standard transformer attention, a source token sends the same value vector to every receiver. The query determines \emph{how much} to attend but not \emph{what} to extract. This work introduces \textbf{attention manifolds}: learned 2D B-spline surfaces $S_d(q_d, k_d)$ that modulate each value dimension based on the query-key interaction. Each surface is a tensor-product cubic B-spline initialized to zero, preserving pretrained behavior. Applied to LLaMA 3.2-1B-Instruct and 3B-Instruct, attention manifolds reduce WikiText-2 validation perplexity by 2--2.5 points with 0.3\% parameter overhead. Across 112 diverse prompts, surfaces change greedy-decoded output for 69\% (1B) to 83\% (3B) of cases, with the strongest effects on ambiguous and polysemous inputs (94--100\% change rate). The surfaces improve output quality: correcting factual errors (\emph{``the CAP theorem has three main components''} $\to$ \emph{``it is impossible to guarantee all three''}), increasing precision (\emph{``impossible to know certain properties''} $\to$ \emph{``impossible to know both position and momentum''}), and adding specificity (a generic quote $\to$ an attributed Saint Augustine citation, consistently at both scales). The learned surfaces are also mechanically editable: inverting a layer's coefficients changes greedy output for 9/10 prompts (KL~0.010), providing a geometric mechanism for model steering. Setting surface coefficients to $-1$ creates ``attention walls'' that block value flow through specific dimensions. In a preliminary experiment, a layer-wide wall redirects an explosive-device prompt from specific instructions to general educational content, suggesting a path toward safety-oriented manifold shaping.

</details>


### [190] [Large Language Bayes Is Not Reparameterisation-Invariant](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00265)
*Jian Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Large Language Bayes (LLB) weights sampled programs by an exponentiated evidence bound, but this weighting depends on parameterization choice. The authors demonstrate that equivalent probabilistic programs (by measure) can have drastically different weights (up to 31.9× discrepancy), inverting Bayes factors, and that this is controlled by a Hilbert-distance bound involving the spread of bound shortfalls.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether LLB's weighting scheme produces consistent results across different parameterizations of the same probabilistic program, since the log marginal likelihood is mathematically invariant to reparameterization but the evidence bound used by LLB is not.

Method: Experimental analysis across: (1) Eight schools problem comparing centered vs non-centered parameterizations; (2) Various likelihood families, dimensions, and funnel severities; (3) 360 programs from six language models; (4) Testing importance weighting and full-covariance Gaussian matching as corrections.

Result: The evidence bound weights depend heavily on parameterization: 6.1× difference on eight schools (reduced to 2.2× with importance weighting, 1.9× with Gaussian matching); up to 31.9× discrepancy in higher dimensions with sign reversal. Parameterization preference varies from 0% to 100% centered across models. This inverts Bayes factors against eight competitors. The error is controlled by spread Δ through a Hilbert-distance bound.

Conclusion: No single parameterization is uniformly preferable; the induced error in posterior estimates is bounded by the spread Δ of bound shortfalls. Detecting equivalent programs statistically can falsely merge different models; verifying reparameterizations generated internally closes this window.

Abstract: Large Language Bayes (LLB) answers an informal modelling question by sampling candidate probabilistic programs from a language model, running approximate inference on each, and averaging them with weights proportional to an exponentiated evidence bound. We show that this weighting depends on how a model is written. The log marginal likelihood is invariant to reparameterisation; the evidence bound is not. On eight schools the centered and non-centered programs are the same measure to $5.7\times10^{-14}$, yet their weights differ by $6.1\times$; importance weighting reduces this only to $2.2\times$, and reproducing the inference LLB actually runs, a full-covariance Gaussian matched to the posterior moments, still leaves $1.9\times$ on eight schools and $8.9\times$ in $64$ dimensions. Across likelihood families, dimensions and funnel severities the discrepancy reaches $31.9\times$ and reverses sign, so no single writing is uniformly preferable. It inverts Bayes factors against eight natural competitors, and the induced error in the model posterior, and in any downstream target, is controlled by the spread $Δ$ of the bound shortfalls through a known sharp Hilbert-distance bound. Across $360$ programs from six language models the parameterisation written ranges from $0\%$ to $100\%$ centered and is stable within a model. Detecting equivalent programs statistically can falsely merge genuinely different models at practical sample budgets; verifying reparameterisations we generate ourselves cannot, and closes the window.

</details>


### [191] [FastCI: Efficient GPU-Intensive CI for LLM Training Frameworks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01967)
*Tianshuo Qiao,Naiqian Zheng,Xiaopeng Liu,Shuguang Wang,Diandian Gu,Xuanzhe Liu,Xin Jin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FastCI is a framework designed to address CI bottlenecks in LLM training frameworks by leveraging runtime evidence for test selection, pruning equivalent tests, prioritizing high-risk tests, and optimizing test workloads. It achieves 77.5% CI latency reduction and 63.9% GPU resource reduction while improving coverage retention by 3.2%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid evolution of LLM training frameworks creates a need for efficient CI pipelines. However, unlike traditional software, LLM CI relies on GPU-intensive tests involving complete model training/evaluation, making CI itself a development bottleneck. Existing CI approaches are inadequate for the fast-paced development cycles of LLM frameworks.

Method: FastCI employs four key techniques: (1) Runtime evidence-based test selection to identify affected tests, (2) Test pruning for equivalent contexts where changed code executes similarly, (3) High-risk test prioritization to expose failures earlier, (4) Workload optimization along dimensions outside each test's intended validation scope.

Result: Evaluated on ByteDance's LLM training framework CI workload, FastCI achieves: 77.5% CI latency reduction, 63.9% GPU resource usage reduction, and 3.2% improvement in modified code coverage retention compared to existing CI pipelines.

Conclusion: FastCI successfully addresses CI bottlenecks in LLM training frameworks through intelligent test selection and optimization. It has been deployed in production at ByteDance's LLM training CI pipelines, demonstrating practical viability while maintaining quality metrics.

Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) keep growing in size and complexity, their training frameworks evolve at a rapid pace as well. Therefore, continuous integration (CI) is critical for maintaining the quality and stability of these frameworks. However, unlike traditional software, CI for LLM training frameworks relies on GPU-intensive tests, which usually involve complete model training or evaluation. This leads CI itself to become a new bottleneck for fast-paced development. In this paper, we introduce FastCI, a framework that improves the efficiency of CI for LLM training frameworks. FastCI leverages runtime evidence to select affected tests and prune tests that execute changed code in equivalent contexts. Then FastCI prioritizes high-risk tests to expose potential failures earlier, and optimizes test workloads along dimensions outside the intended validation scope of each test. Evaluated on the CI workload of our LLM training framework, FastCI reduces the CI latency by 77.5% and the GPU resource usage by 63.9%, while improving the modified code coverage retention by 3.2%, compared with the currently deployed CI pipelines. FastCI has now been integrated into the CI pipelines of our LLM training framework at ByteDance.

</details>


### [192] [MOVE: Multimodal Open-world Verification and Expansion for Graph Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00268)
*Zekai Chen,Jiayang Xing,Xun Wu,Miao Zhang,Xunkai Li,Kairui Yang,Zhengyu Wu,Xu Wang,Rong-Hua Li,Guoren Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MOVE addresses the open-world problem in multimodal graph learning where new classes may emerge after deployment. It identifies unknown nodes using multimodal information, generates candidate classes via multimodal LLM, and selectively expands the class space only when candidates are consistently supported by multimodal evidence without introducing redundant categories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In multimodal graph learning, models are trained with a fixed label space but new classes may emerge after deployment. Existing approaches fail to determine whether existing classes are insufficient or whether generated classes are reliable enough. The empirical study reveals three key challenges: multimodal information is required for unknown-node identification, LLM-generated descriptions may not capture multimodal characteristics, and directly adding candidates introduces redundant categories.

Method: MOVE proposes a three-stage framework: (1) Unknown node identification by jointly considering visual tokens, textual attributes, and graph context; (2) Candidate class generation using multimodal LLM; (3) Selective class space expansion only when candidates are consistently supported by multimodal evidence without introducing unnecessary categories.

Result: MOVE achieves an average improvement of 11.87% across unknown recognition, open-domain annotation, and downstream graph learning tasks.

Conclusion: The proposed MOVE framework effectively addresses the open-world class expansion problem in multimodal graph learning by combining multimodal information for unknown identification, leveraging multimodal LLM for candidate generation, and implementing a verification mechanism to avoid redundant categories.

Abstract: Multimodal graph learning faces a fundamental challenge: new classes may emerge after deployment, while models are trained with a fixed label space. Existing approaches typically detect unknown nodes and use LLMs to generate candidate class descriptions, but they do not determine whether existing classes are insufficient to cover these nodes or whether a generated class is reliable enough to expand the class space. Our empirical study reveals three challenges: multimodal information beyond individual modalities is required for unknown-node identification, LLM-generated class descriptions may not fully capture multimodal class characteristics, and directly adding candidate classes can introduce redundant categories. Based on these observations, we propose MOVE, a multimodal open-world class verification and expansion framework. MOVE identifies nodes that cannot be assigned to existing classes by jointly considering visual tokens, textual attributes, and graph context, leverages a multimodal LLM to generate candidate classes, and selectively expands the class space only when candidates are consistently supported by multimodal evidence without introducing unnecessary categories. Experiments demonstrate that MOVE achieves an average improvement of 11.87\% across unknown recognition, open-domain annotation, and downstream graph learning tasks.

</details>


### [193] [Coupling Perception and Reasoning in Federated Multimodal Graph Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00277)
*Zekai Chen,Xun Wu,Hailin Zhang,Xunkai Li,Yu Liu,Kairui Yang,Muyan Huang,Xuaner Chen,Rong-Hua Li,Guoren Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FedCORE is a federated adaptation framework for multimodal graph foundation models (GFMs) that addresses the incompatibility issue between separately parameterized Encoder and GNN updates by representing both through a shared low-dimensional latent state, achieving an 80.7% reduction in the Encoder-GNN pairing gap.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing federated GFM adaptation methods only update graph-side modules (GNN) while keeping the multimodal Encoder frozen, limiting adaptation to how information is propagated without considering what information is extracted. Empirical studies revealed that Encoder and GNN adaptations are not independent.

Method: FedCORE represents Encoder and GNN updates through a shared low-dimensional latent state ("core"). It jointly optimizes this core from multimodal and structural signals and performs federated evolution directly in the shared state space, preserving compatibility between perception (Encoder) and reasoning (GNN) adaptations.

Result: FedCORE reduces the Encoder-GNN pairing gap from 30.6 to 5.9, corresponding to an 80.7% reduction over independent joint adaptation.

Conclusion: The proposed shared latent state approach effectively addresses the pairing sensitivity problem between separately parameterized Encoder and GNN updates in federated multimodal graph learning, enabling more compatible and effective joint adaptation.

Abstract: Federated multimodal graph foundation models (GFMs) aim to adapt pretrained multimodal models to decentralized graph data, where each client owns a private multimodal graph and cannot share raw information. These models typically combine a multimodal Encoder that extracts semantic evidence from heterogeneous modalities and a graph neural network (GNN) that performs relational reasoning over graph structures. However, existing federated GFM adaptation methods mainly update graph-side modules while keeping the multimodal Encoder frozen, limiting adaptation to \emph{how information is propagated} while fixing \emph{what information is extracted}. Through empirical studies, we reveal that Encoder and GNN adaptations are not independent: Encoder adaptation is affected by graph relations, while cross-client module swapping reveals substantial pairing sensitivity between separately parameterized Encoder and GNN updates. Motivated by this observation, we propose \textbf{FedCORE}, a federated adaptation framework that represents Encoder and GNN updates through a shared low-dimensional latent state. FedCORE jointly optimizes this core from multimodal and structural signals and performs federated evolution directly in the shared state space, preserving compatibility between perception and reasoning adaptations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedCORE reduces the Encoder--GNN pairing gap from $30.6$ to $5.9$, corresponding to an $80.7\%$ reduction over independent joint adaptation.

</details>


### [194] [Stable and Counterfactually Robust Physical World Models from Imposed Structure and Learned Physics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00280)
*Yufeng Wang,Parivesh Priye,Lu Wei,Haibin Ling*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a world model architecture that incorporates general physical structure (energy-based dynamics with reversible operators, confining energy, one-way energy dissipation port) to ensure physical law compliance. The learned model successfully recovers constitutive functions, maintains stability far beyond training horizon, and generalizes to unseen interventions, outperforming unstructured models by orders of magnitude.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: World models learn to forecast physical systems from recorded trajectories, but they may violate physical laws - creating energy, drifting, or diverging over long rollouts. The paper investigates how much general physical structure should be hard-coded into a world model versus learned from data, while ensuring four key properties: second law compatible dissipation, correct responses to interventions on physical parameters, stability beyond training horizon, and robustness to disturbances.

Method: The approach imposes general physical structure: dynamics generated from gradient of learned energy through fixed reversible operator, energy restricted to confining class, one-way port to remove energy (not inject), known drive channel, and intervened parameter enters through separable map. The model learns energy functional, constitutive relations, dissipation rate, and couplings. Evaluated on electromagnetic cavity, particle-in-cell grid, and shallow-water fluid.

Result: Models with ~9,000 parameters recover constitutive functions with unit slope, separate conserving from dissipating worlds by four orders of magnitude using single set of weights, and transfer changes in sign, magnitude, rate, and gravity to unseen values. Equal-capacity models without the same structure perform at chance or worse. Nonlinear constitutive law recovered with curvature preserved and predicts held-out intervention 2-17× better than converged linear model.

Conclusion: Hard-coding general physical structure enables world models to respect physical laws while learning system-specific physics from data. The imposed structure allows the model to satisfy second law dissipation, respond correctly to interventions, maintain stability over 100× training horizon, and achieve superior generalization on held-out interventions compared to unstructured models.

Abstract: A world model learns to forecast how a physical system evolves from recorded trajectories, yet the systems it imitates obey physical laws that are neither fully supplied nor reliably respected. The model may create energy, drift or diverge over long rollouts, and answer a changed law query using the law observed during training. We ask how much general physical structure must be hard coded into a world model, and how much system-specific physics can then be learned from data, for four properties to hold simultaneously: second law compatible dissipation, correct responses to interventions on physical parameters, stability out to one hundred times the training horizon, and robustness to disturbances. The imposed structure is general: dynamics are generated from the gradient of a learned energy through a fixed reversible operator, the energy is restricted to a confining class, a one way port can remove energy but never inject it, the drive channel is known, and the intervened parameter enters through a separable map. The model learns the energy functional, constitutive relations, dissipation rate, and couplings. Across an electromagnetic cavity, a particle in cell grid, and a shallow-water fluid, models with roughly nine thousand parameters recover constitutive functions with unit slope, separate conserving from dissipating worlds by four orders of magnitude using a single set of weights, and transfer changes in sign, magnitude, rate, and gravity to unseen values, where equal-capacity models without the same structure perform at chance or worse. A nonlinear constitutive law is recovered with its curvature preserved and predicts a held-out intervention $2$-$17\times$ better than a converged linear model.

</details>


### [195] [Partial AUC Maximization from Positive-unlabeled Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00284)
*Atsutoshi Kumagai,Tomoharu Iwata,Taishi Nishiyama,Hiroshi Takahashi,Kazuki Adachi,Yasuhiro Fujiwara*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A method for maximizing partial AUC (pAUC) from positive and unlabeled (PU) data only, without requiring negative data for training. The approach represents pAUC using positive and marginal densities within an empirical risk minimization framework and derives a smoothed empirical estimator for training classifiers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In many real-world applications (cybersecurity, medical care, advertising), high pAUC is desirable but labeled negative data are difficult to collect due to privacy concerns or annotation expertise requirements. Existing pAUC maximization methods require both labeled positive and negative data.

Method: Empirical risk minimization framework - showing that pAUC (including FPR-dependent thresholds) can be represented using only positive and marginal densities, then deriving a smoothed empirical pAUC estimator from PU data for classifier training.

Result: Effectiveness demonstrated through experiments on ten real-world datasets.

Conclusion: The proposed method successfully maximizes pAUC using only positive and unlabeled data, enabling classifier training in scenarios where negative data are unavailable due to privacy or expertise constraints.

Abstract: The partial area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (pAUC) is an important performance metric for binary classification that summarizes true positive rates within a specific range of false positive rates (FPRs). Classifiers that achieve high pAUC need to be obtained in many real-world applications such as cybersecurity, medical care, and advertising. Although many methods for maximizing the pAUC have been proposed, they typically require both labeled positive and negative data for training. However, in practice, labeled negative data are often difficult to collect due to privacy concerns or the need for high expertise to annotate them. In this paper, we propose a method for maximizing the pAUC from positive and unlabeled (PU) data without negative data. Within an empirical risk minimization framework, we show that the pAUC, including its FPR-dependent thresholds, can be represented using only the positive and marginal densities, and derive an empirical estimator from PU data. A classifier is then trained by maximizing the derived smoothed empirical pAUC estimator. We experimentally demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method with ten real-world datasets.

</details>


### [196] [Bellman-Certified Rounding for Sparse Policy Deployment in MDPs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00325)
*Zhaojun Peng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies the problem of rounding continuous policy optimization outputs to sparse binary policies in finite MDPs. The authors analyze how much discounted return can be retained when continuous row mixtures are rounded to discrete policies, addressing the mismatch between continuous optimization and discrete deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Continuous policy optimization methods can spread updates across many states, but real-world deployment often permits only a few complete state-level changes. This creates a practical gap between optimization and implementation that requires understanding the loss incurred by rounding continuous policies to sparse binary ones.

Method: The authors derive reusable envelopes from 2d+2 Bellman solves to provide uniform and candidate-specific guarantees before rounding. They use a rank-two rational representation to enable weighted curvature integration along realized trajectories. They prove theoretical bounds showing linear dimension dependence is unavoidable and that exact global curvature thresholding is computationally hard.

Result: Theoretical results: (1) Linear dimension dependence is unavoidable when the budget scales, (2) Exact global curvature thresholding is hard. Empirical results: (1) Candidate-specific bounds raise pre-rounding certification coverage from 48.2% to 74.1% on the structured suite, (2) At γ=0.95, local integration lowers the median bound-to-loss ratio from 402.3 to 2.08 on coupled instances.

Conclusion: The paper provides a framework for certifying policy quality before rounding in MDPs, with candidate-specific bounds significantly improving coverage compared to uniform bounds. The rank-two representation with weighted curvature integration substantially improves bound-to-loss ratios, making practical certification more feasible.

Abstract: Continuous policy optimization may spread an update across many states, even when deployment permits only a few complete state-level changes. We study how much discounted return can be retained when continuous row mixtures are rounded to sparse binary policies in finite MDPs. Policy-dependent visitation couples the row edits, while long horizons make global curvature bounds conservative. From $2d+2$ Bellman solves, we derive reusable envelopes that support uniform and candidate-specific guarantees before rounding. A rank-two rational representation of each exchange further permits weighted curvature integration along the realized trajectory. We prove that linear dimension dependence is unavoidable when the budget scales, and that exact global curvature thresholding is hard. Candidate-specific bounds raise pre-rounding certification coverage from $48.2\%$ to $74.1\%$ on the structured suite. At $γ=0.95$, local integration lowers the median bound-to-loss ratio from $402.3$ to $2.08$ on coupled instances.

</details>


### [197] [Beyond Diagonal State Space Models: Exact Non-Abelian Group Tracking, Solvability Barriers, and Geometric Physical Manifolds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00329)
*Zeyu Jia*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes Non-Commutative State Space Models (NC-SSM) to address limitations of existing SSMs (Mamba, S4D, LRU) that are constrained by transition matrix commutativity and solvable affine transformation groups. The authors lift state transitions to compact Lie groups (SU(2), SO(3), SO(N)) using Euler-Rodrigues maps and Cayley transforms, achieving norm-preserving isometry and significant improvements on non-abelian group tracking tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing selective state space models (SSMs) face severe optimization degradation when modeling non-solvable simple groups (e.g., A_5) because they require exponential circuit emulation depth to simulate non-commutative operations. This limits their ability to handle complex group structures in sequence modeling.

Method: The authors propose three key innovations: (1) NC-SSM lifting state transitions to compact Lie groups SU(2), SO(3), SO(N); (2) Closed-form Euler-Rodrigues maps and rational Cayley transforms for exact norm-preserving isometry; (3) Pure Hopf-filiation Bloch projective readouts, true quaternion parallel prefix scans (9.06x speedup), and Identity-Gated Lie SSMs to eliminate phase drift.

Result: Extensive benchmarks across 14 experimental regimes show: (1) NC-SSM achieves 100% tracking on S_3, D_4, Q_8, A_5 vs 6.60% baseline (p=8.81e-4); (2) Cayley-SO(5)-SSM breaks Klein's 1884 ceiling on S_5 (50.92% vs 5.25%, p=0.0015, 7.8x variance reduction); (3) SO(3)-SSM achieves <3.12e-6 drift over 300 steps (>580,000x advantage), 0.04° dead-reckoning error; (4) NC-SSM achieves 74.36% on Dyck-2 and 30.26% on deep AST scope tracking (p=0.0081); (5) Ablation confirms strict isometry is mathematically necessary for lossless long-range associative memory.

Conclusion: Lifting SSMs from commutative diagonal matrices to non-commutative Lie groups (SU(2), SO(3), SO(N)) enables exact isometry and solves optimization degradation on non-abelian groups. The proposed NC-SSM, SO(3)-SSM, and Cayley-SSM variants demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on group tracking, language parsing (Dyck-2), and AST scope tracking, with strict isometry proven necessary for long-range memory.

Abstract: Selective state space models (SSMs), such as Mamba, S4D, and LRU, are bounded by transition matrix commutativity (A_t A_t' = A_t' A_t) and solvable affine transformation groups (Aff_D of derived length <= 2). Consequently, stacked multi-layer diagonal networks face severe optimization degradation on non-solvable simple groups such as A_5 due to the exponential circuit emulation depth required to simulate non-abelian commutators. We propose Non-Commutative State Space Models (NC-SSM), their real-orthogonal counterpart SO(3)-SSM, and arbitrary-dimension Cayley-SSM, lifting state transitions to compact Lie groups SU(2), SO(3), and SO(N). Via closed-form Euler-Rodrigues maps and rational Cayley transforms, NC-SSM achieves exact norm-preserving isometry (||U_t|| = 1). We introduce pure Hopf-fibration Bloch projective readouts (S^3/{+-1} =~ S^2 =~ SO(3)) to eliminate sign ambiguity, true quaternion parallel prefix scans (9.06x speedup at T=2048), and Identity-Gated Lie SSMs to eliminate sparse syntax phase drift. Extensive benchmarks across 14 experimental regimes show: (1) NC-SSM achieves 100% tracking on S_3, D_4, Q_8 and simple group A_5, where a 3-layer deep diagonal baseline collapses to 6.60% (p = 8.81e-4); (2) Cayley-SO(5)-SSM breaks Klein's 1884 ceiling on symmetric group S_5 (50.92% vs diagonal 5.25%, p = 0.0015, delivering 7.8x variance reduction over SO(3)); (3) SO(3)-SSM preserves Riemannian manifolds across 300 steps (< 3.12e-6 drift, > 580,000x advantage), achieving 0.04 deg dead-reckoning error and active tangent denoising; (4) NC-SSM achieves 74.36% on Dyck-2 and 30.26% on deep AST scope tracking (p = 0.0081); and (5) ablation confirms strict isometry is mathematically necessary for lossless long-range associative memory.

</details>


### [198] [The Weakest Link: Distilling LLM Reasoning with Worst-Case Constrained Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00332)
*Matthieu Zimmer,Xiaotong Ji,Tu Nguyen,Haitham Bou-Ammar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses reasoning distillation from LLMs to smaller models by formulating it as a constrained RL problem that maximizes task reward while enforcing worst-case constraints on teacher log-likelihood at every trajectory prefix. This approach avoids reward hacking (correct answers with flawed reasoning) and the dilution problems of KL-based distillation. The method achieves superior accuracy-fidelity tradeoffs on math reasoning and code generation tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current reasoning distillation methods face a fundamental tension: pure RL optimization leads to reward hacking (correct answers via flawed reasoning), while KL-based regularization dilutes task performance and allows compensation across reasoning steps. The key insight is that reasoning chain quality is determined by its weakest link, not averages.

Method: Formulated reasoning distillation as a constrained RL problem maximizing task reward subject to worst-case teacher log-likelihood constraints on every trajectory prefix. Derived an unaugmented constrained MDP with reward transformation that preserves hard-constraint semantics, enabling low-variance policy gradient decomposition into single-step and long-term terms.

Result: Significantly expands the accuracy-fidelity Pareto front. Matches high Final Answer Correctness of pure RL while drastically reducing teacher constraint violations. Achieves highest rigorous Reasoning Success Rate across all evaluated settings on mathematical reasoning and code generation tasks.

Conclusion: The worst-case constraint formulation along every trajectory prefix is more appropriate for reasoning distillation than averaging-based approaches. The proposed unaugmented constrained MDP provides a tractable solution that avoids dual Lagrangian solvers and test-time teacher dependence while provably satisfying constraints.

Abstract: Distilling the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) into smaller students is a central challenge for efficient deployment. Current approaches face a fundamental tension: optimizing purely for verifiable task rewards (e.g., via GRPO) leads to reward hacking, where students arrive at correct final answers through flawed intermediate logic, while regularizing with soft divergence penalties against a teacher (e.g., KL-based distillation) dilutes task performance and, critically, allows the student to compensate for severe logical violations at one step with high teacher agreement at others. We argue that this averaging is fundamentally misaligned with the nature of reasoning: a chain-of-thought is only as valid as its weakest link. Motivated by this observation, we formulate reasoning distillation as a constrained reinforcement learning problem in which the task reward is maximized subject to a worst-case constraint on the teacher log-likelihood along every prefix of the trajectory. To avoid the prohibitive cost of dual Lagrangian solvers and the test-time teacher dependence of state-augmented methods such as Saute, we derive an unaugmented constrained MDP whose reward transformation preserves the hard-constraint semantics, admits a low-variance policy gradient decomposition into single-step and long-term terms, and provably satisfies the worst-case constraint almost surely in the penalty limit. Through extensive experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation tasks, we demonstrate that our method significantly expands the accuracy-fidelity Pareto front. By matching the high Final Answer Correctness of pure RL and drastically reducing teacher constraint violations, we ultimately achieve the highest rigorous Reasoning Success Rate across all evaluated settings.

</details>


### [199] [Benchmarking System One decision models against trained classifiers and language models for automated decision gates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00346)
*Amir Rafe,Subasish Das*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper compares three classes of AI models (decision models, supervised classifiers, and generative language models) for automated decision-making tasks across workflow, intent, and social-science domains under various conditions. Key findings show that model performance depends heavily on available labels, task type, and threshold settings, with no single model class dominating all scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation appears to be establishing empirical design rules for when to use different types of AI models (decision models vs. classifiers vs. generative models) for automated decision gates in software applications. The authors note that the ranking of model classes depends on specific conditions, suggesting a need for systematic comparison.

Method: The methodology involved testing 8 decision-model checkpoints from 6 families plus a hosted model ("Jev") alongside 2 generative comparators. They evaluated supervised classifiers and zero-shot classifiers across workflow, intent, and social-science items under matched conditions. They tested various configurations including: with/without task labels, different probability thresholds (5% risk), temperature settings, and fine-tuning vs. untuned variants. They also tested an intent-trained first stage escalating to Jev.

Result: Key results include: (1) With labels, small trained classifiers are most accurate on intents and comparable to best decision models on workflows; (2) Without labels, decision models (except encoder-based) exceed zero-shot entailment classifiers; (3) A larger generative model matches Jev on workflows/intents and accepts more workflow decisions at 5% risk; (4) Fine-tuned decision checkpoints gain intent accuracy over untuned backbones; (5) Temperature calibration degrades with more options; (6) Jev accepts 0.310 of out-of-scope requests at 5% in-scope risk threshold; (7) Yes/no flipping affects Jev's answers (50.5 per hundred); (8) Intent-trained first stage escalating to Jev matches accuracy at 43% of the cost.

Conclusion: The results yield condition-dependent design rules for automated decision gates. The choice of model type should depend on: availability of labeled data, task type (workflow vs. intent), acceptable risk threshold, computational cost constraints, and whether the model needs calibration across varying numbers of options. No single model class is optimal across all conditions.

Abstract: Software that hands branching decisions to a model needs a declared option and a probability it can threshold. Typed decision models, also called System One models, return such probabilities without generating text, while supervised classifiers and generative language models are the established alternatives. Under matched conditions, one harness sends eight decision-model checkpoints from six families, including the hosted model Jev, and two generative comparators the same semantic requests, and scores supervised and zero-shot classifiers on the same workflow, intent and social-science items. The ranking of the model classes depends on the conditions. With the task's own labels, small trained classifiers are the most accurate on intents and not significantly different from the best decision models on workflows. Without labels, every decision model except the encoder-based checkpoints exceeds a zero-shot entailment classifier on workflows and intents. Read through option-key likelihoods, a larger generative model is level with Jev on workflows and intents and accepts more workflow decisions at five percent risk, and fine-tuned decision checkpoints gain intent accuracy over their untuned backbones. Stored temperatures fitted on few options raise calibration error with many options, and a held-out threshold for five percent in-scope risk still lets Jev accept 0.310 of out-of-scope requests. Swapping yes and no flips 50.5 answers per hundred for Jev, while fine-tuned checkpoints cut their backbones' social-science flips. An intent-trained first stage escalating to Jev matches its accuracy at 0.43 of its cost at full graphics-processor utilization. The results yield condition-dependent design rules for automated decision gates.

</details>


### [200] [Deep Learning for Anomaly Detection in Railway Systems: A Structured Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00363)
*Ammar Bouketta,Smail Niar,Hamza Ouarnoughi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A structured survey paper organizing deep learning-based anomaly detection approaches for railway systems using a unified taxonomy covering anomaly location, data representation, sensing modality, and temporal characteristics. The survey covers convolutional, recurrent, attention-based architectures, autoencoders, GANs, and transformers, organized into classification-based, prediction-based, reconstruction-based, and hybrid learning paradigms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The increasing need for safe and reliable operation of modern railway systems, driven by the growing availability of heterogeneous sensor data from rolling stock and infrastructure, and the effectiveness of deep learning as a paradigm for railway anomaly detection.

Method: A structured survey using a unified taxonomy that classifies methods by anomaly location, data representation and manifestation, sensing modality, and temporal characteristics. Existing approaches are organized into classification-based, prediction-based, reconstruction-based, and hybrid learning paradigms.

Result: The survey provides a comprehensive classification of deep learning approaches for railway anomaly detection, examines data-centric challenges, evaluation practices, performance metrics, and practical deployment aspects including edge-cloud architectures, computational constraints, and hardware-aware optimization. A decision-oriented framework is presented linking anomaly characteristics, data properties, and operational constraints to suitable detection paradigms.

Conclusion: This work provides a structured reference for selecting and deploying deep learning solutions for railway anomaly detection, while highlighting open challenges toward reliable and scalable intelligent monitoring systems.

Abstract: Ensuring safe and reliable operation of modern railway systems increasingly relies on data-driven monitoring and intelligent fault detection. Deep learning has emerged as an effective paradigm for railway anomaly detection, driven by the growing availability of heterogeneous sensor data from rolling stock and infrastructure. This paper presents a structured survey of deep learning-based anomaly detection approaches for railway systems. The surveyed methods are organized using a unified taxonomy covering anomaly location, data representation and manifestation, sensing modality, and temporal characteristics. Existing approaches, including convolutional, recurrent and attention-based architectures, autoencoders, generative adversarial networks, and transformers, are structured into classification-based, prediction-based, reconstruction-based, and hybrid learning paradigms. The survey also examines data-centric challenges, evaluation practices, performance metrics, and practical deployment aspects, including edge-cloud architectures, computational constraints, and hardware-aware optimization. Finally, a decision-oriented framework links anomaly characteristics, data properties, and operational constraints to suitable detection paradigms and deployment configurations. This work provides a structured reference for selecting and deploying deep learning solutions for railway anomaly detection and highlights open challenges toward reliable and scalable intelligent monitoring systems.

</details>


### [201] [Manifold-Constrained Initial Noise Optimization for Efficient Generative Model Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00365)
*Jinho Chang,Jong Chul Ye*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ZeNOVA is a gradient-free method for optimizing initial noise in generative models to align with black-box rewards, using annealed soft-value guidance, manifold-constrained hyperspherical Langevin dynamics, and Metropolis-Hastings jumping to achieve stable and efficient reward alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing initial-noise optimization methods rely on first-order gradient information, which is either inapplicable or suffers from instability and inefficiency in black-box reward scenarios where gradient access is unavailable.

Method: ZeNOVA addresses black-box reward alignment through three key components: (1) annealed soft-value guidance for gradual reward optimization, (2) manifold-constrained hyperspherical Langevin dynamics to exploit the geometry of the Gaussian prior, and (3) Metropolis-Hastings jumping for stable exploration.

Result: ZeNOVA outperforms all evaluated zeroth-order baselines by optimizing initial noise toward higher rewards substantially more stably while exploiting the geometry of the Gaussian prior.

Conclusion: ZeNOVA demonstrates practical applicability to various black-box reward alignment tasks in image and video generative models, offering a stable and efficient alternative to gradient-based methods.

Abstract: Recent advances in distillation and flow-map models have enabled deterministic one- or few-step generation for high-quality data, facilitating a new branch of reward alignment approaches that directly optimize the initial noise from a Gaussian distribution. However, most existing initial-noise optimization methods rely on first-order gradient information, which is either inapplicable or suffers from instability and inefficiency in black-box reward scenarios. Here, we introduce ZeNOVA, a stable and efficient initial noise alignment method in a gradient-free manner. Specifically, we address existing algorithms' major challenge in black-box scenarios through annealed soft-value guidance, manifold-constrained hyperspherical Langevin dynamics, and Metropolis-Hastings jumping. Extensive experiments on image and video generative models show that ZeNOVA outperforms all evaluated zeroth-order baselines by optimizing the initial noise toward higher rewards substantially more stably while exploiting the geometry of the Gaussian prior, demonstrating its practical applicability to various black-box reward alignment.

</details>


### [202] [MoRA: MoE Pruning via Router Bias Learning and Expert Approximation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00367)
*Yushuai Sun,Zikun Zhou,Lin Gao,Jun Yu,Wenjie Pei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MoRA is a structured expert pruning framework for MoE models that introduces learnable router biases and an expert approximation mechanism to reduce memory usage while maintaining model performance. It outperforms SOTA pruning algorithms on multiple models and benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MoE models require loading all experts into memory despite only activating a subset per token. Existing pruning methods either use poorly-aligned expert ranking criteria or are computationally expensive, and they overlook routing-behavior redundancy among retained experts.

Method: 1) Router bias learning: Learnable bias for each expert, optimized by minimizing language-modeling loss + routing-diversity regularizer to identify critical experts and encourage diverse routing preferences. 2) Expert approximation: Post-pruning enhancement using remaining experts to approximate pruned experts' outputs via affine transformation.

Result: Outperforms state-of-the-art pruning algorithms on Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-V2-Lite, and Moonlight-16B-A3B, removing 25% and 50% of routed experts, evaluated on 9 zero-shot benchmarks.

Conclusion: MoRA effectively reduces MoE memory usage through structured expert pruning while maintaining or improving performance, validated across multiple models and benchmarks.

Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models enable parameter scaling with limited per-token computation by activating only a small subset of experts for each token, but deploying them still requires loading the complete expert pool into memory.
