Structured expert pruning can effectively reduce the memory usage by removing experts. However, existing pruning methods either use expert ranking criteria that are not well aligned with model performance or rely on effective expert subset searching that is computationally expensive. Moreover, these methods typically overlook the routing-behavior redundancy among the retained experts. In this paper, we propose MoE Pruning via Router Bias Learning and Expert Approximation (MoRA), a framework for structured MoE expert pruning. We introduce a learnable router bias for each expert and optimize these biases by minimizing the language-modeling loss and a routing-diversity regularizer. The learned router biases sharpen the routing probability distributions to identify experts critical to model performance while encouraging the selection of experts with diverse routing preferences. In addition, we introduce an expert approximation mechanism as a post-pruning enhancement. It leverages the remaining experts to approximate the outputs of pruned experts by affine transformation, further improving the performance of the pruned model. We evaluate MoRA on Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-V2-Lite, and Moonlight-16B-A3B, removing 25\% and 50\% of the routed experts in each MoE layer. Extensive experiments on nine zero-shot benchmarks show that MoRA outperforms state-of-the-art pruning algorithms. Our code will be released.

</details>


### [203] [M$^2$Weather: A Benchmark for Joint Multi-Station and Multi-Variable Weather Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00370)
*Rongwen Li,Xiao Wang,Mingyang Wang,Hongwu Liu,Changjian Chen,Zhuo Tang,Kenli Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: M²Weather is a benchmark for joint multi-station and multi-variable weather forecasting, featuring 2,809 high-quality stations with 5 physically coupled variables across three spatial scales (France, Europe, Global). It includes a lightweight plug-and-play adapter to examine station-variable relationships without retraining. Evaluation of 16 models shows that jointly modeling station and variable relationships improves forecasting accuracy, with MSE reduction across all adapted models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Station weather forecasting is shaped by complex spatial dependencies across stations and physical coupling among weather variables. However, existing studies consider these relationships separately using different datasets and experimental settings, hindering systematic assessment of their individual and joint contributions.

Method: 1) Multi-criteria quality control and station stratification to collect 2,809 high-quality stations with 5 physically coupled weather variables across three spatial scales (France, Europe, Global). 2) Unified training and evaluation protocols for fair comparison. 3) Lightweight plug-and-play adapter to introduce missing station or variable relationships without retraining. 4) Systematic evaluation of 16 representative models.

Result: Jointly modeling station and variable relationships provides benefits. Completing missing relationships further reduces MSE for all adapted models on all three datasets. The complementary information across stations and variables is identified as an important resource for improving station weather forecasting.

Conclusion: The complementary information across stations and variables represents an important resource for improving station weather forecasting. M²Weather enables fair and efficient investigation of station-variable relationships through its unified benchmark and adapter design.

Abstract: Station weather forecasting is fundamentally shaped by both complex spatial dependencies across stations and strong physical coupling among weather variables. However, existing studies often consider these relationships separately and use different datasets and experimental settings, hindering systematic assessment of their individual and joint contributions. In this paper, we introduce $M^2$Weather, a benchmark for joint multi-station and multi-variable weather forecasting. Through multi-criteria quality control and station stratification, we collect 2,809 high-quality stations with 5 physically coupled weather variables across three spatial scales: France, Europe, and Global. This multi-scale design lets us examine whether conclusions persist from national to global station networks. We also introduce unified training and evaluation protocols to enable fair comparison of different station-variable modeling paradigms. To further examine the benefits of modeling station-variable relationships, we design a lightweight, plug-and-play adapter. With a trained weather forecasting model, this adapter can introduce missing station or variable relationships without retraining the model. This enables fair and efficient investigation of station-variable relationships. Systematic evaluation of 16 representative models shows the benefits of jointly modeling station and variable relationships. Completing missing relationships further reduces MSE for all adapted models on all three datasets. Together, these results identify the complementary information across stations and variables as an important resource for improving station weather forecasting. Our code can be obtained at https://github.com/hnu-vis/M2-Weather.

</details>


### [204] [When Do Attention-Head Ablations Support Causal Claims? Projection-Level Confounds, Floor Effects, and Matched Controls](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00373)
*Juli Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper demonstrates that attention-head ablation in language models (GPT-2 small, DistilGPT2) can produce misleading results if intervention semantics, evaluation metrics, and controls are not carefully validated. The authors show that different ablation implementations yield nearly uncorrelated results (Pearson r=0.057), and proper methodology with matched controls yields highly stable rankings (Spearman rho=0.974).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses the common practice of using attention-head ablation to infer causal responsibility of specific components in language models for task performance. The authors noticed that this inference method could be fragile and wanted to validate the methodology.

Method: The authors compared post-projection ablation with corrected pre-projection ablation on GPT-2 small, evaluated binary accuracy vs gold-token log-probability, used discovery/held-out splits with 1,000 matched random-head and layer-matched-head control draws, and replicated findings on DistilGPT2.

Result: Post-projection and pre-projection ablations are nearly uncorrelated (r=0.057) and select disjoint top-5 heads. Binary accuracy hides effects at floors/ceilings while log-probability remains graded. With proper controls, rankings are highly stable (rho=0.974) and top-5 heads exceed controls (p=0.001). Task specificity is not robust on GPT-2, but findings replicate on DistilGPT2.

Conclusion: Single-head ablation does not justify causal claims by itself. Defensible interpretation requires correct intervention placement (pre-projection), non-saturated continuous metrics (log-probability), and matched held-out controls. Without these, ablation studies may produce spurious or unreliable conclusions about which model components are causally responsible for behaviors.

Abstract: Attention-head ablation, zeroing a head and measuring the resulting change in task performance, is a common method for inferring which components of a language model are causally responsible for a behavior. We show using GPT-2 small that this inference can be fragile unless the intervention semantics, evaluation metric, and controls are carefully validated. A natural post-projection implementation of "zeroing a head" is nearly uncorrelated with a corrected pre-projection ablation (Pearson r = 0.057) and selects a completely disjoint top-5 set of important heads. We also show that binary accuracy can hide effects at behavioral floors and near ceilings, whereas gold-token log-probability remains graded. Using a discovery/held-out split and 1,000 matched random-head and layer-matched-head control draws, the corrected per-head effect ranking is highly stable across splits (Spearman rho = 0.974), and the top-5 selected heads significantly exceed both control distributions (Monte Carlo p = 0.001). However, evidence for task specificity is not robust on GPT-2. Replication on DistilGPT2 preserves the intervention-semantic and matched-control findings. These results show that single-head ablation does not by itself justify a causal claim; defensible interpretation requires correct intervention placement, a non-saturated continuous metric, and matched held-out controls.

</details>


### [205] [A First Glance at Jev for Network Traffic Classification: Accuracy, Processing Time, and Cost](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00376)
*Shenghe Xu,Lifan Mei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: First empirical study evaluating general-purpose decision model Jev for application classification of network flows using only first 10 packets' features. Jev improves significantly with few labeled examples but underperforms traditional tree ensembles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate whether general-purpose decision models (Jev) can perform application classification of network flows, which was previously unexplored. Also compare against traditional ML methods and large language models.

Method: Used CESNET-QUICEXT-25 dataset with 52,000 records from 26 collection weeks. Classification based on first 10 packets' sizes, directions, and inter-packet times. Tested Jev with varying context (40 and 150 examples), compared against Random Forest, Extra Trees, and GPT-5.6 Sol.

Result: Jev accuracy improved from 9.80% to 28.42% with 40 examples, and 34.50% with 150 examples. Random Forest achieved 69.95%, Extra Trees 66.80%. In paired 100-record subset, Jev (29%, 0.750s) vs GPT-5.6 Sol (37%, 6.036s). Tree ensembles consistently outperformed Jev.

Conclusion: Labeled examples substantially improve Jev's performance, but Jev remains less accurate than trained tree ensembles. Unequal supervision budgets and fixed configurations prevent attributing the accuracy gap to a single cause. No significant accuracy advantage between Jev and GPT-5.6 Sol in the paired subset.

Abstract: We evaluate Jev on ten dataset-defined application labels in CESNET-QUICEXT-25 using only the first ten packets' sizes, directions, and inter-packet times. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first empirical study of general-purpose decision models, represented here by Jev, for application classification of network flows. Across 52,000 records from 26 collection weeks following the training period, 40 fixed labeled examples raise Jev's accuracy from 9.80% to 28.42%. Random Forest and Extra Trees trained on 8,000 records achieve 69.95% and 66.80% and outperform Jev in every week. Increasing Jev's context to 150 examples yields 34.50% on the first test week. On a paired 100-record subset, Jev with 40 examples achieves 29% accuracy at a median request time of 0.750 s, versus 37% and 6.036 s for the generative language model OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol with high reasoning effort through Azure; Jev also incurs lower API charges. The paired subset does not establish an accuracy advantage for either service, and the timing reflects different service configurations. Thus, labeled examples substantially improve Jev, but the tested Jev configurations remain less accurate than trained tree ensembles; unequal supervision budgets and fixed configurations prevent attributing the gap to a single cause.

</details>


### [206] [STCFormer: Adaptive Spatio-Temporal Modeling with Dynamic Cluster Transformer for Station-based Weather Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00377)
*Rongwen Li,Haixin Xie,Mingyang Wang,Hongwu Liu,Kun Fang,Changjian Chen,Zhuo Tang,Kenli Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: STCFormer is an adaptive spatio-temporal Transformer for station-based weather forecasting that dynamically groups stations within each temporal patch based on local evolution, combining fine-grained local attention within clusters with global attention over regional state summaries. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across eight temperature and wind forecasting tasks on three real-world datasets, with theoretical justification via a Lipschitz bound analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Station-based weather forecasting requires modeling complex spatial dependencies among stations. Existing clustering-based selective modeling uses a fixed grouping across the observation window, which may obscure local changes in station relationships. Additionally, intra-cluster interactions alone may miss important global context, and the theoretical advantages of selective interactions over dense connectivity remain insufficiently understood.

Method: STCFormer employs a Cluster-Guided Attention Block that dynamically groups stations according to their local evolution within each temporal patch. The architecture combines: (1) fine-grained local attention within clusters for detailed spatial modeling, and (2) global attention over regional state summaries, allowing each station to access information beyond its own cluster. The theoretical contribution includes deriving a Lipschitz upper bound for cluster-conditioned local attention that is no larger than its fully connected counterpart, explaining potential robustness benefits.

Result: Experiments on three real-world weather datasets spanning eight temperature and wind forecasting tasks show that STCFormer achieves the lowest 24-hour mean squared error on all eight tasks and ranks first or second in 47 of 48 comparisons across metrics and forecasting horizons.

Conclusion: STCFormer demonstrates the effectiveness of locally adaptive grouping and complementary local-global interactions for weather forecasting. The proposed dynamic clustering approach within temporal patches better captures evolving station relationships compared to static grouping. The theoretical Lipschitz bound analysis provides insight into why selective attention may offer robustness benefits over dense connectivity.

Abstract: Station-based weather forecasting supports daily life and economic activity, yet accurate forecasts require modeling complex spatial dependencies among stations. Recent clustering-based selective modeling offers a promising alternative to dense inter-station interactions. However, a grouping shared across an observation window may obscure local changes in station relationships, while intra-cluster interactions alone may miss important global context. The theoretical advantages of selective interactions over dense connectivity also remain insufficiently understood. We therefore propose STCFormer, an adaptive spatio-temporal Transformer that dynamically groups stations according to their local evolution within each temporal patch. Its Cluster-Guided Attention Block combines fine-grained local attention within clusters and global attention over regional state summaries, allowing each station to access information beyond its own cluster. We further show that a derived Lipschitz upper bound for cluster-conditioned local attention is no larger than its fully connected counterpart, explaining a potential robustness benefit and motivating the design of InfoLoss. Experiments on three real-world weather datasets spanning eight temperature and wind forecasting tasks show that STCFormer achieves the lowest 24-hour mean squared error on all eight tasks and ranks first or second in 47 of 48 comparisons across metrics and forecasting horizons. Ablations and case studies further confirm the benefits of locally adaptive grouping and complementary local-global interactions. Our code can be obtained at https://github.com/hnu-vis/STCFormer.

</details>


### [207] [Fusion techniques of time frequency-based images to predict the outcome of rTMS depression therapy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00380)
*Wael Korani,Md Fahimul Kabir Chowdhury,Mohammed Aledhari,Reza Rostami,Reza Kazemi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes using EEG-derived Time-Frequency (TF) images with fusion techniques (montage and blending) and a lightweight CNN to predict repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) treatment response for depression. The study reveals a significant performance gap between segment-level cross-validation (99.90% accuracy on primary dataset, 91.90% on secondary) and strict subject-disjoint cross-validation (performance collapses, AUC 0.31-0.54), highlighting the challenge of generalizing to new patients.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Predicting rTMS treatment response for depression is clinically challenging due to high inter-subject variability and limited features from single-domain EEG analysis. Existing methods struggle with generalizability across patients.

Method: The study introduces two fusion techniques (montage and blending) to extract richer features from EEG-derived Time-Frequency (TF) images. A lightweight custom CNN is trained on fused TF representations. Experiments were conducted on two datasets (15 and 46 patients) using two validation approaches: segment-level 10-fold cross-validation (allowing patient overlap) and strict subject-disjoint cross-validation (no patient overlap between training and testing). Four time-frequency methods, six fusion mechanisms, and fourteen model architectures were tested.

Result: In segment-level 10-fold CV, Montage CWT_ST fusion achieved 99.90% accuracy on the primary dataset and 91.90% on the secondary dataset. However, in strict subject-disjoint CV, performance collapsed across nearly all configurations (AUC 0.31-0.54, 95% CI containing 0.5). The best subject-level result was Montage CWT_ST on the primary cohort (AUC 0.874 ± 0.183, 82.7% accuracy), but a patient-level permutation test returned p = 0.703, indicating the results are not statistically significant.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that while segment-level validation shows high accuracy, it significantly overfits due to data leakage (segments from same patient in train and test). Strict subject-disjoint validation reveals that current EEG-based TF analysis methods fail to generalize to new patients. The fusion techniques and CNN architecture proposed do not solve the fundamental challenge of inter-subject variability in rTMS response prediction. The authors conclude that significant methodological advances are needed before EEG-based prediction can be clinically useful.

Abstract: Depression is a mental condition that can lead to suicide and self-harm. Predicting the outcome of depression treatment is one of the most difficult tasks for clinicians. Among various treatment options, repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) is a widely used non-invasive method. Predicting rTMS response using Electroencephalogram (EEG) data is difficult because of high inter-subject variability and limited features from single-domain analysis. We introduce two fusion techniques, montage and blending, to overcome these limitations and extract richer features from EEG-derived Time-Frequency (TF) images. We then propose a lightweight custom Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) trained on fused TF representations. \textcolor{black}{We use a primary dataset of 15 patients and a secondary dataset of 46 patients. We run two sets of experiments. The first set uses segment-level 10-fold cross-validation. In this setup segments from the same patient can appear in both training and testing. The Montage CWT\_ST fusion reaches 99.90\% accuracy on the primary dataset and 91.90\% on the secondary dataset. The second set uses strict subject-disjoint cross-validation. All segments of a patient stay in one fold and no patient appears in both training and testing. Performance collapses. We test four time-frequency methods, six fusion mechanisms, and fourteen model architectures. With one exception, every configuration on both cohorts falls between AUC 0.31 and 0.54 and every 95\% confidence interval contains 0.5. A patient-level permutation test on the best standalone method returns $p = 0.703$. The best subject-level result is Montage CWT\_ST on the primary cohort, which reaches AUC $0.874 \pm 0.183$ and 82.7\% accuracy.

</details>


### [208] [OmniMed-Jev: Calibrating LVLM Confidence for Trustworthy Medical Multimodal Decisions via System One](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00381)
*Luyao Tang,Cheng Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OmniMed-Jev is a decision-native interface for medical imaging that represents decisions as Choices, Nouls, or Scores over candidate sets, providing better calibrated confidence scores compared to generative approaches. It reduces calibration error by up to 10x and reliability error by up to 2x while maintaining comparable point-prediction performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generalist multimodal medical models express decisions as generated text, where reported probabilities reflect next-token predictions rather than actual decision probabilities. This means the reported confidence does not match actual accuracy, making confidence scores unreliable for clinical decision-making.

Method: OmniMed-Jev represents each medical decision as a Choice (mutually exclusive classes), Noul (binary presence of a finding), or Score (bounded ordered value) over a runtime-supplied candidate set. It uses one candidate-conditioned probability model to make heterogeneous outputs comparable probabilities. The study compares OmniMed-Jev against a generative baseline trained on the same backbone, data, and training schedule.

Result: OmniMed-Jev's reported probabilities track observed correctness more closely than the generative baseline: reducing calibration error by up to an order of magnitude (10x) and reliability error by up to two (2x). Point-prediction performance remains comparable. The exception is counting tasks, where the generative baseline performs better.

Conclusion: Making the decision distribution the model's output transforms reported numbers into meaningful probabilities. Explicit decision modeling improves confidence calibration within evaluated tasks. However, results do not demonstrate clinical readiness because the comparison cannot separate the interface from associated training differences. Code is available at github.com/lytang63/OmniMed-Jev.

Abstract: Medical models are judged not only on correctness, but on whether reported confidence matches actual accuracy. Generalist multimodal medical models have expanded what a single model can perceive, yet they still express bounded decisions such as diagnoses, findings or cell counts as generated text, so the reported probability reflects the next token rather than the decision itself. Motivated by decision-native interfaces such as Jev, we introduce OmniMed-Jev, which represents each medical decision as a Choice, Noul or Score decision over a runtime-supplied candidate set and returns a full distribution over that set: mutually exclusive classes, binary presence of a finding, or a bounded ordered value. The design is omni in three respects: it accepts diverse imaging modalities, covers different prediction tasks, and expresses them through one candidate-conditioned probability model, so heterogeneous outputs become comparable probabilities rather than task-specific strings. In an interface-controlled comparison against a generative baseline trained on the same backbone, data and schedule, OmniMed-Jev's reported probabilities track observed correctness far more closely, reducing calibration error by up to an order of magnitude and reliability error by up to two, while point-prediction performance remains comparable; counting is the one family where the generative baseline stays ahead. Making the decision distribution the model's output is not a format change but what turns reported numbers into probabilities that mean what they say. These results support explicit decision modeling as a way to make reported confidence meaningful within the evaluated tasks, and they are not evidence of clinical readiness: the comparison cannot separate the interface from associated training differences, which we state alongside the results. Code is available at github.com/lytang63/OmniMed-Jev.

</details>


### [209] [EvoGen-Harness: Learning Where and How to Evolve Image-Generation Harnesses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00383)
*Jiabin Luo,Yinan Liu,Chunlei Meng,Yufei Guo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EvoGen-Harness is a generator-agnostic framework that improves frozen text-to-image systems by coordinating evolution across multiple external responsibilities (prompts, routing, workflows). It uses Trace, which aggregates evidence across stochastic executions, uses failure attribution as a search prior, and progressively re-attributes residual failures to coordinate evolution. Achieves significant improvements on GenEval2, T2I-CompBench++, and WISE benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing T2I improvement approaches typically optimize a single predefined dimension (prompts, routing, or workflows), restricting the space for correcting generation failures. While allowing multiple generator-external responsibilities to evolve provides broader adaptation space, it introduces a challenge: visual feedback reveals what failed but not where evolution should occur or how to explore the space efficiently.

Method: Trace aggregates evidence across stochastic executions, uses failure attribution as a search prior to focus candidate updates, and progressively re-attributes residual failures to coordinate evolution across responsibilities. No-Patch and held-out validation prevent unnecessary or harmful updates.

Result: Across GenEval2, T2I-CompBench++, and WISE, EvoGen-Harness improves over the strongest evaluated baselines by +0.2633, +0.0720, and +0.0752 respectively, while achieving 87.9-91.4% attribution recall, 94.8% No-Patch accuracy, and only 1.9% regression.

Conclusion: Attribution-guided multi-responsibility evolution can substantially enhance frozen T2I systems beyond single-dimension adaptation, demonstrating the value of coordinating evolution across multiple external responsibilities rather than limiting optimization to a single dimension.

Abstract: Modern text-to-image (T2I) systems can be improved without modifying generator parameters by adapting the external system around frozen generators. However, existing approaches typically optimize a predefined dimension, such as prompts, routing, or workflows, restricting the space in which generation failures can be corrected. Allowing multiple generator-external responsibilities to evolve provides a broader adaptation space, but introduces a new challenge: visual feedback reveals what failed, but not where persistent evolution should occur or how this space should be explored efficiently. We introduce EvoGen-Harness, a generator-agnostic framework for multi-responsibility image-generation harness evolution, together with Trace (Trajectory-Relative Attribution and Coordinated Evolution). Trace aggregates evidence across stochastic executions, uses failure attribution as a search prior to focus candidate updates, and progressively re-attributes residual failures to coordinate evolution across responsibilities, while No-Patch and held-out validation prevent unnecessary or harmful updates. Across GenEval2, T2I-CompBench++, and WISE, EvoGen-Harness improves over the strongest evaluated baselines by +0.2633, +0.0720, and +0.0752, respectively, while achieving 87.9-91.4% attribution recall, 94.8% No-Patch accuracy, and only 1.9% regression. These results demonstrate that attribution-guided multi-responsibility evolution can substantially enhance frozen T2I systems beyond single-dimension adaptation.

</details>


### [210] [FAER: Auditable Utility-Aligned Trajectory Replay for Language Model Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00385)
*Miaobo Hu,Shuhao Hu,Xiaobo Guo,Xin Wang,Bokun Wang,Tianshu Fu,Daren Zha,Jun Xiao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FAER is an auditable full-trajectory replay framework that addresses the gap between cache-level correctness metrics and downstream learner utility in replay selection. It introduces training-free fixed selectors and learner-aware selectors (FAER-UTILITY) fitted on calibration blocks, achieving 0.6624 quality on GSM8K with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct compared to 0.5482 for uniform selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Replay selectors typically rank cached trajectories by format feedback, confidence, freshness, or response length. However, cache-level correctness and downstream learner utility are distinct objectives—metrics that select "good" records don't necessarily produce the best downstream learner. This selection-to-learning gap motivates the need for an auditable framework that explicitly aligns replay selection with actual learner utility.

Method: FAER framework with three key components: (1) Training-free fixed selector as protocol baseline; (2) FAER-UTILITY learner-aware selector fitted on disjoint calibration blocks using metadata-only cross-fitted calibration; (3) Disposable optimizer-aware virtual update for magnitude-aware utility surface. The audit contract freezes observed fields and replay traces before evaluation labels are joined.

Result: On GSM8K with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (128 updates): Fixed selector achieves quality 0.6329 vs uniform 0.5482 vs format-feedback 0.6037. Metadata-only cross-fitted calibration reaches 0.6476 ± 0.0139 at 63,276 tokens (cost: 189,642 tokens, 3.48 GPU-hours). FAER-UTILITY achieves 0.6624 at 62,844 tokens (4.26 GPU-hours). Format-feedback selects records with correctness 0.6953 vs 0.3594 for fixed selector, despite different downstream ranking.

Conclusion: FAER demonstrates that learner-aware selection significantly outperforms format-feedback and uniform selection. The gap between cache-level correctness (0.6953 for format-feedback) and downstream utility (0.6037) confirms the selection-to-learning problem. FAER-UTILITY's superior performance (0.6624) validates the importance of calibration-based selection aligned with actual learner utility, with reported ablations including same-seed gap, policy-optimization, and zero-shot transfer.

Abstract: Replay selectors often rank cached trajectories by format feedback, confidence, freshness, or response length, although cache-level correctness and downstream learner utility are distinct objectives. We formalize this selection-to-learning gap and introduce FAER as an auditable full-trajectory replay framework. Its training-free fixed selector is a protocol baseline; FAER-UTILITY is the learner-aware selector fitted on disjoint calibration blocks. The normalized gradient alignment is reported as a baseline, while a disposable optimizer-aware virtual update supplies a magnitude-aware utility surface. The audit contract freezes observed fields and replay traces before evaluation labels are joined. On GSM8K with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, the matched learner study reports quality 0.6329 for the fixed selector, compared with 0.5482 for uniform and 0.6037 for format-feedback under 128 updates. Metadata-only cross-fitted calibration reaches $0.6476\!\pm\!0.0139$ over eight seeds (median 0.6481; paired 95% interval $[+0.079,+0.122]$) at 63,276 target-run tokens; its recorded full cost is 189,642 tokens and 3.48 GPU-hours including calibration. The completed FAER-UTILITY row reaches 0.6624 at 62,844 target-run tokens and 4.26 GPU-hours. Format-feedback selects records with correctness 0.6953, compared with 0.3594 for the fixed selector, despite the different downstream ranking. The completed comparison surfaces report the learner-aware ablation, same-seed gap, policy-optimization rows, and strict zero-shot transfer.

</details>


### [211] [T2SPO: Trajectory-to-Step Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00388)
*Bo-Wen Zhang,Junwei He,Maoqi Liu,Feiran Li,Song-Lin Lv,Wentao Ma,Rongyi Lin,Shuhan Zhong,Lan-Zhe Guo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: T2SPO is a reinforcement learning method that addresses the sparse reward problem in multi-step LLM agent tasks by using past successful trajectories to provide step-level feedback. It uses a pretrained TabPFN regressor to estimate remaining distance to success at each state, deriving auxiliary credit from changes in distance estimates across consecutive states.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In multi-step interactive tasks, rewards typically reflect only final outcomes, providing limited guidance on intermediate decisions. This sparse reward problem makes it difficult for RL agents to learn which intermediate steps advance toward task completion.

Method: T2SPO derives remaining-distance targets from successful trajectories and pairs them with state representations. A pretrained TabPFN regressor estimates remaining distance to success at each state of new rollouts. Changes in distance estimates across consecutive states yield auxiliary credit for agent steps alongside task-level supervision. The estimator's context is refreshed with newly completed trajectories without updating its parameters.

Result: Experiments with 1.5B and 7B language models on ALFWorld and WebShop show that T2SPO consistently improves overall task success over GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization).

Conclusion: T2SPO provides an effective approach for step-level credit assignment in LLM agent training by leveraging successful trajectory data and distance estimation, demonstrating consistent improvements over baseline methods on benchmark tasks.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning enables large language model (LLM) agents to learn multi-step behaviors through interaction with their environments. However, rewards in many interactive tasks reflect only the final outcome, providing limited guidance on which intermediate decisions advance the task. Successful training trajectories contain intermediate states that can provide supervision for subsequent interactions. We introduce Trajectory-to-Step Policy Optimization (T2SPO), a method that uses past interaction trajectories to provide step-level feedback for policy learning. T2SPO derives remaining-distance targets from successful trajectories and pairs them with representations of the states visited along the way. Conditioned on these examples, a pretrained TabPFN regressor estimates the remaining distance to success at each state of a new rollout. Changes in this distance estimate across consecutive states yield auxiliary credit for agent steps alongside task-level supervision. As training proceeds, newly completed trajectories refresh the estimator's context, incorporating new experience without updating its parameters. Experiments with 1.5B and 7B language models on ALFWorld and WebShop show that T2SPO consistently improves overall task success over GRPO.

</details>


### [212] [MatrixReward: Reward from Rubric Matrix for Open-Ended Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00389)
*Zihan Shen,Qi Liu,Zixuan Yang,Yiqun Chen,Chenglong Zhao,Xiaozhao Wang,Lei He*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Open-ended query generation lacks standard answers, thus necessitating an effective reward mechanism. Pointwise scoring rubrics provide limited information about the relative quality of sample answers under the same prompt; merging multiple rubric judgments into a single score may also mask the differences between these answers. We propose MatrixReward, which constructs rewards from a rollout-by-rubric win-rate matrix obtained by comparing every pair of sampled responses under each rubric. The spread of each matrix column captures how strongly that rubric distinguishes the current rollouts, while correlations between columns reveal rubric repetition; together, these statistics yield data-dependent rubric weights. We combine these weights with the prior weights of rubrics. After column normalization and weighting, the observed per-rubric maxima and minima define positive and negative ideal profiles. Each rollout's distances to these two ideals determine its relative-closeness quality reward. Evaluated using Qwen3-8B on four open-ended query-answering benchmarks, MatrixReward achieves an average score of 63.02, outperforming the strongest baseline by approximately 2.0%. These results support the idea that matrices derived from relative comparisons can be used to construct rewards more reasonably for open-ended generative reinforcement learning.

</details>


### [213] [Interpretable Synthetic Medical Tabular Data Generation for Clinical Decision Support Using Fuzzy Cognitive Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00391)
*Michael Vasilakakis,Dimitris K. Iakovidis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes using Fuzzy Cognitive Maps (FCMs) for generating synthetic medical tabular data with explicit causality and privacy preservation. The approach uses linguistically interpretable fuzzy sets to describe clinical features and encodes inter-feature dependencies as FCM edge weights. Synthetic patient records are generated through propagation and defuzzification, achieving competitive performance on UCI benchmarks while running on CPU.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Synthetic medical tabular data generation is essential for developing computer-based medical systems (CBMSs) when real clinical data is restricted due to privacy, ethical, or data availability limitations. Existing probabilistic and deep generative models lack interpretability and fail to preserve clinically meaningful dependencies, limiting their suitability for safety-critical medical applications.

Method: The paper proposes a novel framework using Fuzzy Cognitive Maps (FCMs) for synthetic medical tabular data generation. Clinical features are described using linguistically interpretable fuzzy sets, and inter-feature dependencies are encoded as FCM edge weights computed from fuzzy set intersections. Synthetic patient records are generated by propagating randomly initialized linguistic activation vectors through the FCM until convergence, followed by defuzzification to produce clinically coherent numerical values. The approach natively handles mixed data types and domain constraints common in health records.

Result: Experimental evaluation on UCI medical benchmark datasets under TSTR (Train-on-Synthetic-Test-on-Real) protocol shows: accuracy up to 0.81 and AUROC up to 0.90 on Heart Disease dataset; performance matching or exceeding TVAE and Gaussian Copula baselines; runs exclusively on CPU; fidelity metrics: KS Complement up to 0.91, Correlation Similarity up to 0.95; DCR Baseline Protection scores consistently exceed those of TVAE, confirming adequate privacy guarantees.

Conclusion: Causally grounded, interpretable fuzzy modeling offers a computationally efficient and transparent alternative to deep generative models for trustworthy synthetic data generation in CBMSs.

Abstract: Synthetic medical tabular data generation has become essential for developing and validating computer-based medical systems (CBMSs) when real clinical data is restricted due to privacy, ethical, or data availability limitations. Existing probabilistic and deep generative models often lack interpretability and fail to preserve clinically meaningful dependencies, limiting their suitability for safety-critical applications. This paper proposes a novel application of Fuzzy Cognitive Maps (FCMs) in a framework for synthetic medical tabular data generation with explicit causality and privacy preservation. Clinical features are described using linguistically interpretable fuzzy sets, and inter-feature dependencies are encoded as FCM edge weights computed from fuzzy set intersections. Synthetic patient records are generated by propagating randomly initialized linguistic activation vectors through the FCM until convergence, followed by defuzzification to produce clinically coherent numerical values. The approach natively handles mixed data types, and domain constraints common in health records. Experimental evaluation on UCI medical benchmark datasets demonstrates competitive performance under a Train-on-Synthetic-Test-on-Real (TSTR) protocol. The proposed method achieves accuracy of up to 0.81 and AUROC of up to 0.90 on the Heart Disease dataset, matching or exceeding TVAE and Gaussian Copula baselines while running exclusively on CPU. Fidelity metrics including KS Complement (up to 0.91) and Correlation Similarity (up to 0.95) confirm strong statistical coherence, and DCR Baseline Protection scores consistently exceed those of TVAE, confirming adequate privacy guarantees. These results demonstrate that causally grounded, interpretable fuzzy modeling offers a computationally efficient and transparent alternative to deep generative models for trustworthy synthetic data generation in CBMSs.

</details>


### [214] [Forking: Sudden Overfitting Under Replay](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00394)
*Shanbin Yu,Shaoyang Guo,Haoran Zhao,Danni Yu,Ziming Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper identifies "forking," a generalization failure in language models where training and validation loss sharply diverge at epoch boundaries under data replay conditions. The phenomenon occurs in models with over-encoding n-gram memory branches and is reproduced in DeepSeek-style models. The effect is caused by repeated updates sharpening observed continuations while suppressing unseen ones, with low-frequency contexts contributing most to the gap.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors aim to study and characterize forking, a generalization failure discovered in NanoGPT autoresearch. This phenomenon resembles "forks" in shape due to the sharp separation of training and validation loss at epoch boundaries. The motivation includes both discovering a new phenomenon in deep learning and highlighting the need for caution when evaluating results from autoresearch agents.

Method: The authors conducted controlled experiments using vanilla NanoGPT and reproduced the phenomenon in a DeepSeek-style model with Engram. They analyzed the mechanistic behavior under data replay, examining how repeated updates affect training versus validation loss, and studied the role of n-gram modules, context frequency, training budgets, and table crowding. They also tested short-budget, heavily repeated SFT and RL-like regimes.

Result: Forking is confirmed as a generalization failure where training and validation loss sharply diverge at epoch boundaries. The n-gram module creates weakly interacting context-specific subspaces that amplify this effect. Low-frequency contexts contribute most to the gap. Larger training budgets and heavily crowded tables suppress forking. The phenomenon also appears in short-budget, heavily repeated SFT and RL-like regimes.

Conclusion: Forking represents another curious phenomenon in deep learning, alongside grokking and double descent. It serves as an unexpected and unpleasant by-product of tricks proposed by autoresearch agents. The authors emphasize that while these agents produce many seemingly useful results, careful evaluation is necessary. The paper contributes by documenting this new phenomenon and warning about uncritical adoption of autoresearch findings.

Abstract: This paper studies forking, a generalization failure discovered in NanoGPT autoresearch. Under data replay, models with an over-encoding n-gram memory branch show a sharp separation of training and validation loss at epoch boundaries, resembling the shape of forks. We study this phenomenon in a controlled vanilla NanoGPT setting and reproduce it in a DeepSeek-style model with Engram. Mechanistically, repeated updates sharpen the continuations observed in training while suppressing the probability of unseen continuations, whose loss grows with each pass. The n-gram module creates weakly interacting context-specific subspaces, amplifying this effect. Low-frequency contexts contribute most of the gap, whereas larger training budgets and heavily crowded tables suppress it. We also observe forking in short-budget, heavily repeated SFT and RL-like regimes. The contributions of this paper are twofold: (1) Forking reveals yet another curious phenomenon in deep learning, in addition to grokking and double descent. (2) Forking is an unexpected and unpleasant by-product of tricks proposed by autoresearch agents. While these agents produce an enormous number of results that seem useful, we should always be careful with their results.

</details>


### [215] [Specificity-Aware Diffusion Steering via Variance-Reduced Sequential Monte Carlo](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00395)
*Luran Wang,Linrui Ma,Hannes Stärk,Regina Barzilay*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses inference-time steering for pretrained diffusion models, focusing on "specificity-aware generation" - the ability to suppress undesired (negative) reference distributions while preserving desired (positive) distributions, especially in overlapping regions. The authors propose an overlap-based objective to derive a target distribution, combined with a Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) sampler and fixed-noise optimization procedure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that existing negative guidance methods for diffusion models tend to erode the positive distribution when trying to repel negative samples, particularly in regions where the two distributions overlap. This limits specificity - the ability to precisely target generation toward desired regions while effectively suppressing undesired ones. This is important for applications like text-to-image generation and peptide-MHC binding prediction where precise control over output distributions is critical.

Method: The authors formulate specificity-aware steering as a target-design problem. They derive a target distribution from an overlap-based objective that retains the desired reference distribution only in regions where it is sufficiently preferred over the undesired distribution (giving a likelihood-ratio interpretation). They develop a Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) sampler with a variance-minimized local proposal for sampling from the time-dependent target path. Additionally, they introduce a practical fixed-noise optimization procedure using Jacobian-vector products with both desired and undesired score fields.

Result: Experiments across four domains - synthetic task, class-contrastive generation, text-to-image, and peptide-MHC (p-MHC) binder prediction - demonstrate that the proposed method: (1) suppresses undesired regions more effectively, (2) reduces mode shift, and (3) improves sampling stability by decreasing SMC weight collapse compared to negative-guidance baselines.

Conclusion: The paper presents a principled approach to specificity-aware diffusion steering that addresses the overlap problem through an overlap-based objective and likelihood-ratio interpretation. The combination of SMC sampling with variance-minimized proposals and fixed-noise optimization provides a practical solution that outperforms existing negative-guidance methods in terms of specificity, mode preservation, and sampling stability.

Abstract: Inference-time steering enables pretrained diffusion models to satisfy new constraints without full retraining. However, specificity-aware generation is difficult: repelling samples from a negative reference distribution can also erode the positive distribution where the two overlap. The key challenge is to suppress negative mass while minimally distorting the positive distribution. We address this problem by formulating specificity-aware steering as a target-design problem and deriving a target distribution from an overlap-based objective. The resulting target keeps the desired reference distribution only in regions where it is sufficiently preferred over the undesired reference distribution, giving a likelihood-ratio interpretation of specificity. To sample from the corresponding time-dependent target path, we develop a Sequential Monte Carlo sampler with a variance-minimized local proposal. We further introduce a practical fixed-noise optimization procedure with the Jacobian--vector products with the desired and undesired score fields. Experiments on synthetic task, class-contrastive generation, text-to-image tasks and peptide-MHC (p-MHC) binder show that the proposed method suppresses undesired regions more effectively, reduces mode shift, and improves sampling stability by decreasing the SMC weight collapse compared with negative-guidance baselines. Code is available at: https://github.com/WangLuran/Specificity-Aware-Diffusion-Steering

</details>


### [216] [NEUROTOKEN: Joint Source and Directional AAD with Envelope Decoding via Conditional Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00397)
*Ali Alavi,Donald S. Williamson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NEUROTOKEN is a neural network with three heads sharing an EEG front-end that solves the cocktail-party problem by computing conditional likelihoods of attended audio envelopes given EEG signals. It uses ATTUNEFLOW (conditional flow-matching) to score candidate streams and two inference ensembles (QUADTRACK and ENV-FLOW) to achieve state-of-the-art auditory attention decoding at 5-second windows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The cocktail-party problem (identifying which speaker a listener attends to in noisy environments) is critical for next-generation hearing aids and brain-computer interfaces. Current AAD methods have limitations: directional-AAD cannot map side to stream; regression-based source-AAD uses noisy Pearson correlation; envelope reconstruction lacks native AAD rules. The authors argue the correct approach is computing conditional likelihoods rather than single statistics.

Method: NEUROTOKEN uses a single network with three heads sharing one EEG front-end: (1) ATTUNEFLOW head using conditional flow-matching with integrated velocity-residual likelihood ratio for scoring candidates; (2) Two inference-time ensembles - QUADTRACK (four complementary statistics) and ENV-FLOW (z-normalized QUADTRACK+ATTUNEFLOW) to absorb per-statistic failure modes. Evaluated on KU Leuven, DTU, and NJU datasets at 5-second windows.

Result: ATTUNEFLOW improves per-segment source-AAD by 9%-16% over the strongest non-generative baseline and reduces across-subject variance by ~3x. Trial-level fusion exceeds 93% accuracy on two of three datasets. Canonical 95-97% direction-AAD numbers collapse by 17%-45% under strict trial-disjoint protocols, revealing true performance ceilings.

Conclusion: A likelihood-based formulation (conditional likelihood of attended envelope given EEG) is superior to single-statistic approaches for auditory attention decoding. NEUROTOKEN achieves state-of-the-art performance at practical 1-5 second windows, with ATTUNEFLOW and ensemble methods effectively addressing limitations of prior approaches. The findings also clarify that previous high direction-AAD accuracy numbers may be inflated due to non-disjoint protocols.

Abstract: Identifying which speaker a listener is attending to in a noisy room -- the cocktail-party problem -- is the missing ingredient for next-generation hearing aids and brain-computer interfaces: it tells the device whose voice to amplify. Auditory attention decoding (AAD) reads this answer from EEG, but the literature splits into disconnected pieces: directional-AAD classifies side but does not map side to stream; regression-based source-AAD ranks candidate streams by a single Pearson correlation that is intrinsically noisy at the 1-5 s windows real devices need; and envelope reconstruction has no native AAD rule. We argue the right object is not any single statistic but the conditional likelihood of the attended envelope given EEG, and we make this practical with NEUROTOKEN: a single network whose three heads share one EEG front-end, with a conditional flow-matching head (ATTUNEFLOW) that scores candidates by an integrated velocity-residual likelihood ratio. Two inference-time ensembles -- QUADTRACK (four complementary statistics) and ENV-FLOW (z-normalised QUADTRACK+ATTUNEFLOW) -- absorb per-statistic failure modes for free. On KU Leuven, DTU, and NJU at 5 s, ATTUNEFLOW lifts per-segment source-AAD by 9%-16% over the strongest non-generative baseline and shrinks across-subject variance by ~3x; trial-level fusion exceeds 93% on two of three datasets. In parallel reproductions we show that canonical 95-97% direction-AAD numbers collapse by 17%-45% under a strict trial-disjoint protocol, clarifying both the true ceiling and why a likelihood-based formulation is needed.

</details>


### [217] [WIPSNet: Deep Learning for Paediatric Wheeze Detection from Overnight Impedance Pneumography](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00398)
*Felix Oury,Harley Day,Karina Mayoral,Ville-Pekka Seppä,Sejal Saglani,Reiko J. Tanaka*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: WIPSNet uses 3D ResNet on continuous wavelet transform scalograms of overnight impedance pneumography signals to classify nocturnal wheeze in pediatric patients, achieving AUC of 0.783 compared to 0.633 for the standard EVI method.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current clinical method (EVI) compresses overnight IP recordings into a single scalar, resulting in poor classification performance (AUC 0.633). This oversimplification fails to capture the complex temporal dynamics of nocturnal respiratory patterns.

Method: Proposed WIPSNet: a 3D ResNet architecture operating on stacked continuous wavelet transform (CWT) scalograms of overnight IP signals. The approach preserves time-frequency information and uses 3D convolutions to capture multi-scale temporal patterns.

Result: WIPSNet achieves AUC of 0.783 ± 0.026, outperforming EVI (0.633), a state-space model (Mamba), and two modern sleep-staging architectures. Best performance occurs at 32 minutes of temporal context, indicating multi-scale temporal aggregation is crucial for modeling nocturnal respiratory dynamics.

Conclusion: Structured time-frequency representations combined with 3D convolutional architectures provide an effective approach for learning from long, irregular physiological time series. The 32-minute optimal context suggests important temporal patterns exist at this scale for wheeze classification.

Abstract: Overnight impedance pneumography (IP) is used to monitor paediatric respiratory health. Its current clinical readout, the Expiratory Variability Index (EVI), compresses each IP recording into a single scalar and achieves an AUC of 0.633 for night-level wheeze classification. We introduce Wheeze Impedance Pneumography Scalogram Network (WIPSNet), a 3D ResNet operating on stacked continuous wavelet transform scalograms of overnight IP signals. On a 15-patient cohort (60 nights, 281 hours), WIPSNet achieves an AUC of $0.783 \pm 0.026$, outperforming EVI, a state-space model (Mamba), and two modern sleep-staging architectures. Performance peaks at a volumetric depth corresponding to 32 minutes of temporal context, suggesting that multi-scale temporal aggregation is important for modelling nocturnal respiratory dynamics. Overall, these results indicate that structured time-frequency representations combined with 3D convolutional architectures provide an effective approach for learning from long, irregular physiological time series.

</details>


### [218] [Metacognitive Reasoning in Energy Based Models using Instance Based Learning Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00399)
*Tailia Malloy,Prateek Kumar Rajput,Serge Lionel Nikiema,Cleotilde Gonzalez,Tegawendé F. Bissyandé*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces MERITED, a framework combining Energy-Based Models (EBMs) with Instance-Based Learning Theory (IBLT) to enable metacognitive reasoning in AI systems. It allows dynamic allocation of computational resources based on uncertainty estimation, addressing limitations of current LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI systems relying on LLMs cannot estimate uncertainty before responding or dynamically allocate compute resources. While EBMs offer interpretable uncertainty modeling and dynamic compute allocation, they lack metacognitive control mechanisms for determining how much reasoning effort to allocate based on uncertainty.

Method: The authors combine Energy-Based Models with Instance-Based Learning Theory (IBLT), which models human decision-making from experience. They trained a 191M parameter reasoning EBM and implemented the MERITED framework for dynamic compute allocation using an IBL model that determines computational effort based on uncertainty estimates.

Result: The paper contributes: (1) a trained 191M parameter reasoning EBM with open weights, and (2) an implementation of the MERITED framework enabling metacognitive control over reasoning effort based on uncertainty while maintaining computational efficiency.

Conclusion: The MERITED framework enables AI systems to mimic human metacognitive processes by dynamically allocating computational resources based on uncertainty, potentially making AI reasoning more efficient and interpretable.

Abstract: Metacognition involves reasoning about cognitive processes themselves. An example is in resource allocation where we choose how much time and effort to put into a reasoning task before we begin based on our confidence. Current Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems that rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) cannot estimate their uncertainty about an output without first responding, and cannot dynamically allocate resources to producing an output, making this type of metacognitive process difficult. A recently proposed alternative to classic transformer architectures that addresses these two concerns is the Energy Based Model (EBM) which allows for interpretable uncertainty modeling and dynamic allocation of compute resources. While EBMs can allow for control of these two processes, the actual metacognitive task of determining compute allocation based on uncertainty is not directly addressed. Instance-Based Learning Theory (IBLT) provides an approach to modeling human-like decisions from experience that has previously been applied to predicting human metacognitive reasoning. In this paper we introduce a framework for MEtacognitive Reasoning with Instance-based Learning Theory and Energy Dynamics (MERITED). Grounded in IBLT, this framework allows for control of the computational effort allocated in an EBM to allow for metacognitive control over reasoning effort based on uncertainty while remaining computationally efficient. This work has two main contributions, the training and open weight sharing of a 191M parameter reasoning EBM, and an implementation of the MERITED framework for dynamic compute allocation using an IBL model.

</details>


### [219] [Representation Transitions Reveal Emerging Safety Risks in Multi-Turn LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00400)
*Haoyu Wang,Wei Zhao,Yedi Zhang,Christopher M. Poskitt,Jun Sun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DART is a runtime defense framework that detects multi-turn attacks on agentic systems by analyzing accumulated representation transitions in internal representations, using a denoising technique to filter benign drift, achieving significant attack reduction with minimal overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-turn attacks compose individually harmless actions into harmful outcomes, evading defenses that assess actions in isolation. Existing defenses lack effective detection for these attacks, and naive representation monitoring fails due to benign drift.

Method: 1) Identify accumulated representation transitions across context updates as attack signature; 2) Use contrastive safety direction but denoise it by anchoring benign traffic at zero and removing leading variation directions; 3) Implement DART framework with detection, attribution, and targeted reminder interventions.

Result: On MT-AgentRisk: attack success reduced from 84% to 25% with 12% false-alarm rate, outperforming ToolShield (55%). On ASEval: reduced from 97% to 52% with 0% benign non-refusal cost. Denoising critical:undenoised catches 7-40% vs denoised 60-85%. Adds 0.14-0.56s overhead per step without auxiliary model.

Conclusion: Representation transitions provide a detectable signature for multi-turn attacks. DART's denoising approach is essential for effective detection, offering a lightweight complement to computation-heavy defenses with strong empirical results across six models and two benchmarks.

Abstract: Multi-turn attacks on agentic systems can compose individually permissible actions into harmful outcomes, challenging defenses that assess actions or states in isolation. We show that such attacks leave a detectable signature in the agent's internal representations: harmful behavior emerges as an accumulated representation transition across context updates, whose triggering context can be identified from the same signal. We further find that naive aggregation is confounded by benign representation drift, as a contrastive safety direction need not assign zero to benign transitions. We address this by denoising the direction, anchoring benign traffic at zero and removing its leading variation directions, with no runtime cost.
  These findings motivate DART, a runtime framework that detects and attributes representation shifts and intervenes with targeted reminders. Across six models and two multi-turn benchmarks, DART reduces attack success from 84% to 25% on MT-AgentRisk, catching every attack at a mean false-alarm rate of 12%, and from 97% to 52% on ASEval, at costs in benign non-refusal of 8% and 0%, respectively. On MT-AgentRisk, it outperforms ToolShield, the state-of-the-art multi-turn defense, on all six models: under the same protocol, ToolShield reaches only 55%. Denoising is critical: on ASEval, the undenoised monitor catches only 7%-40% of attacks, while the denoised monitor catches 60%-85%. The same monitor covers single-turn indirect injection without modification and adds only 0.14-0.56 s overhead per monitored step without requiring an auxiliary model, making it a lightweight complement to computation-heavy speculative defenses.

</details>


### [220] [The Conflict Between Logic and Memory: Learning Higher-Order Interactions in Shallow MLPs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00403)
*Gongyue Zhang,Honghai Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates how single-hidden-layer MLPs can achieve perfect training accuracy while failing to learn the true data-generating rule. Using synthetic tasks with controlled interaction order and nuisance inputs, the authors benchmark different optimizers (SGD, Adam, Muon) and show significant variation in their ability to learn higher-order rules, with optimizer choice and nuisance weight learning significantly affecting the final representations learned.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors investigate the "double descent" phenomenon where networks can fit training data perfectly but fail to generalize or recover the true underlying rule. This separation between training performance and rule recovery is examined in shallow MLPs using synthetic tasks that control interaction order and nuisance inputs.

Method: The study uses single-hidden-layer ReLU MLPs on synthetic tasks: (1) pure parity tasks with controlled interaction order, (2) mixed-order tasks with nuisance inputs, and (3) compact signal-only regimes. Experiments compare SGD, Adam, and Muon optimizers across different task orders (2-11), test freezing first-layer weights for nuisance inputs, and apply bias interventions to examine target symmetry.

Result: Key findings: (1) At order 2, all optimizers achieve 100% test accuracy; at order 3, SGD reaches 96.25%, Adam 50.87%, and Muon 76.82%; at order 4, Muon achieves 99.21%. (2) Freezing nuisance-connected weights raises AdamW's accuracy from 44.73% to 95.07%; removing them at test time only raises it to 48.38%. (3) In compact signal-only regimes, both SGD and Muon learn orders 5-8, with SGD outperforming at orders 9-11. (4) Pure parity contains no predictive lower-order marginals and admits exact Bayes posterior.

Conclusion: The results demonstrate that optimization method and nuisance weight learning significantly constrain the higher-order rules realized by shallow networks. The study bridges optimization dynamics with representation learning, showing that optimizer choice substantially affects whether networks recover the true rule or get trapped in spurious solutions.

Abstract: A network can fit its training examples while failing to recover the rule that generated their labels. We examine this separation in single-hidden-layer multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), using synthetic tasks that control interaction order and the presence of nuisance inputs. We establish elementary benchmark properties: pure parity contains no predictive lower-order marginals, admits an exact Bayes posterior, and can be represented on clean latent inputs by a width-$k$ ReLU network. Experiments then identify distinct optimization outcomes. In a matched order-2--4 sweep, SGD, Adam, and Muon all reach 100\% peak test accuracy at order two; at order three they reach 96.25\%, 50.87\%, and 76.82\%, respectively, while Muon reaches 99.21\% at order four. In a separate mixed-order task, freezing only the first-layer weights connected to independent nuisance inputs raises AdamW's epoch-10 accuracy from 44.73\% to 95.07\%. Removing the same inputs only at test time raises it to 48.38\%. Thus, nuisance-weight learning changes the training outcome beyond its immediate effect on prediction. Bias interventions expose a connection between target symmetry and shallow ReLU representations. In a compact signal-only regime, both SGD and Muon learn orders five through eight, with higher SGD peak accuracy at orders nine through eleven. Together, the results show how optimization and nuisance learning constrain the higher-order rules realized by a shallow network.

</details>


### [221] [RACE: Residual-Aware Test-Time Adaptation for Neighbor-Rich Time-Series Foundation Model Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00405)
*Hao-Nan Shi,Tong Wu,Chen-Cong Sun,Yuan Jiang,Han-Jia Ye,De-Chuan Zhan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RACE is a two-stage framework that improves time-series foundation model forecasting by using query-compatible neighbor evidence without modifying the backbone model. It retrieves neighbors, aligns residuals, and uses a lightweight Gate to selectively apply corrections.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: TSFMs perform strongly but are ill-suited for neighbor-rich forecasting settings like CGM and Web/cloud workloads. Existing methods either fine-tune for each domain (costly, limited transferability) or append neighbors without verification. Key challenges include conflicting residual evidence from neighbors and varying residual patterns across TSFMs and tasks.

Method: RACE uses a two-stage approach: (1) RACE-TF retrieves query-compatible neighbors, aligns their residuals to query scale, and aggregates coherent evidence into training-free correction; (2) Full RACE adds a lightweight domain-specific Gate to determine when correction is beneficial, with reusable training workflow across TSFM backbones.

Result: Across four TSFMs, RACE improves all three domain-aggregate metrics on both primary domains (CGM and Web/cloud workloads), with largest gains on high-error queries. The Gate trained on one TSFM transfers to other backbones without adaptation, improving all 72 cross-backbone metric comparisons over matched frozen targets.

Conclusion: RACE successfully formulates test-time neighborhood scaling as a training-free problem, enabling TSFMs to leverage same-domain neighbor evidence without backbone modification. The approach achieves consistent improvements across multiple backbones and domains, with the Gate mechanism enabling effective transfer across different forecasting models.

Abstract: Time-series foundation models (TSFMs) perform strongly across forecasting tasks, but their per-series inference is ill-suited to neighbor-rich forecasting, where each query has access to related but nonidentical historical series. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) and Web/cloud workloads exemplify this setting: CGM trajectories share physiological patterns but vary across individuals, devices, and conditions, while Web/cloud workloads combine common operating regimes with non-stationarity, heavy tails, and bursts. These histories share useful structure, yet neighbors are not equally relevant. Existing methods either fine-tune TSFMs for each target domain, incurring additional costs and offering limited transferability across backbones, or append retrieved series without verifying whether they support the current forecast. The key challenges are conflicting residual evidence from neighboring series and residual patterns that vary across TSFMs and forecasting tasks. We formulate test-time neighborhood scaling: using same-domain neighbor evidence without modifying the backbone. We propose RACE (Residual-Aware Correction of Forecasting Errors), a two-stage framework for using historical neighbors. We first retrieve query-compatible neighbors, align their residuals to the query scale, and aggregate coherent evidence into the training-free RACE-TF correction. Full RACE then uses a lightweight, domain-specific Gate to determine when applying the correction is beneficial, with a reusable training workflow across TSFM backbones. Across four TSFMs, RACE improves all three domain-aggregate metrics on both primary domains, with the largest gains on high-error queries. Within each domain, a Gate trained on one TSFM transfers to other backbones without adaptation, and the resulting pipeline improves all 72 cross-backbone metric comparisons over the matched frozen targets.

</details>


### [222] [VANDAM: Viewing a nucleotide sequence with DNA molecular priors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00411)
*Jeremy Levy,Ariel Larey,Yury Nahshan,Raizy Kellerman,Elay Dahan,Amit Bleiweiss,Guy Leib,Omri Nayshool,Dan Ofer,Tal Zinger,Dan Dominissini,Gideon Rechavi,Marissa Wirth,Simon Lee,Dung Hoang,Noam D. Beckmann,Shane O'Connell,Nicole Bussola,Alexander W. Charney,Yoli Shavit,Nati Daniel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: VANDAM extends Genomic Foundation Models (GFMs) training by incorporating DNA molecular priors (biophysical properties) alongside traditional masked token prediction objectives, improving performance across multiple architectures and tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current GFMs treat DNA as a string and use masked token prediction, but this paradigm ignores biochemical, structural, and physical properties crucial for biological function. These molecular properties can be estimated from sequence using biophysical models and could provide valuable priors for training.

Method: Two-pronged approach: (1) Self-supervised: predict regional molecular properties from pooled representations; (2) Supervised: inject local molecular features at input when functional labels are available. Tested across four architecture families and nine genomic tasks.

Result: Consistent improvement in downstream performance across all tested architectures and tasks. Probing experiments show molecular priors generalize to unseen molecular properties.

Conclusion: VANDAM demonstrates that integrating molecular priors with token-based objectives is a promising direction for improving GFMs, with benefits extending beyond the specific properties used during training.

Abstract: Contemporary Genomic Foundation Models (GFMs) rely on a DNA-as-a-string paradigm that employs masked token prediction objectives for pretraining. However, this abstraction does not explicitly model the biochemical, structural, and physical properties essential to biological function. Many molecular properties can be estimated from sequence using established biophysical models, so their utility lies not in providing an independent modality, but in introducing priors that training objectives can explicitly exploit. We introduce VANDAM, a framework that extends the training of GFMs with DNA molecular priors. In self-supervised training, VANDAM predicts regional molecular properties from pooled representations. When functional labels are available and can reward retaining molecular priors, local features are additionally injected at the input. VANDAM consistently improves downstream performance across four architecture families and nine held-out genomic tasks by complementing token-based objectives. Probing experiments further demonstrate that the use of molecular priors generalizes to other unseen molecular properties.

</details>


### [223] [EchoPress: Query-Agnostic KV Cache Pruning via Virtual Context Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00412)
*Jiawei Lin,Saibo Geng,Thomas Bourgeat*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EchoPress is a training-free KV cache pruning method that approximates reconstruction-based importance scores using prefill attention, achieving 1.7-19.6x compression overhead reduction and up to 2.9x faster prefill while matching KVzip's accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: KV cache pruning reduces memory in long-context inference but existing methods either require expensive reconstruction (KVzip) or model-specific training (learned approximations). There is a need for a training-free method that can efficiently identify important key-value pairs without additional computational overhead.

Method: EchoPress analyzes how KVzip identifies important cached information through context reconstruction, then shows how to approximate reconstruction scores using information already computed during standard prefill. For each request, it reconstructs only the first chunk to calibrate importance scores for the remaining context.

Result: EchoPress matches KVzip in task accuracy across eviction ratios from 50% to 90% on LongBench and RULER benchmarks with Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, while reducing compression overhead by 1.7-19.6x and total prefill time by up to 2.9x.

Conclusion: EchoPress provides an effective training-free alternative to KVzip that achieves comparable compression quality with significantly reduced computational overhead, making it practical for real-world long-context inference applications.

Abstract: KV cache pruning reduces long-context inference memory usage by evicting less important key-value pairs. KVzip estimates importance through context reconstruction: prompting a model to repeat the context chunk by chunk. This achieves strong compression quality at the cost of additional forward passes. Learned approximations reduce this cost but require model-specific training. We analyze how KVzip identifies important cached information and show how to approximate its reconstruction scores using information already computed during prefill. These findings motivate EchoPress, a training-free method that approximates reconstruction attention using queries and keys from standard prefill. For each request, it reconstructs only the first chunk to calibrate importance scores for the remaining context. Experiments on LongBench and RULER with Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct show that EchoPress matches KVzip in task accuracy across eviction ratios from 50% to 90%, while reducing compression overhead by a factor of 1.7-19.6 and total prefill time by a factor of up to 2.9. Code is available at https://github.com/ljwljwljwljw/kvpress/tree/echo-press.

</details>


### [224] [Do Better Scores Mean Better Physics? Physics-Grounded Explanations for Sim2Real Neural Operators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00415)
*Somyajit Chakraborty,Xizhong Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether lower prediction error in machine-learning surrogates for fluid dynamics corresponds to lower error in physically relevant flow statistics. Using flow around a NACA4418 airfoil with paired CFD simulations and experimental PIV measurements, the authors find that standard benchmark errors do not reliably predict errors in physically important quantities like fluctuation energy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Machine learning surrogates are increasingly used to accelerate physical simulations, but there's an assumption that lower velocity field error automatically means better physical predictions. This paper questions that assumption by examining whether benchmark errors correlate with errors in physically meaningful flow statistics.

Method: The study used paired CFD simulations and experimental PIV measurements of flow around a NACA4418 airfoil. They tested four neural operators with a mean-preserving input intervention that removes velocity fluctuations from selected regions. They also conducted an output attenuation stress test and compared a CNO against a reference model, analyzing both velocity-field error and two-component fluctuation-energy error.

Result: Key findings: (1) Removing fluctuations from the most energetic 10% of cells changes forecasts more than equal-area random removal, but masks aren't matched for removed fluctuation energy, so this measures sensitivity rather than physical importance. (2) CNO has lower velocity-field error but substantially higher two-component fluctuation-energy error than the reference on both analysis subsets. (3) The output attenuation stress test demonstrates disagreement between benchmark errors and domain-summed fluctuation energy.

Conclusion: Single benchmark results (like velocity-field error) are insufficient for evaluating machine-learning surrogates in physical simulations. The authors recommend reporting complementary physical diagnostics alongside aggregate prediction scores, though they note this doesn't establish counterfactual physical correctness.

Abstract: Machine-learning surrogates accelerate physical simulation, but lower prediction error need not coincide with lower error in physically relevant flow statistics. We examine this question for flow around a NACA4418 airfoil using paired computational-fluid-dynamics simulations and experimental particle-image-velocimetry measurements. A mean-preserving input intervention removes velocity fluctuations from selected regions of observed flow histories. Across four neural operators, removing fluctuations from the most energetic 10% of valid observed cells changes forecasts more than equal-area random removal. Because the masks are not matched for removed fluctuation energy, this contrast measures sensitivity, not independent evidence of physical importance. Separately, a CNO has lower velocity-field error but substantially higher two-component fluctuation-energy error than the reference on both analysis subsets. An output attenuation stress test also demonstrates disagreement between benchmark errors and domain-summed fluctuation energy. These single-benchmark results motivate reporting complementary physical diagnostics alongside aggregate prediction scores; they do not establish counterfactual physical correctness.

</details>
