### [225] [Source Identification Is Not Fitness Testing: Measuring the Limits of Synthetic-Data Attribution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00417)
*Joss Armstrong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether provenance tracking (identifying the source of generated data) can help select better training data when models are repeatedly trained on synthetic data. The study finds that while source attribution works well on original passages (98.7% accuracy), it degrades significantly after paraphrasing (53.1%) or style rewriting (29.0%). Neither provenance-based selection nor reference model scoring shows a clear advantage in preventing model degradation over multiple training rounds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses the problem of model degradation when models are repeatedly trained on their own generated data (a phenomenon related to model collapse). The authors investigate whether tracking the provenance of generated examples and selecting based on source information can mitigate this degradation, compared to using a criterion-facing proxy (reference model scores).

Method: The study used financial-risk text as the dataset. Experiments included: (1) Testing generator attribution accuracy on original passages, paraphrased passages, and style-rewritten passages; (2) Testing generated-versus-human detection; (3) Comparing two selection methods over three rounds of generation and retraining - one based on source information and one based on reference model scores.

Result: Generator attribution achieved 98.7% accuracy on original passages but dropped to 53.1% after paraphrasing and 29.0% after style rewriting. Generated-versus-human detection remained near-perfect against the human comparison set. The two selection methods (provenance-based vs. reference model scoring) selected different examples, but no stable difference in model degradation was detected across the three training rounds.

Conclusion: Identifying data provenance and identifying useful training data are separate problems. Neither provenance tracking nor the tested criterion-facing proxy is sufficient to prevent model degradation in recursive training scenarios. The experiment disentangles source identity, criterion-facing selection, and recursive training outcome, showing that both tested approaches have limitations for future recursive behavior.

Abstract: Repeated training on model-generated data can degrade later models. One possible response is to use provenance when deciding which generated examples to reuse. We test both how reliably that provenance can be recovered and whether it helps identify better training data. Using financial-risk text, we first identify the source of generated passages and then repeat the test after rewriting them. Generator attribution is 98.7% accurate on the original passages but falls to 53.1% after paraphrasing and 29.0% after style rewriting. Generated-versus-human detection remains close to perfect against the tested human comparison set. We then compare two ways of selecting generated examples over three rounds of generation and retraining. One uses source information. The other uses a score from a separate reference model. The two rules select different examples, but the planned comparison does not detect a stable difference in the degradation of the resulting models. The results show that identifying where data came from and identifying which data are useful for training are separate problems. The experiment therefore separates source identity, criterion-facing selection, and recursive training outcome: neither the provenance score nor the tested criterion-facing proxy is established as sufficient for future recursive behaviour.

</details>


### [226] [CommunityKV: Efficient Long-Context Decoding via Graph Partitioning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00418)
*Joe McKenna,Anastasios Alexandridis,Nathan Susanj,Jing Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CommunityKV is a framework that formulates sparse attention as a community detection problem to scale Transformers to long contexts. It partitions token graphs into communities for semantic retrieval and uses local update rules for constant-time token assignment during decoding, achieving up to 1.71x throughput improvement over dense attention.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scaling Transformers to long contexts is constrained by two major bottlenecks: (1) the quadratic cost of self-attention, and (2) the linear growth of key-value cache memory transfer. Existing sparse attention methods either require large-scale training or rely on semantically coarse heuristics or expensive clustering that is difficult to update efficiently during decoding.

Method: CommunityKV constructs a token graph from QK^T scores computed during standard prefill, then partitions this graph into communities to enable retrieval of semantically coherent token groups. It uses a local update rule to assign newly generated tokens to communities in constant time, enabling sparse retrieval throughout streaming decoding without global re-partitioning. Two variants are proposed: one graph per query head, and query-group graph aggregation.

Result: Evaluated on Qwen3 and Llama-3.1 models across three long-context benchmarks: (1) one graph per query head delivers up to 1.25x end-to-end generation throughput of dense attention; (2) query-group graph aggregation yields up to 1.71x throughput with comparable accuracy.

Conclusion: CommunityKV successfully addresses the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff in long-context Transformers by formulating sparse attention as a community detection problem. The local update mechanism enables efficient decoding without expensive global re-partitioning, making it practical for streaming applications.

Abstract: Scaling Transformers to long contexts is constrained by the quadratic cost of self-attention and the linear growth of key-value cache memory transfer. Sparse attention mitigates this by retrieving only relevant tokens, but current approaches either require large-scale training or, within the training-free regime, rely on semantically coarse heuristics or expensive clustering that is difficult to update efficiently during decoding. We introduce CommunityKV, a framework that formulates sparse attention as a community detection problem. CommunityKV constructs a token graph from the $QK^T$ scores already computed during standard prefill, and partitions the graph into communities to enable retrieval of semantically coherent token groups. A local update rule assigns newly generated tokens to communities in constant time, enabling sparse retrieval throughout streaming decoding without global re-partitioning. We evaluate CommunityKV on Qwen3 and Llama-3.1 models across three long-context benchmarks. With one graph per query head, CommunityKV delivers up to $1.25\times$ the end-to-end generation throughput of dense attention, while query-group graph aggregation yields up to $1.71\times$ with comparable accuracy.

</details>


### [227] [The Life Cycle of a Massive Activation: Stochastic Birth, Weight-Decay-Driven Growth, and Competitive Consolidation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00423)
*S. Aaron McClendon,Jorge Gallego-Feliciano,Antonios Saravanos*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates how massive activations (large-magnitude residual-stream coordinates associated with attention sinks) are regulated during transformer training. Through training-trajectory analyses and controlled interventions, the authors discover that weight decay is the key factor controlling the turnover of global activation scale, with peak magnitude scaling approximately as λ^(-1/2) where λ is the decay coefficient.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While massive activations associated with attention sinks in transformers have been observed, how their scale is regulated during training remains incompletely understood. The researchers seek to trace the emergence, growth, and consolidation of these activations throughout training.

Method: The authors combined training-trajectory analyses with controlled interventions, including ablation studies and controlled training continuations with varying weight decay coefficients.

Result: Sink-carrying channels vary across random seeds but stabilize early. Over longer training, surrounding channels erode and sinks concentrate onto few redundant carriers. Gradient attenuation follows the sink token's collective RMS magnitude. Weight decay causally controls activation scale: removing decay near the peak allows scale to keep rising, while retaining it produces decline. Peak timing scales approximately log-linearly with decay coefficient λ, and peak magnitudes scale as λ^(-1/2), consistent with a balance model where AdamW-preconditioned growth opposes weight decay.

Conclusion: Weight decay serves as a training-time lever for controlling activation magnitude. The lifecycle of massive activations is governed by scale-regulating training dynamics, specifically the balance between AdamW preconditioning and weight decay.

Abstract: Massive activations, residual-stream coordinates with magnitudes far larger than typical activations, are associated with attention sinks in transformers, but how their scale is regulated during training remains incompletely understood. Combining training-trajectory analyses and controlled interventions, we trace their emergence, growth, and consolidation. Sink-carrying channels vary across random seeds but stabilize early within each run. Over longer training, surrounding channels erode and the sink concentrates onto a few redundant carriers. Across ablations, gradient attenuation follows the sink token's collective root-mean-square magnitude rather than any single channel, making collective scale central to understanding their effects. Our central result is that weight decay causally controls the turnover of global activation scale. In controlled continuations, removing decay near the peak allows this scale to keep rising, whereas retaining it produces decline even at constant learning rate. We develop a balance model for the rise and peak of massive-activation magnitude, in which AdamW-preconditioned growth opposes weight decay. Sweeping the decay coefficient $λ$ shifts peak timing approximately log-linearly and yields peak magnitudes scaling approximately as $λ^{-1/2}$, consistent with this balance. Optimizer measurements further show that preconditioning sustains the large-channel cohort against decay even when raw maintaining forces are too small to do so. Together, these findings connect the observed life cycle to scale-regulating training dynamics and establish weight decay as a training-time lever on activation magnitude.

</details>


### [228] [IrekoGPT: Turning Structured Pruning into Post-Hoc Slimmable LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00426)
*Pietro Moriello,Pietro Buzzega,Angelo Porrello,Simone Calderara*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: IrekoGPT is a post-hoc method for converting pretrained LLMs into slimmable models with adjustable width at inference time. It builds on SliceGPT by retaining projection matrices without pruning, enabling a single model to expose nested subnetworks at different widths.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to enable flexible LLM deployment that can dynamically adjust computational resources at inference time, while improving upon existing PCA-based slimming approaches that show degradation especially at high compression ratios.

Method: IrekoGPT builds on SliceGPT architecture with three key innovations: (1) Retaining projection matrices without pruning to expose nested subnetworks at different widths; (2) Calibrating each layer across multiple compression ratios to improve robustness; (3) Correcting downstream linear layers through gradient-free ridge regression.

Result: Preliminary results on Llama and Qwen models show improvements over naive PCA-based slimming, with the largest gains achieved at high compression ratios.

Conclusion: IrekoGPT demonstrates the feasibility of converting pretrained LLMs into slimmable models with better performance at various compression levels, particularly excelling at high compression where traditional methods struggle.

Abstract: We introduce IrekoGPT, a post-hoc method for converting pretrained LLMs into slimmable models whose width can be adjusted at inference time. Building on SliceGPT, we retain its projection matrices without pruning them, allowing a single model to expose nested subnetworks at different widths. We improve robustness by calibrating each layer across multiple compression ratios, and correct downstream linear layers through gradient-free ridge regression. Across Llama and Qwen models, preliminary results show improvements over naive PCA-based slimming, with the largest gains at high compression. Code is available at https://github.com/aimagelab/IrekoGPT

</details>


### [229] [XOR-Trellis: Ultra-Low-Complexity Dequantization and Curvature-Aware Hadamard-Free LLM Quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00432)
*Xiaofan Que,Nir Elkayam,Spandan Pyakurel,Shuokai Pan,Dibakar Gope*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses challenges in deploying trellis-coded quantization for compressing large language model (LLM) weights at ultra-low bit widths. The authors propose two techniques: an ultra-low-complexity trellis dequantizer with hardware-efficient state-to-value mapping, and a curvature-aware objective for trellis path optimization. These enable high-quality compression with parallel reconstruction without requiring Hadamard-based incoherence transformations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to enable practical deployment of high-dimensional LLM weight compression at ultra-low bit widths. Conventional vector quantization requires exponentially large codebooks, making it impractical. Additionally, existing approaches face two key challenges: (1) achieving sufficient parallel throughput during dequantization to avoid inference bottlenecks, and (2) maintaining quantization accuracy without costly incoherence transformations (like Hadamard transforms).

Method: The authors propose two complementary techniques: (1) An ultra-low-complexity trellis dequantizer that uses a structured, hardware-efficient state-to-value mapping while preserving diverse reconstruction choices for trellis search. (2) A reformulation of discrete trellis path optimization with a curvature-aware objective that reflects model sensitivity directly in the original coordinate space, rather than using conventional approaches.

Result: The proposed techniques enable high-quality ultra-low-bit trellis quantization with inexpensive, highly parallel runtime reconstruction. The approach eliminates the need for Hadamard-based incoherence processing, which is typically required in conventional methods.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates that trellis-coded quantization can be practically deployed for LLM weight compression by addressing both the computational efficiency (parallel throughput) and accuracy challenges. The curvature-aware optimization and hardware-efficient dequantizer provide a practical solution for ultra-low-bit quantization without relying on costly incoherence transformations.

Abstract: Trellis-coded quantization enables high-dimensional compression of large language model (LLM) weights at ultra-low bit widths without the exponentially large codebooks required by conventional vector quantization. Practical deployment, however, presents two challenges: reconstructing compressed weights at sufficient parallel throughput to avoid making dequantization an inference bottleneck, and maintaining quantization accuracy without costly incoherence transformations. We address these challenges with two complementary techniques. First, we introduce an ultra-low-complexity trellis dequantizer that uses a structured, hardware-efficient state-to-value mapping while preserving diverse reconstruction choices for trellis search. Second, we reformulate discrete trellis path optimization with a curvature-aware objective that reflects model sensitivity directly in the original coordinate space. Together, these techniques enable high-quality ultra-low-bit trellis quantization with inexpensive, highly parallel runtime reconstruction and without relying on Hadamard-based incoherence processing.

</details>


### [230] [Every Batch Is Its Own Validation Set: Leave-One-Out Gradient Matching for Online Data Selection in LLM Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00436)
*Hongyu Chen,Xinyi Luo,Ming Zhao,Lin Tang,Zihan Xu,Jing Li,Yuxuan Wang,Haoran Deng,Wei Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses online batch selection for LLM fine-tuning, identifying that in-sample gradient matching selectors fail because the diagonal of the gradient Gram matrix (covariance penalty) steers selection toward noisy examples. The proposed solution LOOM removes this diagonal to create an unbiased estimate of update error, weighting examples by their gradient SNR. The method achieves 2.3-2.4 point improvements over full-batch training and outperforms prior methods by 1.6-2.4 points across four fine-tuning tasks and seven backbones (1.5B-8B parameters).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current in-sample gradient matching selectors for online batch selection rarely beat training on the whole batch, despite being attractive (no held-out data needed). The authors investigate why this occurs and seek to fix it.

Method: The paper identifies that the diagonal of the gradient Gram matrix (covariance penalty) makes training error optimistic by crediting each example with its own gradient noise. The fix: remove the diagonal so the matching objective becomes an unbiased estimate of the update's error with respect to the population gradient. LOOM computes the Gram matrix in the metric of the Adam preconditioner during the ordinary backward pass, selects a weighted subset greedily with a (1-e^{-γ}) guarantee, and uses no held-out data.

Result: LOOM improves on full-batch training by 2.3 and 2.4 points on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B, exceeds every in-sample gradient matcher by 2.4 points and validation-guided GREATS and OPUS by 1.6--2.0 points, and selects injected label noise at under a fifth of its base rate. Validated across four fine-tuning tasks and seven backbones from 1.5B to 8B parameters.

Conclusion: By removing the diagonal from the gradient Gram matrix, the leave-one-out objective weights examples by their gradient signal-to-noise ratio, enabling half of a batch to yield lower-error updates than the full batch when per-example SNR is sufficiently heterogeneous. This simple fix at no cost enables effective online batch selection without held-out data.

Abstract: Online batch selection fine-tunes a language model on the most useful part of each candidate batch. Selectors that match the gradient of the candidate batch are attractive because they need no held-out data, yet they rarely beat training on the whole batch. We show why. In-sample gradient matching uses every example as part of its own target, so its objective credits each example with its own gradient noise. This is the covariance penalty that makes training error optimistic, now sitting on the diagonal of the gradient Gram matrix: it steers selection toward the noisiest examples and makes the full batch the best solution the objective can reach. The fix costs nothing. For each example, the other candidates form an independent sample of the data distribution, so removing the diagonal turns the matching objective into an unbiased estimate of the update's error with respect to the population gradient. The minimizer of this leave-one-out objective weights examples by their gradient signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and whenever per-example SNR is heterogeneous enough, half of a batch yields a lower-error update than the whole batch; we give the exact condition. We build \method{} on this principle. It computes the Gram matrix in the metric of the Adam preconditioner during the ordinary backward pass, selects a weighted subset greedily with a $(1-e^{-γ})$ guarantee, and uses no held-out data. Across four fine-tuning tasks and seven backbones from 1.5B to 8B parameters, LOOM improves on full-batch training by 2.3 and 2.4 points on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B, exceeds every in-sample gradient matcher by 2.4 points and the validation-guided GREATS and OPUS by 1.6--2.0, and selects injected label noise at under a fifth of its base rate.

</details>


### [231] [One pool, many targets: a conservation layer and what archival data can identify](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00445)
*Zahra Khodagholi,Niloofar Yousefi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses a fundamental limitation in CRISPR off-target prediction: pairwise guide-transcript scores incorrectly treat independent occupancy predictions rather than modeling a finite conserved RISC pool. The authors develop a differentiable scalar equilibrium layer with conservation equations and exact implicit gradients, providing theoretical results including a redistribution theorem and rank-invariance properties. Experimental validation on archival off-target data shows weak predictive value, with the coupling not establishing clear added predictive value. The dose fits are heterogeneous and violate model constraints, though a saturable compression method maintains accuracy targets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current pairwise guide-transcript scoring methods for CRISPR off-target prediction treat independent occupancy predictions without enforcing conservation of a finite guide-loaded RISC pool. This fundamental limitation leads to inaccurate predictions because the model doesn't account for competition among multiple guide-target pairs for a limited cellular resource (RISC).

Method: The authors formulate a differentiable scalar equilibrium layer with one conservation equation that has a unique positive root and exact implicit gradients. This approach yields several theoretical results: a redistribution theorem, a qualified high-resource limit, analysis of the retrieval approximation, and a conditional rank-invariance result. They then validate this framework experimentally on archival off-target data using paired permutation tests and construct-cluster bootstraps.

Result: Corrected thermodynamic affinities show weak association with measured repression in the direction required by a working predictor. However, paired permutation tests and construct-cluster bootstrap analyses do not establish added predictive value from the coupling. GapNet emerges as a descriptive measure of equilibrium association's cluster standard error. Dose fits are heterogeneous and frequently violate the model-implied superlinear exponent constraint, failing to identify the competition parameter. A saturable compression of the competitor set maintains accuracy targets on held-out guide families but doesn't improve speed at the size measured.

Conclusion: The paper provides a reusable conservation operator for modeling finite RISC pools in CRISPR off-target prediction, along with experimental methodology needed to test this framework. While the theoretical equilibrium model provides valuable insights, the experimental data does not conclusively support the coupling's predictive value. The heterogeneous dose responses and constraint violations suggest the need for further refinement of the model or additional experimental data to properly identify the competition parameter.

Abstract: Pairwise guide--transcript scores do not enforce conservation of a finite guide-loaded RISC pool when they are interpreted independently as occupancies. We formulate a differentiable scalar equilibrium layer: one conservation equation with a unique positive root and exact implicit gradients. It yields a redistribution theorem, a qualified high-resource limit, an analysis of the retrieval approximation, and a conditional rank-invariance result: within one construct at one dose, rankings by fractional occupancy cannot distinguish equilibrium from independent scoring. We therefore audit the two experiments that proposition leaves open, dose and cross-context, on archival off-target data. Corrected thermodynamic affinities associate weakly with measured repression in the direction a working predictor requires, but a paired permutation test and a construct-cluster bootstrap do not establish added predictive value from the coupling: what survives their differing permutation-null baselines is \GapNet{}, a descriptive \GapNetOverSE{} of the equilibrium association's cluster standard error. The dose fits are heterogeneous and frequently violate the model-implied exponent constraint, which is superlinear rather than sublinear, so these data do not identify the competition parameter. A saturable compression of the competitor set holds both accuracy targets on held-out guide families but is not faster at the size measured. The contribution is a reusable conservation operator and the experimental information needed to test it. The code for this study is available at https://github.com/shadi97kh/One-Pool-Many-Targets.

</details>


### [232] [Exact information accounting for SGD methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00446)
*Akshay Balsubramani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents an exact information-theoretic analysis of SGD and its variants, showing that preconditioned SGD corresponds to posterior-mean updates in a Gaussian Bayes model. The analysis introduces an identity that decomposes one-step regret (and the objective) into intrinsic-time cost and change in comparator information, with this decomposition applying to various SGD variants and phenomena including convex convergence, saddle-point escape, flatness-generalization links, learning-rate schedules, and adaptive optimizers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to provide an alternative to standard geometric analyses of SGD by offering an exact, information-theoretic framework. The authors aim to address limitations in classical convergence bounds and to better understand generalization, optimizer performance, and the effects of various SGD modifications.

Method: The method involves an information-theoretic analysis treating preconditioned SGD as posterior-mean updates in a Gaussian Bayes model. This allows derivation of an identity splitting one-step regret into intrinsic-time cost and comparator information change. The framework is then applied to analyze various SGD variants and phenomena empirically on synthetic and real training runs.

Result: The key results show: (1) The identity applies to convex convergence, saddle-point escape, flatness-generalization relationships, learning-rate schedules, and adaptive optimizers; (2) On real networks, the identity attributes classical convergence bound slack to dropped terms and separates optimizers reaching same training loss based on step number/consistency; (3) Generalization performance varies between networks; (4) For gradient-free SGD, the identity determines curvature preconditioner entry; (5) Sharpness-based generalization certificates are vacuous at network scale unless curvature spectrum is nearly flat.

Conclusion: The information-theoretic identity provides a unified framework for understanding SGD behavior, revealing that classical convergence bounds lose accuracy due to specific dropped terms. The approach successfully distinguishes optimizers with identical training loss and connects to generalization, though data-independent certificates become vacuous for large networks with non-flat curvature spectra.

Abstract: As an alternative to the standard geometric analyses, we give an exact, information-theoretic analysis of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants. We show that a preconditioned SGD step is the posterior-mean update of a Gaussian Bayes model, and that its one-step regret splits into an intrinsic-time cost and a change in comparator information. The split extends to an identity for the objective itself. Convex convergence, strict-saddle-point escape, the link between flatness and generalization, the standard learning-rate schedules, adaptive optimizers, and the noisy, momentum, heavy-tailed, and gradient-free variants of SGD each correspond to a term or a special case of this identity. We measure its terms on synthetic and real training runs. On real networks it attributes the slack of classical convergence bounds to the terms their derivations drop and separates optimizers that reach the same training loss. That separation follows the number and consistency of their steps. Its relation to which of them generalizes better differs between networks. For gradient-free SGD the identity determines how a curvature preconditioner should enter the update. The sharpness-based generalization certificate it yields, with a data-independent isotropic prior, is vacuous at network scale unless the curvature spectrum is nearly flat across all parameters.

</details>


### [233] [Score the Update, Not the Token: Descent-Aligned Routing for Combinatorial LoRA Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00493)
*Priya Nair,Lukas Brenner,Maya Lindqvist,Daniel Whitmore,Wen-Hsuan Liu,Tom Saliencro,Amara Okonkwo,Rohan Desai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: VANE proposes a novel routing mechanism for Mixture-of-LoRA-experts that scores expert updates based on their alignment with the loss gradient descent direction ("compass") rather than routing based on token features alone. It splits each expert into reader and writer components, enabling efficient scoring of all expert pairs from combined vectors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current MoE-LoRA methods route tokens based on token features without seeing what experts would write. The authors argue the router should score the expert's update (usefulness) based on alignment with the loss gradient, not just token features. Token-based routers miss the quadratic token dependence and output factors entirely.

Method: 1) Split each LoRA expert into a reader (down-projection) and writer (up-projection)
2) Use a low-rank "compass" to predict the descent direction for each token
3) Score every reader-writer pair by alignment between its update and the compass without forming the update
4) Activate top-k pairs with additive gates
5) Provide exact first-order router gradient for each pair
6) Achieves N_A + N_B scoring from N_A × N_B possible pairs efficiently

Result: On single-domain commonsense reasoning: best average among 12 PEFT and MoE-LoRA baselines, improving by 0.9-1.1 points. On four-domain multi-task mixture with Llama-3.2-3B and Llama-3.1-8B: best average, improving by 1.3-1.5 points. Uses less than half the trainable parameters of an 8-expert MoE-LoRA. Router scores track measured usefulness more closely than token routers.

Conclusion: VANE demonstrates that scoring expert updates by their alignment with the loss gradient is more effective than token-based routing. By decomposing experts into readers and writers and using a compass-based scoring mechanism, it achieves superior performance with fewer parameters than existing MoE-LoRA approaches, while providing more accurate usefulness predictions.

Abstract: Mixture-of-LoRA-experts methods raise the capacity of low-rank adaptation by routing each token to a few low-rank experts. Nearly all of them tie one input-side factor to one output-side factor per expert, and nearly all of them route by scoring the token: the router picks experts without seeing what any of them would write. We argue that the router should score the update. To first order, adding an expert's update to a layer output lowers the loss by the inner product between that update and the negative loss gradient at the output. This usefulness is quadratic in the token, so a router that is linear in the token sees only the part of it that runs through the token mean, and routers that rank experts by the norm of their own activations never see the output factor. If each expert is split into a reader (down-projection) and a writer (up-projection), the usefulness of every reader--writer pair becomes an inner product in the shared rank-$r$ space, and all $N_AN_B$ pairs can be scored from $N_A+N_B$ vectors. We build VANE on this identity. A low-rank compass predicts the descent direction of each token. VANE scores every pair by the alignment between its update and the compass without forming any update, activates the top-$k$ pairs with additive gates, and gives every pair its exact first-order router gradient. On single-domain commonsense reasoning and a four-domain multi-task mixture with Llama-3.2-3B and Llama-3.1-8B, VANE attains the best average among twelve PEFT and MoE-LoRA baselines, by 0.9--1.1 and 1.3--1.5 points respectively, with less than half the trainable parameters of an 8-expert MoE-LoRA. Its router scores also track the measured usefulness of experts far more closely than token routers do.

</details>


### [234] [Gumbel Straight Flow: Distilling Autoregressive Models into One-step Flow Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00497)
*Yeongmin Kim,Arnaud Doucet,Andrew Campbell,Valentin De Bortoli,Thomas Mensink,David Ruhe*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Gumbel Straight Flow (GSF) is a continuous flow-based language model that combines noise-data coupling from pretrained autoregressive models with flow map techniques to achieve high-quality few-step text generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of high-quality few-step text generation in flow-based language models. Existing methods often struggle with the trade-off between sampling speed and generation quality, particularly when using few sampling steps.

Method: The paper proposes Gumbel Straight Flow (GSF), which leverages the noise-data coupling of a pretrained autoregressive (AR) language model. The key theoretical contribution is demonstrating that the coupling between Gumbel noise and one-hot token sequences induced by an autoregressive model yields non-intersecting linear paths connecting noise to sequence representations. The method uses a flow map semigroup objective with velocity guidance from the AR teacher.

Result: GSF outperforms current few-step language generation baselines across various benchmarks, including both pretraining and downstream tasks.

Conclusion: The proposed GSF approach successfully combines flow-based modeling with autoregressive teacher guidance to achieve superior few-step text generation performance, representing a promising direction for efficient high-quality text generation.

Abstract: We present Gumbel Straight Flow (GSF), a continuous flow map language model that leverages the noise-data coupling of a pretrained autoregressive language (AR) model. We theoretically demonstrate that the coupling between Gumbel noise and one-hot token sequences induced by an autoregressive model yields non-intersecting linear paths connecting the noise to the sequence representations. To further enhance high-quality few-step path sampling, we use a flow map semigroup objective where the tangent (velocity) condition is guided directly by the AR teacher. Across various benchmarks, including pretraining and downstream tasks, GSF can outperform current few-step language generation baselines.

</details>


### [235] [Denoising Surface: Modeling and Predicting Inference Cost for Diffusion LLM Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00499)
*Haoyu Zheng,Fangcheng Fu,Binhang Yuan,Yongqiang Zhang,Liang Deng,Hao Wang,Yuanyuan Zhu,Xiao Yan,Jiawei Jiang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes Denoising Workload Surface (DWS), a novel cost estimation framework for diffusion large language models (dLLMs) that preserves the two-dimensional execution structure of block-autoregressive generation to accurately predict inference costs for real-world serving scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current cost proxies (output length, denoising-step count) fail for dLLMs because they ignore that one forward pass can unmask multiple tokens and that per-step costs are heterogeneous. Existing scalar-based proxies collapse the essential two-dimensional block-step execution structure into a single value, leading to inaccurate inference cost predictions critical for request management in serving systems.

Method: The authors propose DWS that preserves the two-dimensional block-step structure as a probability surface to weight heterogeneous per-step costs. They design a coarse-to-fine training scheme enabling a lightweight prompt-only predictor to accurately predict the complex DWS. This predictor runs efficiently on a single CPU core, avoiding GPU contention with the serving model. Since DWS decouples request-dependent execution behavior from deployment-specific cost factors, the predictor transfers across hardware configurations without retraining.

Result: In real-world serving experiments, DWS reduces cost-prediction error by up to 2.50× over scalar-based predictors. The DWS-guided shortest-job-first scheduler reduces end-to-end latency by up to 1.92× for online chatbots.

Conclusion: DWS provides a novel approach to cost estimation for dLLMs that captures the two-dimensional execution structure of block-autoregressive generation. The method achieves significant improvements in prediction accuracy and enables more efficient scheduling, demonstrating substantial practical value for real-world dLLM serving systems.

Abstract: As diffusion large language models (dLLMs) become more capable, they are moving from research settings to real-world \textit{serving}, where request management (such as scheduling and resource allocation) relies on accurate estimation of per-request inference cost. However, common cost proxies fall short for dLLMs: output length ignores that one forward pass can unmask multiple tokens, and denoising-step count ignores the \textit{heterogeneous} per-step costs. We observe that the block-autoregressive generation mechanism induces a two-dimensional execution structure over output blocks and within-block denoising steps, whereas these proxies collapse it into a scalar, discarding information essential for characterizing the cost. Motivated by this insight, we propose the Denoising Workload Surface (DWS), which preserves this two-dimensional block-step structure as a probability surface to weight the heterogeneous per-step costs. We then design a coarse-to-fine training scheme that enables a lightweight prompt-only predictor to accurately predict the complex DWS. This predictor runs efficiently even on a single CPU core, avoiding GPU contention with the serving model. Since DWS decouples request-dependent execution behavior from deployment-specific cost factors, the predictor transfers across hardware configurations without retraining. In \textit{real-world} serving experiments, DWS reduces cost-prediction error by up to $2.50\times$ over scalar-based predictors, while the DWS-guided shortest-job-first scheduler reduces end-to-end latency by up to $1.92\times$ for online chatbots.

</details>


### [236] [One-Step Generative Modeling via Training Dynamics Action](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00518)
*Zhangyong Liang,Ying Huang,Haibin Ling*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces Training Dynamics Action (TDAction), a method for one-step generative models that selects transport targets according to local shared-parameter realization cost while retaining prescribed distributional progress. It formulates the cost as a soft-terminal control problem and derives a closed-form Batch Tangent Action-to-Go value accounting for parameter effort and terminal mismatch.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses a fundamental question in one-step generative model training: when training becomes the iterative process that constructs the final one-step map, what should be optimized - the next distributional move, or the route by which the finite generator learns the final map? Existing transport objectives primarily assess distributional motion, but a neural generator needs to realize requested sample displacements jointly through shared parameter updates.

Method: The authors propose TDAction which selects transport targets according to local shared-parameter realization cost. They formulate the cost as a soft-terminal control problem and derive a closed-form Batch Tangent Action-to-Go value that accounts for parameter effort and terminal mismatch. The criterion captures cross-sample interactions omitted by independent pairwise costs. Under isotropic mobility, the criterion agrees with quadratic Euclidean assignment for deterministic balanced couplings. Randomized tangent probes provide a low-rank implementation that constructs shared detached targets without adding inference-time trajectory.

Result: On ImageNet 256×256, TDAction achieves an FID (Fréchet Inception Distance) below 1.1 without distillation.

Conclusion: The proposed criterion captures cross-sample interactions that are omitted by independent pairwise costs. Under isotropic mobility, the criterion agrees with quadratic Euclidean assignment for deterministic balanced couplings. The method demonstrates that selecting transport targets based on local shared-parameter realization cost, while retaining distributional progress, enables high-quality image generation with a one-step model.

Abstract: One-step generative models construct a static generator through iterative training-time transport. Existing transport objectives primarily assess distributional motion, although a neural generator needs to realize the requested sample displacements jointly through shared parameter updates. The training-time construction raises the question: \emph{once training becomes the iterative process that constructs the final one-step map, what to optimize: the next distributional move, or the route by which the finite generator learns the final map?} To address the question, we introduce \textbf{T}raining \textbf{D}ynamics \textbf{A}ction (\textbf{TDAction}), which selects transport targets according to local shared-parameter realization cost while retaining a prescribed level of distributional progress. We formulate the cost as a soft-terminal control problem and derive a closed-form Batch Tangent Action-to-Go value that accounts for parameter effort and terminal mismatch. The criterion captures cross-sample interactions omitted by independent pairwise costs; under isotropic mobility, the criterion agrees with quadratic Euclidean assignment for deterministic balanced couplings. Randomized tangent probes provide a low-rank implementation that constructs shared detached targets without adding an inference-time trajectory. Controlled studies examine the relationship between generator geometry, transport selection, and realized local action. On ImageNet $256\times256$, TDAction attains an FID below $1.1$ without distillation.

</details>


### [237] [SimplexUQ: An Evaluation Framework and Benchmark for Conformal Uncertainty on Simplex-Valued Predictions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00523)
*Liang You,Hengyu Shi,Dongwen Ou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SimplexUQ is a benchmark protocol for measuring how conformal prediction methods allocate coverage unevenly across different data subgroups (strata) when making simplex-valued predictions. It reveals that while marginal coverage may look good, worst-stratum coverage can be significantly lower, and no single conformal wrapper dominates across all tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conformal prediction guarantees marginal coverage but can spread that coverage unevenly—over-covering easy regions while under-covering hard ones. Existing methods are typically compared in isolation, and there was no standardized benchmark to measure this allocation problem on simplex-valued predictions (class probabilities, topic mixtures, etc.).

Method: The authors created SimplexUQ, a reproducible protocol comparing existing conformal wrappers (not proposing new ones). They built SimplexTasks-12 with 12 tasks: 6 controlled synthetic regimes and 6 real tasks (class probabilities, topic mixtures, spectral abundances, cell-type fractions, age distributions, emotion mixtures). Each comparison fixed the predictor, score, and response-free stratification map, varying only the wrapper. Metrics: marginal coverage, worst-stratum coverage, max disparity, within-task radius and compute.

Result: Key findings: (1) Global calibration can appear valid while failing badly—on CIFAR-10, it achieves 0.900 marginal coverage but only 0.542 in worst entropy stratum; (2) Mondrian calibration raises worst stratum to 0.886 and reduces max disparity from 0.358 to 0.022; (3) No wrapper dominates across all tasks; (4) Rankings depend on evaluation groups and protocol; (5) Mondrian has lower disparity on single target partition for all 12 tasks, while BatchMVP has lower disparity over overlapping groups on 5 tasks; (6) Removing predictor bias only partly reduces global-threshold disparity.

Conclusion: This work provides the first benchmark (SimplexUQ) and reproducible protocol for measuring coverage allocation in conformal prediction on simplex-valued outputs. The empirical comparisons show that wrapper selection should be treated as a diagnostic choice rather than a universal ranking, as performance varies significantly across tasks and evaluation criteria. The authors release task cards, result provenance, and rebuild instructions to enable reproducibility.

Abstract: Conformal prediction guarantees marginal coverage, but a single calibration threshold can still spread that coverage unevenly, over-covering easy regions and under-covering hard ones. SimplexUQ is, to our knowledge, the first benchmark and reproducible protocol for measuring this allocation problem on simplex-valued predictions; it compares existing conformal wrappers rather than proposing a new one. Its task suite, SimplexTasks-12, combines six controlled synthetic regimes with six frozen-predictor real tasks spanning class probabilities, topic mixtures, spectral abundances, cell-type fractions, age distributions, and emotion mixtures. Each comparison fixes the predictor, score, and response-free stratification map, varies only the wrapper, and reports marginal coverage, worst-stratum coverage, max disparity, and within-task radius and compute. Global calibration can look valid while failing badly: on CIFAR-10 it attains 0.900 marginal coverage but only 0.542 in the worst entropy stratum, and Mondrian calibration raises that stratum to 0.886 while reducing max disparity from 0.358 to 0.022. No wrapper dominates, however. Under smooth synthetic heterogeneity, several repairs are competitive; fixed-map analyses show that rankings depend on the evaluation groups and protocol; and in a 12-task comparison, Mondrian has lower disparity on its single target partition for all 12 tasks, whereas BatchMVP has lower disparity over overlapping groups on five. These are empirical comparisons, not new coverage guarantees. A controlled predictor-bias sweep shows that removing predictor bias only partly reduces global-threshold disparity. We release task cards, result provenance, permitted derived arrays, and rebuild instructions, and treat wrapper selection as a diagnostic comparison rather than a universal ranking.

</details>


### [238] [Random Recursive Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00541)
*Jama Hussein Mohamud,Mirco Ravanelli*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The Random Recursive Model (RRM) introduces a flexible recursive architecture that samples layers from a pool of L learned layers for each recursive step, enabling flexible layer reuse with parameter efficiency. It matches or exceeds baseline performance on reasoning tasks with 50-75% fewer parameters and supports variable depth at inference without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional recursive models restrict computation to a fixed layer order by repeatedly applying one learned transformation or a prescribed sequence. This limits the flexibility of layer reuse despite the parameter efficiency offered by recurrence.

Method: RRM maintains a pool of L learned layers and performs T recursive steps by sampling one layer independently with replacement for each example and step. This enables flexible layer reuse while retaining parameter efficiency.

Result: RRM matches or exceeds baseline performance on challenging reasoning tasks, often with 50-75% fewer parameters. It can vary depth at inference beyond training without retraining or adding parameters. It also supports Monte Carlo inference and probabilistic test-time scaling, both improving performance without retraining.

Conclusion: RRM demonstrates that random layer sampling during recursion can achieve strong performance with significantly fewer parameters. The ability to vary depth at inference and support probabilistic test-time scaling may open new directions in neural network architecture design.

Abstract: Recursive models create computational depth through parameter reuse, offering a parameter-efficient alternative to increasing model size. However, most recursive models repeatedly apply one learned transformation or a prescribed sequence of transformations, restricting computation to a fixed layer order. We introduce the Random Recursive Model (RRM), which maintains a pool of $L$ learned layers and performs $T$ recursive steps by sampling one layer independently with replacement for each example and step. This enables flexible layer reuse while retaining the parameter efficiency of recurrence. We evaluate RRM on challenging reasoning tasks, where it matches or exceeds the baselines, often with 50-75 % fewer parameters. RRM can vary its depth at inference, including beyond that seen during training, without retraining or adding parameters, improving tasks that benefit from deeper iterative computation. RRM also supports Monte Carlo inference and probabilistic test-time scaling, both of which improve performance without retraining. These insights may open new directions in neural network architecture design.

</details>


### [239] [Geometry-Dependent Bounds for Online Non-Monotone DR-Submodular Maximization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00545)
*Vaneet Aggarwal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper studies adversarial online maximization of nonnegative, non-monotone DR-submodular functions over compact convex down-closed sets. The learner selects actions before observing objectives and competes with the best fixed action in hindsight. The main contribution is a comparator-uniform first-order inequality achieving coefficient 4/9, improving the prior online benchmark of 0.401, with O(√T) expected regret using one gradient query and one projection per round.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to improve the competitive ratio in adversarial online optimization for DR-submodular functions. The existing 0.401 benchmark was insufficient, and the goal is to achieve a better coefficient while maintaining practical query complexity (one gradient query and one projection per round).

Method: The proof uses a direct ordered-coordinate argument with an objective-independent rational action. The paper also employs a three-group symmetry-gap construction for the upper bound analysis, and provides parameterized extensions with exact finite-instance bounds.

Result: Key results include: (1) Improved coefficient 4/9 ≈ 0.444, beating the 0.401 benchmark; (2) For ζ1 ∈ K ⊂ [0,1]^d, coefficient improves to α(ζ) = 1/2 - (1-2ζ)_+^2/[2(3-2ζ)^2]; (3) Offline oracle upper bound β* = 0.470438... at ζ = 0; (4) Bounds match at 1/2 for ζ ≥ 1/2, with optimal deficit Θ((1/2-ζ)^2); (5) For coefficient-revealed polynomials: 1/2 for quadratics, 8/17 for cubics; (6) O(T^{3/4}) regret with one noisy value per round.

Conclusion: The paper establishes improved first-order algorithms for adversarial online DR-submodular maximization, achieving 4/9 coefficient with low query complexity. The lower and upper bounds match at 1/2 for ζ ≥ 1/2, and the optimal deficit from 1/2 is Θ((1/2-ζ)^2). The work provides nonanticipating adaptive-adversary and value-feedback guarantees, including O(T^{3/4}) regret with noisy feedback.

Abstract: We study adversarial online maximization of nonnegative, non-monotone DR-submodular functions over compact convex down-closed sets. A learner commits each action before observing its objective and competes with the best fixed action in hindsight. We prove a comparator-uniform first-order inequality that gives coefficient $4/9$, improving the online $0.401$ benchmark, with one gradient query and one projection per round and $O(\sqrt T)$ expected approximate regret. If $ζ{\bf 1} \in K\subseteq[0,1]^d$, the coefficient improves to $\underlineα(ζ)=\tfrac12-(1-2ζ)_+^2/[2(3-2ζ)^2]$. The proof is a direct ordered-coordinate argument with an objective-independent rational action. Conversely, a three-group symmetry-gap construction yields an offline oracle upper bound $β_*=0.470438681380894\ldots$ at $ζ=0$, even with exact value and full-gradient responses. A parameterized extension and exact finite-instance bounds define an upper function for every $ζ$. The lower and upper bounds match at $1/2$ for $ζ\ge1/2$, and show that the optimal deficit from $1/2$ is $Θ((1/2-ζ)^2)$ as $ζ\uparrow1/2$. For coefficient-revealed polynomials we obtain $1/2$ for quadratics and a geometry-dependent cubic coefficient starting at $8/17$, including $0.49$ at $ζ=1/5$. A constant objective sequence yields an offline $(4/9-\varepsilon)$ approximation with polynomially many first-order queries on the cube and projections, without requiring a supplied positive lower bound on the optimum. We also give nonanticipating adaptive-adversary and value-feedback guarantees, including $O(T^{3/4})$ regret with one noisy value per round.

</details>


### [240] [Evaluating Hybrid Quantum-Classical Models for Reduced-Order Brain Deformation Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00554)
*Tao Liu,Ge He,Dongyu Liang,Wujie Wen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper evaluates hybrid quantum-classical machine learning for predicting spatiotemporal brain deformation fields using Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) for dimensionality reduction. It compares classical baselines (POD-MLP, POD-LSTM) against quantum variants (VQC, QLSTM) for static regression and temporal forecasting tasks. Results show classical networks outperform quantum approaches in fidelity and stability, though enhanced VQC improves upon minimal VQC.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The computational intractability of high-dimensional displacement fields in brain deformation modeling necessitates reduced-order methods. The study aims to investigate whether hybrid quantum-classical architectures can offer advantages over classical baselines for this physical field learning problem.

Method: Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) projects high-dimensional data into compact latent space. Two learning objectives: (1) static temporal-to-latent regression, and (2) autoregressive latent state forecasting. Benchmarking of classical baselines against minimal and enhanced hybrid quantum architectures (VQC, QLSTM).

Result: Classical networks provide strongest baselines. For static regression, POD-MLP outperforms all quantum variants, though enhanced VQC substantially improves over minimal VQC. For temporal forecasting, POD-LSTM delivers superior accuracy and robustness compared to enhanced QLSTM across varying history windows and random initializations.

Conclusion: Reduced-order physical field learning serves as a rigorous testbed for near-term quantum machine learning. While hybrid enhancements successfully recover expressivity in weak quantum circuits, classical architectures retain definitive advantage in both fidelity and stability.

Abstract: We evaluate hybrid quantum-classical machine learning for the reduced-order prediction of spatiotemporal brain deformation fields. To mitigate the computational intractability of high-dimensional displacement fields, we employ Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) to project the data into a compact latent space. Within this framework, we formulate two distinct learning objectives: static temporal-to-latent regression and autoregressive latent state forecasting. We systematically benchmark compact classical baselines against both minimal and enhanced hybrid quantum architectures. Our results demonstrate that classical networks provide the strongest baselines in the present setting. For static regression, a classical POD-MLP outperforms all evaluated quantum variants, although an enhanced Variational Quantum Circuit (VQC) substantially improves upon a minimal VQC baseline. For temporal forecasting, a classical POD-LSTM delivers superior predictive accuracy and statistical robustness compared to an enhanced Quantum LSTM (QLSTM) across varying history windows and random initializations. Overall, this study establishes reduced-order physical field learning as a rigorous testbed for near-term QML, highlighting that while hybrid enhancements successfully recover expressivity in weak quantum circuits, classical architectures retain a definitive advantage in both fidelity and stability.

</details>


<div id='cs.SD'></div>

# cs.SD [[Back]](#toc)

### [241] [High-Value Synthetic Supervision for Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of a Compact Japanese Speech Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00026)
*Sidi Chang,Peiying Zhu*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper presents an auditable synthetic pipeline for converting Japanese care handoff audio to six-field structured notes. Using 182 synthetic training clips, they adapt a 1.47B audio model via full fine-tuning and rank-16 LoRA. LoRA achieves 97.7% of full-tuning performance (0.8461 vs 0.8664 factuality-recall) with only 12.4M trainable parameters (0.85% of backbone).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Private domain speech is difficult to collect and redistribute, while compact models need task-specific supervision. The study aims to investigate whether a compact model can acquire a narrow audio-to-structure transformation from synthetic examples without requiring large amounts of real private data.

Method: The study uses 182 synthetic training and development clips to adapt a 1.47B audio model through two approaches: full fine-tuning and rank-16 LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation). Evaluation is performed on a 39-clip scenario-seed-disjoint synthetic test set using a model-judged factuality-recall metric.

Result: On the synthetic test set, the unadapted model achieved 0.0500 factuality-recall, while full fine-tuning achieved 0.8664 and LoRA achieved 0.8461. LoRA reaches 97.7% of full-tuning aggregate performance while using only 12.4M trainable parameters (0.85% of the backbone). The full-versus-LoRA performance interval crosses zero, meaning neither method is definitively superior.

Conclusion: The evidence demonstrates that a compact model can acquire a narrow audio-to-structure transformation from a few hundred provenance-linked synthetic examples. However, this is a parameter-efficient capability-acquisition result, not a device-performance result. The study does not establish clinical validity, real-speech transfer, or superiority to a clean cloud system. All evaluation data is synthetic, references are model-proposed, and the judge is uncalibrated.

Abstract: Private domain speech is difficult to collect and redistribute, while compact models need task-specific supervision. We study an auditable synthetic pipeline that maps Japanese care handoffs directly to six-field structured notes. Using 182 synthetic training and development clips, we adapt a 1.47B audio model by full fine-tuning and rank-16 LoRA. On a 39-clip scenario-seed-disjoint synthetic test, an unadapted model obtains a model-judged factuality-recall score of 0.0500, full tuning 0.8664, and LoRA 0.8461. LoRA reaches 97.7% of the full-tuning aggregate as a descriptive ratio while project telemetry reports 12.4M trainable parameters, about 0.85% of the backbone. Both adaptations show large paired gains over the same base; the full-versus-LoRA interval crosses zero, and differing optimization settings preclude an equivalence claim. This is a parameter-efficient capability-acquisition result, not a device-performance result: latency, memory, energy, and real-time factor were not measured. All evaluation speech and targets are synthetic, references are model-proposed, and the judge is uncalibrated. The evidence shows that a compact model can acquire a narrow audio-to-structure transformation from a few hundred provenance-linked synthetic examples; it does not establish clinical validity, real-speech transfer, or superiority to a clean cloud system.

</details>


### [242] [How Robust Are Neural Audio Codecs for African Speech? A Multi-Task Benchmark and the Limits of Perceptual Quality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00154)
*Chibuzor Okocha,Christan Earl Grant*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper benchmarks seven neural audio codecs on three African speech datasets, evaluating signal-level quality metrics and downstream ASR/ASV tasks. It finds that reference-based metrics (ViSQOL, STOI, F0-RMSE) predict downstream performance better than neural MOS predictors, intelligibility and speaker identity preservation conflict across architectures, degradation is worst for conversational dialog, and LoRA adaptation can partially recover recognition performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural audio codecs are increasingly used for speech compression and tokenization, but their robustness on accented and multilingual speech (particularly African languages) remains under-evaluated. This gap motivates a comprehensive benchmark to assess inclusive deployment readiness.

Method: The authors benchmarked seven open-source neural codecs (DAC, EnCodec, FocalCodec, LanguageCodec, SemantiCodec, UniCodec, WavTokenizer) on three African speech datasets (afrinames, afrispeech dialog, afrispeech multilingual). They evaluated signal-level quality using NISQA, UTMOS, ViSQOL, STOI, and F0-RMSE, plus two downstream tasks: automatic speech recognition (ASR) and speaker verification (ASV). They also tested parameter-efficient codec adaptation using LoRA on ~35 hours of African speech.

Result: Four key findings: (1) Reference-based structural/intelligibility measures (ViSQOL, STOI) and F0-RMSE track ASR/ASV degradation more reliably than neural MOS predictors (NISQA, UTMOS); (2) Intelligibility and speaker-identity preservation diverge across architectures, with identity ranking depending on ASV backend; (3) Degradation is strongly domain-dependent, largest for conversational dialog; (4) LoRA adaptation (~1-3% of parameters) on ~35 hours of African speech partially recovers compression-induced WER gap toward uncompressed baseline.

Conclusion: Task-aware, domain-representative, and adaptation-aware evaluation of speech codecs is essential for inclusive deployment. Reference-based metrics better predict downstream task performance, and parameter-efficient adaptation can mitigate codec-induced degradation in underrepresented speech varieties.

Abstract: Neural audio codecs enable low-bitrate speech compression and tokenization, yet their robustness on accented and multilingual speech remains under-evaluated. We benchmark seven open-source neural codecs (DAC, EnCodec, FocalCodec, LanguageCodec, SemantiCodec, UniCodec, WavTokenizer) on three African speech datasets afrinames, afrispeech dialog, afrispeech multilingual, reporting signal-level quality (NISQA, UTMOS, ViSQOL, STOI, F0-RMSE) alongside two downstream tasks: automatic speech recognition (ASR) and speaker verification (ASV). Our analysis yields four findings. First, signal metrics differ sharply in downstream validity: reference-based structural/intelligibility measures (ViSQOL, STOI) and prosodic error (F0-RMSE) track ASR and ASV degradation far more reliably than neural mean-opinion-score predictors (NISQA, UTMOS). Second, intelligibility and speaker-identity preservation diverge sharply across architectures, and the apparent identity ranking itself depends on the ASV backend. Third, degradation is strongly domain-dependent and largest for conversational dialog. Fourth, the resulting degradation is partly recoverable: parameter-efficient \emph{codec} adaptation (LoRA, $\sim$1--3\% of parameters) on roughly 35 hours of African speech reduces the compression-induced word-error-rate gap, recovering recognition toward the uncompressed baseline (developed in companion work). These results motivate task-aware, domain-representative, and adaptation-aware evaluation of speech codecs as a prerequisite for inclusive deployment.

</details>


### [243] [ProxyMOS: Label-Free Speech Quality Assessment by Multi-Teacher Distillation with Adaptive Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00419)
*Maxim Trokunov,Kirill Borodin,Nikita Vasiliev,Grach Mkrtchian*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: ProxyMOS combines multiple public MOS predictors into a stronger model without human labels, using ensemble routing to label 807k utterances for training a wav2vec 2.0 student that outperforms all individual teachers on both English (URGENT) and Russian (mos260) TTS benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human MOS is costly to collect, and non-intrusive MOS predictors degrade outside their training domain. This work aims to create a better MOS predictor by ensembling existing public predictors without requiring new human labels.

Method: Benchmarked 8 public MOS predictors against human ratings, selected top 5 most informative via subset search under 5 routing strategies (uniform, correlation-weighted, error-weighted, MSE-optimized, adaptive). Used best 4-model ensemble to label 807k unlabeled utterances, then trained a wav2vec 2.0 student model.

Result: On URGENT: student achieves ρ=0.802 vs 0.773 for best teacher. On mos260 (Russian TTS, 4,600 utterances, 38 conditions): student achieves ρ=0.636 vs 0.613 per utterance, 0.95 per condition, matching the routed ensemble in one forward pass. Adaptive routing is the only method not degrading with weak predictors added.

Conclusion: ProxyMOS successfully creates a stronger MOS predictor by ensembling multiple public predictors, achieving new state-of-the-art results on both English and Russian TTS benchmarks. The adaptive routing strategy proves most robust. Model, ONNX exports and mos260 dataset are released.

Abstract: Human mean opinion scores (MOS) are costly to collect, and non-intrusive MOS predictors degrade sharply outside their training domain. ProxyMOS turns a pool of public MOS predictors into a single stronger model without new human labels. Eight predictors are benchmarked against human ratings; the five most informative enter a subset search under uniform, correlation-weighted, error-weighted, MSE-optimised and adaptive per-utterance routing; and the best routed four-model ensemble labels 807k unlabeled utterances that train a wav2vec 2.0 student. On URGENT the student reaches Spearman $ρ=0.802$ against $0.773$ for the best teacher. On mos260, a new Russian TTS benchmark of 4,600 utterances from 38 synthesis conditions, it reaches $ρ=0.636$ against $0.613$ per utterance and $0.95$ per condition, matching its own routed ensemble in one forward pass. Adaptive routing is the only rule that does not degrade when weak predictors are added. Model, ONNX exports and mos260 are released. It's about 950 characters; arXiv's limit is 1,920. I kept $ρ$ because arXiv renders it on the abstract page. If you'd rather avoid math, replace $ρ=0.802$ with rho = 0.802 and do the same for the other $...$ values.

</details>


### [244] [Collapse, Not Invariance: Diagnosing Auxiliary Objectives in Speech Anti-Spoofing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00539)
*Ksenia Lysikova,Kirill Borodin,Maxim Maslov,Grach Mkrtchian*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether auxiliary objectives (that shape embedding spaces) improve speech anti-spoofing countermeasures across different generators, codecs, and channels. The authors compare seven auxiliary objectives with cross-entropy over 113 runs on five corpora and find that none consistently outperform cross-entropy when normalized by embedding spread.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Speech anti-spoofing countermeasures degrade when generators, codecs, or channels change. While auxiliary objectives that shape embedding spaces are commonly used as a remedy, their effectiveness is evaluated using EER (Equal Error Rate), which is a pure ranking metric that cannot reveal whether improvements come from a more stable or simply smaller embedding space.

Method: The authors compared seven auxiliary objectives with cross-entropy over 113 runs across five corpora. They tested AASIST3 (a specific anti-spoofing model) with three different seeds plus four pre-trained detectors, resulting in 24 AASIST3 runs. They directly measured the embedding space properties to understand what drives the performance differences.

Result: Raw augmentation displacement makes cosine consistency appear effective, but the gain actually comes from a smaller embedding space, not a more stable one. When normalized by spread, no configuration consistently improves over cross-entropy. Every trained space is dominated by a single decision axis (as expected for two-class problems), and the training-set structure does not transfer to test scenarios. Four runs collapsed to near-constant outputs, which displacement rewards and EER reports as poor accuracy.

Conclusion: No auxiliary objective maintains an advantage over cross-entropy across different architectures, corpora, and seeds. The study reveals that EER improvements from auxiliary objectives often stem from embedding space compression rather than genuine generalization improvements, challenging the effectiveness of these commonly-used training strategies.

Abstract: Speech anti-spoofing countermeasures degrade when the generator, codec or channel changes, and a common remedy is an auxiliary objective that shapes the embedding space; whether it does is invisible to EER, a pure ranking metric. We compare seven such objectives with cross-entropy over 113 runs on five corpora, AASIST3 at three seeds plus four pre-trained detectors, and measure the embedding space of the 24 AASIST3 runs directly. Raw augmentation displacement makes cosine consistency look effective, but the gain is a smaller space, not a more stable one: normalised by the spread, no configuration consistently improves on cross-entropy. Every trained space is dominated by the single decision axis expected for two classes, whose training-set structure does not transfer, and four runs collapse to a near-constant output that displacement rewards and EER reports as poor accuracy. No auxiliary objective keeps an advantage over cross-entropy across architectures, corpora and seeds.

</details>


### [245] [PLACE: Positional Latent Adaptation via Conditioned Embeddings for Binaural Audio Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00630)
*Tiernon Riesenmy,You Zhang,Gautam Bhattacharya,Andrea Fanelli*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: PLACE extends the pretrained AudioX model for binaural generation from arbitrary combinations of text, video, and optional audio prompts. It uses Perception Encoder Core features for video conditioning, aligns text/video representations for spatial cues, and applies conditioning-dependent low-rank transformation with interaural level and time difference objectives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research aims to enable flexible binaural audio generation from multimodal inputs (text, video, audio prompts) with improved spatial consistency, addressing limitations in existing video-to-audio generation methods.

Method: PLACE extends the pretrained any-to-audio model AudioX through: (1) Perception Encoder Core features for enhanced video conditioning, (2) text-video representation alignment for spatial cue derivation, (3) conditioning-dependent low-rank transformation on generated latents, and (4) adapter training using decoded-audio interaural level difference (ILD) and interaural time difference (ITD) objectives. Trained on MRSAudio dataset.

Result: PLACE improves most metrics over ViSAGe on FAIR-Play and achieves improved SpatialCLAP score over SpatialSonic on BEWO-1M Single Static test split. Listener evaluations favor PLACE for video-to-audio and out-of-distribution text-to-audio generation.

Conclusion: PLACE demonstrates flexible multimodal control and improved spatial consistency in binaural audio generation, with strong performance across both objective metrics and subjective listener evaluations.

Abstract: We present PLACE, a method that extends the pretrained any-to-audio model AudioX for binaural generation from arbitrary combinations of text, video, and optional audio prompts. PLACE augments video conditioning with Perception Encoder Core features, aligns text and video representations to derive spatial cues, and applies a conditioning-dependent low-rank transformation to the generated latent. The adapter is supervised via decoded-audio interaural level and time difference objectives. Trained on MRSAudio, PLACE improves most metrics over ViSAGe on FAIR-Play and achieves an improved SpatialCLAP score over SpatialSonic on the BEWO-1M Single Static test split. Listener evaluations favor PLACE for video-to-audio and out-of-distribution text-to-audio generation, demonstrating flexible multimodal control and improved spatial consistency.

</details>


### [246] [On Evaluating Quantum Kernel Robustness for Low-Resource Cross-Corpus Audio Deepfake Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00649)
*Lisan Al Amin,Lei Zhang,Vandana P. Janeja*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This study compares quantum kernel methods (QSVM) with classical SVM and MLP for cross-corpus audio deepfake detection under limited training data (200 samples). Under severe domain shift (ASVspoof 2019 → ADD 2023), QSVM significantly outperforms MLP (AUC 76.0% vs ~50%), but this advantage is inconsistent across transfer directions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Synthetic speech detection performance degrades under cross-corpus scenarios with limited labeled data. This work investigates whether quantum kernel methods can provide advantages over classical approaches under such challenging low-resource, domain-shift conditions.

Method: Three models (QSVM, classical SVM, MLP) were trained on wav2vec 2.0 embeddings reduced to 4 dimensions via PCA, using only 200 training samples. Experiments spanned four datasets (ASVspoof 2019, ASVspoof 5, ADD 2023, In-the-Wild) with various transfer directions to evaluate cross-corpus robustness.

Result: Under severe domain shift (ASVspoof 2019 → ADD 2023), MLP degrades to near-random (AUC ~50%, EER 50.0%) while QSVM maintains meaningful discrimination (AUC 76.0%, EER 27.0%). However, when trained on ADD 2023, QSVM falls below chance on 2/3 transfers while MLP performs better.

Conclusion: Quantum kernel methods can be competitive under severe cross-corpus shifts with strict low-resource constraints, but do not provide consistent advantage across transfer directions. Results characterize quantum kernel inductive bias under distribution shift rather than demonstrating quantum advantage, as the 4-qubit kernel can be classically simulated.

Abstract: Synthetic speech detection is critical for audio security, but performance can degrade when labeled data are scarce and evaluation conditions differ from training. This study examines quantum kernel methods and lightweight neural models for cross-corpus audio deepfake detection under limited training data. We compare a Quantum Support Vector Machine (QSVM), a classical support vector machine (SVM), and a multilayer perceptron (MLP), all trained on frozen wav2vec 2.0 embeddings using a strict budget of 200 training samples. To match the qubit budget of near-term quantum hardware, embeddings are reduced to four dimensions using principal component analysis, and all models use the same reduced features. Experiments on ASVspoof 2019, ASVspoof 5, the ADD 2023 Challenge, and the In-the-Wild dataset show that under severe domain shift from ASVspoof 2019 to ADD 2023, the MLP degrades to near-random performance, with an area under the curve of approximately 50% and an equal error rate of 50.0%. In contrast, the QSVM maintains meaningful discrimination, achieving an area under the curve of 76.0% and an equal error rate of 27.0%. This advantage is not consistent across transfer directions. When trained on ADD 2023, the QSVM falls below chance on two of three transfers, while the MLP performs better. These results suggest that quantum kernel methods can be competitive under severe cross-corpus shifts and strict low-resource constraints, but do not provide a consistent advantage under near-domain transfer. We interpret these findings as an empirical characterization of quantum kernel inductive bias under distribution shift, rather than evidence of quantum advantage, since the four-qubit kernel can be simulated exactly on classical hardware.

</details>


### [247] [Balalaika-Longform: A Russian Speech Corpus for Continuous Long-Form Text-to-Speech](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00658)
*Nikita Vasiliev,Kirill Borodin,Vasilii Kudryavtsev,Maxim Maslov,Grach Mkrtchian*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: Balalaika-Longform is an open Russian TTS corpus (189 hours) with continuous units (30s-15min) designed to evaluate long-form synthesis. Experiments fine-tuning CosyVoice3, Qwen3-TTS, VoxCPM2, and F5-TTS on matched short/long windows reveal that training sequence length significantly impacts performance: CosyVoice3 WER drops from 99.9% (short-window) to 16.6% (long targets with punctuated transcripts) at 1,200 words.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-form text-to-speech must retain requested words over extended generations, but sentence-level training and evaluation can hide omissions and early stops, masking real-world performance issues.

Method: Introduced Balalaika-Longform corpus (189 hours, continuous units 30s-15min) with matched short windows for fine-tuning comparisons. Fine-tuned CosyVoice3, Qwen3-TTS, VoxCPM2, and F5-TTS on either view. Tested continuous synthesis on 50 text-voice pairs with unseen voices at ~75, 300, and 1,200 words, retaining every synthesis attempt.

Result: At 1,200 words, CosyVoice3 WER fell from 99.9% (short-window fine-tuning) to 47.3% (long targets) to 16.6% (punctuated, format-matched transcripts). Paired intervals favored long targets for Qwen3-TTS and VoxCPM2, and by small margin for F5-TTS, whose absolute WER remained above 90%.

Conclusion: Training sequence length under fixed continuous-generation protocol is a critical factor in long-form TTS performance. Long-target training combined with punctuated, format-matched transcripts yields substantial WER improvements.

Abstract: Long-form text-to-speech must retain requested words over extended generations, yet sentence-level training and evaluation can hide omissions and early stops. We introduce Balalaika-Longform, an open Russian corpus of 189 hours in continuous units of 30 seconds to 15 minutes.
