Long units and matched short windows support fine-tuning comparisons on the same source recordings, and the accompanying evaluation retains every synthesis attempt. We fine-tune CosyVoice3, Qwen3-TTS, VoxCPM2 and F5-TTS on either view and test continuous synthesis on 50 text-voice pairs with voices unseen in fine-tuning, at about 75, 300 and 1,200 words. At 1,200 words, CosyVoice3 WER falls from 99.9% after short-window fine-tuning to 47.3% with long targets, and to 16.6% with punctuated, format-matched transcripts; paired intervals favor long targets for Qwen3-TTS and VoxCPM2, and by a small margin for F5-TTS, whose absolute WER stays above 90%. The results isolate the effect of training sequence length under a fixed continuous-generation protocol.

</details>


### [248] [AnchorPrompt: Self-Distilled Soft Prompts for Robust Audio-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00706)
*Pooneh Mousavi,Amir Ivry,Mirco Ravanelli,Cem Subakan*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: AnchorPrompt is an efficient adaptation method for Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) that addresses sensitivity to input perturbations (noise, corruption, adversarial injections). It learns prompt vectors inserted at the decoder input between audio and question embeddings, trained via self-distillation over diverse perturbations, using clean predictions as targets and refusal targets for unanswerable inputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large Audio-Language Models are sensitive to input perturbations like noise, waveform corruption, and adversarial injections, leading to hallucinations and inconsistent answers when audio quality degrades.

Method: AnchorPrompt keeps the model frozen and learns a single block of prompt vectors inserted at the decoder input between audio and question embeddings. Training uses self-distillation over diverse audio and text perturbations: clean recording predictions serve as targets for answerable inputs, while refusal targets are assigned when audio lacks sufficient evidence. The method is perturbation-agnostic at inference, requiring no prior perturbation detection.

Result: Evaluated on three LALMs across three benchmarks, AnchorPrompt improves answer consistency in most conditions. Clean accuracy improves in 6 of 9 model-benchmark pairs, with minimal impact on remaining pairs (≤1.2%). It reduces hallucinations under severe audio corruption while keeping false refusals on clean audio rare. Consistency gains transfer to unseen perturbations including choice permutations and reverberation.

Conclusion: AnchorPrompt provides an efficient adapter-free approach that enhances robustness of LALMs to various perturbations without degrading clean performance. It enables zero-shot transfer to unseen distortions and effectively mitigates hallucinations while maintaining answer accuracy on clean inputs.

Abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) are sensitive to input perturbations, such as noise, waveform corruption, and adversarial injections. We propose AnchorPrompt, an efficient adaptation method that keeps the model frozen and learns a single block of prompt vectors inserted at the decoder input, between the audio and question embeddings. We train these vectors through self-distillation over diverse audio and text perturbations. To improve answer consistency and mitigate hallucination, we use the model's prediction on the clean recording as the target for answerable inputs, and assign a refusal target when the audio lacks sufficient evidence to answer. Furthermore, AnchorPrompt is perturbation-agnostic at inference, requiring no prior detection of perturbations and enabling zero-shot transfer to unseen distortions. We evaluate three LALMs across three benchmarks and show that AnchorPrompt improves answer consistency in most tested conditions. Clean accuracy improves in six of nine model-benchmark pairs, with minimal impact on the remainder of 1.2% at most. Crucially, AnchorPrompt reduces hallucinations under severe audio corruption while keeping false refusals on clean audio rare. Finally, these consistency gains transfer to unseen perturbations, such as choice permutations and reverberation.

</details>


### [249] [Where the Body Keeps the Beat: Structured Motion Conditioning and Music Dynamics Supervision for Dance-to-Music Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00726)
*Changchang Sun,Lu Cheng,Yan Yan*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: Dyna2Music is a latent flow-matching framework for dance-to-music generation that addresses limitations in existing methods by introducing structured motion conditioning (decomposing joint velocities into slow/fast components with hierarchical fusion) and latent dynamics consistency (LDC), an auxiliary objective for supervising local music-latent dynamics without adding inference computation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing dance-to-music (D2M) methods do not explicitly distinguish motion cues across body parts and frequency bands, and standard flow matching lacks a dedicated objective for supervising local music-latent dynamics. These limitations lead to poor rhythmic alignment and audio quality.

Method: Dyna2Music uses a latent flow-matching framework with two key components: (1) Structured motion conditioning - decomposes joint velocities into slow/fast components and hierarchically fuses part-wise motion energy with pretrained joint features; (2) Latent dynamics consistency (LDC) - an auxiliary objective that matches adjacent-frame change magnitudes between single-step clean-latent estimates and paired references, making local music-latent variation explicit without adding trainable parameters or inference computation.

Result: Experiments on AIST++ and TikTok datasets demonstrate improved rhythmic alignment and audio quality over representative D2M baselines. Empirical analysis on AIST++ quantifies how spatial partitioning and frequency separation affect raw music-to-kinematic beat alignment and motion-reference density.

Conclusion: Dyna2Music successfully addresses the limitations of prior D2M methods through structured motion conditioning and explicit supervision of music-latent dynamics via LDC, achieving superior performance in both rhythmic alignment and audio quality while supporting variable-length music generation.

Abstract: Dance-to-music (D2M) generation aims to synthesize musically plausible soundtracks whose temporal structure aligns with a given dance performance. Representative D2M methods do not explicitly distinguish motion cues across body parts and frequency bands, while standard flow matching lacks a dedicated objective for supervising local music-latent dynamics. To address these issues, we propose Dyna2Music, a latent flow-matching framework that combines structured motion conditioning with explicit supervision of music-latent dynamics. An empirical analysis on AIST++ quantifies how spatial partitioning and frequency separation affect raw music-to-kinematic beat alignment and motion-reference density, informing the conditioning design. Accordingly, Dyna2Music decomposes joint velocities into slow and fast components and hierarchically fuses the resulting part-wise motion energy with pretrained joint features to condition music generation. To complement this representation, we introduce latent dynamics consistency (LDC), an auxiliary objective that matches adjacent-frame change magnitudes between a single-step clean-latent estimate and the paired reference. LDC makes local music-latent variation an explicit training target without adding trainable parameters or inference computation. Dyna2Music supports variable-length music generation, and experiments on AIST++ and TikTok demonstrate improved rhythmic alignment and audio quality over representative D2M baselines.

</details>


### [250] [RMS-AQA: A Two-Stage Spatial Audio Question Answering Benchmark for Real-World Domestic Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00935)
*Peihao Chen,Qing Wang,Lichun Fan,Yufeng Hao,Zhifeng Kong,Mengyao Zhu,Hengyi Hong,Hang Chen,Hang Su,Yujie Jian,Chao-Han Huck Yang,Shichao Hu,Jun Du,Jian Luan,Ke Li*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: RMS-AQA is a spatial audio question answering benchmark for domestic environments that assesses audio-language models' ability to ground sound events and perform spatio-temporal reasoning, using real-world FOA recordings combined with RIR-synthesized synthetic data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Embodied assistants in domestic environments need to understand what happened, where, when it occurred, and how to respond - requiring complex spatio-temporal reasoning about audio events in real-world settings.

Method: Introduces a two-stage QA format: (1) grounding audible sound events, then (2) performing complex spatio-temporal reasoning. Dataset combines authentic first-order Ambisonics (FOA) recordings with high-fidelity synthetic data using measured room impulse responses (RIRs). Provides a lightweight spatial plug-in that injects FOA-format data into frozen audio-language backbones.

Result: Experimental results identify three primary challenges: (1) concurrent sound sources, (2) far distance recording scenarios, and (3) sim-to-real domain gap between RIR-synthesized and authentic recordings.

Conclusion: The benchmark successfully reveals key limitations in current audio-language models for domestic embodied AI applications, particularly in handling realistic acoustic complexities.

Abstract: Embodied assistants in domestic environments must infer what happened, where and when it occurred, and how to respond. To address this, we introduce RMS-AQA, a spatial audio question answering (SAQA) benchmark for real-world domestic environments. The benchmark features a two-stage question-answering (QA) format to comprehensively assess the ability of audio-language models (ALMs) to first ground audible sound events and subsequently perform complex spatio-temporal reasoning based on that grounding. To maximize acoustic realism, our dataset combines authentic real-world first-order Ambisonics (FOA) recordings with high-fidelity synthetic data generated using measured room impulse responses (RIRs). Furthermore, we provide a lightweight spatial plug-in that injects FOA-format data into frozen audio-language backbones. Experimental results reveal that the primary challenges stem from concurrent sources, far distance, and sim-to-real domain gap between RIR-synthesized and authentic recordings.

</details>


### [251] [Toward Elastic Speech Inference: Training-Free Wake-Word Detection from Pretrained ASR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01182)
*Hwayeon Kim,Youngwon Choi,Hyeonyu Kim*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper explores using pretrained ASR models for wake-up word (WuW) detection without fine-tuning, applying SliceGPT (a PCA-based structured pruning method) to extract compact encoders. Experiments show stable WuW detection performance even with 50% reduction in encoder channel dimension.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address generalization across diverse domains and acoustic conditions in ASR systems, while avoiding the need for gradient-based fine-tuning when adapting pretrained models to downstream tasks like wake-up word detection.

Method: The authors use SliceGPT, a PCA-based structured pruning approach, to extract compact encoders from pretrained ASR models (Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 and Moonshine-base) without gradient-based fine-tuning.

Result: WuW detection performance remains relatively stable when the encoder channel dimension is reduced by 50%, demonstrating that task-relevant compact encoders can be derived from pretrained ASR models without fine-tuning.

Conclusion: Task-relevant compact encoders can be successfully extracted from pretrained ASR models using structured pruning (SliceGPT) without requiring fine-tuning, enabling efficient deployment for wake-up word detection while maintaining performance.

Abstract: Recent ASR development has placed growing emphasis on generalization across diverse domains and acoustic conditions. Existing approaches typically adapt pretrained ASR models to front-end functions such as wake-up word (WuW) detection through additional training or task-specific modules. In this work, we explore the use of a shared pretrained ASR backbone for WuW detection without gradient-based fine-tuning and examine whether a compact encoder can be extracted using the PCA-based structured pruning approach of SliceGPT. Experiments with Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 and Moonshine-base show that WuW detection performance remains relatively stable when the encoder channel dimension is reduced by 50%. These results suggest that task-relevant compact encoders can be derived from pretrained ASR models without fine-tuning.

</details>


### [252] [AudioJev: Direct Audio Decisions with Order-Calibrated Probabilities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01293)
*Sihan Lv,Zhen Li,Zhiqi Cao,Jinshan Zhang,Ying Li,Meng Xi,Jianwei Yin*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: AudioJev is a direct audio-to-answer model that maps waveforms, questions, and answer alternatives to a candidate distribution through a shared full-parameter model. It addresses order sensitivity in multiple-choice audio QA by introducing order calibration (preserving answer probability under option permutations) and training with random-derangement SKL loss. The model achieves 68.88%/55.33% accuracy on MMAU/MMAR benchmarks while maintaining probability stability across option orderings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Audio decisions often depend on evidence that transcripts do not preserve, and probability estimates can vary depending on how answer options are ordered. Existing approaches may not adequately handle these issues in audio question answering tasks.

Method: AudioJev uses a shared full-parameter model to directly map waveforms, questions, and alternatives to candidate distributions. The training employs random-derangement SKL: each question is paired with a reordered view where every alternative changes position, both answers are supervised, distributions are aligned, and a symmetric KL penalty is applied. Inference uses a single candidate-scoring forward pass without calibration heads or order ensembles.

Result: Across three training seeds, AudioJev achieves 68.88% mean accuracy on MMAU and 55.33% on MMAR. It reduces random-order SKL by 43.8% (MMAU) and 60.5% (MMAR) relative to single-view removal ablation. The same model handles multiple audio understanding tasks: intent recognition, environmental sound classification, note properties, speech activity detection, and conversational transitions.

Conclusion: AudioJev establishes a direct audio interface with built-in order calibration that acts on candidate meaning rather than presentation position. The approach demonstrates that a single model can handle diverse audio QA tasks while maintaining probability stability across option orderings, without requiring calibration heads or ensemble methods at inference time.

Abstract: Audio decisions often depend on evidence that a transcript does not preserve, while their probability estimates can depend on how answer options are ordered. AudioJev maps a waveform, question and supplied alternatives directly to a candidate distribution through one shared full-parameter model. We define order calibration as preserving an answer's probability under meaning-preserving option permutations. Random-derangement SKL training pairs each question with a reordered view in which every alternative changes position, supervises both answers, and aligns the two distributions before applying a symmetric KL penalty. Inference retains a single candidate-scoring forward, with no calibration head or order ensemble. Across three training seeds, AudioJev reaches 68.88%/55.33% mean accuracy on complete MMAU/MMAR and reduces random-order SKL by 43.8%/60.5% relative to the single-view removal ablation. The same model handles intent, environmental sound, note properties, speech activity and conversational transitions. Paired removal ablations and multi-order evaluation measure predictive accuracy and probability stability together, establishing a direct audio interface whose calibration objective acts on candidate meaning rather than presentation position. Inference code and model weights are available at https://github.com/SihanLv/AudioJev-Inference and https://huggingface.co/shlv/AudioJev.

</details>


### [253] [Multi-Party Backchannel Prediction: a Diagnosis, a Benchmark, and a Ceiling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01488)
*Mohammed Hafsati,Ahmed Loughzali*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper introduces a multi-party benchmark for backchannel prediction based on the AMI corpus, revealing that state-of-the-art dyadic models fail zero-shot (AUROC 0.499), but retraining improves performance to 0.751. The key finding is that listener identity is deeply entangled with backchannel cues - listener conditioning helps seen listeners but not unseen ones, and this gap persists despite various interventions including adversarial training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Backchannel prediction has been studied almost entirely in dyadic (two-person) conversation, but real-world meetings involve multiple parties. This work addresses the gap by creating a multi-party benchmark to investigate whether dyadic models generalize to group settings.

Method: The authors created a benchmark from the AMI corpus with 682 masked-listener views from 171 meetings, 190 speakers, and 18,697 backchannel events, using a person-disjoint held-out split. They tested a state-of-the-art dyadic model zero-shot, then applied linear probing, retraining, and various interventions (capacity reduction, listener-adversarial training, per-listener adaptation, oracle lexical conditioning) to address the listener generalization gap.

Result: Key findings: (1) Zero-shot dyadic model performs at chance (AUROC 0.499); (2) Linear probe reaches 0.704, retraining reaches 0.751; (3) Listener conditioning improves prediction for seen listeners but not unseen listeners; (4) The gap persists under all interventions; (5) Adversarial training only partially removes speaker-identity information while stronger removal hurts prediction; (6) Turn-onset prediction transfers to unseen listeners but backchannel prediction does not; (7) Backchannel rates vary ~2x more across individuals than turn-onset rates.

Conclusion: Speaker/listener identity is entangled with useful backchannel cues, making it difficult to generalize to unseen listeners. The authors recommend reporting AUROC alongside event-F1 on listener-active regions due to the low base rate (1% of frames). They release the benchmark and evaluation tools.

Abstract: Backchannel prediction has been studied almost entirely in dyadic conversation. We introduce a multi-party benchmark based on the AMI corpus, comprising 682 masked-listener views from 171 meetings, 190 speakers, and 18,697 backchannel events, with a person-disjoint held-out split. A state-of-the-art dyadic model applied zero-shot to meeting audio performs at chance (AUROC 0.499); nevertheless, its frozen acoustic features remain informative: a linear probe reaches 0.704, and retraining the predictor raises performance to 0.751. Retraining reveals a second limitation. Listener conditioning improves prediction for listeners seen during training but not for unseen listeners, and the gap remains under capacity reduction, listener-adversarial training, per-listener adaptation, and oracle lexical conditioning. Adversarial training removes only part of the speaker-identity information, while stronger removal hurts prediction, suggesting that identity is entangled with cues that are useful for backchanneling. A within-model control helps explain this pattern: with the same features and data splits, turn-onset prediction transfers to unseen listeners, while backchannel prediction does not. Backchannel rates also vary about twice as much across individuals as turn-onset rates. Since backchannels occupy only about 1% of frames, frame-level F1 is strongly affected by the base rate. We therefore report AUROC alongside event-F1 on listener-active regions. We release the benchmark and evaluation tools at https://github.com/HafsatiMohammed/bc_multiparty_release.

</details>


### [254] [Q-SPT: Learnable Query-Based Compression for Low-Frame-Rate Speech Tokenization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01492)
*Jeeyoung Yun,Seohwan Yun,Sungwoong Kim*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: Q-SPT is a low-frame-rate dual-stream speech tokenizer that uses separate, context-aware, learnable query-based compressors for semantic and acoustic representations, achieving superior reconstruction quality and downstream performance in SLMs compared to existing codecs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Lowering the frame rate of neural speech codecs reduces computational and memory costs for speech language models (SLMs), but existing rule-based compression methods (like average pooling or similarity-based merging) struggle to preserve both linguistic information and acoustic detail simultaneously.

Method: Q-SPT proposes a dual-stream tokenizer with two separately learned compressors: (1) query-based compressors that attend to semantic and acoustic streams as separate key-value sources at a fixed rate, enabling stream-specific context-aware aggregation; (2) an autoregressive text loss that explicitly supervises the semantic compressor to preserve linguistic information.

Result: Q-SPT achieves the best reconstruction quality among evaluated codecs at the same frame rate. In downstream SLMs, it yields the best speech recognition accuracy and text-to-speech perceptual quality with competitive intelligibility.

Conclusion: The learnable, stream-specific query-based compression approach with explicit linguistic supervision effectively addresses the trade-off between low frame rate and preservation of both semantic and acoustic information, making Q-SPT a promising tokenizer for efficient SLMs.

Abstract: Neural speech codecs increasingly serve as tokenizers for speech language models (SLMs). Lowering the frame rate reduces the computational and memory costs of SLMs, but makes it difficult to preserve both linguistic information and acoustic detail. Existing approaches rely on rule-based compression: average pooling can discard linguistic information, whereas similarity-based merging uses a fixed threshold on adjacent-frame similarity and applies the resulting boundaries to the acoustic stream. We propose Q-SPT, a low-frame-rate dual-stream speech tokenizer with separate, context-aware, learnable query-based compressors specialized for semantic and acoustic representations. In particular, queries at a fixed rate independently attend to the semantic and acoustic streams as separate key-value sources, enabling stream-specific, context-aware aggregation through two separately learned compressors. In addition, an autoregressive text loss explicitly supervises the semantic compressor to preserve linguistic information. Experimental results show that Q-SPT achieves the best reconstruction among the evaluated codecs at the same frame rate. In downstream SLMs, it yields the best speech recognition accuracy and text-to-speech perceptual quality with competitive intelligibility.

</details>


### [255] [Beyond Decodability: Do Acoustic Factors Drive Predictions in Speech-Based Alzheimer's Assessment?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01846)
*Serli Kopar,Alkis Koudounas,Roshan P. Rane,Sam Gijsen,Paula A. Perez-Toro,Kerstin Ritter*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether acoustic recording factors (noise, reverberation) in speech-based Alzheimer's disease (AD) assessments are merely encoded in self-supervised learning (SSL) representations or can systematically alter AD predictions. Using ADReSSo dataset and three SSL backbones, the study applies controlled interventions and finds that acoustic factors significantly influence AD predictions, even when no significant diagnostic-group difference exists in the original data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address a critical concern in clinical speech-based AD assessment: whether high predictive performance of SSL-based models is actually capturing disease-related biomarkers or is instead influenced by acoustic recording factors (noise, reverberation). The authors argue that absence of significant diagnostic-group differences in acoustic factors does not guarantee robustness.

Method: The study employs: (1) Controlled noise and reverberation interventions on participant-speech-only, non-speech, and full-recording audio; (2) Layer-wise linear decoding to analyze representations; (3) Input-space and representation-space interventions; (4) Geometric alignment analysis to distinguish acoustic decodability from prediction influence.

Result: Key findings: (1) Controlled acoustic interventions alter AD predictions across all three SSL backbones; (2) Noise produces the strongest intervention effects despite showing no significant diagnostic-group difference in original data; (3) Effects are systematically structured relative to classifier's decision direction; (4) Results replicate on held-out test set and reverse when intervention direction is reversed.

Conclusion: High predictive performance and absence of significant diagnostic-group difference in acoustic factors are insufficient for robustness. The authors recommend that intervention-based robustness tests should become standard for trustworthy clinical speech models.

Abstract: Speech-based Alzheimer's disease (AD) assessments increasingly rely on pretrained self-supervised learning (SSL) models that learn acoustic representations directly from raw audio, exposing the model to recording factors. We ask whether such factors are merely encoded in SSL representations or can systematically alter predictions. Using ADReSSo and three large SSL backbones, we apply controlled noise and reverberation interventions to participant-speech-only, non-speech, and full-recording audio. We combine layer-wise linear decoding, input- and representation-space interventions, and geometric alignment analysis to distinguish acoustic decodability from influence on AD prediction. Our results show that controlled acoustic interventions alter AD predictions across all three SSL backbones. Noise, despite showing no significant diagnostic-group difference in the original data, produces the strongest intervention effects. Importantly, these effects are systematically structured relative to the classifier's decision direction, replicate on the held-out test set and reverse when the representation-space intervention direction is reversed. Together, these findings show that high predictive performance and the absence of a significant diagnostic-group difference in a measured acoustic factor are not sufficient for robustness. We argue that intervention-based robustness tests should become standard for trustworthy clinical speech models.

</details>


### [256] [From Isolated Feature to Orbits: Discovering Music Concepts via Multi-SAE Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01864)
*Liwei Lin,Gus Xia*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper proposes a structure-based analysis framework for interpreting music foundation models, using pitch transposition as an inductive bias with multi-view SAE alignment to discover organized representations of chords, keys, and melodic patterns rather than isolated features.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current interpretability approaches (probing, SAEs) focus on individual features, but many music concepts are better understood as structured relations (e.g., chord transpositions, diatonic systems). The authors argue that understanding how learned representations emerge as organized structures over features is crucial for music AI.

Method: The framework uses pitch transposition as an inductive bias to generate pitch-shifted input pairs, then applies multi-view SAE alignment to discover structured groups of pitch-related features (orbits). This requires only minimal grounding with anchor examples to interpret entire concept families.

Result: Experimental results demonstrate that the approach successfully recovers orbit structures corresponding to chords, keys, and melodic patterns across two state-of-the-art music foundation models.

Conclusion: The proposed structure-based analysis framework effectively reveals how music concepts are organized internally in foundation models, providing a new paradigm for interpretability that captures relational structure rather than isolated features.

Abstract: How can we understand what a music foundation model has learned \textit{internally}? Most interpretability approaches, such as probing and Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), focus on identifying individual features with minimal structural assumptions. We argue that many concepts are better understood as \textit{structured relations} rather than isolated features. This is especially prominent in music, where tonal structures are organized in the space of pitch and time. For example, concepts such as chords or keys are naturally expressed as structured sets (e.g., the 12 transpositions of a chord or the diatonic system within a key), rather than isolated features. In this study, \textbf{we shift from feature identification to structure-based analysis}, asking whether the learned inner representations of music foundation model emerge as organized structures over features. To this end, we introduce a framework that uses pitch transposition as an inductive bias to induce ordered orbits via multi-view SAE alignment. Concretely, we generate pitch-shifted input pairs and align their SAE representations to discover structured groups of pitch-related features. Experimental results show that this approach recovers orbit structures corresponding to chords, keys, and melodic patterns across two state-of-the-art music foundation models, while requiring only minimal grounding (e.g., a few anchor examples) to interpret entire concept families.

</details>


### [257] [LAST: Looped Audio Spectrogram Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01926)
*Haider Al-Tahan,Sean O'Brien,Anastasia Razdaibiedina,N. Apurva Ratan Murty*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: LAST (Looped Audio Spectrogram Transformer) reuses the same transformer blocks to iteratively refine only the class token over fixed audio features, rather than adding more layers. This approach achieves better accuracy than a deeper sequential transformer while using significantly fewer parameters and computations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Increasing transformer depth improves accuracy but requires more parameters and computational cost. The authors explore whether additional processing can focus on integrating already-computed features rather than adding new layers.

Method: LAST first processes all tokens in initial passes, then reuses the same transformer blocks in subsequent passes to refine only the class token over fixed audio features. This makes later passes computationally inexpensive since the audio features remain fixed.

Result: On AudioSet, ten-pass LAST achieves 0.345 mAP, exceeding a twelve-layer sequential transformer by 2.1% relative with 49.4% fewer parameters, 42% fewer MACs, and 9.8% higher throughput. Increasing passes from 2 to 10 adds only 1.2% computation. The method shows improved robustness to temporal masking and auditory augmentations, with better generalization on music, environmental, and event sound classification.

Conclusion: Looped/iterative refinement of the class token using fixed audio features is an efficient alternative to deeper transformers, achieving superior accuracy with fewer parameters and computations while also improving robustness and generalization.

Abstract: Increasing depth of transformer models improves recognition, but it comes at a substantial cost. Each additional layer requires more parameters, which makes the process computationally inefficient. We ask whether additional processing can focus on integrating features already computed. Looped Audio Spectrogram Transformer (LAST) first processes all tokens, then reuses the same blocks to refine only the class token over fixed audio features, thereby making later passes inexpensive. On AudioSet, ten-pass LAST achieves 0.345 mean average precision, exceeding a twelve-layer sequential transformer by 2.1% relative with 49.4% fewer parameters, 42% fewer multiply-accumulate operations, and 9.8% higher measured throughput. Across separately trained models, increasing the pass count from two to ten improves accuracy while adding only 1.2% computation. Further evaluations show improved robustness to temporal masking and various other auditory augmentations, with better generalization on classification tasks with music, environmental, and event sounds.

</details>

### [258] [Supporting Perspective Acquisition and Opinion Formation on Societal Issues Through AI-Generated Japanese Rap Battle Debates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01179)
*Ryota Mibayashi,Toru Urakawa,Dai Takanashi,Tomoya Morohoshi,Kanata Yamagishi,Ryuho Sekikawa,Yasuhiko Nishimura,Yuta Takeuchi,Hideaki Tamori,Takehiro Yamamoto,Hidenari Kiyomitsu,Hiroaki Ohshima*

Main category: cs.MM

TL;DR: This study investigates whether AI-generated rap battle-style debates can help audiences acquire diverse perspectives and form opinions on societal issues. Using GPT-5.4-mini to generate 40 brief debates (~1.5 minutes each) on topics from Japanese high school debate championships, researchers found that participants nearly doubled their identified opinions and reconsidered or changed stances in over half of evaluated cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Acquiring diverse perspectives and forming informed opinions are essential for critical thinking and decision-making. While observing debates between opposing viewpoints can promote perspective acquisition, conventional debates require substantial time and human resources, limiting their accessibility. This study seeks a more engaging and accessible alternative format.

Method: The researchers automatically generated rap battle-style debates using GPT-5.4-mini and presented them to participants with synthesized audio through a web-based interface. A user study was conducted with six participants who viewed 40 debates covering societal issues from the All Japan Junior and Senior High School Debate Championships.

Result: Watching approximately 1.5-minute rap battle-style debates nearly doubled the number of opinions and discussion points identified by participants. Furthermore, participants reconsidered or changed their stances in 52.5% of the evaluated cases.

Conclusion: Even brief AI-generated rap battle-style debates can effectively support perspective acquisition and opinion formation on societal issues, demonstrating potential as an accessible educational tool for promoting critical thinking.

Abstract: Acquiring diverse perspectives and forming informed opinions on societal issues are essential for critical thinking and informed decision-making. Although observing debates between opposing viewpoints can promote perspective acquisition, conventional debates require substantial time and human resources, limiting their accessibility. This study investigates whether brief AI-generated rap battle-style debates can support perspective acquisition and opinion formation on societal issues. Rap battles are debate-style performances in which opposing viewpoints are expressed through rhymed verses, making them engaging while preserving the structure of argumentative dialogue. To conduct this investigation, we automatically generated rap battle-style debates using GPT-5.4-mini and presented them to participants with synthesized audio through a web-based viewing interface. We evaluated the educational effectiveness of this approach through a user study involving six participants who viewed 40 debates generated from topics on societal issues used in the All Japan Junior and Senior High School Debate Championships. The results showed that watching approximately 1.5 minute rap battle-style debates nearly doubled the number of opinions and discussion points identified by participants. Furthermore, participants reconsidered or changed their stances in 52.5% of the evaluated cases. These findings demonstrate that even brief AI-generated rap battle-style debates can effectively support perspective acquisition and opinion formation on societal issues.

</details>
