# cs.SE [[Back]](#toc)

### [259] [Software Project Management with LLM-Based Automation: Coordination, Validation, and Governance in Practice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00027)
*Ronnie de Souza Santos,Cleyton Magalhaes,Italo Santos*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates how software project managers perceive changes in their work and learning demands due to LLM-based automation in a large software organization. Using an exploratory case study, it finds that LLMs become embedded in everyday project work, affecting planning, estimation, coordination, monitoring, and governance activities while increasing reliance on managerial judgment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address a gap in software engineering research, which has largely focused on task-level and developer-centered uses of LLMs, by capturing managerial perspectives on LLM-based automation in practice.

Method: Exploratory case study approach based on the experience of software project managers working in a large, multi-project software organization.

Result: LLM-based automation influences planning, estimation, coordination, monitoring, and governance activities without introducing new formal management practices. LLMs become embedded in everyday work, producing uneven productivity effects, increasing need for review/validation, and reducing visibility into task execution. Learning demands are experiential and incremental, focused on understanding LLM capabilities/limitations, critically assessing outputs, and guiding responsible use.

Conclusion: The findings provide empirical evidence on how software project management work is adapted when LLM-based automation is integrated into ongoing software development practice, highlighting greater reliance on managerial judgment and coordination.

Abstract: As software engineering has evolved, development environments have increasingly integrated automated support for tasks such as testing, analysis, and code generation, requiring project management to coordinate both human work and automated workflows. In this paper, we investigate how software project managers perceive changes in their work and learning demands associated with LLM-based automation. Motivated by a gap in software engineering research, which has largely focused on task-level and developer-centered uses of LLMs, we adopted an exploratory case study approach to capture managerial perspectives on automation in practice. Based on the experience of software project managers working in a large, multi-project software organization, our analysis indicates that LLM-based automation influences planning, estimation, coordination, monitoring, and governance activities rather than introducing new formal management practices. Participants described LLMs as becoming embedded in everyday project work, producing uneven effects on productivity, increasing the need for review and validation, and reducing visibility into task execution. These effects contribute to greater reliance on managerial judgment and coordination. Learning demands were perceived as experiential and incremental, centered on understanding LLM capabilities and limitations, critically assessing generated artifacts, and guiding responsible use within teams. The findings provide empirical evidence on how software project management work is adapted in contexts where LLM-based automation is integrated into ongoing software development practice.

</details>


### [260] [Localizing Post-Wire Semantic Changes in MCP Agent Frameworks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00182)
*Aditi Patodiya*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper presents a differential testing method to verify whether agent frameworks preserve Model Context Protocol (MCP) message distinctions that downstream software requires. Testing 18 designed fixtures across four Python integrations (Google ADK, OpenAI, and two others), the method identified 13 unique fixture-task divergences involving structured values, declared errors, and rich content. Google ADK satisfied all primary contracts, while others showed interface-specific changes or failures. The study concludes that post-wire regression tests need to specify both information requirements and consumer reading behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agent frameworks implementing MCP may not preserve critical message distinctions through their public interfaces, potentially causing downstream software to receive incorrect or incomplete data. Existing testing approaches don't systematically verify whether consumer requirements are met across different framework implementations.

Method: The authors developed a differential testing method that traces a fixed tool result through each framework's public interfaces and checks explicit consumer requirements. They applied this to 18 designed fixtures across four pinned Python integrations.

Result: The method identified 13 unique fixture-task divergences involving structured values, declared errors, and rich content. Google ADK satisfied every primary contract in its observed path, while other integrations showed interface-specific changes or execution failures. Most of OpenAI's strict rich-content failures were explained by treating absent optional fields as equivalent to null. In exploratory replay, parsing JSON text recovered more structured values but also returned incorrect values and values for fields absent at the source.

Conclusion: Post-wire regression tests need to specify both the information required and how the consumer reads it. The study provides reproducible, interface-specific evidence from controlled cases rather than production failure rates or model-behavior measurements.

Abstract: Valid Model Context Protocol (MCP) messages do not guarantee that an agent framework preserves the distinctions downstream software needs. We present a differential testing method that follows a fixed tool result through each framework's public interfaces and checks explicit consumer requirements. Applied to 18 designed fixtures in four pinned Python integrations, the method identifies 13 unique fixture-task divergences involving structured values, declared errors, and rich content. Google ADK satisfies every primary contract in its observed path; the other integrations show interface-specific changes or an execution failure. Whether a change matters depends on the consumer: treating absent optional fields as equivalent to null explains most of OpenAI's strict rich-content failures. In an exploratory replay, parsing JSON text recovers more structured values but also returns incorrect values and values for fields absent at the source. Documented settings help in conflicting-output stress cases without restoring a separate structured slot. Fault challenges expose an oracle weakness and test its repair on fresh cases. The study provides reproducible, interface-specific evidence from controlled cases, not production failure rates or model-behavior measurements. Its practical implication is that post-wire regression tests need to specify both the information required and how the consumer reads it.

</details>


### [261] [Testing and Verification of Quantum Compilers through Assurance Contracts and Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00255)
*Furqan Nasir,Muhammad Arif Shah,Iftikhar Alam*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This survey paper compares multiple methods for quantum compiler assurance, including verified transformations, equivalence checking, differential/metamorphic testing, and property-based testing. It provides a source catalogue, extraction matrix, four documented failure cases, and a worked example demonstrating validation gaps. The paper proposes a regression architecture but notes it remains unevaluated.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address the critical need for quantum compiler assurance by establishing semantic relations that match intended use and can expose violations at the delivered interface. Current methods have limitations that need systematic comparison.

Method: The authors conduct an integrative survey comparing verified transformations, equivalence checking, differential and metamorphic testing, property-based testing, and evidence for assurance across revisions. They create a source catalogue and focused extraction matrix to distinguish formal guarantees, empirical findings, analytical deductions, and proposed practices. They document four failure cases and provide a worked example involving layout metadata, parameter bindings, and ancillary qubits.

Result: The study identifies that published bug counts, mutation results, and processing benchmarks support different claims but do not establish a common effectiveness ranking. The proposed regression architecture remains unevaluated. A key finding is that validating a circuit under a reconstructed interpretation can leave the delivered interface unchecked.

Conclusion: The conclusion provides guidance on method applicability, complementary observations, and treatment of inconclusive outcomes. The authors note that practical value of the proposed regression architecture requires controlled comparisons on independently adjudicated compiler-change events. Four documented failure cases connect conditional applicability, parameter association, termination, and phase conventions to method selection.

Abstract: Quantum compiler assurance requires a semantic relation that matches the intended use and observations that can expose violations at the delivered interface. This critical integrative survey compares verified transformations, equivalence checking, differential and metamorphic testing, property-based testing, and evidence for assurance across revisions. A source catalogue and focused extraction matrix distinguish formal guarantees, reported empirical findings, analytical deductions, and proposed practice. A recorded coverage update and source-level selection decisions make the review auditable within its declared scope. Four documented failure cases connect conditional applicability, parameter association, termination, and phase conventions to method selection. A worked example involving layout metadata, parameter bindings, and ancillary qubits demonstrates why validating a circuit under a reconstructed interpretation can leave the delivered interface unchecked. An illustrative revision scenario then separates fault detection from change attribution. The resulting guidance specifies applicability, complementary observations, and treatment of inconclusive outcomes. Published bug counts, mutation results, and processing benchmarks support different claims and do not establish a common effectiveness ranking. The proposed regression architecture remains unevaluated as a complete system; its practical value requires controlled comparisons on independently adjudicated compiler-change events.

</details>


### [262] [Code That Works, Environments That Don't: Measuring Environment Reproducibility in AI-Generated Software](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00425)
*Bhanu Prakash Vangala,Tanu Malik*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper addresses a critical gap in code generation quality assessment: environment specification - the accurate identification of dependencies required to execute generated code. The authors develop a three-layer framework (declared, runtime-installed, and necessary-and-sufficient dependencies) and an agent protocol to evaluate how well coding agents specify software environments. Across 3 agents, 4 languages, and 50 tasks, they find systematic failures including inconsistent, redundant, or incomplete dependency specifications, with dependency set agreement as low as 7% for identical tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While functional correctness of generated code has been the primary quality metric, environment specification - accurately identifying dependencies needed to execute code - is equally critical but neglected. Current benchmarks do not capture this dimension, and the authors hypothesize that coding agents exhibit systematic generalization failures in specifying dependencies.

Method: The authors develop: (1) an agent protocol for environment specification, and (2) a three-layer framework comprising declared dependencies (explicitly listed), runtime-installed dependencies (actually needed at execution), and necessary-and-sufficient dependencies (minimal complete set). They evaluate across three coding agents, four programming languages, and fifty programming tasks, measuring dependency set agreement and variations across layers.

Result: Coding agents show systematic generalization failures in environment specification: dependency specifications are inconsistent, redundant, or incomplete in ways that functional tests do not detect. Dependency set agreement is as low as 7% for identical tasks across agents. Newer agents show no meaningful improvement, suggesting the failure is not resolved by scale or recency. The largest divergence occurs between declared and runtime dependency layers, implicating environment priors learned from training distributions as the primary driver.

Conclusion: Environment specification is a distinct, measurable axis of code generation quality that current benchmarks fail to capture. The findings motivate training objectives and evaluation protocols that jointly optimize for functional correctness and environmental portability. The failure appears fundamental to current approaches rather than solvable by simply scaling models.

Abstract: Code generation has emerged as a central capability of large language models, with coding agents now able to produce functionally correct software projects from natural language prompts. However, functional correctness alone does not capture a critical dimension of generation quality: environment specification, defined as the accurate identification of the dependencies required to execute generated code, is equally critical. We develop an agent protocol for environment specification and introduce a three-layer framework comprising declared, runtime-installed, and necessary-and-sufficient dependencies to systematically assess coding agents for environment specification. Using this protocol, we evaluate the extent to which coding agents systematically misspecify software environment dependencies and how this misspecification varies across three agents, four languages, and fifty programming tasks. Our results show that current coding agents exhibit systematic generalization failures along this dimension, producing dependency specifications that are inconsistent, redundant, or incomplete in ways that functional tests do not detect. Across agents, dependency set agreement is as low as 7% for identical tasks, and newer agents show no meaningful improvement, suggesting the failure is not resolved by scale or recency. The largest divergence occurs between the declared and runtime dependency layers, implicating environment priors learned from the models' training distributions as the primary driver. Our findings establish environment specification as a distinct, measurable axis of code generation quality that current benchmarks do not capture, and motivate training objectives and evaluation protocols that jointly optimize for functional correctness and environmental portability.

</details>


### [263] [Extending LLM-based support for software engineers with ADHD](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00555)
*Aarsh Shah,Ronnie de Souza Santos,Italo Santos,Cleyton Magalhaes,Kiev Gama*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Tether 2.0 is an LLM-based assistant designed to support software engineers with ADHD by providing structured workflow-oriented interaction across planning, coding, debugging, and review phases, with activity-aware context and persistent memory to support task progression and continuity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Software engineering workflows are not designed for developers with ADHD, who face challenges with task initiation, sustained attention, and completion. Existing LLM-integrated programming tools do not account for neurodiversity or support structured progression across development tasks.

Method: Tether 2.0 combines structured interaction modes, activity-aware context, and persistent memory. The system was evaluated through expert feedback and hands-on use with a software engineer with ADHD.

Result: Tether 2.0 supports requirement clarification, task decomposition, incremental implementation, debugging, and completion. It enables users to maintain progress and resume work after interruptions.

Conclusion: LLM-based assistants can support direction, sustained progress, and learning in software development when designed with workflow structure and context-aware interaction, specifically for neurodiverse users.

Abstract: Software engineering workflows are often not designed to accommodate the needs of developers with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), despite known challenges related to task initiation, sustained attention, and completion. At the same time, large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into programming tools, but existing systems do not account for neurodiversity or support structured progression across development tasks. In this work, we present Tether 2.0, an LLM based assistant designed to support software engineers with ADHD through workflow oriented interaction across planning, coding, debugging, and review. The tool was named Tether 2.0 because it builds upon the open source code and foundations of the original Tether system. Our approach combines structured interaction modes, activity aware context, and persistent memory to support task progression and continuity. We evaluate the system through expert feedback and hands on use with a software engineer with ADHD. Our results indicate that Tether 2.0 supports requirement clarification, task decomposition, incremental implementation, debugging, and completion, while enabling users to maintain progress and resume work after interruptions. These findings suggest that LLM based assistants can support direction, sustained progress, and learning in software development when designed with workflow structure and context aware interaction.

</details>


### [264] [Understanding and Mitigating Library-Related Issues in LLM-Generated Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00622)
*Yacine Majdoub,Rinad Hamid,Eya Ben Charrada,Ahmad Abdellatif,Haifa Touati*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper addresses library-related errors in LLM-generated code by proposing an agentic approach that combines task analysis, documentation grounding, code generation, and automated validation. The study analyzes 100 LLM-generated files to characterize errors, then evaluates the approach on 300 tasks across five LLMs, achieving 38.1%-54.6% error reduction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs frequently produce incorrect library usage (invalid imports, outdated APIs, hallucinated dependencies), leading to compilation/runtime failures and reducing reliability of AI-assisted software development.

Method: 1) Exploratory study on 100 LLM-generated code files to characterize library-related issues; 2) Agentic approach integrating task analysis, documentation grounding, code generation, and automated validation; 3) Evaluation on 300 code generation tasks from LangChain and AutoGen across five LLMs (GPT-5, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3, Mistral, Llama 3).

Result: 84% of generated files contain at least one library-related error. Error patterns include incorrect import paths, missing imports, hallucinated libraries, deprecated library usage, and unused imports. The approach reduces library-related errors by 38.1%-54.6% and increases code correctness by up to 16%.

Conclusion: The proposed agentic approach consistently improves code generation quality across all evaluated models, effectively mitigating library-related errors in LLM-generated code.

Abstract: Software practitioners increasingly rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate code that integrates external libraries. However, LLMs often produce incorrect library usage, such as invalid imports, outdated API calls, and hallucinated dependencies, leading to compilation or runtime failures that reduce the reliability of AI-assisted software development. In this paper, we propose an agentic approach to mitigate libraryrelated errors in LLM-generated code. More specifically, we first conduct an exploratory study to characterize the library-related issues produced by LLMs. Our analysis of 100 LLM-generated code files reveals that 84% of generated files contain at least one library-related error, with recurring patterns including incorrect import paths, missing imports, hallucinated libraries, deprecated library usage, and unused imports. Based on these findings, we design an agentic approach that integrates task analysis, documentation grounding, code generation, and automated validation to improve library usage during code synthesis. We evaluate our approach on 300 code generation tasks derived from realworld implementations of rapidly evolving Python frameworks, including LangChain and AutoGen, across five LLMs: GPT-5, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3, Mistral, and Llama 3. The results show that our approach consistently improves code generation quality across all evaluated models, reducing library-related errors by 38.1% - 54.6% and increasing code correctness by up to 16%.

</details>


### [265] [ASAD: Adaptive Software Agents for Debugging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00629)
*Yacine Majdoub,Eya Ben Charrada,Haifa Touati*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: ASAD is an adaptive multi-agent debugging system that dynamically configures agent teams based on bug complexity, rather than using fixed predefined architectures. It analyzes faulty code to determine optimal number of agents, roles, and collaboration strategies, using a central coordinator for iterative planning, reflection, and execution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM-based multi-agent debugging systems use rigid, predefined architectures where the number of agents, roles, and interaction patterns are fixed before bug analysis. This one-size-fits-all approach is mismatched to the heterogeneous nature of software defects: simple bugs waste resources on unnecessary coordination, while complex bugs suffer from insufficient or poorly aligned expertise.

Method: ASAD initiates debugging by analyzing the faulty code and dynamically determining: (1) the number of agents to deploy, (2) the specialized roles they should have, and (3) the collaboration strategy they should follow. A central coordinator orchestrates this process through iterative planning, reflection, and execution—applying fast single-pass repairs for simple issues while assembling purpose-built teams for complex failures.

Result: Evaluated on Defects4J, DebugBench, and CodeFlaws benchmarks using multiple LLMs (DeepSeek-V3, Qwen-3, GPT-5). ASAD improves bug-fix rates by 12-20% over chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, outperforms static multi-agent systems by 4-9% in fix precision, and reduces average agent usage by 32%. The system dynamically adjusts agent number and roles—resolving simple bugs with minimal coordination and scaling involvement only for complex cases.

Conclusion: ASAD demonstrates that adaptive agent configuration based on bug characteristics significantly improves debugging effectiveness and efficiency. The key innovation is dynamic team composition that matches agent resources to bug complexity, achieving better fix rates while reducing resource consumption.

Abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into multi-agent systems has shown great potential for automated debugging. Yet nearly all current frameworks rely on rigid, predefined architectures: the number of agents, their roles, and their interaction patterns are fixed before any analysis of the bug occurs. This one-size-fits-all approach is fundamentally mismatched to the heterogeneous nature of software defects. Simple bugs waste resources on unnecessary coordination, while complex ones suffer from insufficient or poorly aligned expertise. This paper introduces ASAD, an adaptive agentic system for debugging that configures its team according to the nature and complexity of each bug. ASAD initiates the debugging process by analyzing the faulty code and dynamically determines the number of agents to deploy, the specialized roles they should have, and the collaboration strategy they should follow. A central coordinator orchestrates this process through iterative planning, reflection, and execution; applying fast single-pass repairs for simple issues while assembling purpose-built teams to tackle more complex failures. We evaluate ASAD on three established benchmarks: Defects4J, DebugBench, and CodeFlaws, using multiple LLMs, such as DeepSeek-V3, Qwen-3 and GPT-5. ASAD consistently improves bug-fix rates by 12--20% over chain-of-thought(CoT) prompting and consistently outperforms static multi-agent systems by 4--9% in fix precision while reducing average agent usage by 32%. Crucially, our system dynamically adjusts the number and roles of agents: it resolves simple bugs with minimal coordination and scales agent involvement only for more complex cases.

</details>


### [266] [FORALL-LEAN-AGENT for Auditable Reasoning in Formal Mathematics and Software Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00885)
*Naing Oo Lwin*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: FORALL-LEAN-AGENT is a framework for auditable reasoning in formal mathematics and software verification, addressing the gap between successful Lean proof compilation and proof correctness verification. It combines isolated workspaces, Lean tools, and review mechanisms to provide traceable verification evidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coding agents increasingly automate Lean proof development, but successful compilation alone does not establish that a candidate proves the intended statement under acceptable assumptions. There is a need for auditable reasoning that goes beyond aggregate solve counts.

Method: The framework combines isolated workspaces, Lean tools, and fresh review with statement comparison, axiom audits, and independent proof checking where supported. Verification evidence and reviewer decisions are bound to the same candidate artifact, making acceptance traceable.

Result: On the 100-task VeriSoftBench subset, integration with FORALL-LEAN-AGENT raises benchmark-rule success from 93 to 100 for GPT-5.6 Sol at low effort while reducing cost from $69 to $62. The PutnamBench evaluation accepts all 672 problems at an average of $4.72 each.

Conclusion: Agent harness design can improve correctness and efficiency while providing evidence beyond aggregate solve counts. The framework successfully achieves auditable reasoning with improved success rates and reduced costs.

Abstract: Coding agents increasingly automate Lean proof development, but successful compilation alone does not establish that a candidate proves the intended statement under acceptable assumptions. We present FORALL-LEAN-AGENT, a frontend-agnostic framework for auditable reasoning in formal mathematics and software verification. The framework combines isolated workspaces, Lean tools, and fresh review with statement comparison, axiom audits, and independent proof checking where supported. Verification evidence and reviewer decisions are bound to the same candidate artifact, making acceptance traceable. We evaluate the framework on VeriSoftBench, PutnamBench, and both problems in the Lean Eval softwareverification track. On the 100-task VeriSoftBench subset, integration with FORALLLEAN-AGENT raises benchmark-rule success from 93 to 100 for GPT-5.6 Sol at low effort while reducing cost from $69 to $62. The PutnamBench evaluation accepts all 672 problems at an average of $4.72 each. These results show that agent harness design can improve correctness and efficiency while providing evidence beyond aggregate solve counts.

</details>


### [267] [Understanding Issues, Causes and Solutions in Open-Source LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00905)
*Asad Ur Rehman,Syed Mohammad Kashif,Ruiyin Li,Peng Liang,Zengyang Li,Arif Ali Khan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper conducts an empirical study on 22,848 closed issues from 21 open-source LLM-based multi-agent systems to understand the challenges practitioners face, their causes, and potential solutions. The study identifies Orchestration & Execution Issues as most common, with Workflow Problems, Tool Integration Problems, and Memory Problems being the top causes. Optimize Workflow is the predominant solution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLM-based multi-agent systems are increasingly adopted in open-source projects, there is limited understanding of the practical challenges developers face, their root causes, and available solutions. This gap motivates an empirical investigation into real-world issues from open-source projects.

Method: The authors collected 22,848 closed issues from 21 open-source LLM-based MAS projects. They applied a mixed automated and manual filtering approach to narrow down to 944 issues directly related to LLM-based MAS. These were then analyzed to identify frequent issues, underlying causes, and solutions.

Result: Three key findings emerged: (1) Orchestration & Execution Issue is the most common issue, (2) Workflow Problem, Tool Integration Problem, and Memory Problem are the most frequent causes, and (3) Optimize Workflow is the predominant solution category.

Conclusion: The study provides empirically grounded implications for improving orchestration, tool integration, and memory mechanisms in LLM-based MAS for both practitioners and researchers.

Abstract: With the advancement of LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS), an increasing number of opensource projects are adopting multi-agent architectures as the foundation of their core functionality. Although research and practice on MAS have attracted considerable attention, limited studies have explored the challenges faced by practitioners of open-source LLM-based MAS, the causes of these challenges, and potential solutions. To address this gap,we conducted an empirical study to understand the issues that practitioners encounter when developing and using open-source LLM-based MAS, the possible causes of these issues, and potential solutions. We collected 22,848 closed issues from 21 open-source LLM-basedMASand applied a mixed automated and manual filtering approach to reduce the dataset to 944 issues related to LLM-based MAS.We then analyzed these issues to understand the frequent issues encountered by practitioners, their underlying causes, and potential solutions. Our study results show that (1) Orchestration & Execution Issue is the most common issue faced by practitioners, (2) Workflow Problem, Tool Integration Problem, and Memory Problem are identified as the most frequent causes of the issues, and (3) Optimize Workflow is the predominant solution to the issues. Based on the study results, we derive empirically grounded implications for practitioners and researchers aimed at improving orchestration, tool integration, and memory mechanisms in LLM-based MAS.

</details>


### [268] [Groundability, Not Scale Alone: When Weak Reviewers Can Audit Strong Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01023)
*Junyu Guo,Shangding Gu,Ming Jin,Javad Lavaei*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether a weaker reviewer can reliably determine if a code patch solves its intended issue. The authors study 411 execution-labeled traces from three agents and 101 controlled cases, finding that structured evidence (even unchecked) can improve defect detection but also increases false rejections. A frozen cascade using static errors and generated tests achieves 0.89 coverage on GPT-5.4 traces and 0.86 on Gemini traces, with the main bottleneck being producing reliable checks without official tests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coding agents can produce plausible patches that miss required behavior, but these failures are difficult to review because long execution traces and confident summaries obscure what was actually missed. The authors seek to determine when a nominally weaker reviewer can reliably decide whether a patch solves its issue.

Method: The study analyzed 411 execution-labeled traces from three agents (including GPT-5.4 and Gemini) and 101 controlled cases. Experiments included: (1) testing structured but unchecked evidence on 154 GPT-5.4 traces, (2) providing official execution evidence as an upper-bound diagnostic, (3) having five of six reviewers evaluate 122 held-out traces after choosing and freezing one of two formats per reviewer, and (4) evaluating a frozen cascade combining patch-caused static errors with generated tests that first fail on the unpatched repository.

Result: On 121 held-out GPT-5.4 traces: coverage 0.89, risk 0.33, catch 0.76, over-rejection 0.66. On 59 Gemini traces: coverage 0.86, risk 0.26, catch 0.80, over-rejection 0.67. Five of six reviewers improved both defect catch and over-rejection rates on 122 held-out traces; two classified every trace correctly. Reviewer size was not a consistent quality predictor. Most false rejections occurred when unresolved cases reached the reviewer.

Conclusion: Official execution evidence demonstrates the potential of weak review when decisive checks are available. The primary bottleneck remains producing equally reliable checks without access to official tests. A frozen cascade using static error detection and generated tests shows promise but still produces significant false rejection rates (0.66-0.67).

Abstract: Coding agents can return plausible patches that omit required behavior. These failures are hard to review because long traces and confident summaries often hide what was missed. We ask when a nominally weaker reviewer can reliably decide whether a patch solves its issue. We study 411 execution-labeled traces from three agents and 101 controlled cases. On 154 GPT-5.4 traces, structured but unchecked evidence raises both defect catch and over-rejection. We then provide official execution evidence as an upper-bound diagnostic. After choosing and freezing one of two formats per reviewer, five of six reviewers improve both rates on 122 held-out traces; two classify every trace correctly. Reviewer size is not a consistent predictor of quality. Because official tests are unavailable in deployment, we also evaluate a frozen cascade with patch-caused static errors and generated tests that first fail on the unpatched repository. On 121 scored held-out GPT-5.4 traces and 59 Gemini traces, its coverage is 0.89 and 0.86, risk is 0.33 and 0.26, catch is 0.76 and 0.80, and over-rejection is 0.66 and 0.67. Most false rejections occur when unresolved cases reach the reviewer. Official execution evidence shows the potential of weak review when decisive checks are available. Producing equally reliable checks without official tests remains the main bottleneck.

</details>


### [269] [Safety Must Survive Self-Improvement: Why Failures Persist and How Agents Recover](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01073)
*Yunbei Zhang,Janet Wang,Saiyue Lyu,Yingqiang Ge,Kaiqu Liang,Zijian Jin,Chandan K Reddy,Jihun Hamm*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper studies safety challenges in recursive self-improvement (RSI) systems where AI agents optimize themselves across generations. Using a controlled testbed of stateful authorization tasks with LLM editors, the authors show that unsafe programs can persist across generations (22/48 cases) and that recovery depends on choosing which implementation to edit. Full validation and validated rollback achieve correct programs while retaining 43% deployment savings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address safety concerns in recursive self-improvement systems, where agents can pass modifications across generations. The key challenge is preventing unsafe behavior from persisting while enabling recovery when failures occur. This is particularly important as AI systems become more capable of self-modification.

Method: The authors use a controlled testbed of stateful authorization tasks where fixed LLM editors optimize executable agent components. Independent traces record the effects of modifications. Paired interventions separate which revisions pass validation, which program continues running, and which program the editor revises next. They test various intervention strategies including score refreshing, full validation, and validated rollback.

Result: Key findings include: (1) Historical scores preserve unsafe programs in 22 out of 48 framework histories despite correct alternatives existing; (2) Refreshing scores restores correctness on original tests but leaves residual failures on independently composed tests; (3) Failures persist even under unchanged contracts when all proposals are rejected and the failed incumbent remains active; (4) Editing the initial implementation instead of the failed one improves recovery, though the advantage varies across editors; (5) Full validation and validated rollback achieve fully correct programs in the core trajectory while retaining over 43% deployment savings.

Conclusion: The conclusion emphasizes that preserving agent safety in RSI systems requires both checking what will run under current conditions and carefully choosing which implementation to edit next. The authors propose that full validation and validated rollback are effective strategies for maintaining safety while achieving computational efficiency gains.

Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) allows agents to carry useful changes across generations. Maintaining safety across these generations involves both preventing unsafe behavior from persisting and enabling recovery when failures occur. We study these challenges through a controlled testbed of stateful authorization tasks, where fixed LLM editors optimize executable agent components and independent traces record their effects. Paired interventions separate which revisions pass validation, which program continues running, and which program the editor revises next. After a new authorization dependency invalidates previously tested optimizations, historical scores preserve the same unsafe programs in 22 of 48 framework histories despite a correct alternative in every affected archive. Refreshing scores restores correctness on the original suite, with residual failures on independently composed tests. Failures also persist under an unchanged contract when all proposals are rejected and the failed incumbent remains active. Starting from shared failures, editing the initial implementation instead of the failed one improves recovery, although the advantage varies across editors. Full validation and validated rollback end with fully correct programs in the core trajectory study while retaining over 43% deployment savings. Preserving agent safety requires checking what will run under current conditions and choosing which implementation to edit next.

</details>


### [270] [CompProv Produces Machine Readable Graphs Encoding Microscopic Algebraic Provenance for Reproducible Computation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01203)
*Minas Abramyan,Mohammed Alaa Ala'anzy,Nasir Saeed*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CompProv is a Java-based provenance framework that captures lineage at the atomic level of individual algebraic operations by encapsulating numerical values in high-precision wrapper objects, producing a serializable Calculation Provenance Graph (CPG) that enables deterministic replay and auditability without exposing proprietary source code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing provenance systems operate at the granularity of files, datasets, or pipeline stages, leaving the internal sequence of algebraic transformations connecting an algorithm's inputs to its outputs unrecorded. This creates a gap where rounding errors, undocumented substitutions, or missing intermediate values can propagate to final results without recoverable trace, undermining reliability in scientific research and financial modeling.

Method: CompProv encapsulates numerical values in high-precision wrapper objects and generates a serializable Calculation Provenance Graph (CPG) that persists as a self-contained artifact. The framework was evaluated through three heterogeneous case studies: a decentralized-finance NAV calculation, an interferometric gauge-block calibration in metrology, and a hydrological model performance evaluation.

Result: Deterministic replay reproduced each result exactly in a fresh environment. CPG-based input substitution supported sensitivity analysis without exposing underlying source code. The CPG allows numerical integrity to be audited without disclosing proprietary business logic, and its self-contained structure supports temporal auditability once an execution environment has become deprecated.

Conclusion: CompProv establishes an operation-level foundation for auditable-by-design computational systems. The framework enables numerical integrity auditing while preserving proprietary business logic, with scaling to high-throughput computing identified as a direction for future work.

Abstract: The reliability of computational results in scientific research and financial modeling increasingly depends on verifiable traceability, not merely on trust in a reported output. Existing provenance systems operate at the granularity of files, datasets, or pipeline stages, leaving the internal sequence of algebraic transformations connecting an algorithm's inputs to its outputs unrecorded; a rounding error, an undocumented substitution, or a missing intermediate value can propagate to a final result with no recoverable trace. This work presents CompProv, a Java-based, audit-oriented provenance framework that captures lineage at the atomic level of individual algebraic operations by encapsulating numerical values in high-precision wrapper objects, producing a serializable Calculation Provenance Graph (CPG) that persists as a self-contained artifact rather than a discarded byproduct. The framework is evaluated through three heterogeneous case studies: a decentralized-finance NAV calculation, a reconstruction of an interferometric gauge-block calibration in metrology under explicitly documented input assumptions, and a hydrological model performance evaluation. Deterministic replay reproduced each result exactly in a fresh environment, and CPG-based input substitution supported sensitivity analysis without exposing the underlying source code. These results indicate that, provided the CompProv runtime and wrapper classes are available in the replay environment, a CPG allows numerical integrity to be audited without disclosing proprietary business logic, and that its self-contained structure supports temporal auditability once an execution environment has become deprecated. This framework establishes an operation-level foundation for auditable-by-design computational systems, with scaling to high-throughput computing identified as a direction for future work.

</details>


### [271] [A Design Theory for AI-Assisted Software Development Derived from Christopher Alexander's Theory of Form](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01372)
*Chien-Tsun Chen,Yu Chin Cheng*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper proposes Misfit-Governed Development (MGD), a methodology for ensuring LLM-generated code meets specified requirements by using a dual-loop process with deterministic misfit detectors, pattern languages, and human-gated legislative circuits. Evidence is provided from building a Scrum system with 64 specifications, 1,300 tests, and 28 blocking gates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-generated code cannot be assumed to meet specified requirements. While reviews, testing, and static analysis apply, there is no clear framework for what harness is sufficient and in what role. The paper addresses Alexander's 1996 OOPSLA challenge regarding the generativity dimension.

Method: The authors derive a design theory from Christopher Alexander's theory of form, treating the LLM as a "non-native vernacular builder." They engineer four components: (1) Jackson's problem frames for problem representation and a four-form pattern language for tradition; (2) deterministic misfit detectors; (3) a fix loop; and (4) a human-gated legislative circuit. The resulting MGD methodology uses a dual-loop process: an autonomous inner loop where the LLM iterates against gates, and a human outer loop where specifications are judged against the world.

Result: The authors report evidence from building and rebuilding a Scrum system with four event-sourced aggregates from 64 problem-frame specifications, verified by approximately 1,300 generated tests and 28 blocking gates, with one gate applying 188 rules.

Conclusion: The S = P = T = W assurance model (specification, program, tests, world) is proposed, where equals signs denote relations rather than identity. The generativity dimension of Alexander's 1996 OOPSLA challenge is addressed. However, the moral dimension—whether the specification still fits the world—requires human judgment and belongs to the outer loop.

Abstract: Code generated by large language models (LLMs) cannot be assumed to meet specified requirements. Reviews, testing, and static analysis still apply, but which of them a sufficient harness needs, and in what role, is open. We propose a design theory derived from Christopher Alexander's theory of form, and a methodology for applying it. In Alexander's account, fit between a form and its context can be perceived only negatively, through the absence of identified misfits. We make the organization's tradition explicit and derive the misfits from it and from the problem's classification. The theory models the LLM as a non-native vernacular builder, trained on many codebases but native to none, whose output tends to drift toward mainstream conventions rather than the local tradition. We engineer four pieces of machinery: explicit representations of the problem (Jackson's problem frames) and of the tradition (a four-form pattern language); deterministic misfit detectors; a fix loop; and a human-gated legislative circuit governing the representations and detectors. We call the resulting methodology, a practice of harness engineering, Misfit-Governed Development (MGD). Its dual-loop process separates an autonomous inner loop, where the LLM iterates against the gates, from a human outer loop, where specifications are judged against the world. Together they form the S = P = T = W assurance model (specification, program, tests, world), whose equals signs name relations, not identity. We report evidence from building and rebuilding a Scrum system of four event-sourced aggregates from 64 problem-frame specifications, verified by about 1,300 generated tests and 28 blocking gates, one applying 188 rules. This addresses the generativity dimension of Alexander's 1996 OOPSLA challenge. The moral dimension, whether the specification still fits the world, requires human judgment and belongs to the outer loop.

</details>


### [272] [Refactoring React Component Hierarchies to Eliminate Prop Drilling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01376)
*Vangelis Gkinis,Vassilis E. Zafeiris*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper addresses Prop Drilling in React applications - a practice where data is passed through multiple component hierarchy levels via props. The authors propose a static analysis method to identify Prop Drilling instances and eliminate them using two automated refactoring strategies (Context API and Component Composition). The method is implemented as ReactRefactor tool and evaluated on open-source React applications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite being discouraged by React documentation and characterized as a code smell, there is limited knowledge about Prop Drilling's prevalence, complexity, and potential for automated refactoring. This work aims to fill this gap by providing empirical evidence and automated solutions.

Method: The authors developed a static analysis method implemented as a Node.js command line tool called ReactRefactor. They evaluated it on a benchmark dataset of open-source React applications, using two automated refactoring strategies: Context API and Component Composition.

Result: Key findings: (a) Prop drilling occurs frequently across benchmark projects regardless of project size; (b) generally low to moderate complexity in data propagation depth, but more prevalent complexity from simultaneous forwarding of multiple properties along the same path; (c) 76.3% of prop drillings can be automatically eliminated, primarily through refactoring to Context API.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that Prop Drilling is a common issue in React codebases, and a substantial majority (76.3%) of these instances can be automatically refactored, with Context API being the preferred refactoring approach. This provides practical tools and empirical evidence for addressing this code smell in React development.

Abstract: In React front-end development, Prop Drilling is the practice of propagating data through component properties across multiple levels of the component hierarchy. Despite being discouraged by React documentation and characterized as a code smell by recent research, little is known about its prevalence, complexity, and potential for automated refactoring. In this work, we propose a static analysis method for identifying Prop Drilling instances in a React codebase and eliminating them using two automated refactoring strategies based on Context API and Component Composition. The proposed method is implemented as a Node.js command line tool, ReactRefactor, and empirically evaluated on a benchmark dataset of open-source React applications. The main findings of the empirical evaluation indicate (a) the frequent occurrence of prop drillings across benchmark projects, irrespective of project size; (b) their generally low to moderate complexity in terms of data propagation depth, contrasted with the more prevalent complexity arising from the simultaneous forwarding of multiple properties along the same path; and, (c) the potential for automated elimination of a substantial share (76.3%) of prop drillings, primarily through refactoring to the Context API.

</details>


### [273] [Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01611)
*Noman Ahmad,Ruoyu Su,Matteo Esposito,Andrea Janes,Valentina Lenarduzzi,Davide Taibi*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A Multivocal Literature Review consolidating 284 studies on architectural degradation, identifying 277 measurement approaches, 357 metrics, 238 tools, and 395 remediation strategies. The field shows strong concentration on static/structural analysis and detection, but less progress in connecting diagnosis with effective remediation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Architectural degradation undermines software maintainability, evolvability, and quality, but existing research is fragmented across measurement approaches, metrics, tools, and remediation strategies, limiting understanding of how these elements relate across the degradation lifecycle.

Method: Multivocal Literature Review of 284 peer-reviewed and grey-literature studies, using LLM-assisted pipeline combining Retrieval-Augmented Generation, multi-model validation, and human adjudication for screening, data extraction, and classification.

Result: Identified 277 measurement approaches, 357 metrics, 238 tools, and 395 remediation approaches. Research strongly concentrates on static and structural analysis, structural metrics, and detection-oriented tools. Remediation spans heterogeneous code-level, architectural, and organizational interventions with substantially less consolidation.

Conclusion: The field has developed a mature diagnostic apparatus but has made less progress in connecting degradation detection with effective remediation. The diagnosis-remediation gap is identified as a key direction for future research.

Abstract: Context. Architectural degradation undermines software maintainability, evolvability, and quality. However, existing research remains fragmented across measurement approaches, metrics, tools, and remediation strategies, limiting our understanding of how these elements relate across the degradation lifecycle. Aim. We consolidate the state of the art on architectural degradation by examining how researchers measure it, which metrics and tools support its assessment, and how existing approaches address remediation. Method. We conducted a Multivocal Literature Review of 284 peer-reviewed and grey-literature studies. We supported screening, data extraction, and classification with a locally executed LLM-assisted pipeline combining Retrieval-Augmented Generation, multi-model validation, and human adjudication. We then analyzed the resulting taxonomies and their cross-dimensional relationships. Results and Conclusions. We identified 277 measurement approaches, 357 metrics, 238 tools, and 395 remediation approaches. Research strongly concentrates on static and structural analysis, structural metrics, and detection-oriented tools. In contrast, remediation spans heterogeneous code-level, architectural, and organizational interventions and shows substantially less consolidation. Overall, the field has developed a mature diagnostic apparatus but has made less progress in connecting degradation detection with effective remediation. Our results provide a structured view of the available techniques and identify the diagnosis-remediation gap as a key direction for future research.

</details>


### [274] [Code Detectors Have a Half-Life: Obsolescence and Metric Illusions in LLM-Generated Code Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01664)
*Alberick Euraste Djire*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper introduces the concept of "detector half-life" to describe how code detectors become obsolete as code-generating models evolve. It evaluates 8 general-purpose LLM judges and 3 dedicated detectors across human-written and AI-generated code from 7 generators in C++, Java, and Python. Results show that general-purpose LLM judges outperform dedicated detectors, but reliability varies based on judge model, code generator, and prompting strategy. The study also reveals that accuracy can mask severe prediction bias.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address the problem that code detectors validated on one generation of models may not transfer to the next, limiting their practical usefulness. This is increasingly important as AI-generated code becomes more prevalent.

Method: The researchers evaluated eight general-purpose LLM judges and three dedicated detectors on human-written code and code produced by seven generators across C++, Java, and Python. They assessed performance across different generators and prompting strategies.

Result: General-purpose LLM judges achieved stronger accuracy and F1 scores compared to dedicated detectors. However, performance varies considerably across generators and prompting strategies. Some detectors like DetectCodeGPT and GPT-Sniffer achieved 0.50 accuracy but 0.00 F1 due to classifying almost every sample as AI-generated, revealing that accuracy can conceal severe prediction bias.

Conclusion: General-purpose LLMs are promising training-free judges of code provenance and can outperform dedicated detectors. However, their reliability depends on the judge model, the code generator, and the prompting strategy. The recommendation is to evaluate LLM judges across multiple generators and report macro-F1 alongside class-specific precision and recall.

Abstract: Code detectors can become obsolete as code-generating models evolve: a detector validated on one generation of models may not transfer to the next. We call this limited useful life a detector half-life. We evaluate eight general-purpose LLM judges and three dedicated detectors on human-written code and code produced by seven generators across C++, Java, and Python. Our results reveal two problems. First, performance varies considerably across generators and prompting strategies, suggesting that some detectors rely on generator-specific patterns rather than general evidence of code provenance. Second, accuracy can conceal severe prediction bias. DetectCodeGPT and GPT-Sniffer achieved an accuracy of 0.50 but an F1 score of 0.00 across all generators because they classified almost every sample as AI-generated. However, general-purpose LLM judges achieved stronger accuracy and F1 scores. Our results show that general-purpose LLMs are promising training-free judges of code provenance and can outperform dedicated detectors. However, their reliability depends on the judge model, the code generator, and the prompting strategy. We therefore recommend evaluating LLM judges across multiple generators and reporting macro-F1 alongside class-specific precision and recall.

</details>


### [275] [CONTRA: Discovering and Qualifying Behavior-Changing Questions for Selective Clarification in LLM Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01769)
*Zheng Fang,Yongmin Li,Yichang Zhang,Dongming Jin,Haoyu Wang,Shuai Wang,Zhi Jin,Ge Li*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CONTRA is a training-free method for coding agents to identify key clarification questions by combining broad question discovery with semantic and execution-based qualification, preventing behavior mismatches from underspecified requirements without unnecessary interruptions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coding agents can silently resolve underspecified requirements through their own assumptions, leading to code that appears correct but implements unintended behavior. Correcting this later becomes increasingly costly. While early clarification can help, existing methods struggle to identify key questions while avoiding unnecessary ones that interrupt developers.

Method: CONTRA combines three components: (1) broad question discovery to generate candidate questions, (2) semantic filtering to remove questions unrelated to required behavior or already resolved by requirements, (3) execution-based qualification that generates programs conditioned on two plausible answers and checks for stable behavioral differences on shared inputs. The interaction history is used to select among qualified questions or decide to stop asking.

Result: CONTRA achieves the highest F1 on ClarifyCodeBench with all four coding agents, exceeding the best baseline macro-average F1 by 13.88 percentage points. It also achieves higher clarification recall and F1 than Claude Code and OpenHands harnesses. A practical Claude Code plugin implementation is also provided.

Conclusion: CONTRA effectively balances the trade-off between preventing behavior mismatches and avoiding unnecessary interruptions in coding agent development workflows, providing a practical solution for selective clarification in everyday development.

Abstract: Coding agents can generate code that appears correct but implements behavior the user never intended. This mismatch can arise when an agent silently resolves underspecified requirements through its own assumptions. As subsequent development builds on these assumptions, correcting the resulting behavior can become increasingly costly. Early clarification can help prevent such mismatches, but unnecessary questions can interrupt developers and slow down development. Existing methods struggle to identify key clarification questions while avoiding unnecessary ones. Therefore, we propose CONTRA, a training-free method that combines broad question discovery with semantic and execution-based question qualification. CONTRA first generates candidate questions and filters out those unrelated to required behavior or already resolved by the requirement. For each remaining question, it generates programs conditioned on two plausible answers and checks for stable behavioral differences on shared inputs. It then uses the interaction history to select among qualified questions or stop asking. Experiments on ClarifyCodeBench show that CONTRA achieves the highest F1 with all four coding agents, exceeding the best baseline macro-average F1 by 13.88 percentage points. With the same LLM and evaluation protocol, CONTRA also achieves higher clarification recall and F1 than the coding harnesses Claude Code and OpenHands. To support practical use, we also implement CONTRA as a Claude Code plugin that integrates selective clarification into everyday development.

</details>


### [276] [Detecting Inconsistencies in Model Specifications with LLM-as-Verifier Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01847)
*Zichen Xie,Mrigank Pawagi,Lize Shao,Yang Hu,Wenxi Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: VeriSpec is the first method to directly detect inconsistencies in LLM model specifications by auditing the specification text itself, using an LLM as a verifier to identify conflicting rules.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model specifications may contain defects where two reasonable principles prescribe incompatible behavior, but detecting such inconsistencies is challenging as formalization risks losing subtle distinctions and behavior-based testing cannot distinguish specification defects from model behavior differences.

Method: VeriSpec preserves specifications in natural language while using an LLM as verifier. It extracts structured context-aware rules, constructs a topic-guided graph to cluster behaviorally related rules at the same authority level, and applies LLM-as-verifier reasoning to detect inconsistencies.

Result: Applied to OpenAI Model Spec, VeriSpec extracted 405 rules and manually validated five inconsistencies (all reported to developers who responded positively). It achieved highest precision (38.5%) and lowest cost per validated inconsistency ($11.12) compared to five baselines.

Conclusion: Direct specification auditing is a practical complement to behavioral alignment evaluation, catching defects at the source before they shape any model.

Abstract: Model specifications define how large language models (LLMs) should behave, guiding alignment training, inference-time behavior, and evaluation. Yet these specifications may themselves contain defects: two individually reasonable principles may prescribe incompatible behavior when applied to the same situation, leaving no response that satisfies both. Detecting such inconsistencies is challenging. Formalizing natural-language specifications risks losing subtle distinctions, while behavior-based testing cannot reliably distinguish specification defects from differences in model behavior. We introduce VeriSpec, the first approach to directly detect inconsistencies in model specifications by auditing the specification text itself. Our key insight is to preserve the specification in natural language while using an LLM as a verifier. VeriSpec extracts structured, context-aware rules, constructs a topic-guided graph to cluster behaviorally related rules at the same authority level, and applies LLM-as-verifier reasoning to detect inconsistencies. Applying VeriSpec to the OpenAI Model Spec, we extract 405 rules and manually validate five inconsistencies, all reported to its developers, who responded positively and have initiated internal discussions. Compared with five baselines, VeriSpec identifies the most validated inconsistencies, achieves the highest precision (38.5%), and incurs the lowest cost per validated inconsistency ($11.12). These results establish direct specification auditing as a practical complement to behavioral alignment evaluation, catching defects at the source before they shape any model. The code is available at https://github.com/HIPREL-Group/VeriSpec.

</details>
