### [277] [Smooth Curves from Curvature-Driven Subdivision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00020)
*Hassan Ugail*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: This paper introduces a novel interpolatory subdivision scheme where new points are defined by a curvature-profile model rather than affine combinations. The scheme uses curvature estimation from circumscribed circles, Frenet integration with geodesic shooting, and places new points at half arc length. It works in both planar and spherical settings, reproducing geodesics and circles exactly, and achieves higher smoothness (C² in arc length) compared to traditional approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to develop a subdivision scheme that reproduces circles and geodesics exactly, and to address the limitation that the straightening condition of Ewald, Reif, and Sabin fails for this scheme. The authors aim to prove that the refined polygons converge to a regular interpolatory limit curve with continuous tangent direction and curvature, and to demonstrate that regularity is governed by the normal companion scheme alone.

Method: The method involves: (1) estimating curvature from circumscribed circles on each edge, (2) using Frenet integration with geodesic shooting to reconstruct the segment, (3) placing new points at half arc length. A unique curvature prefilter is used to turn the planar linearization into the six-point Deslauriers-Dubuc scheme. The theory is repaired by measuring only the normal part of the relative distortion.

Result: The scheme works identically in the plane and on the sphere, reproduces geodesics and circles exactly. The refined polygons converge to a regular interpolatory limit curve with continuous tangent direction and curvature, twice continuously differentiable in arc length (C²). Regularity is governed by the normal companion scheme alone, confirming the conjecture of Ewald, Reif, and Sabin.

Conclusion: The curvature-profile model provides a geometrically meaningful approach to subdivision that achieves high smoothness (C² in arc length) while preserving exact reproduction of circles and geodesics. The key insight is that regularity is determined solely by the normal companion scheme, not by the full straightening condition. This connects the scheme to the classical Deslauriers-Dubuc scheme through the curvature prefilter.

Abstract: We introduce and analyse an interpolatory subdivision scheme in which each inserted point is defined by a curvature-profile model rather than by an affine combination of its neighbours, and we establish its convergence and geometric regularity. On each edge, curvatures estimated from circumscribed circles prescribe a curvature profile, the segment is reconstructed by Frenet integration with geodesic shooting, and the new point is taken at half arc length. The construction works identically in the plane and on the sphere, reproduces geodesics and circles exactly, and a unique curvature prefilter turns its planar linearisation into the six-point Deslauriers-Dubuc scheme. The straightening condition of Ewald, Reif, and Sabin fails for this scheme. Measuring only the normal part of the relative distortion repairs their theory, and we prove that the refined polygons converge to a regular interpolatory limit curve with continuous tangent direction and curvature, twice continuously differentiable in arc length. Regularity is thus governed by the normal companion scheme alone, as these authors conjectured.

</details>


### [278] [GS-PQM: A Parameter-Domain Quality Metric for Compressed Gaussian Splatting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00195)
*Pedro Martin,António Rodrigues,João Ascenso,Maria Paula Queluz*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: GS-PQM is a novel full-reference quality metric for post-training Gaussian Splatting compression that operates directly in the GS parameter domain, using Support Vector Regression to estimate perceptual quality from parameter-domain distortion errors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recent advances in GS compression have enabled significant model size reductions, creating a need for reliable objective quality assessment to compare compression methods and guide development of more efficient GS codecs. Existing approaches rely on rendering predefined viewpoints, making quality estimates dependent on selected views.

Method: GS-PQM estimates perceptual quality using a set of parameter-domain distortion errors fed into a Support Vector Regression model, avoiding the need for rendering-based assessment.

Result: GS-PQM outperforms 25 existing image, video, and point-cloud quality metrics in assessing compressed GS content, providing accurate and computationally efficient quality assessment.

Conclusion: GS-PQM offers an accurate and computationally efficient alternative to rendering-based quality assessment for Gaussian Splatting compression, operating directly in the parameter domain.

Abstract: Recent advances in Gaussian Splatting (GS) compression have enabled substantial reductions in GS model size. Reliable objective quality assessment is therefore essential for comparing compression methods and guiding the development of more efficient GS codecs. Existing GS quality assessment typically relies on image and video quality metrics, requiring rendering of predefined viewpoints and making the quality estimate dependent on the selected views. This paper introduces GS-PQM, a novel full-reference quality metric for post-training GS compression that operates directly in the GS parameter domain. GS-PQM estimates perceptual quality from a set of parameter-domain distortion errors using a Support Vector Regression model. Experimental results show that GS-PQM outperforms 25 existing image, video, and point-cloud quality metrics in assessing compressed GS content, providing an accurate and computationally efficient alternative to rendering-based quality assessment.

</details>


### [279] [Diffusion Editing with Soft Mask: Pixel Level Redo of Image and Video with Adjustable Strength](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00359)
*Candi Zheng,Yuan Lan*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: SoftPaint is a zero-shot sampling method that enables pixel-level control in diffusion models by using soft masks, allowing continuous edits from full preservation to complete re-synthesis of masked regions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing diffusion model editing methods lack fine-grained pixel-level control; training with pixel-wise annotations is expensive, and zero-shot methods produce unsatisfactory results for tasks requiring spatial precision.

Method: A Langevin-iteration-based sampler that respects per-pixel soft mask strengths, applied universally to image and video diffusion models. The method is gradient-free and memory-efficient.

Result: Achieves smooth, pixel-level edits across multiple image and video backbones, enabling tasks such as video editing with continuous control over edit strength.

Conclusion: SoftPaint provides an effective zero-shot solution for fine-grained diffusion-based editing, balancing quality and flexibility without requiring training or annotations, with broad applicability to both images and videos.

Abstract: Diffusion models with prompt and reference image-guided editing have seen rapid progress, yet they remain too coarse for pixel-level control. One promising direction is to incorporate a soft mask that specifies spatially varying edit strengths but training such fine-grained control demands expensive pixel-wise annotations, while existing zero-shot methods often yield unsatisfactory results. We introduce SoftPaint, a new zero-shot sampling method that leverages soft masks to enable a continuous spectrum of edits, from fully preserving the original content to completely re-synthesizing the masked region. Going beyond zero-shot inpainting methods, we design a Langevin-iteration-based sampler that respects per-pixel soft mask strengths, which applies universally to image and video diffusion models, enabling tasks such as video editing. The method is gradient-free, memory-efficient, and achieves smooth, pixel-level edits across multiple image and video backbones.

</details>


### [280] [Implementation Note 2: Approximating a Smooth Three-Dimensional Function on a Coarse Lattice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00203)
*Dennis Luxen*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: A method for efficiently approximating smooth 3D functions using a 3D lookup table with tetrahedral interpolation, optimized for integer-only arithmetic. Applied to RGB to CMYK color conversion, requiring only 38 KiB for a 16-cell table with 0.08% mean error.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the need for efficient, accurate color conversion (RGB to CMYK) in low-power devices and real-time applications where computational resources are limited, while avoiding floating-point operations and minimizing memory usage.

Method: Sample a 3D function on a coarse grid (preprocessing), locate the enclosing grid cube for each input, select one of 6 tetrahedra within the cube, and combine the 4 corner values using weighted sum. The implementation uses integer arithmetic only (no floating point, no division), with all intermediate values fitting in 32 bits.

Result: A 16-cell-per-axis table (17³ nodes, 16-bit values) requires 38 KiB and achieves 0.08% mean error per channel. The integer implementation differs from exact fractional tetrahedral interpolation by at most 1 unit in 16-bit output, with exact reproduction of white and black.

Conclusion: The approach is highly suitable for low-power devices and real-time applications with limited computational resources, as it requires no floating-point operations or division, uses minimal memory, and provides sufficient accuracy for color conversion.

Abstract: A smooth 3D function can be efficiently and accurately approximated by a 3D lookup table of significantly lower resolution combined with tetrahedral interpolation. The function is sampled once on a coarse grid in a preprocessing step. For each input, the enclosing grid cube is located, one of the 6 tetrahedra in this cube is selected, and the values at its 4 corners are combined by a weighted sum.
  For RGB to CMYK color conversion, a particularly frequent application of this, a table with $n = 16$ cells per axis ($17^3$ nodes, 16-bit values) requires 38\,KiB. A full 8-bit table requires 64\,MiB. As shown in an experimental evaluation, the mean error of the $n = 16$ table is 0.08\,\% ink per channel. For 8-bit input, the lookup uses integer arithmetic only (Section~\ref{sec:integer}). It requires no floating point and no division, and all intermediate values fit in 32 bits. Floating point is needed only to build the table, once and offline. The integer result differs from tetrahedral interpolation with exact fractions by at most 1 unit of the 16-bit output, and white and black are reproduced exactly. This makes the approach suitable for low-power devices and real-time applications where computational resources are limited.

</details>


### [281] [Plate-Local River Generation: Deterministic, Terrain-Aware, Downhill-Flowing Rivers for Infinite Procedural Worlds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00301)
*Michael K. Davis*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: This paper presents a deterministic algorithm for generating coherent, downhill-flowing river networks in infinite procedural worlds. The approach uses tectonic plate seeds to define bounded Voronoi-like domains, enabling lazy per-plate river preprocessing. Rivers are traced downhill on low-resolution grids, with heights monotonically adjusted to guarantee downhill flow. Full-resolution terrain evaluation computes exact distances to cached river networks and interpolates river heights on-demand without caching the blended result.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing procedural terrain generation methods face a trade-off: coherent downhill-flowing river networks only work on fixed domains, while infinite world approaches sacrifice network coherence or downhill-flow guarantees. There was a need for a terrain-aware river generation method that supports efficient on-demand evaluation for interactive procedural worlds.

Method: The method uses tectonic plate seeds to define both continuous terrain fields and bounded Voronoi-like plate domains. Within each plate, terrain is sampled on a low-resolution grid, and rivers are traced downhill from highland sources to coastlines, local minima, or existing confluences. River heights are monotonically adjusted along paths to ensure downhill flow. The river network is lazily cached per plate, processed independently. During full-resolution sampling, exact distance to the cached river network is computed, and river height is interpolated and blended with local terrain on-demand without caching the blended result.

Result: The bounded warp of plate borders below the river border margin guarantees downhill flow along every river channel of the final terrain. The design enables terrain-aware river generation for interactive procedural worlds with efficient on-demand evaluation, as demonstrated by the performance analysis.

Conclusion: The proposed algorithm successfully achieves deterministic, terrain-aware, downhill-flowing river generation for infinite procedural worlds. By combining tectonic plate seeds, lazy per-plate caching, and on-demand river-terrain blending, the method supports efficient evaluation suitable for interactive applications while maintaining network coherence and downhill-flow guarantees.

Abstract: Existing procedural terrain generation methods produce coherent, downhill-flowing river networks only on fixed domains, whereas approaches that extend to infinite worlds typically sacrifice network coherence or downhill-flow guarantees. This work presents a deterministic, terrain-aware, downhill-flowing river algorithm for infinite procedural worlds. Tectonic plate seeds define both continuous terrain fields and corresponding bounded Voronoi-like plate domains, so localized river preprocessing can operate directly on the geometric domain without sampling terrain fields for the purpose of locating plate boundaries. Within each plate, the terrain field is sampled on a low-resolution grid, and rivers are traced downhill from highland source nodes to coastlines, local minima, or existing confluences. River heights are then monotonically adjusted along each path so that every stored segment descends. The resulting river network is generated and cached lazily per plate, so each plate is processed independently of its neighbors. During full-resolution terrain sampling, the distance to the cached river network is computed exactly, and river height is interpolated along nearby segments and blended with the locally evaluated terrain on demand, without caching the blended result itself. Because the warp of the plate borders is bounded below the river border margin, this guarantees downhill flow along every river channel of the final terrain. Together, these design choices make terrain-aware river generation practical for interactive procedural worlds by supporting efficient on-demand evaluation, as demonstrated by the performance analysis presented in this work.

</details>


### [282] [Dirichlet Splatting: Differentiable Rendering for Wave-Based Inverse Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00618)
*Xingyu Chen,Wuqiong Zhao,Xinyu Zhang,Tzu-Mao Li*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: This paper proposes a novel approach for wave-based coherent imaging (terahertz tomography, synthetic-aperture acoustics, millimeter-wave radar) by replacing Gaussian splatting with a Dirichlet kernel-based primitive that matches the physics of finite-window DFT measurements. The method uses a specialized solver (DSFW) and achieves 10-50x speedup over waveform-level automatic differentiation while recovering reflector centers with 0.018 bin RMSE.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Wave-based coherent imaging forms images via Fourier-processing finite-length signals with an exact point spread function that is a Dirichlet kernel (complex-valued, oscillatory, periodic). However, Gaussian splatting fails in this domain because it discards sidelobe energy (10-20% of total) and the phase that governs coherent interference between reflectors. Gaussian splatting is fundamentally incompatible with coherent sensing physics.

Method: The key innovation is replacing the learned Gaussian footprint with the physically exact Dirichlet kernel of the finite-window DFT, modulated by a surfel carrying area, normal, and material properties. This is paired with a specialized solver called Dirichlet Sliding Frank-Wolfe (DSFW) that combines: (1) variable projection, (2) residual dual certificates, (3) certificate-driven hard replacement of low-utility surfels, and (4) periodic low-resolution coupled Levenberg-Marquardt correction to navigate the rugged loss landscape that breaks generic first-order optimizers.

Result: The Dirichlet kernel admits O(1) closed-form evaluation, enabling the forward model to match FFT ground truth to machine precision while remaining differentiable end-to-end. On dense terahertz reconstruction, the method recovers reflector centers to 0.018 bin RMSE, achieving 10-50x speedup over waveform-level automatic differentiation, where Gaussian splats fundamentally fail.

Conclusion: The proposed Dirichlet kernel-based primitive successfully bridges the gap between 3D reconstruction and coherent wave physics. By matching the measurement physics instead of approximating it with Gaussians, the method achieves superior accuracy and efficiency for coherent imaging applications. The O(1) evaluation and exact FFT alignment make this approach both practical and theoretically sound for wave-based sensing modalities.

Abstract: Wave-based coherent imaging, including terahertz tomography, synthetic-aperture acoustics, and millimeter-wave radar, forms images by Fourier-processing finite-length signals, with an exact point spread function that is not Gaussian but a Dirichlet kernel: complex-valued, oscillatory, and periodic. However, transplanting 3D Gaussian splatting to coherent sensing fails by construction; Gaussian splats discard the sidelobe energy (10-20% of the total) and the phase that governs coherent interference between reflectors. Our key idea is to replace the learned Gaussian footprint with the physically exact Dirichlet kernel of the finite-window DFT, modulated by a surfel that carries area, normal, and material, so that the rendering primitive matches the measurement physics instead of approximating it. We pair this primitive with a specialized solver, Dirichlet Sliding Frank-Wolfe (DSFW), that combines variable projection, residual dual certificates, and certificate-driven hard replacement of low-utility surfels, with periodic low-resolution coupled Levenberg-Marquardt correction, navigating the rugged loss landscape that breaks generic first-order optimizers. The Dirichlet kernel admits an O(1) closed-form evaluation, so the forward model matches FFT ground truth to machine precision while remaining differentiable end-to-end. On dense terahertz reconstruction, our method recovers reflector centers to 0.018 bin RMSE, 10-50x faster than waveform-level automatic differentiation, where Gaussian splats fail.

</details>
